Surah Hud, peace be upon him, is Meccan.

As Ibn al-Nahhas in his History, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related through various chains from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Ibn Mardawayh from Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they excepted nothing from it. This is the view of the majority, while some excepted three verses from it: ﴿So perhaps you would abandon﴾, ﴿Is one who has a clear proof from his Lord﴾, and ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day﴾. It is also narrated that the third was excepted from Qatadah. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: Its evidence is what is authentically related through several chains, that it was revealed in Medina concerning Abu al-Yusr. According to al-Dani in the book of the Count, it has one hundred and twenty-one verses in the later Medinan count, two in the earlier Medinan count, and three in the Kufan count.

As for its connection with Surah Yunus, peace be upon him: the story of Noah, peace be upon him, was mentioned in Surah Yunus in a very brief and summary form, so it is explained in this surah and expanded upon in ways not expanded in other surahs, nor in Surah al-A'raf despite its length, nor in the surah (Indeed We sent Noah), which was devoted to his story. Thus this surah is an explanation of what was summarized in that surah and an elaboration of it. Moreover, its opening is strongly linked to the opening of that one, for His saying here, ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm﴾, is similar to His saying there, ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra. These are the verses of the wise Book﴾. Indeed, there is also a strong link between the opening of this surah and the close of that one, as that one ended with the negation of polytheism and following revelation, and this one opens with the explanation of revelation and warning against polytheism.

Concerning its merits, what has been reported is that al-Darimi, Abu Dawud in his Marasil, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, and others related from Ka'b who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Recite Hud on Friday." Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wa al-Nushur related through the route of Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas who said: Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O Messenger of Allah, you have grown gray." He said: "Hud, al-Waqi'ah, al-Mursalat, 'Amma yatasa'alun, and 'Idha al-shamsu kuwwirat have made me gray." Ibn Asakir related through the route of Yazid al-Raqashi from Anas, from al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, gray hair has come upon you quickly." He said: "Indeed. Surah Hud and its sisters, al-Waqi'ah, al-Qari'ah, al-Haqqah, 'Idha al-shamsu kuwwirat, and Sa'ala sa'il have made me gray."

It has also come in some narrations that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to him, peace be upon him: "Gray hair has come upon you quickly, O Messenger of Allah." He answered him with something similar to what was mentioned, except that he mentioned among the sisters al-Waqi'ah, 'Amma, and 'Idha al-shamsu kuwwirat. In another narration from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, you have grown gray. He said: Hud and al-Waqi'ah have made me gray," and so on until the end of the report of Umar. In some of them it is limited to "Hud and its sisters have made me gray," and in another with the addition "and what was done to the nations before me." Ibn Asakir related this from Ja'far ibn Muhammad from his father, may Allah be pleased with them both, as a marfu' report.

Ibn Mardawayh and others related from Imran ibn Husayn that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was told by his companions: "Gray hair has come upon you quickly." He said: "Hud and its sisters from the mufassal, and al-Waqi'ah have made me gray." All of this indicates its importance and the magnitude of what it contains and alludes to, and this is what became the cause of the hastening of gray hair upon him (ﷺ). Some interpreted it as referring to the mention of the Day of Resurrection and the stories of the nations, and some reports support this. Al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from Abu Ali al-Shatri who said: I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) in a dream and I said: "O Messenger of Allah, it has been related from you that you said: Hud has made me gray." He said: "Yes." I said: "What made you gray in it: the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them, and the destruction of the nations?" He said: "No, but rather His saying: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾." This is what some of the Sufi masters relied upon, may Allah sanctify their secrets, and he explained it in the manner he explained. The truth is that what made the Prophet (ﷺ) gray is what this surah includes, which is more general than this matter and others, of what was great in his affair for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) according to his sublime knowledge and exalted station. This is what occurs to the mind of the hearer, and for this reason his companions did not ask him what had made him gray in it and its sisters, but were content with what is immediately understood from such statements.

As for the claim that what was immediately understood by them, may Allah be pleased with them, was what was hidden from Abu Ali, so they did not ask about it, even if this is granted: it remains that they did not ask about what made him, peace be upon him, gray among the sisters, although there is in them nothing but mention of the Day of Resurrection and the destruction of nations, apart from that matter. And the claim that they knew the cause of gray hair in it and its sisters is something else, namely the mention of the Day of Resurrection and the destruction of nations, is refuted by what is in Abu Ali's report of the negation by him (ﷺ). And that what was mentioned as causing gray hair is understood to be in one surah and not others is of obvious weakness. In sum, one should not rely upon this narration, even if it is granted that it was authentically transmitted from Abu Ali. Accusing the reporter of poor memory or of failing to verify what he saw is easier than asserting the correctness of the vision and straining to justify what is in it. The complete discussion on this point will come, Allah willing, at the end of the surah, so let it be understood.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra﴾: it is a name of the surah according to what al-Khalil and Sibawayh and others held, or a name of the Qur'an according to what is related from al-Kalbi and al-Suddi. It was said that it refers to one of Allah's names or one of His attributes, glory be to Him. It was also said that it is an oath by Him, the Exalted, by what is among the origins of languages, the beginnings of His revealed books, and the letters of His noble names. And it was said, and it was said, and the discussion of what benefits you here has already been presented in the most complete detail. Many later scholars preferred that it is a name of the surah and that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., this surah is named "Ra." It was said that its position is nominative as a subject, or accusative by supposing a verb suited to the context, such as "Mention" or "Recite." His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿A Book﴾ is its predicate on the supposition that it is independent, or the predicate of an omitted subject according to other views. The tanwin in it is for glorification, i.e., a Book of great status and lofty worth. ﴿Whose verses have been made firm﴾, i.e., arranged in a firm order not subject to disorder, so that there is no contradiction in it, nor opposition to reality and wisdom, nor anything that impairs its eloquence and rhetoric. Thus "ihkam" is borrowed from the firmness of a structure, meaning its perfection, or they were protected from abrogation, either some of them or all of them, by another book, as happened to the earlier books. Thus "ihkam" is from "ahkama," when one prevents something; one says "ahkamtu al-safih" when one prevents him from foolishness, and from it is the verse of Jarir:

"O sons of Hanifa, restrain your foolish ones; indeed I fear for you if he becomes angry."

It was said: the meaning is that they were protected from corruption, taken from "ahkamtu al-dabba" when one places the hikmah in its mouth, which is an iron piece placed in the animal's mouth to keep it from bolting. So it is as if the proofs of the origin and the return are like a beast that the proofs have prevented from bolting. Thus there is a metaphor in the speech, either a figurative (tamthili) or implicit (makniyya) one. It was objected that comparing it to a beast is objectionable and unnecessary, though taste distinguishes this from comparing it to the stiff-necked camel mentioned in some reports, since it submits to those who interpret it, because of the multiplicity of its possible meanings that suit their purposes.

Some objected to taking the meaning of "preventing corruption" on the grounds that it suggests something hardly fitting to the honored verses, namely a tendency toward corruption were it not for the preventer. The first, when the meaning of prevention is intended, is that prevention from abrogation is meant, and by "Book" the Qur'an is meant, and that its not being abrogated, whether entirely or partly, is according to what we have indicated. That this is contrary to the apparent meaning falls within the scope of prevention.

Some claimed that by the verses are meant the verses of this surah, and that all of them are firm and not abrogated by anything at all. This was related from Ibn Zayd, but it was disputed. He claimed that it contains four abrogated verses: His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿You are only a warner, and Allah is over all things a Disposer of affairs﴾, and ﴿Say to those who do not believe: Work according to your position; indeed we are working﴾, and the one following it. All of them were abrogated by the verse of the sword. And ﴿Whoever desires the worldly life and its adornment﴾, the verse, which was abrogated by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Whoever desires the hastened [life], We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We wish﴾. This is not free from scrutiny. It may be that the meaning is that they were protected from doubts through overwhelming proofs and supported by manifest evidence, or that it was made wise, i.e., possessing wisdom, as it includes the foundations of beliefs and righteous deeds, admonitions and wisdoms. On this reading the verb is derived from "hakuma" (with a damma) when one becomes wise, and from it is the verse of Nimr ibn Tawlab:

"And hate your enemy with a gentle hatred, when you attempt to become wise."

Al-Asma'i said that the meaning is "when you attempt to be wise." In attributing the ihkam in the aforementioned senses to the verses rather than to the Book itself, especially if what is intended includes the excellent placement of each verse and its indication that it is at the utmost of perfection, there is what is not hidden. ﴿Then it was detailed﴾, i.e., made detailed, like a necklace distinguished by jewels placed between the pearls. The reason for making it so is that it includes proofs of monotheism, rulings, admonitions and stories. Or, the vital affairs of servants in livelihood and the hereafter were detailed in it, by metaphorical attribution. Or it was made into separate sections, one section after another, of the surahs. By "Book" the Qur'an is meant. It was also said that it is valid to mean by it this surah as well, on the basis that the meanings of its verses were placed in surahs. It is not hidden that this is an artificial reading for which there is no need. Or it was separated in revelation, so it was not revealed all at once, but was revealed piece by piece according to what wisdom and benefit require. In this reading, "then" (thumma) clearly indicates temporal delay. This is because what is immediately understood by "revelation in installments" is the actual installment revelation. If it is intended that it is in itself such that its revelation is in installments according to wisdom, then it is a delay of rank, because that is an inherent attribute of it, worthy of being ranked after the attribute of its rulings. On the first of these readings, the delay is only of rank. It was also said that it indicates delay between the two reports. It was objected that there is no delay there unless "delay" is meant figuratively as sequence, or it is said that it exists with respect to the beginning of the first report and the end of the second.

You know that the view of delay in rank is preferable, except that the delay of the rank of detailing, under either of the first two meanings, from the rank of firm construction is an obvious matter; while under the third meaning there is some obscurity. And you should not fail to notice that the possibilities in the verse arising from multiplying the four meanings of ihkam by the meanings of tafsil are similarly many, and multiplying the total by the possible meanings of the intended "thumma" reaches thirty-two or forty-eight possibilities, and there is no restriction on that. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned three aspects for ihkam, according to what is in al-Kashshaf.

Its formation from solid construction, in view of the composition reaching the limit of inimitability, or from firmness, by making it wise or possessing wisdom, which conveys the meaning of protection from corruption. As for the detailing, there are four views. The first is that it was made like necklaces set with jewels, because of the proofs of tawhid (oneness of God) and related matters in it. The second is that it was divided into sections, surah by surah and verse by verse. The third is that it was spread out in the revelation and detailed what the servants need, with its explanation. This was narrated from Mujahid, who said: the meaning of "thumma" (then) is not delay in time but delay in state, as you say, "It is firmly constructed in the best firmness, then it is detailed in the best detail," and "So-and-so is noble in origin, then noble in deed."

The apparent meaning is that he intended this in all the possibilities. It also follows that if "ihkam" is taken in one of the first two senses and "tafsil" in one of the two ends, then the delay is one of rank, because firmness in the first sense relates to the wording and detailing to the meaning. In the second sense, although it is a matter of meaning, detailing completes what is brief in it. If one of the middle two is intended, then the delay is literal, because firmness is considered in each verse on its own, and making them sections is considered in relation to some of them with others, or because each verse contains phrases of arranged words, and this is a delay of existence. Since the discourse was a matter of questions, it was also temporal. But al-Zamakhshari preferred the delay of state absolutely, reading it as a delay in reporting in these two aspects, so that the word matches its lexical meaning and so that the reason for the shift from "fa" to "thumma" becomes clear. If the third is intended, and "tafsil" is one of the two ends, then it is one of rank; otherwise it is one of reporting. The better view is that "ihkam" refers to the first and "tafsil" to one of the two ends, and on this the correspondence between "Hakim" (All-Wise) and "Khabir" (All-Aware), and between "uhkimat" and "fussilat," applies. Then he said: from this it is clear that the delay of state includes the delay of rank and of reporting. End. So consider this carefully.

It was read as "uhkimat" (with the passive form changed to an active first-person verb, "I have made firm") and "fasalt" with two fathas and lightening, narrated from Ibn Kathir. The meaning is: then I distinguished between truth and falsehood. It was also said that "fussilat" here is like its use in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when the caravan set out﴾, meaning it separated and departed, ﴿from the presence of One who is All-Wise, All-Aware 1﴾. This is an attribute of the Book, described after its verses were described as firm and detailed, which indicate the loftiness of its rank in terms of its essence, to show the greatness of its status in terms of its source. Or it is a second predicate of the subject, whether stated or implied, or it is a complement of one of the two verbs by the dispute over a shared complement (tanazu'), while it is also linked to both of them in meaning, that is, from Him comes its firmness and its detailing. This is what al-Kashf (al-Kashshaf) chose. In al-Kashshaf it is said that there is a good correspondence in it, because the meaning is that the All-Wise firmly established it and the All-Aware detailed it, that is, explained and clarified it, knowing the modes of matters. So in the verse there is laff and nashr (a rhetorical pairing of items with their corresponding referents). The original wording, according to al-Tibi, was: "The All-Wise firmly established its verses and the All-Aware detailed them," then it was changed to "uhkimat, All-Wise; and fussilat, All-Aware," in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿In it, morning and evening, glorify Him men﴾, with "men" as the subject in the reading of the passive form.

And the saying of the poet:

Let Yazid weep, one who is humbled by a dispute,
and one who is stricken by what the calamities bring down.

Then, beyond what is in this sublime arrangement, there is the beauty of the metonymy together with conveying the utmost magnification, whose true nature no describer's description can reach, especially since the two noble names are brought in indefinite form with the indefiniteness of magnification. "Ladun" is one of the indeclinable adverbs, and it is for the first limit of time or place, while the meaning here is the last limit, metaphorically. It was built (made indeclinable) because of its resemblance to the particle in being constantly used in one fixed way, which is that it is a starting point of a limit, and in that it cannot be reported about or reported from, and a subject cannot be predicated upon it. This differs from "ʿinda" and "ladā," for these are not constantly used in one way; rather they are used for the starting of a limit and for other things, and a subject can be predicated upon them, as in His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen, and with Us is more﴾. It was said: because of the strength of its resemblance to the particle and its departure from its counterparts, it is not inflected when it is put in the genitive by an added noun. Yes, it was narrated from Qays that it is inflected, by analogy to "ʿinda." On this basis the reading of ʿĀṣim was explained: ﴿a severe punishment from Him﴾, with the genitive and the sukun of the dal with the pronounced dhamma, and its being joined with "min," as in the verse. Likewise its addition to a singular noun, whatever it is, is the most common, though it may be stripped of "min," and it may be added to a nominal clause, as in the saying:

And remember His favors from when you were a youth.

And to a verbal clause, as in the saying:

A fallen one, of the beauties who pleased them and whom they pleased,
from when he grew up until his black locks turned white.

Ibn al-Dahhan prohibited its addition to a clause, and he interpreted what came of that as if "an" (the verbal particle) were implied, based on its appearing with it in the saying:

If only you had not cut, from when you and we went away,
the kinship of a close relative nor the right of a Muslim.

There is no hiding the strain of maintaining that, especially in an example like "ladun anta yafiʿun." It becomes purely temporal when added to a clause. The accusative "ghadwatan" came after it in the saying:

From the morning until it drew close to sunset.

It was interpreted as a specification of a noun, and the Kufans narrated its nominative after it, and it was explained as an ellipsis of "kāna" (was). It has eight dialectal forms. Some say "ladun" with a fatha on the lam, a damma on the dal, and sukun on the nun, which is the well-known form, and the damma is lightened as in ʿaḍud. In that case two sukuns meet, so some drop the nun for this reason, leaving "lad," with a fatha on the lam and sukun on the dal. Others do not drop it and vowel the dal with a fatha, saying "ladan," with fatha on the lam and dal and sukun on the nun. Others do not drop it and vowel the dal with a kasra, saying "ladin," with fatha on the lam, kasra on the dal, and sukun on the nun. Others do not drop it and vowel the nun with a kasra, saying "ladnin," with fatha on the lam, sukun on the dal, and kasra on the nun. It may also be lightened by moving the dammah of the dal to the lam, as is said of ʿaḍud as ʿuḍd with a damma on the ʿayn and sukun on the ḍad, which is rare. In that case two sukuns also meet, so some drop the nun for this reason, saying "lud" with a damma on the lam and sukun on the dal. Others do not drop it and vowel the nun with a kasra, saying "ludnin" with a damma on the lam, sukun on the dal, and kasra on the nun. These are seven dialectal forms. "Lud" also came, with the nun of "ladun," which is the mother of them all, dropped, and with that the eight are complete. What shows that the original form of "lad" is "ladun" is that when you add it to a pronoun you bring in the nun, saying "min ladunka," and it is not permitted to say "min laduka," as Sibawayh pointed out. In Hamʿ al-Hawāmiʿ, he mentioned ten dialectal forms for it, besides the Qaysi dialect, so let it be consulted.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 2:**

﴿That you worship none but Allah﴾ is in the position of the reason (ʿilla) for the two preceding verbs, on the reading that *anna* is verbal (*maṣdariyya*, forming a verbal noun with the following verb) and the *lam* of causation is understood with it. It is as if it were said: "A Book whose verses were made firm and then distinguished, so that you may not worship except Allah." That is, so that you may abandon the worship of other than Him, Mighty and Majestic, and devote yourselves sincerely to worshipping Him, glorified is He. For the making firm and the distinguishing are among the things that call people to faith and monotheism (tawhid), and to all the acts of obedience that branch from them.

It is also permitted that it be explanatory (*mufassira*) of what is in "distinguished" (*fuṣṣilat*) of the meaning of speech, though not of its letters. It is as if it were said: "It was distinguished and said: 'Do not worship except Allah,'" or "He was commanded that he not worship except Allah." It has also been said that this is a statement disconnected from what precedes it, not verbally connected to it, but rather the beginning of a statement intended as an incitement (*igh'rāʾ*) to monotheism upon his tongue, peace and blessings be upon him. The *anna* and what follows it are in the place of the direct object (*maf'ūl bihi*) of an implied verb, as if it were said: "Hold fast to abandoning the worship of other than Him, exalted is He." The possibility that what came before it is also a direct object, by supposing an implied "say" at the beginning of the speech, is contrary to the apparent sense. Similar is the possibility that *anna* and the verb are in the position of the absolute object (*maf'ūl muṭlaq*); some verifiers have stated that this is among the things that are not good, or not permissible, so one should not heed it.

﴿Indeed I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good news﴾ (2). The pronoun in *minhu* refers to Allah, Exalted is He, and *min* denotes the starting point (*ibtidāʾ al-ghāya*). The prepositional phrase, in origin, is a qualifier (*ṣifa*) of an indefinite noun; when it was placed before it, it became a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*), as is well known in such constructions. That is: "Indeed I am to you, from His direction, exalted is He, a warner: I warn you of His punishment if you do not abandon what you are upon of worshipping other than Him, glorified is He, and a bringer of good news: I give you good news of His reward if you believe and devote yourselves sincerely to His worship, Mighty and Majestic is He."

It is also permitted that *min* be a complement (*ṣila*) of "warner," and the pronoun then refers either to Allah, Exalted is He, as well, and the meaning in that case, as Abu al-Baqa' said, is "a warner on account of His punishment"; or it refers to the Book, with the meaning: "Indeed I am to you a warner against opposing it, and a bringer of good news to whoever believes in it."

[p. 207]

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that you seek forgiveness from your Lord﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿that you worship none but Allah﴾, whether the latter is a prohibition or a negation. The two possibilities mentioned earlier apply to ﴿that﴾ (an). You already know that the correct view is that the verbal ﴿that﴾ (an al-maṣdariyya) may be joined to an imperative and a prohibition just as it is joined to other forms. The insertion of the clause ﴿Indeed I am to you﴾ etc. between the two coordinated elements carries an evident indication of the exalted status of monotheism (tawḥīd) and the lofty rank of the Prophet (ﷺ). In placing the warning before the good news, the same principle was observed as in the discourse, where negation precedes affirmation and emptying (of vices) precedes adornment (with virtues), so that the parts correspond to one another. The mention of the attribute of lordship (rubūbiyya) is an instruction to the addressees and a guidance for them to the way of earnest supplication in asking, and an reinforcement of what is mentioned concerning enjoyment (tamtīʿ) and the bestowal of grace. As for His saying, glorified is He: ﴿then repent to Him﴾, it is coordinated with ﴿seek forgiveness﴾, and there has been disagreement about the explanation of the insertion of ﴿then (thumma)﴾ between them, given that seeking forgiveness, in common usage, means repentance. Al-Jubbāʾī said: the intended meaning of seeking forgiveness here is repentance from the sins that have occurred, and the intended meaning of repentance is seeking forgiveness from what occurs of them after it has occurred. That is: seek forgiveness from your Lord for your sins which you have committed, then repent to Him from sins which you will commit. Thus the word ﴿then﴾ is upon its apparent meaning of delay in time. Al-Farrāʾ said: ﴿thumma﴾ here has the meaning of waw (and), as in the verse:

*With a shaking like the shaking of the Rudaynī spear, that ran through its joints, then trembled.*

and the coordination is explanatory (tafsīrī). It has also been said: we do not grant that seeking forgiveness is repentance; rather, it is abandoning disobedience, while repentance is returning to obedience. And even if it is granted that the two have the same meaning, then ﴿thumma﴾ indicates delay in rank (rutba), and by repentance is meant sincerity in it and persistence upon it. This is the view of the author of al-Farāʾid. Some of the verifiers (muḥaqqiqūn) said: seeking forgiveness is repentance, except that by repentance in the coordinated element is meant the attainment of the sought goal, metaphorically, by the figure of mentioning the cause for the effect; and ﴿thumma﴾ is upon its apparent meaning, and it is an indication of this.

You know that the original meaning of seeking forgiveness (istighfār) is requesting ghafr, that is, covering, and the meaning of repentance (tawba) is return. The first is used for asking God, exalted is He, to cover the sin and pardon it, and the second for regret over it together with resolve not to return to it. Thus there is no identity between them, nor even a necessary logical connection; but the regret for sin together with resolve not to return to it has been stipulated by the Law (sharʿan) as a condition for the validity and acceptance of that request. The use of the first term for the second has also occurred. The need for an explanation of the coordination is evident according to this view. As for the other view, it is because the apparent meaning is that the intended seeking forgiveness commanded is seeking forgiveness preceded by repentance in the sense of regret, so that it is as if it were said: seek forgiveness from your Lord after repentance, then repent to Him. There is no doubt that the need for explanation then becomes manifest. The heart inclines in this case to take the second command as referring to sincerity in repentance and persistence in it, and the delay in it may be either in rank or in time, as is not hidden.

﴿He will give you good enjoyment﴾ is jussed (majzūm) by the imperative. ﴿Enjoyment (matāʿan)﴾ is in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq, a verbal noun not from its own verb), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾. It may also be a direct object (mafʿūl bihi), as a name for what one benefits from among the worldly benefits, such as wealth, children and other things. The meaning, as has been said, is: He will let you live in security and comfort. Perhaps this does not conflict with the world being a prison for the believer and a paradise for the unbeliever, nor with the fact that the people most severely tested are the best and then the next best, because the intended security is security from other than Allah, exalted is He, ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him﴾, and by comfort is meant the goodness of his life through hope in Allah, exalted is He, and drawing near to Him, to the point that he counts the trial a gift:

*Your punishment is sweet to me, and your injustice upon me, according to what desire decides for you, is justice.*

Al-Zajjāj said: the intended meaning is that He will preserve you and not uproot you with punishment, as He uprooted the people of the towns who disbelieved. The address is to the whole community, regardless of each individual. ﴿Until a specified term (ajal musamman)﴾, determined with Allah, exalted is He, which is the end of your lifespans, or the end of the days of the world, as the words of al-Zajjāj imply. There is no indication in the verse that a human has two terms, as the Muʿtazila claimed. ﴿And He will give﴾, that is, He will bestow ﴿to every possessor of grace (kulla dhī faḍl)﴾, that is, increase in righteous deed, ﴿His grace (faḍlahu)﴾, that is, the reward of His grace in this world or in the Hereafter, because the deed is not what is given. It may be said: there is no need to posit an omitted noun (muḍāf), and the intended meaning is hyperbole, in the manner of His saying: ﴿He will recompense them for their description﴾. The pronoun refers to each one. It is also permissible that it refers to the Lord, and by the first grace is meant what was meant by it first, and by the second the increase in reward, by the indication that bestowing is reward; and then the need for interpretation is dispensed with.

Some of the verifiers chose the first explanation, and then said: this is a completion of what was summarized in the enjoyment until a specified term, and a clarification of what might be difficult to understand regarding its wisdom from some of what happens in the world, namely the variation of conditions among those who act. Many a person has the grace of obedience and deed yet is not given more enjoyment in the world than another who is inferior to him in grace, and perhaps the inferior one is given more enjoyment. So it is said: He gives every superior one the reward of his grace, either in this world, as happens in some cases, or in the Hereafter, and that is something that cannot be averted. End.

It is understood from the words of some of them that the distinction is not considered; that He, glorified is He, bestows upon the possessor of grace both in this world and the Hereafter, and His beneficence is not restricted to one of the two abodes. There is no doubt that everyone who has righteous deeds is blessed in the Hereafter with what Allah, exalted is He, knows, and likewise in this world through the adornment of righteous deeds in his heart, comfort according to the hope placed in his Lord, and the like. There is no difficulty in this, as is clear to the reflective person. It has also been said that the verse contains a *laff wa nashr* (an arrangement in which two items are mentioned and then each is matched to its counterpart), for enjoyment is ordered upon seeking forgiveness, and the bestowal of grace is ordered upon repentance. End.

In any case, the speech contains a detailed explanation of what was summarized earlier in the good news. Then he began the warning with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿But if they turn away﴾, that is, persist in turning away from what has been conveyed to you of monotheism, seeking forgiveness and repentance. Its origin is ﴿tatawallaw﴾, which is a present-tense verb beginning with the feminine second-person prefix, because what follows requires it, and one of the two tāʾs has been deleted, as is done in similar forms. It has also been said that ﴿tawallaw﴾ is a past-tense third-person verb, so there is no deletion, and something like ﴿say to them﴾ is understood after it; but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. He placed the warning after the good news, following the pattern of mercy preceding wrath, or because punishment has been made conditional upon turning away from what was mentioned of monotheism and what accompanies it, and this requires that it be mentioned beforehand.

ʿĪsā ibn ʿAmr and al-Yamānī read ﴿tuwallū﴾ with a damma on the tāʾ, a fatḥa on the wāw, and a ḍamma on the lām. This is the present tense of *wallā*, from their saying: *wallā hāriban*, meaning he turned his back and fled. ﴿Indeed I fear for you﴾, by the requirement of compassion and tenderness, or I anticipate, ﴿the punishment of a great day﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection. It is described as great because of the greatness of what occurs in it, and for this reason it is also described as heavy. It is also permissible to describe it as great because it is so in itself. It has been said that the intended meaning is the time in which Allah tested them in this world, and it has been narrated that they were afflicted with a great famine in which they ate carrion. In any case, the attribution of the punishment to it contains intimidation and horrifying.

﴿To Allah is your return﴾ is a *maṣdar mīmī* (a verbal noun formed with the letter *mīm*). Its regular form would have been with a fatḥa on the *jīm*, since it belongs to the pattern *ḍaraba*. The analogical form of its *mīmī* verbal noun is that, as is known from its position. That is, to Him, exalted is He, is your return, by death and then resurrection for recompense on a day like that day, not to other than Him, all of you, none of you will be exempt. ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾ 4.

Page 209

Thus His power over causing your death, then your resurrection and your recompense, is included in that universality, so He will punish you with various kinds of punishment. This is an affirmation and emphasis of what preceded of the mention of the Day, and a reason for the fear.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 5 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Ala innahum yathnuna sudurahum liyastakhfu minhu﴾ ("Behold, they fold their breasts so that they may hide from Him"). This seems to be an answer to an implied question. That is because, when what was cast to them was cast, and the encouragements and warnings that were driven to them were driven, it occurred to the hearer: after they heard such a speech before which the solid mountains crumble, did they respond to it with acceptance, or did they persist in their aversion and misguidance? So it was said, prefaced with the word of alerting (ala), to indicate that what follows of their conduct is a matter that ought to be understood and wondered at: "Behold, they..." etc. The pronoun in "innahum" refers to the polytheists addressed earlier. "Yathnuna" with a fatha on the ya' is the present tense of thanā al-shay'a, meaning to bend or turn a thing, and from it, according to what has been said, comes al-ithnan (the pair), for one of the two bends toward the other; and al-thana' (praise) is the bending of virtues, one upon another; likewise al-istithna' (exception) is the turning toward what was excluded by taking it out. Its original form is yathniyuna, and it underwent the familiar elision seen in yarmuna. Regarding its intended meaning there are several possibilities. One is that the bending is a metaphor or a figure of speech for turning away from the truth, because whoever faces something presents his breast to it, and whoever turns away turns it from it; that is, they fold their breasts away from the truth and swerve from it. The intended meaning is their persistence in the aversion and turning away mentioned by His words, glorified be He: "But if they turn away" etc. Another is that it is a metaphor for concealment, because what is placed inside the breast is hidden; that is, they conceal disbelief, aversion from the truth, and enmity toward the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. Another is that it remains on its literal sense, and the meaning is that when they saw the Prophet, peace be upon him, they did this and turned their backs to him. The apparent view is that the lam is connected to "yathnuna" on all the other possibilities. It seems some scholars regarded the connection as invalid on the first possibility, since turning away from the truth cannot be explained by seeking concealment, as there is no causal relation; so they supplied for it a verb of intention, either as a circumstantial clause or as coordinated with what precedes it: that is, "and they intend, in order to hide from Allah, the Exalted, so that He does not inform His Messenger, peace be upon him, and the believers of their aims." He considered it, in the course of the meaning leading to it, as one of the cases of implied elision in His words, exalted be He: "Strike with your staff the sea, and it split," meaning: he struck, and it split. But it is not hidden that the mind's leap to inserting the intention between the bending of the breasts and the concealment is not like its leap to inserting the striking between the command and the splitting, as mentioned by the scholar al-Qastallani and others. It has also been said that there is no need for supposition in the first two possibilities, because their deviation from the truth in their hearts, the folding of their breasts over disbelief, turning away, and enmity toward the Prophet ﷺ, and their not displaying that, may be for the sake of hiding from Allah, the Exalted, because of their ignorance of what is impermissible for Allah, the Exalted. As for the third possibility, the apparent view is that supposition is necessary, unless the pronoun is returned to the Messenger ﷺ, and this is what the occasion of revelation requires according to what Abu Hayyan reported: that the verse was revealed concerning some of the disbelievers who, whenever the Prophet ﷺ met them, would lower themselves, fold their breasts as if hiding, turn their backs to him, cover their faces with their garments, out of aversion and dislike of meeting him, peace be upon him, while they thought that it would be hidden from him ﷺ. But the apparent sense of His words to come:
﴿He knows what they conceal and what they disclose﴾ requires the pronoun to return to Him, exalted be He. Some verifiers chose the second of the three possibilities, and the matter of the causal clause and the pronoun is clear according to it, and he supported it with what is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, who was a man sweet of speech and fine in relating talk, who showed love to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while concealing in his heart what opposed it. But it is not agreed upon, as you have heard from Abu Hayyan.
Page 210
It was also said: a man of the disbelievers would enter his house, let down his curtain, bow his back, cover himself with his garment, and say: "Does Allah know what is in my heart?" So it was revealed. Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Abdullah ibn Shaddad that it was revealed concerning the hypocrites: whenever one of them passed by the Prophet ﷺ, he folded his breast and covered himself so that he would not see him. This has the same meaning as what was mentioned from Abu Hayyan, except that it includes some disbelievers and not only hypocrites, so the objection raised against this view is not applicable: that the verse is Meccan while hypocrisy only arose in Medina, so how can it be said that it was revealed about the hypocrites? It has been answered that by hypocrisy is not meant its apparent sense, but what proceeded from some polytheists who had a diplomacy resembling hypocrisy. It may also be said: the claim that hypocrisy arose in Medina is not granted without dispute; rather its manifestation was there, and the distinction into three groups occurred there. Even if it be granted, there is no difficulty, and it would be like His words, glorified be He: "As We sent down upon the dividers" if it is interpreted as referring to the Jews, meaning what befell the Banu Qurayza, for it is a report of what would occur, treated as already occurred because of its certainty, and this is among the signs of inimitability, since it happened exactly so; similarly what we are discussing. Yes, what is established in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, and related by Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh through the chain of Muhammad ibn Abbad ibn Ja'far, is that he heard Ibn Abbas reciting the verse and asked him about it, and he said: "There were people who were shy to relieve themselves, lest they expose themselves to the sky, and to have intercourse with their wives, lest they expose themselves to the sky; so this was revealed concerning them." The earlier narrations do not match this one in soundness. The meaning of "yathnuna" on it is clear, except that if by "people" is meant a group of Muslims, as Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti explicitly stated, the matter becomes problematic. That is because the apparent condition of a Muslim who is shy before his Lord, glorified be He, is that he would not, for example, uncover his nakedness in private, since his intention is merely to show courtesy toward Allah, the Exalted, while knowing that He, majestic is His affair, is not screened from His sight by any screen and nothing prevents His knowledge. Such shyness is something no one would hardly blame; rather, in the reports there is what is explicit in commanding it, and it is the motto of many of the great leaders of the Ummah. As for the claim that the shyness of those Muslims was joined with ignorance of His attributes, mighty and majestic, so that they thought the folding could screen them from Allah, glorified be He, and He refuted them with what He refuted, I do not think you would accept it. In sum, the matter on these reports is not free of difficulty, and it is hardly resolved by taking the matter at face value. What the context requires and the connection of the verses calls for is that the verse concerns the polytheists as previously stated, so reflect. And Allah, the Exalted, knows best.

Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), Mujahid, and others read "tathnuni" with the ta' for the feminine plural and with the yā' for the fact that the feminine is not real; it is the present of ithnawiya, like iḥlawlā, so its pattern is tafa'wala with doubling of the 'ayn, which is among the augmented forms used for intensification, since one says ḥalā, and when intensification is intended one says iḥlawlā, and it is intransitive. So "ṣudūruhum" is its subject, and the meaning is the same as the meanings intended in the reading of the majority, except that intensification is implied in it; so it is said, for example: the meaning is that their breasts turn aside with a strong turning. From the same Ibn Abbas also, and from Urwa and others, it is related that they read "tathnūna" with a fatha on the upper ta', sukūn on the thā', fatha on the nūn, kasra on the wāw, and shadda on the final nūn; the original is tathnūnan, on the pattern tafa'wal, from al-thinn, with kasra on the thā' and shadda on the nūn, which means the soft, weak herbage. Abu Zayd recited:
O you, the favored one, the one meant, indeed you are sated, so you have turned silent toward me.
A single mouthful of thinn suffices the milk-camel.
Idghām (assimilation) was obligatory because the 'ayn is repeated, when it is not an elongated form. And "ṣudūrahum" on this reading is also in the nominative as subject, and the meaning, by describing their hearts with flimsiness and weakness, is like that weak plant; so "ṣudūr" is a figure of speech for what is within them of hearts. It was also allowed that it be the intransitive of thanāhu, for one says thanāhu, then infanā, and "ithnūnī," as Ibn Malik explicitly stated in al-Tashil, saying: "Ifa'wala is for intensification, and it may match istaf'ala and be intransitive of fi'l," and they gave this verb as an example. So the meaning is that their breasts accepted the bending, and it returns to the sense of "they swerved," as was explained with the majority reading. And from Mujahid, and likewise Urwa al-A'sha, that he read "tathna'inn," like "tatma'inn," whose original is yathnān, so the alif was changed to a hamza with a kasra, out of desire to avoid two consecutive sukūns, though it is on its usual rule. It is said of its past tense: ithna'anna, like iḥmarra and ibyaḍḍa. It was also said: the original is tathnūn with a kasra on the wāw, so the kasra was felt heavy on the wāw and it was changed into a hamza, as was said of wishāḥ becoming ishāḥ and wisāda becoming isāda. Its pattern on this view is tafa'wal, and on the first view tif'āl; the latter was preferred for its regularity, and it is also from al-thinn, the weak herbage. It was also read "tathnawī," like tarʿawī, and this is attributed to Ibn Abbas as well; but the transmission has been called into question, on the ground that the waw has no place in this verb, since one does not say thanawtuhu then infanā, as ra'awtuhu then irtawā is not said. The pattern of irtawā is among the rare patterns; in the Ṣiḥāḥ its measure is given as ifwala, and its pattern is if'alla. It was not assimilated only because of the quiescence of the yā' and the completion of the discussion of it is sought in its proper place. It was read in other ways, and some scholars brought the readings up to thirteen, detailing them in al-Durr al-Maṣūn. Among the strange ones is that it was read "yuthnūna" with a ḍamma, and Ibn Jinni found this problematic, since one does not say athnaytuhu in the sense of thanaytuhu, and it is not heard outside this reading. Abu al-Baqa' said: "This is not known in the language, unless it is said that its meaning is that they exposed them to bending, as one says abi'ta al-faras when one offers the horse for sale."

﴿Ala ḥīna yastaghshūna thiyābahum﴾ ("Behold, when they cover themselves with their garments"), that is, they make them into coverings, and from it is the saying of al-Khansa':
I pasture the stars, though I was not charged with their pasturing, and at times I cover myself beyond my rags.
Its substance is: when they retire to their beds and wrap themselves in what the sleeper wraps himself with, and this is a time in which the discourse of the soul frequently occurs customarily. And from Ibn Shaddad: when they cover themselves with their garments for concealment. In any case, "thiyab" is meant in its literal sense. It was also said that what is meant is the night, which conceals as garments conceal, and from this is the saying: "The night is more concealing for the wrongdoer." The adverbial phrase is connected to His words, glorified be He: "He knows," meaning: does He not know "what they conceal and what they disclose" when they cover themselves with their garments? It does not follow from this that the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, is restricted to that time, because whoever knows then knows at other times all the more. It was allowed that it be connected to an omitted element, and al-Samin and Abu al-Baqa' supposed it to be "they hide" or, for some, "they intend." The "mā" in both places is either verbal-masdar or relative, its resumptive pronoun omitted, meaning "that which they conceal in their hearts" and "that which they disclose, whatever it may be," and what the context requires enters first and foremost; some restricted it to that. Here the secret is mentioned before the open, as a rebuke against them from the outset for what they did, and as a notice of their exposure and the occurrence of what they fear, and to establish equality between the two knowledges in the most eloquent manner. So His knowledge, glorified be He, of what they conceal is, as it were, prior to His knowledge of what they disclose. The sum of the meaning is that, in relation to His all-encompassing knowledge, their secret and their open are equal, so how could what they might disclose be hidden from Him, glorified be He?

Ibn Abbas read "ʿalā ḥīna yastaghshūna." Ibn Atiyya said: from this usage is the saying of al-Nabigha:
"On the time when I rebuked gray hair for youth..."

﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ is a justification for what preceded it and a confirmation of it. What is meant by "what is within the breasts" is either the secrets concealed therein, or the hearts that are in the breasts. Whichever it is, "dhat" (essence, or "possessor of") is not superfluous, as in "dhat ghadwa" (on a morning), nor is it an idafa (construct) of the named to its name, as has been imagined. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, is thorough in encompassing the hidden thoughts and secrets of all people, or the hearts and their states, so no secret of them is hidden from Him. How, then, could what they conceal and what they disclose be hidden from Him? The use of the nominal sentence indicates that He, glorified is He, has always been knowing of this. There is in it evidence that He, exalted is He, knows things before their external existence. This is something no one denies except a small group of the Mu'tazila (the Mu'tazilites), who said: He, exalted is He, knows things only after they come into being. Exalted is He far above that. This does not apply to some of the speculative theologians who deny mental existence (al-wujud al-dhihni, existence in the mind).

[Page 212]

For if they do not hold it, while denying mental existence, they are obliged to say that knowledge relates to the purely non-existent, and its impossibility is self-evident. Denial of it is either obstinacy or ignorance of the meaning of relating to the purely non-existent. Al-Muhaqqiq al-Dawani (the verifier al-Dawani) raised this objection against them. It is said that it arises from forgetfulness of the meaning of denying mental existence. After verifying what is meant by it, the objection is dispelled.

Its explanation is that their denial does not mean that no image (sura) arises in the intellect when we conceive of something or assent to it, for its occurrence in the intellect in reality is self-evident, and no one denies it except an obstinate person. How would the majority deny it, when for them the temporal knowledge is created, and creation relates only to the particular existents? Rather, it means that this occurrence is not another mode of the existence of the known quiddity, such that one single quiddity, like the sun for example, would have two existences, one external and the other mental, as its proponents claim. For they do not deny existence for the images (suwar) and shapes (ashbah) of things, which are external existents and psychic qualities, and these are what is created for them. They deny only mental existence for the very essences of those things. This is shown by their proofs, where they said: If fire occurred in minds, the minds would be burned by conceiving of it. The consequent is false. For, as you see, this only negates existence from the essence of fire, not from its shape and likeness. Thus the truth is that the majority only denied what the verifying philosophers (muhaqqiqu al-hukama) held, namely that what is present in minds is the very quiddities of things, and they did not deny what the people of the shapes (ahl al-ashbah) held. In that case it is said: the knowledge of the Necessary Being (al-Wajib) according to them is either its relating to the shapes of things, or an attribute of the essence of that relation. Thus they are not obliged to say what that small group said. Nor does it hold against them that the relation to those shapes, which exist in eternity, is, because it is a relation between them and Him, exalted is He, posterior to them, so that the creation of those shapes would be without knowledge, which is impossible. For we say: since the Necessary Being (al-Wajib) (1), exalted is He, is an agent by necessity in His knowledge and His other essential attributes, the existence of those perceptual forms, which are those shapes, is a requirement of His essence, exalted is He. So there is no harm in their being prior to the knowledge of the essence. What is preceded by knowledge is only His voluntary acts.

Then it should be known that the statement of theirs, that the knowledge of the Necessary Being, blessed and exalted is He, concerning things is eternal while its relation to them is temporal, does not mean that there is nothing but a temporal relation, for that would entail the temporality of knowledge itself, and so we would return to what that small group committed, for it would mean the known does not become known before knowledge relates to it. That is utter corruption. Rather, its meaning is that the relation which the reality of knowledge does not require is temporal, and there is a relation which that reality requires, and it is eternal. That is because the shapes and likenesses are known in themselves, and through them things are known. So the relation of knowledge for them is more general than its relation to the essence of the known thing or to its likeness and shape. Since the temporal events did not exist in eternity, the knowledge that relates to them was by relation to their likenesses and shapes. After their coming into being, the relation is renewed by being to the very essences of those temporal events. In sum, the relation of knowledge to the likenesses of temporal events and their shapes is eternal, and its relation to their selves and essences is temporal. There is no difficulty in this at all. By this verification many doubts are dispelled, as is said. However, it has been objected to this that the argument of application (burhan al-tatbiq) applies to those shapes, since they are individually distinct in reality, so one of the two undesirable consequences follows.

There are lengthy discussions on this subject. Mawlana Isma'il Afandi al-Kalnabawi has expounded on this matter in his glosses on the Commentary on the Adudiyya (Sharh al-'Adudiyya). Mawla al-Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani has a verification in another style, which he mentioned in his book Mutla' al-Jud, so refer to it. In sum, the difficulty of this question is not hidden. It is among the matters in which the feet of peoples have slipped, and perhaps Allah, glorified is He, will grant you its verification by His bounty, glorified is He. Mawlana Isma'il Afandi al-Kalnabawi, the most excellent of the later scholars, held this view.

The eleventh part is completed by the power and strength of Allah. Following it is the twelfth part, whose beginning is (Wa ma min dabbatin 12).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 6:

Page 2
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾. Al-dabba (creature) is the name for every living animal, whether male or female, rational or otherwise. It is derived from al-dabib (crawling), which in its original sense means light walking. From it is the verse:

They claimed me an old man, and I am not an old man; rather, the old man is one who crawls along crawling.

In common usage it is specifically applied to quadrupeds, and it may be restricted to the horse. Here, by the agreement of the exegetes, it is meant in its linguistic sense; that is: there is no animal that crawls upon the earth but that its nourishment and sustenance are upon Allah the Exalted. The meaning is that this is as if it were obligatory upon Him, the Exalted, since there is no obligation upon Him, glorified is He, according to the People of Truth, as has been explained in the discourse. Thus the word "upon" (ʿalā), which is used for obligation, is employed metaphorically through a subsequent (tabaʿiyya) metaphor on account of what resembles it, and it is a metaphor of two levels.

Al-Imam mentioned that provision is obligatory by reason of promise, bounty and beneficence, in the sense that it remains a matter of His grace; but since He, glorified is He, whose majesty is great, does not fail to fulfil what He has promised, He has depicted it in the form of obligation for two benefits: the confirmation of its arrival, and the urging of the servants towards reliance upon Him in it. Reliance upon Allah does not preclude engaging with the means, while knowing that He, glorified is He, is the one who causes them. In a report: "Use your reason and rely upon Allah." And it has come: "No soul will die until it has completed its provision and its term, so fear Allah the Exalted and be moderate in seeking." It should not be believed that provision is not obtained without engaging a means, for He, glorified is He, provides abundantly without any means at all. In some reports: "When revelation descended upon Musa, peace be upon him, his heart became attached to the circumstances of his family, so Allah the Exalted commanded him to strike a rock with his staff. He struck, and the rock split, and a second rock emerged; he struck it, and a third emerged; he struck it, and it split open to reveal a worm like a grain of dust, and in its mouth was something that served as its food. He heard it say: 'Glory be to Him who sees me, hears my speech, knows my place, remembers me and does not forget me.'" How fine is the saying of Ibn Udhayna:

Indeed she knows, and I am not one of ostentatious ways, that the one who is my provision will surely come to me.
I strive towards it, and its seeking does not tire me; and even if I remain seated, it does not concern me.

Allah the Exalted confirmed this for him on the day he came to Hisham, who rebuked him with these words; so he returned to Medina, and Hisham regretted this and sent his reward to him. Close to his story is the story of al-Thaqafi with Ubayd Allah ibn Amir, the maternal uncle of ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, may Allah be pleased with him, which is well known; it was related by Ibn Abi al-Dunya and transmitted by more than one. Someone who entirely disregarded the matter of means said:

The likeness of the provision you seek is like the shadow that walks along with you: you cannot catch it while pursuing it, and when you turn away from it, it follows you.

Page 3
In sum, one should trust in Allah the Exalted and attach the heart to Him, glorified is He; whatever He wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be. (The People of the Sunna) argued from the verse that the forbidden is provision; otherwise, whoever has eaten nothing but the forbidden throughout his life would necessarily not be one who is provided for. It was answered that this is a mere supposition, since there is at least nourishment by the mother's milk, for example, which is lawful. Moreover, what is meant is that every animal that needs provision, when it is provided for, its provision is from Allah the Exalted; and this does not preclude that there may be someone for whom there is no provision, such as one who is nourished by the forbidden, and likewise one who is not provided for at all until he dies of hunger. This was reported from Mujahid, and the discussion of this has already preceded.

﴿And He knows its settled place and its place of storage﴾: its settled place is the place of its lodging in the loins (al-aslab), and its place of storage (mustawdaʿ) is its place in the wombs and what runs in their course, such as eggs and the like. So "mustaqarr" and "mustawdaʿ" are both nouns of place, and it is permitted that both be verbal nouns, and that "mustawdaʿ" be a passive participle since its verb is transitive; but this is not permitted for "mustaqarr", since its verb is intransitive. The first is the apparent one. Each of the two nouns has been specified with the place assigned to it, as some of the learned men have said, because the drop of semen, for example, in relation to the loins is in its natural receptacle and its created origin; but in relation to the wombs, for instance, it is deposited in them until a specified time. From ʿAṭāʾ the interpretation of "mustaqarr" as the wombs and "mustawdaʿ" as the loins is reported, and he seems to have taken the interpretation of the first from His words, glorified is He: ﴿and We settle in the wombs what We will﴾. It is also permitted that "mustaqarr" means their dwellings on the earth wherever they are actually found, and "mustawdaʿ" their place among the materials and the resting-places when they were still potential; and this is general for all animals, unlike the first, since among animals there are those that are not lodged in a loin, such as one formed from the putrefaction of the earth, for example. Perhaps the mention first of their place, with regard to their final state, is for the sake of the appropriateness between it and the heading of their being a creature on the earth. The meaning, according to what has been said, is: there is no creature on the earth but that Allah provides for it wherever it is from its places, driving it toward it; and He knows its various materials, which are included within the ranks of diverse preparedness, varying in its stages, differing in its states, and its various resting-places; He bestows upon each rank what befits it of the beginnings of its existence and its perfections that branch from it. It is not free from beauty, though it has some remoteness. ʿAbd al-Razzaq and a group related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that its settled place is where it dwells and its place of storage is where it dies. It was objected that interpreting "mustawdaʿ" in this way does not suit the context of the guarantee of their provision; and it may be said: perhaps that is an indication of the end of the term of that guarantee. In the report of Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him, there is an indication of what is, as it were, also its beginning: Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim related from him, and al-Hakim graded it sound, that he said: "Its settled place is the wombs, and its place of storage is where it dies." It is as if it were said: He, glorified is He, is the guarantor of the provision of every creature, and He knows its place when it first needs provision and its place when it last needs it; so He drives it to it, and it is necessary until the term of its need comes to an end. It is permitted that this clause be an explanatory resumption (istiʾnaf bayani), or that it be conjoined to the clause ﴿its provision is upon Allah﴾, falling within the scope of (illa); and al-Ajhuri limited himself to this.

﴿All of it is in a clear Book﴾: that is, each one of the creatures, its provision, its settled place and its place of storage; or, all that has been mentioned and other things are recorded in the Preserved Tablet, which is clear to whoever looks into it among the angels, peace be upon them; or it is the manifest one for what is recorded in it to those who look. The clause, according to al-Tibi, is like a completion for the meaning of the obligation of guaranteeing provision, like one who acknowledges something owed to him and then writes a document about it. In al-Kashf: the more evident view is that it is a confirmation of knowledge; and as if, when He mentioned that He knows what they conceal and what they reveal, He followed it with what indicates the comprehensiveness of His knowledge,

[Page 4]

Then He, glory be to Him, presented, in the words of the Exalted and Blessed One, what indicates the greatness of His power: ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾. This affirms monotheism (tawhid), because the one whose knowledge and power encompass all things is the one who is God, not anyone else who knows nothing and has no power to harm or benefit. It also confirms what preceded concerning promise and threat (wa'd wa wa'id), because the one who is knowing and powerful is hoped in and feared. It is also permitted that this verse is an affirmation of His words: ( ﴿He knows what they conceal and what they reveal﴾ ), and what follows it is an affirmation of His words: ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾. But this is far-fetched. It is as if the intended meaning of "the creation of the heavens and the earth" etc. is the creation of both and what is in them. Or the heavens may be taken as a metaphor for the higher things (al-'Ulwiyyat), so that they include them and what is in them, and the earth may be taken as a metaphor for the lower things (al-Sufliyyat), so that they include them and what is in them, without any restriction. This was needed because the context requires it. Otherwise, their creation within that period does not preclude the creation of other things within it. By "day" is meant time in general, not the commonly known day, since that cannot be conceived when there was no sun and no earth. It was also said: what is meant is the duration of one complete revolution of the sphere called the Throne (al-'Arsh). The Greatest Shaykh (al-Shaykh al-Akbar), may God sanctify his secret, went to this view, and his state is known from what has preceded. Other views have also been stated.

In the fact that they were not created at once, as you have learned, there is evidence, as many have said, of His being capable and choosing, together with what it contains of lessons for observers and an exhortation to deliberation in matters. What has been said concerning the reason for specifying this number rather than a greater one, such as seven, or a smaller one, such as five, for the creation, has already been mentioned. Perhaps we will investigate that in another place. The use of the plural form for "heavens" (al-samawat) is because they differ in origin and essence, unlike the earth. Even if it is said that the earth is like the heaven in being seven layers, with a distance between each earth and another earth and creatures in them, and by this was interpreted His words: ﴿And of the earth, the like of them﴾, most hold that the earth is one sphere divided into seven climes (aqalim), and they took the verse as referring to this.

﴿And His Throne was over the water﴾ is coordinated with the clause "created" (khalaqa) together with its implicit pronoun, or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun, with "qad" assumed, according to what is well known about the circumstantial past clause, that "qad" must be present or implied. The past tense derived from "kana" (was) concerns the judgment, not the speaking. That is, "His Throne was over the water before their creation." This is what the words of Mujahid imply, and al-Qadi al-Baydawi stated it explicitly. Then he said: "Nothing intervened between them, i.e., the Throne and the water, not that it was placed upon the back of the water." It was used as evidence for the possibility of the void (al-khala'), and that water is the first thing created after the Throne from the bodies of this world. End of quote. Likewise, the scholar Abu al-Su'ud, Mufti of the Ottoman lands, stated it explicitly, but he said: "Nothing is beneath it (i.e., the Throne) other than it (i.e., the water), whether there was a gap between them or it was placed upon its back, as reported in the narration. Therefore there is no indication in it for the possibility of the void. How could it be, since if it indicated, it would indicate its existence, not merely its possibility, nor that water was the first thing created in the world after the Throne. It only indicates that their creation was earlier than the creation of the heavens and the earth, without addressing the relation between them." End of quote. There is no hiding the disagreement between the Qadi and the Mufti, and most hold that the truth is with the Mufti, as you will learn, God willing.

Some defended the Qadi by saying: If it were placed upon the back of the water, then before the completion of the world, one of six matters would necessarily follow: either the water leaving its natural place, or the Throne leaving its natural place, or the water rarefying or growing, or the Throne rarefying or growing. And at the time of the creation of the world, one of five matters would follow: either the Throne moving in a straight line to its natural place, or the water condensing or thinning, or the Throne condensing or thinning. And these matters are false, as will be clear to anyone trained in philosophy (hikma). The possibility in his words is to be understood as actual possibility (al-imkan al-waqu'i), or it may mean essential possibility (al-imkan al-dhati), and by "the void" is meant the void in this our world, for this is what is disputed. So it is as if it were said: "It was used as evidence that the void in our world is possible in essential possibility." The way of inferring this is that the void existed before this our world, and the occurrence of a thing at some time is evidence of its essential possibility at all times, for the establishment of possibility for the possible is necessary. So the possible at one time is possible at another time, as the commentator on Hikmat al-'Ayn verified. The way of showing that water is the first thing created after the Throne is that every simple body has a natural place, and that place is a necessary accompaniment of the existence of the body, for when the agent brings a body into existence, he necessarily brings it into a place, as they have stated. The place for light bodies is above, and for heavy bodies is below, according to heaviness and lightness, and the delimitation of these two is only by the Greatest Sphere. So the existence of water within the Throne depends on the existence of its place, which depends on the existence of the Throne, so it comes after it in origin. The flaw in this argument is not hidden. At least one may say: why is it not permissible that God create the Throne and the water together? Moreover, there is in some narrations what is apparent that the water was created before the Throne. Al-Tayalisi, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi who graded it as good (hasan), Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat, and others narrated from Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, where was our Lord before He created the heavens and the earth?' He said: 'He was in 'ama' (a cloud or mist), with air beneath it and air above it, and He created His Throne upon the water.'"

Some explained the meaning of this, saying: Since the meaning of the Throne being "upon the water" is that it is placed above it, not touching it, and since the creation of the heavens and the earth came after both, this entails that the Throne was created earlier, and that water is the first thing created after it. This is from the implication of the address. As for his words: "not that it was placed..." etc., this is because the context is to explain His power, may He be exalted, and this requires it. In it there is what there is, as is not hidden.

Some of the scholars of Rum (Ottoman lands) criticized what was mentioned first, saying: Its summary is that the second part of the two parts mentioned in the words of the second scholar entails one of matters established in the science of philosophy as false, so the first of the two is necessary, and it is what the first scholar held. This is only complete if the premises stated in refuting those matters are certain, and this is disputed, for most of them are based on the principles of the philosophers. The Qadi himself demonstrated the falsity of most of them in al-Tawali'. He only observes the philosophical principles when they do not contradict the Islamic principles. Moreover, in the words of that supporter there are flaws in several respects:

The first: his statement, "It is necessary that either the water leaves its natural place..." etc. It may be answered: It is permissible for water to leave its natural place, and that is not impossible, although its leaving of itself by way of flowing from its natural place is impossible. This is supported by the fact that they mentioned that water, because of its relative heaviness, requires that it be above the earth, and the earth, because of its absolute heaviness, requires that it be entirely submerged within it, such that one can imagine a point within the earth from which the lines drawn to the surface of the water are equal from all directions. Yet the matter today is not like that, because a northern quarter of the earth is uncovered, and the water has receded from it, either because of the nearness of the sun from the south to the earth when it is at perigee, by the thickness of the "mutammim mahwi" (a term from astronomy), as it has been said, or for another matter known to God, may He be exalted.

The second: what he mentioned about the impossibility of the rarefaction (takhalkhul) of water is disputed by them as well. As for what is said, that the view of rarefaction cannot be conceived in simple (non-composite) real substances because it entails composition in what is in it, this is refuted. For it is stated in Hikmat al-'Ayn and its commentary that real rarefaction, which is that the quantity of a body increases without anything being added to it from outside, is possible. And the greatest of the verifiers (Sayyid al-Muhaqqiqin) verified it in his glosses, saying: A body, whether composed of matter and form or not, can undergo rarefaction and condensation, because the quantity of the body is additional to it, and the body as such has no quantity in its essence, so its relation to all quantities is equal, and so it can be characterized by greater or smaller quantity. Also, the body is one continuous unity, and quantity is additional to it, and the simple body, its part is equal to its whole. So when the whole is characterized by a specific quantity, its part, if taken alone, must be capable of being characterized by that quantity. And the whole, by the reverse, is necessary, since equals must share the same judgments. Then the possibility of that is established.

The third: the justification by taking the possibility as essential possibility, etc., is open to criticism, for it does not follow from the occurrence of a thing at some time except the possibility of its existence at that time, even if that possibility is continuous and necessary at all times. So his words, "the establishment of possibility for the possible is necessary, so the possible at one time is possible at every time," if he means by it that its possibility is a fact established for it at every time, with "at every time" as a temporal modifier of the possibility, then this is granted. But what follows from it is that that thing is characterized by possibility in a continuous, perpetual way, not preceded by a state of non-characterization and not prior to it. And it does not follow from it that its existence at every time is possible, because it is permissible that the existence of a thing in general is possible in continuous possibility, while its existence at every time is not possible but impossible. And it does not follow from this that the thing belongs to the category of the impossibles rather than the possibles, for the possibility of a thing does not mean the permissibility of its being characterized by all modes of existence, but rather its permissibility of being characterized by existence in some form. Thus it suffices for the possibility of a thing that it be permissible to be characterized by existence occurring at some time. What is impossible is that which does not accept existence in any way. If he means that it is possible to exist at every time, in the sense that at every time it is a container for existence, then this is denied. It does not follow from the fact that the establishment of possibility for the possible is necessary. For the verifier al-Dawani has verified in some of his works that the possibility of the possible, even if continuous at all times, does not entail the possibility of its existence at those times. On this basis the theologians relied in answering the argument of the philosophers for the eternity of the world, that it is possible for it to exist in pre-eternity, otherwise there would be inversion (inqilab), which is necessarily impossible. And the power of the Exalted Creator is eternal by consensus. So if the world were created, it would follow that the bounty (jud), which is the bestowing of existence and what follows it of perfections upon possible things, would be abandoned for an infinite duration, and this is impossible for the True, Generous, Bountiful Giver.

[Page 6]

(The essence of the answer) is that your statement "the world is possible in eternity," if you mean by it that existence in eternity is possible for it, so that the time-phrase "in eternity" is attached to "existence," then this is disputed, since its existence in eternity may be impossible. If you mean by it that the possibility of its existence, in general, is continuous throughout eternity, with the time-phrase attached to "possibility," then this is accepted. It does not follow that the existence of the world in eternity is possible, since its existence in eternity may be impossible, even though it is characterized in eternity by the possibility of its existence at every moment. This is what is meant by saying that the eternity of possibility does not entail the possibility of eternity. As for what has been said to prove the entailment, namely that its possibility, if it is continuous in eternity, is not in its essence a barrier to receiving existence in any part of the parts of eternity, so that the absence of its barrier from it is a matter continuous in all those parts. Then, when one considers its essence as such, it does not prevent its being characterized by existence in any of them. Rather, its being characterized by it in each of them is permitted, alternately, and even together. The permissibility of its being characterized in each of them is the possibility of its being characterized by continuous existence in all parts of eternity, considered in relation to its essence. So the eternity of possibility entails the possibility of eternity. This is correct, up to his words "it does not prevent its being characterized by existence in any of them." If he means that its essence does not prevent, in any part of eternity, its being characterized by existence in general, with the phrase "in any of them" attached to "non-prevention," then its meaning is that it does not prevent, in any part of eternity, existence after it, and this is exactly the eternity of possibility.
