It does not follow from this that its non-prevention of eternal existence, which is the possibility of eternity, is absent. If he means that its essence does not prevent existence in any part of eternity, with the prepositional phrase attached to "existence," then this is exactly the possibility of eternity, and the dispute arose over precisely this, so it is begging the question. How wondrous is it that this statement came from its speaker, when among existent things there are those that tend toward existence, like some letters, and with the explicit statement that the quiddity of time requires in its essence the non-gathering of its parts and the precedence of some of them over others. For it entails the possibility of the existence of each of those parts in eternity, considered in relation to its essence. The full discussion of this is sought in Sharh al-Mawaqif and its glosses.

And it was objected, regarding the meaning of the void being the void within our world, because it is the point in dispute, that several have stated that the point in dispute is only the void inside the world. Its reality is that two bodies do not touch, and there is nothing between them that touches them, on the basis that it is measurable, [Page 7] definitely. As for the void outside the world, it is agreed upon, since nothing is measurable there according to reality itself. So the dispute concerns only the naming of it as a dimension. The philosophers say that it should not be called a dimension or a void, while the theologians call it an imagined dimension. There is no doubt that the world-space where the Throne is upon the water is inside the world, so the void within it is included in the point in dispute. Some later scholars also stated this explicitly.

Some people objected to his statement: "if it were placed upon the back of the water, there would necessarily follow..." etc., saying that the matters which would necessarily follow from that assumption are false. Most of them were mentioned, and he blackened the face of the paper by explaining that, though it is not needed and not even relied upon. Some claimed that nothing the judge (al-Qadi) observed in this section is contrary to Islamic principles, and his own self whispered to him that the water's leaving its place is impossible, because if God, glory be to Him, is a causer by essence, then removing it from Him, glory be to Him, cannot be conceived, since its relation to Him is equal at all times, so it is impossible that He be deficient in some and not others. If He is a chooser, it is said that this removal is impossible in itself, and He, glory be to Him, does not do the impossible, nor does His power relate to it. The same is said about rarefaction (takhalkhul) and condensation (takaththuf). It is possible that they occur by nature, otherwise they would be permanent, since what the essence requires does not differ from it. Among those who held their impossibility is al-Asfahani in his commentary on Hikmat al-Mata li', then he spoke defending his own position. For the judge there is something that neither fattens nor satisfies. Ibn Sadr al-Din said, after quoting the two scholars: It has been established in the science of dimensions and bodies that the totality of the spheres of the elements has no sensible measure in relation to the greatest sphere, which is what is meant by the Throne. So it cannot be conceived that it is placed upon the back of the water-sphere. That would only be the case if the size of the water-sphere were such that it fills the hollow of the Throne, touching its convex with its concave. Otherwise it would not be placed upon its back, which is the convex surface. Rather, either they do not touch at all, or they touch at a point, as sound imagination testifies. How can it be conceived that it fills it, when it now fills only with the heavens, the earth, the Kursi, and all the elements together? You cannot say: perhaps the water at the beginning of creation was at this small size it now has, then rarefied until it filled its hollow, because of the impossibility of void, and then when He created the rest of the upper and lower bodies, it returned by its nature to what you see. We say: rarefaction is the increase of the quantity of a body without anything being added to it, which requires a local motion, and this requires the existence of an empty space free of occupants, and this is what is meant by void. Likewise, you cannot say: let it at the beginning of creation be of great size, such that it fills the hollow of the Throne, and then condensed after the creation of the rest of the bodies to this small size. We say also: condensation, which is the reduction of the quantity of a body without anything being lost from it, is caused, as established among them, by two things. One is prior rarefaction, which occurs to it by what necessitates it. When that occurring cause disappears, it returns by its nature to its original measure, as in the ebb and flow. In the mentioned case this cannot be conceived, because it is supposed that it was created initially of great size, such that it fills the hollow of the Throne. So how can it be conceived that it rarefied by an accident until, when that accident disappears, it returns to its natural small measure? This is evident. The second is condensation through the overpowering of intense cold. This also cannot be conceived here. First, because water that has solidified into ice, even if smaller than before it solidified, does not fall to a point where it has no sensible measure in relation to its original measure. Rather it approaches it perceptibly, as is seen in frozen waters. And the sphere of water that exists now has no measure in relation to what fills the hollow of the Throne. This is like the sea solidifying until it becomes like a lentil, and no rational person would accept this. Second, because the water-sphere, as observed, is not frozen, but remains in its nature of melting. If you say: there remains, on the assumption that the water at the beginning of creation was of great size, filling the hollow of the Throne, another possibility, namely that some parts of this great sphere are separated and made into matter for the rest of the celestial and terrestrial bodies, as in the Surah of the transformation of some elements into others.

[Page 8]

This is supported by what has been transmitted in the tradition that the Throne was upon the water before the creation of the heavens and the earth. Then He, exalted is He, produced agitation in the water, so it foamed, and smoke rose from it, while the foam remained on the surface of the water. He created dryness in it, and it became earth, and He created the heavens from the smoke. To this His words, glory be to Him, refer: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke﴾. We say: this possibility does not occur. As for the assumption that the body is composed of matter and form, as the Peripatetic philosophers (al-Mashsha'un) held, then the prime matter (hayula) of the elements, though one in individual, is receptive to the forms of the elements coming upon it through successive dispositions that arise. But the prime matter of each sphere differs from the prime matter of another sphere, accepting only the form that has come about in it. As for the assumption that it is composed of indivisible atoms (al-jawahir al-fardah), as is the doctrine of the People of Truth (Ahl al-Haqq), then they differ in realities according to the verifying later scholars, as they have stated. What water is composed of cannot be what the rest of the bodies are composed of. As for what has been transmitted in the tradition and indicated by the verse, namely making the smoke rising from the water a matter for the heavens, it is turned away from its apparent meaning, since smoke consists of fiery parts mixed with small earthy parts that have been refined by heat, and there is no distinction between them to the senses because of their extreme smallness. Before the creation of the heavens and the earth with what is in them, there was no fire and no earth, so from where would smoke be generated? Likewise if by smoke is meant vapor, since it consists of airy parts mixed with small watery parts refined by heat, such that no distinction between them is perceptible either. Where there is no air, there is no vapor. For this reason the judge said, in explaining ﴿and it is smoke﴾, that it is a dark matter, and perhaps he meant by it its matter, or the minute parts of which it was composed. From here it appears that what is in the tradition does not support the Throne's being placed upon the back of the water, adhering to it. Rather it supports that there is no barrier between them, since the rising of smoke and vapor requires the existence of a space in which those parts move. In the case of adherence, this is impossible, as is not hidden from one who has sound imagination.

It is known from what has been mentioned that the verse must be interpreted as the judge interpreted it, and there is no room for saying that it is placed upon the back, so the argument is complete. As for Abu al-Su'ud's statement: "if it indicates..." etc., the reply is that actuality is the strongest proof of the possibility of a thing. Such argument is widespread and common in their discourse. As for whether the intended possibility is actual possibility, this is not so, since the dispute concerns possibility, not actuality. As for what is reported from al-Asma'i, that this is like their saying: "the sky is over the earth," although neither is attached to the other, then the meaning of the judge's statement "there was no barrier between them" would be that there was no perceptible barrier between them, and there was an imperceptible barrier, namely air, which is nothing, and what has been mentioned does not suit as a meaning for that. For the "above-ness" existed before the creation of all the bodies of this world, so on the assumption of non-adherence, no barrier at all can be conceived. Then he explained the manner in which the verse indicates that the water is the first thing created after the Throne, in the manner we previously mentioned. The intended meaning of his words has ended.

[Page 8]

(And I say): This possibility, which he answered according to his own claim, is very strong. What he reported from the later verifying scholars (muhaqqiqi al-muta'akhkhirin) has been explicitly contradicted by the majority. This matter has been verified in its proper place. There is therefore no barrier to Allah, exalted is He, creating the heavenly and earthly bodies, and indeed everything, from water. What he mentioned as a reason for diverting the report from its apparent meaning is not a valid reason at all, for He, glorified is He, may transform part of that water that fills the space into fiery components, and part of it into earthly components, and make the whole of it smoke. Likewise, He may transform part of it into airy components, which then mix with small, subtle watery components, and with heat that He creates wherever He wills, so that vapor forms. In a report from Wahb ibn Munabbih, He, majestic is His glory, grasped a handful of water, then opened the handful, and the smoke rose. Then He decreed them as seven heavens in two days. The hadith about the rising is interpreted in a way that does not require empty space, such as the meaning: He found part of it as rising smoke. It may also be said: it is possible that the water at the beginning of creation filled the Throne. Then, when He, glorified is He, wished to create what He created, He annihilated from it what He wished and created without any separation in which a void would be realized. The creation then came into being from nothing. The claim that this creation is impossible leads to great corruption and a grave matter, which no Muslim would easily accept. This is evident.

[Page 9]

What he mentioned in rebutting the words of Shaykh al-Islam, "that if it indicated, it would indicate…," is not clear in it. It has been said: the objection by way of "if it indicated, it would indicate the existence of the void, not its possibility" is an evasion, because when a thing exists, its existence is necessary, not merely possible, as explained in its proper place. What points to this objection being so is that he restricted the possibility in his expression by a condition only, while asserting that it indicates existence.

Some have objected to his statement, "It is established in the science of dimensions and bodies…," that this is based on the assumption that the water in the verse is elemental water, and that elemental water, according to that assumption, was created only after the creation of the earth. How then can it be conceived that the Throne, which was created before the heavens and the earth, was upon it, let alone that it was placed on its back or not placed on it without a barrier between them? Rather, it is the natural, luminous, cloud-like water from which the Throne was formed. In this there is a diversion of the expression from its apparent meaning. Similar to this is what al-Kamil ibn al-Kamal said: "The intended meaning of the Throne is not the ninth sphere, nor is the water one of the elements, because of what testifies to that with sound testimony that cannot be refuted: what Muslim recorded in his Sahih from the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Allah, exalted is He, existed, and nothing existed with Him, and His Throne was upon the water, and He wrote in the Reminder (al-dhikr) everything, then He created the heavens and the earth.'" So there is no basis for using it as evidence for the possibility of the void, or that water is the first thing created. Rather, His Throne, glorified is He, is an expression of His self-subsistence (qayyumiyya), on the basis that it was originally the throne of sovereignty, which is the manifestation of His authority. Water indicates the attribute of life, in that every living thing is created from it. So the meaning of "and His Throne was upon the water" is: and He was living and self-subsisting. In the word "upon" (ʿalā) there is an indication of the ordering of one of them over the other, so reflect. End of quotation.

Perhaps the point of the report's testimony to that negation is that its inclusion, if affirmed, would contain something that contradicts what the negation contains, for then there would be two things with Him, glorified is He, let alone one thing. It is not hidden that this is only complete if the past clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The apparent view is that it, like the others, is coordinated with the initial (independent) clause. Nothing in the statement requires that the meaning of "and His Throne was upon the water" be with His existence without anything being with Him, which would force interpreting water and Throne according to the two attributes of His that you know. I see in the hadith no more than establishing the existence of what the coordinated clauses contain before the creation of the heavens and the earth. As for whether His being and there being nothing with Him, the Throne of Him, glorified is He, being upon the water, and His writing in the Reminder of what He wrote, all occurred at one time, which is the time of His existence, after which the creation of the heavens and the earth occurred with an interval and delay, I do not see this. In some narrations, the creation is coordinated with what precedes it by "and" (wa), like the rest of the coordinated clauses.

Aḥmad, al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others reported from ʿImran ibn Husayn, who said: "The people of Yemen said: 'O Messenger of Allah, inform us about the beginning of this matter, how was it?' He said: 'Allah existed before everything, and His Throne was upon the water, and He wrote in the Preserved Tablet the record of everything, and He created the heavens and the earth.'" The report continues. Then, the matter of testimony is not completed by what has preceded alone. It is also necessary to take the writing in the Reminder as a supposition, and to negate that there is any writing and any written thing in it, as is understood from the two. He maintains this in the second report also. Yet, with that, the view that the time of the supposition is united with the time of His self-subsistence and His life, blessed and exalted is He, together with the time of His existence, glorified is He, is disturbed by what Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Bayhaqi reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, exalted is He, decreed the measures of the creatures fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, and His Throne was upon the water." Because the parts of the imagined time separating the time of His existence, exalted is He, and the existence of His attributes from the time of the existence of creation, are infinite. How then can it be measured as fifty thousand years? Multiplying it by itself, and multiplying the result by itself a thousand thousand times, is at least a very small amount; indeed, it is nothing at all in comparison to the infinite.

This testimony is also contradicted by what was mentioned in the hadith of Abu Razin al-ʿUqayli, in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him: "And He created His Throne upon the water," for it explicitly states that the Throne is created, and self-subsistence cannot be created. Likewise, what is narrated from Kaʿb: that He, glorified is He, created an emerald green jacinth (yāqūta khaḍrāʾ), and looked at it with awe, and it became water. Then He created the wind and placed the water on its back. Then He placed the Throne upon the water. The hadith that the water was on the back of the wind came from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, al-Bayhaqi and others reported it from him. The rejection of what was mentioned, that water means the attribute of life of Him, exalted is He, is evident. Similar to this is what Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas, that he said: "His Throne, glorified is He, was upon the water. When He created the heavens and the earth, He divided that water into two halves. He placed half beneath the Throne, which is the sea that is kindled (al-bahr al-masjur), so not a drop falls from it until the Trumpet is blown, and then something like dew descends from it, and bodies grow from it. And He placed the other half beneath the lowest earth." Perhaps the reason for the command to reflect on the words of this virtuous man is an allusion to what we have mentioned.

In sum, there is no doubt that what is understood from "water" is one of the elements, and from "Throne" a body whose description in the reports is such as to dazzle the intellects. The testimony of the preceding report, despite being a testimony of negation, is opposed by testimonies of affirmation that are not explicit in the matter sought, as you have known. And from the fact that the Throne is upon the water there is something that covers both parts: that it is placed on its back, touching it, and that it is above it without anything between them touching them. Restricting it to the second part is something that no evidence completes and that is not free from dispute and contention. The verse is not suitable as evidence that water is the first thing created after the Throne. Whoever returns to the reports relied upon sees some of them, such as the report of Abu Razin which al-Tirmidhi graded as good (ḥasan), apparently indicating that water is before the Throne. The most that can be said in this context is: the truth is with Shaykh al-Islam, and the support of al-Qadi, though he is the helper of religion, is support outside the clear path. So do not turn, may Allah guide you, to one who went at length in that without benefit, and brought a statement that does not resemble the speech of a sensible person, and claimed that this is wisdom, when it is far from wisdom, the knowledge of Allah. Had it not been for falling into futility, we would have quoted it and pointed out what is in it, even though its apparent state indicates its hidden state. Yes, it may be said that al-Baydawi only mentioned that he derived from the verse such and such, and did not claim that there is evidence for that in it. So the objections that arise are directed at the one deriving, not at him. It seems that the one to whom that was directed claimed his approval of deriving the evidence from what he prepared for it in speech. Al-Jubba'i (a Mu'tazili theologian) claimed that in the verse there is an indication that before the creation of the heavens and the earth there was a living, accountable being, because creating the Throne upon the water has no wisdom except that there is in it a kindness (lutf) to an accountable being who can derive evidence from it. ʿAli ibn ʿIsa rejected this, saying that this does not necessarily follow, and that it suffices that the report of it is beneficial to the accountable. Al-Murtada chose this view. The origin of this is the Mu'tazili school (the rationalist school). And Allah, exalted is He, is the one who grants success to what is correct, and to Him is the return and the final destination.

**"That He may test you"**: The lam here is the lam of purpose, used figuratively, and it is connected to "created." That is: He created the heavens and the earth and what is in them of created things, among which you are included. He arranged in them all that you need from the beginnings of your existence and the causes of your livelihood, and placed within their folds what you can use as evidence, through the wonders of crafts and lessons, for your religious objectives, so that He may deal with you as one who tests you.

**"Which of you is best in deed"**: so that He may recompense you according to your deeds. It was said: it is connected to a supposed verb, meaning: I make known by that "that He may test you." It was said: the implied meaning is "and He created you, that He may test you." It was said: in the speech there is an omitted clause, meaning: and His creating them was for benefits whose benefit returns to you in this world and not in the Hereafter, and He did that "that He may test you." All of these, as you see, are far-fetched.

Testing (ibtila') originally means examination, and the speech comes out in the form of a figure of speech and metaphor. It is not valid to intend the literal meaning, for it applies only to one who does not know the outcomes of matters.

It was said: it is a metonymic figure (majāz mursal) for knowledge, because of the mutual connection between knowledge and testing. This requires the strain of intending that He may make manifest the eternal relation of His knowledge. Otherwise, His eternal, essential knowledge is not dependent on anything else. What preceded has no strain in it, and it, along with its eloquence, hits its target. By "deed" is meant what includes the deed of the heart and the deed of the body. This is supported by what Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim in his history, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse, 'that He may test you,' etc. I said: 'What is the meaning of that, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'That He may test you: which of you is best in intellect.' Then he said: 'And the best of you in intellect is the most scrupulous of you regarding the prohibitions of Allah, exalted is He, and the most diligent of you in obedience to Allah, exalted is He.'" However, al-Hafiz al-Suyuti mentioned that its chain is weak.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sufyan that the meaning of "best in deed" is most ascetic regarding the world. From Muqatil: most pious toward Allah, exalted is He. From al-Dahhak: most thankful. Perhaps taking "deed" as inclusive of both matters is preferable. And the best of deeds is that which is the deed of the heart. How not, when the basis of the obligatory bodily worship upon the servants is the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, which settles in the heart. And through it, a servant may be raised in a single day to a degree equal to the deeds of the people of the earth.

In some reports: "Reflecting for an hour is equal to seventy years of worship." Considering the creation of the heavens within what is derived from it is because in the heavens there is what is among the beginnings of reflection, and preparation of the causes of earthly livelihood by which the body is sustained, which is not hidden. Close to this is that the mention of the heavens and their creation is so that they may be the places of the stars and the angels who work in them for the sake of man.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 7 (part 4 of 5):

Some of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) said: That the creation of the earth and what is in it is for the trial (al-ibtila') is evident. As for the creation of the heavens, it is mentioned as a completion (tatmim) and by way of digression (istitrad), although the heavens are the abode of the guarding angels (al-hafazah), the direction of supplication (qiblat al-du'a'), the place of descent of revelation (mahbit al-wahy), and other things which have some bearing on the trial in general. Perhaps what was pointed out first is preferable. The clause of interrogation (jumlat al-istifham) is in the position of the second object of the verb of testing (fi'l al-balwa), according to the well-known view. In al-Kashshaf, the verb here is treated as suspended (mu'allaq) because of what it contains of the meaning of knowledge ('ilm). In Surat al-Mulk, he (al-Zamakhshari) denied calling that "suspension" (ta'liq), claiming that it occurs only when, after the verb, there comes something that stands in place of both objects together, like "I knew which of them did such-and-such" (a'alimtu ayyuhuma fa'ala kadha) and "I knew whether Zayd is departing" (a'alimtu azaydun muntaliqun). There is an apparent inconsistency between his two statements in the two surahs. In al-Kashf, he answered this with what amounts to the following: suspension (al-ta'liq) has two meanings. One is technical (mustalah), and it is transitive with "'an" (from), and this is what is negated in that surah. The other is linguistic (lughawi), and it is transitive with "bi" (with) and "'ala" (upon), and it is specific to the verbs of the heart (af'al al-qalb) without restriction to the seven verbs that take two objects. It occurs only with interrogation specifically, not with what contains the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') or the like. The meaning of suspending a verb on what contains that is that the verb becomes connected to it in meaning and in grammatical function (i'rab), whether this is in words or in position (mahallan), and this is what is affirmed here. Al-Tibi said: It is possible that what is here is on the assumption of an implied knowledge, as if it were said: "to test you" (liyabluwakum), so that He knows (fayalamu) "which of you is best in deed" (ayyukum ahsanu 'amalan), and suspension in this is clear. And what is there (in Surat al-Mulk) is on the basis of the verb including the meaning of knowledge, as if it were said: "so that He may make you know which of you..." etc., and thus the negation is valid. Anyone who consults his words will not fail to notice that there is in them what rejects this. It may be said that suspension is not restricted to verbs that have the meaning of knowledge, as Tha'lab, al-Mubarrad and Ibn Kaysan held, although Uways justified it with what is in Hamm' al-Hawami', and al-Shalubin preferred it. Nor is it restricted to the verb of the heart absolutely; rather, it occurs with it and with what has been attached to it, but only with interrogation. Some have limited what is attached to it to "basar" (to see), "tafakkara" (to reflect), and "sa'ala" (to ask), while Ibn Kharuf added "nazara" (to look), and Ibn 'Usfur agreed with him, and Ibn Malik added "nasiya" (to forget), as in his saying: "Who are you? Indeed we have forgotten who you are." Abu Hayyan disputed with him, saying that "man" (who) may be relative (mawsulah) with an omitted returning pronoun, meaning "who they are, you," and similarly he added other verbs close to the mentioned ones, which have some connection with the verb of the heart, such as the sight verb "tara" (you see) in his saying: "Do you not see what lightning is there?", and "yastanbi'una" (they seek information) in the saying of the Exalted: "And they ask you, 'Is it true?'" and "nabluw" (We test) in what we are discussing. Abu Hayyan disputed with him regarding the first, that "tara" is cognitive ('ilmiyyah), and "ayyukum" in the last is a relative (mawsulah) whose first part of the relative clause has been omitted, so it is built (mabniyyah), and it is an apposition (badal) of a part (badal ba'd) from the pronoun of address. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti reported this from him, but I did not find it in his Bahr. In al-Radi, it is stated that all the senses' verbs are suspended from acting, and in al-Tashil there is something that supports this. Yunus permitted the suspension of every verb other than those mentioned, and on this he construed "Then We shall surely draw out from every faction whichever of them is most violent" (thumma lananza'anna min kulli shi'atin ayyuhum ashaddu). The majority did not agree with him on this. Some of the learned have mentioned that the verb of the heart and what runs in its course is either transitive to one object or to two. The first may be suspended whether it is transitive by itself, like "'arafa" (to know), or by a particle, like "tafakkara," because its object can only be a single word (mufrad). By suspension, its action is nullified in the single word which is its requirement, and it is connected to the clause. Suspension has no meaning except nullifying the action in words, not in position, even if it is transitive to two. Then either the second may be a clause, as in the chapter of "'alima" in the first place. If it may be, it is suspended from the two objects, as in "I knew that Zayd is standing" (a'alimtu lazaydun qa'imun), not from the second, because it would be a clause without suspension, so there is no point in counting it among them, since there is no difference between the suspension particle and its absence. Thus suspension does not nullify the verb's action at all, as in "I knew Zayd, his father is standing" and "I knew Zayd, not his father is standing," for its action in the place of the clause does not differ whether the particle of suspension is present or absent. And if it may not be (a clause), and a word of suspension occurs with it, it is of this kind, like "They ask you what they should spend" (yas'alunaka madha yunfiquna), for what is asked about can only be a single word.

The verb in our case may be operative on what follows it, namely the object of testing (al-mukhtabar bihi), not including knowledge. The verb of testing, when it is so, is transitive to the object of testing by "bi" and can only be a single word, as in the saying of the Exalted: "And We will surely test you with something" (wa-lanabluwannakum bishay'in). Interrogation has nullified its requirement in words, which is suspension. It may be that it includes the meaning of knowledge, and knowledge is operative on it, and its second object is it, and then there is no suspension. From here it becomes clear that the suspension of the verb in the verse is only on the assumption that the verb of testing is operative, and its non-suspension on the assumption that knowledge is operative, so there is no contradiction between the two statements. End of quotation. This is a good distinction. In al-Hamm, the clause after the suspender in the chapter of "'alima" and its sisters is in the position of the two objects. If the suspension is after the first object has been fulfilled, it is in the position of the second object. As for outside this chapter, if the verb is transitive by a preposition, the clause is in the position of an accusative by dropping it, as in "I reflected: is this correct or not" (fakkartu ahadha sahihun am la), and Ibn Malik counted from it "then let him look which of them is purer in food" (fal-yanzur ayyuha azka ta'aman). If it is transitive to one object, it is in its position, as in "I knew which of them is Zayd" ('araftu ayyuhum zaydun). If its object is mentioned, as in "I knew Zayd, who is his father" ('arafta zaydan abu man huwa), then the clause is an apposition (badal) from it according to what al-Sirafi and Ibn Malik chose, and it is an apposition of the whole from the whole with an implied noun (mudaf), that is, "the story of Zayd" or "his matter," according to Ibn 'Usfur. He committed to this so that the replaced noun would be a clause in meaning, and an apposition of inclusion (badal ishtimal). According to Ibn al-Sa'igh, there is no need for estimation. Al-Mubarrad, al-A'lam, Ibn Kharuf and others went to the view that the clause is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial (hal). Al-Farisi went to the view that it is in the position of the second object of "'arafta," with "'arafa" implying the meaning of "'alima," and Abu Hayyan chose it, and in it there is a kind of apparent opposition to what has preceded, which becomes clear on reflection. However, he (al-Zamakhshari) objected to the statement that what follows the verb of testing is the object of testing, on the ground that the object of testing is only the creation of the heavens and the earth. It was answered that this, although it is in itself the thing being tested for, the object of testing is what has been mentioned, except that it was made the object of testing by considering its consequence from that. What is in this is not hidden. Some of the people of verification said, in removing the contradiction: al-Zamakhshari made His saying here, "so that He may test you, which of you is best in deed," as a whole an allegorical metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), so its individual words are used in their literal meanings, given what they deserve. The verb of testing is suspended from the second object, because it cannot be a clause, since it is transitive to it by "bi," and a preposition does not enter upon clauses. Suspension occurred there on the basis that it is appropriate to the verbs of the heart in meaning, and more than one has stated that it operates in that and that it is there used metaphorically for the meaning of knowledge. When a verb is used figuratively for the meaning of another verb, it acts as that verb acts and takes its rulings, and "'alima" is not suspended from the second object, so likewise
page 13
what has its meaning, so he has taken in each of the two positions a varied course, and he often does that in his book. Perhaps he did not reverse the matter because what he did in each is more suitable to what precedes it: the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is in them of blessings and benefits, and the creation of death and life. And it is not hidden that this is close to what was mentioned before, and in it is what is in it.

The use of the superlative form (sighat al-tafdil), which indicates specialness with the two tested ones as best in deed, together with the inclusiveness of the testing to the categories of the responsible (al-mukallafin), and the deeds of the disbelievers among them vary between good legally (hasan shar'i) and evil, not between good and better as in the deeds of the believers, is for encouragement toward the best of excellences and for urging ascent always, because it indicates that the principal aim of the testing is that group, so that He may reward them with the most perfect reward. So it is as if it were said: The aim is that He show your excellence to the most excellent of you, for that is settled, from which no person of understanding deviates. It is permitted that it be of the category of absolute increase (al-ziyadah al-mutlaqah), and that it be of the category of "which of the two groups is better in station" (ayyu al-fariqayni khayrun maqaman). In any case, the address is not specific to the believers, because displaying the state of others is also intended, but not directly in the first way.

﴿And if you say, "Indeed you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is nothing but clear magic."﴾

That is, its like in deception and falsehood. So the construction is from the eloquent simile (al-tashbih al-baligh). The reference is to the mentioned statement. It is permitted that it refer to the Qur'an, as if it were said: If you recited to them from the Qur'an what contains the affirmation of resurrection, they would say, "This recited thing is magic." What is meant is the denial of resurrection by way of allusive metonymy (al-kinayah al-ima'iyyah), because denying resurrection is denying the Qur'an. It was said: The report about their being resurrected, even though it does not answer about its being by way of recited revelation, yet when they hear that, they reach the Qur'an, because its reports about it are in every place, and its being knowledge among them in that, so they make it their aim to deny it. Calling it magic is an excess on their part in obstinacy and an evasion from the path of right guidance. This is contrary to the apparent. It was said: The reference is to resurrection itself. It is objected that naming it magic does not suit it, for magic is only applied to something existing apparently that has no root in reality, while resurrection itself, in their view, is pure nonexistence. In this there is a discussion, since it is possible that they meant by magic the false matter and the thing that has no root or reality, because of its prevalence among them, so that it is like a proper name for it. It is permitted that the reference be to the speaker, and the report about him as magic is for hyperbole. The address in "innakum" (indeed you), if it is to all the responsible, then the relative clause with its relation is for specification, that is, "those of them who disbelieve will surely say." If it is to the disbelievers, then the mention of the relative is so that by it one may reach their condemnation by the title of the relation. The connection of the noble verse to what precedes it is either from the standpoint that resurrection is among the completions of the trial mentioned in it, as if it were said: The matter is as mentioned, and despite that, if you inform them of one unique introduction from its introductions and one singular matter from its completions, they say what they say, let alone that they believe in what has occurred. This is a completion of it. Or from the standpoint that resurrection is a new creation, as if it were said: He is the one who created all created things so that consequences follow from them, and despite that, if you inform them that He, glorified is He, will restore them another time, and that this is easier for Him, they count that as they count it. Glory be to Allah above what they describe.

Al-Hasan? No: 'Isa al-Thaqafi recited "wa-la'in qulta" with a damma on the ta', on the basis that the verb is attributed to Him, Exalted is He, meaning "And if I say that in My Book revealed to you, they who disbelieve will surely say" etc. In al-Bahr it is said that the meaning on that reading is "And if you say," establishing the resurrection after death, since in His saying, Exalted is He: "And He is the One who created" etc., there is an indication of great power, so whenever He informs of a possible event, it occurs without doubt, and He has informed of the resurrection, so its acceptance is obligatory and its occurrence is certain. End of quotation. This, for the sound taste, is like the water of the sea.

Al-A'mash recited "innakum" with a fatha on the hamzah, on the basis of implying the meaning of "dhakarta" (you mentioned) in "qulta," so that "wa-la'in qulta" means "mentioning," "innakum mab'uthuna" (that you will be resurrected), and "anna" with what follows it is in the sense of the object of the verb of mentioning. Some have held that the saying with the meaning of mentioning is metaphorical, and it was objected that mentioning and saying are synonymous, so there is no sense of metaphor then. Since the saying remained in the implication, the address came in accordance with its requirement.

Al-Alusi says: It is also permissible for *anna* to mean *'alla* (perhaps). This is related from Sibawayh, and there is the example * i'ti al-suuqa 'allaka tashtari lahman* (go to the market, perhaps you will buy meat) and *wa annaka tashtari lahman* (and that you will buy meat). The word is used to express the addressee's expectation, but not in the sense of a statement, since they do not expect resurrection. Rather it is in the sense of a command, as if it were said: "Expect your resurrection, and do not categorically deny it." By this, the objection is removed that the Prophet (ﷺ) was certain of the resurrection, so how could he say ﴿لَعَلَّكم مَبْعُوثُونَ﴾ (perhaps you will be resurrected)? Also, the well-known reading is explicit in certainty and affirmation, while this reading is explicit in the opposite, so the two would contradict each other. Some have said: it is possible that this is from the fair speech and gradual leading, for perhaps they will take heed if they reflect, and will be certain of the resurrection if they consider.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (except for *sahirun*, a sorcerer) with the reference to the speaker. There is no emphasis in the statement as there was under this possibility in the reading of the majority. It is also possible that the reference is to the speech or to the Qur'an, and in it there is the same emphasis as in the saying: "the poetry of a poet."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 8:**

﴿And if We defer the punishment from them﴾, i.e., the punishment that follows from their resurrection, or the punishment promised by His words, glorified is He: ﴿But if you turn away, indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾. It has also been said: it is the punishment of the Day of Badr. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Jibril, peace be upon him, killed the mockers, who were five men, who were destroyed before Badr. The apparent meaning is that the intended punishment is one that encompasses the disbelievers. This is supported by what Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, who said: When ﴿The reckoning of people has drawn near for them﴾ was revealed, some people said: "The Hour has indeed drawn near." So they desisted, and the people desisted for a little while, then they returned to their deeds, the evil deeds. So Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾. Then some people of misguidance said: "This is the command of Allah, the Exalted, which has already come." So the people desisted, then they returned to their dregs, the evil dregs. So Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse: ﴿To a limited community﴾, i.e., a portion of days, few in number, because what can be restricted by counting is small.

It has been said that the intended meaning of "ummah" is a group of people, i.e., "And if We defer the punishment from them until a group who recognize one another [in wrongdoing] and among whom there is no believer." This was related from 'Ali ibn 'Isa. And al-Jubba'i said that the meaning is "until a community after these, whom We will charge [with obligations], and they will disobey, so wisdom requires their destruction and the establishment of the Resurrection." The Imamiyyah, who are the house of lies, related from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the intended meaning of "the limited community" is the companions of the Mahdi at the end of time, and they are three hundred and some ten men, equal in number to the people of Badr.

﴿They will surely say: "What holds it back?"﴾, i.e., what prevents it from coming? As though he [the questioner] wants it and something prevents it. They used to say this by way of urging haste, and it is a kinayah (metonymy) for mockery and denial, because if they had believed in it, they would not have sought to hasten it. Their aim was not acknowledging its coming or inquiring about what holds it back, as what follows indicates.

﴿Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them﴾, that punishment, whether the punishment of the Hereafter or of this world, ﴿it will not be averted from them﴾, i.e., no one will ever lift it, nor will any repeller repel it from them; rather it will befall them. The apparent view is that "yawma" (the day) is in the accusative case, governed by "masrufan" (averted), which is the predicate (khabar) of "laysa" (is not). The Basran majority used this to argue for the permissibility of placing the predicate of "laysa" before it, just as it is permissible to place it before its subject (ism) without any significant disagreement, because placing the object (ma'mul) first indicates placing the governing element (amil) first, a fortiori. Otherwise it would follow that the branch (far') is superior to its root (asl). The Kufans and al-Mubarrad held that it is not permissible, and claimed that the verse is not valid as evidence, because the rule referred to is not consistent. Do you not see His words, glorified is He: ﴿So as for the orphan, do not oppress [him]﴾, how the object of the verb is placed first despite the prohibition on placing it first, because the verb cannot come directly after "amma". And it is reported from the Hijazis that they say "ma al-yawma Zaydun dhahiban" (Zayd is not going today), although it is agreed that the predicate of "ma" cannot be placed first. Also, the object here is an adverbial of time (zarf), and the matter concerning it is based on leniency. Yet it has been said that it is related to a verb omitted, indicated by what follows it, and the estimated meaning is: "that the punishment not be averted from them, or that it cling to them on the day it comes to them." Some of them made it related to a verb omitted, "yakhafunahum" (they fear), i.e., "that they do not fear on the day, etc." It has also been said that it is a subject (mubtada') that is not related to "masrufan" nor to an omitted element, and it is built on fatha because it is attached to a clause, and a similar case is His words, glorified is He: ﴿This is a day when the truthful will benefit﴾ according to the fatha reading. You know that there is disagreement among the grammarians about building an adverbial of time that is attached to a clause whose beginning is a definite present-tense verb; and the apparent view is that it is related to "masrufan." Yes, the verse's unsuitability as evidence is beyond doubt. In al-Bahr [al-Bahr al-Muhit] it is written: I have traced a number of the Arabs' collections and did not find the predicate of "laysa" placed before it, nor its object placed first, except what the apparent meaning of this noble verse indicates, and the poet's words:

*He refuses, and he only grows more stubborn; and I was one who refused base things, I would not advance into them.*

﴿And there descended upon them﴾, i.e., came down and encompassed them. Its origin is "haqqa," so it is like "zalla and zala" and "dhamma and dhama," and the intended meaning is "yahiqu bihim" (it will befall them).

﴿That at which they used to mock﴾.

Except that he expressed it in the past tense to affirm that it will certainly occur. The intended referent of the relative pronoun is the punishment, and it was expressed in this way to magnify its status, and to indicate that the cause of the descent of what is in the relative clause is their mockery of it, its descent and its encompassing them. And the mockery is placed in the position of hastening, because it was mockery.

[Page 15]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 9:

﴿And if We let man taste mercy from Us﴾ i.e., We bestow upon him a blessing of health, security, wealth, and other things, and We make it reach him in such a way that he finds its pleasure; so "letting him taste" is a metaphor for this bestowing. ﴿Then We withdraw it from him﴾ i.e., We strip him of that mercy. ﴿From him﴾ is the complement of "withdraw," and the expression with it (min, "from") serves to indicate how strongly he is attached to it and how eager he is for it. ﴿Indeed, he is despairing﴾ (ya'us), intensely despairing, much given to it, cutting off his hope of the return of such a blessing, sooner or later, by the grace of Allah the Exalted, because of his lack of patience and his lack of reliance upon Him, glorified is He, and his lack of trust in Him. ﴿Ungrateful﴾ (kafur), greatly ungrateful for the blessings that Allah the Exalted bestowed upon him in the past. The placing of this attribute after the attribute of his despair is for the sake of the rhyme (ri'ayat al-fawasil), and also because despair is itself a form of ingratitude for the past blessing.

﴿And if We let him taste favour﴾ such as health, security and prosperity ﴿after adversity had touched him﴾ such as sickness, fear and poverty. The attribution of the tasting (*idhaqa*) to Him, the Exalted, rather than the touching (*mass*), indicates that the tasting of blessing is intended in its own right, whereas the touching of harm is intended only incidentally. For this reason some have said that the *min* in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿*minhu*﴾ (from Him), should be taken as causal, meaning: We removed it because of his wickedness, his evil conduct and his ugly deeds, so that it would come from Us. And *minhu* indicates this meaning and corresponds to it, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾. There is no concealing that interpreting *minhu* in this way is contrary to the apparent and immediate meaning, and there is no necessity compelling it. The transformation of blessing into hardship and the reverse were not expressed in the same pattern; rather, the expression differs between them. In the first, the beginning is with the bestowal of blessing and the conveying of mercy, whereas in the second the conveying of harm is not begun in the same manner. This alerts to the precedence of mercy over wrath and expresses concern for it. In expressing the contact of mercy and blessing by *dhawq* (tasting), which, it has been said, signals their pleasantness and that they are desirable, and in expressing the contact of adversity by *mass* (touching), which indicates that it is at the lowest level of what is called encounter, there is a gentleness that is not hidden, and perhaps this strengthens the great standing of mercy.

Some have mentioned that in the wording of *idhaqa* (tasting) and *mass* (touching), based on the principle that *dhawq* is what one tests tastes with, and *mass* is the first reaching, there is an alert that what a person finds in this world of gifts and trials is a model of what he will find in the Hereafter, and that he falls into ingratitude and insolence at the slightest thing. ﴿He will surely say, "The evils have gone away from me"﴾, i.e., the calamities that troubled me, and similar ones will not befall me again. ﴿Indeed, he is exultant﴾
[Page 16]
boastful and deceived by it. Its origin is *fariḥ*, but it was changed to what you see for emphasis (*mubalagha*). In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) it is stated that *faʿil* with a kasra on the ʿayn is the regular form of the active participle (*ism al-fa'il*) from an intransitive verb (*fi'l lazim*). It has been read as *faraḥa* with a damma on the rāʾ, as you say *nadusa* and *nataṣa*. The word *fariḥ* occurs in the Qur'an mostly in a dispraising sense; when praise is intended, it is qualified, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾. ﴿Boastful﴾: magnifying himself over people because of the blessings he has been given, preoccupied with that and thereby distracted from fulfilling their due. The *lam* in *la'in* (if indeed) in the four verses is a preparatory *lam* (*lam al-muwatta'a lil-qasam*) introducing an oath, and its answer takes the place of the answer of the conditional, as in the verse:

"If ʿAbd al-ʿAziz returns to me with the like of it, and enables me to get it, then I will not relinquish it."

[p. 17]

**"Except those who are patient"** is an exception (*istithna'*) from "man." It is a connected exception (*muttasil*) if the *alif-lam* in *al-insan* denotes the comprehensiveness of the genus (*istighraq al-jins*). This is the view that al-Tabarsi transmitted from al-Farra', contrary to Ibn al-Khazin. It is a disconnected exception (*munqati'*) if the *alif-lam* is for a specific reference (*al-'ahd*), indicating the disbelieving human in general. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the intended person is a specific disbeliever, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. It was also said that he is 'Abdullah ibn Umayya al-Makhzumi, which al-Wahidi mentioned. The disconnected reading is connected under both reports. Some attributed the unrestricted version to al-Zajjaj and al-Akhfash. In any case, what is meant is those who were patient over the hardships that afflicted them, whether before or after, out of faith in Allah, the Exalted, and submission to His decree, may He be exalted.

**"And did righteous deeds"**: as gratitude for His blessings, glorified is He, both past and future. The author of *al-Kashf* (al-Tibi) said: Since despair includes the absence of patience and ingratitude includes the absence of thankfulness, the exception from that is its opposite, from among those characterised by patience and thankfulness. When it is said "except those who..." and so on, it is as if it said "except those who are patient and thankful," and these are the attributes of the believer. Therefore he referred to them by these two as a metonymy (*kinaya*) for him. This is why al-Zamakhshari interpreted it as "except those who believed," since their custom, when mercy reaches them, is to give thanks, and when a blessing is removed from them, to be patient. Hence it is fitting to refer to this by a metonymy for faith. Then he (al-Tibi) took a dig at his teacher al-Tibi (sic) with the words: As for the indication of "were patient" that righteous deeds are thankfulness, because it has been reported in a narration: "Faith is two halves: half patience and half thankfulness," and the indication of "did" that patience is faith, because these two are typically joined, it does not fit what we are discussing, unless another aspect is intended, as if it were said: "except the righteous believer who is patient and thankful." This is one aspect, but the matter is as Hidham said, because the metonymy conveys that meaning along with its beauty and emphasis.

**"Those"** is a reference to the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*), in view of its being characterised by what is in the scope of the relative clause, and it carries the sense of distance, as has been mentioned more than once. That is, those described by these praiseworthy attributes.

**"For them is forgiveness"**, a great forgiveness, for their sins, whatever they were. **"And a reward"**, a recompense for their good deeds, **"great"**. It is described as such because of the everlasting bliss it contains, the lifting of obligations, security from punishment, Allah's pleasure with them, and looking upon His noble Face in a Garden whose breadth is the heavens and the earth.

As for the connection of the three verses with what precedes them, according to al-Bahr: when He mentioned that the punishment of the disbelievers, though delayed, must certainly befall them, He mentioned what indicates their disbelief and that they deserve punishment, because of their being disposed to ingratitude for Allah's blessings, and what follows from His goodness to them that is not befitting for them, such as insolence and boasting. It was said: This indicates that the aspect is that the verses include the reason for the befalling (*al-hayq*), and this is weakened by the fact that its reason was given earlier by what is in the scope of the relative clause. Some chose that it is sharing in blame, so what the verses contain before the explanation of some of their faults, and what these verses contain is the explanation of another part.

Some of the researchers (*muhaqqiqin*) said: The aspect of connection is that the tasting of blessing and the touching of hardship is a segment of the category of trial, and it falls in the position of detail to the general statement in His words: "that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed" (Q. 11:7). The meaning is that each of the tasting of blessing and its removal, while being a trial for the human, whether he will give thanks or disbelieve, he does not follow the path of right guidance, but deviates in both states from it into the abysses of misguidance. Therefore no good deed appears from him except from the patient righteous. Or, in terms of the fact that their denial of resurrection and their mockery of punishment are due to their insolence and boasting, it is as if it were said: They did what they did because human nature is disposed to that. The end of the quote. The weakness of the first is not hidden. The second is closer. And Allah knows best.

* * *

(And among the allusive (*ishari*) interpretations of the verses: **"Alif. Lam. Ra."** An indication of what has already been indicated. **"Its verses have been made firm"**, that is, its realities and essences in the universal world, so they do not change or alter. **"Then they have been detailed"** in the particular world and made clear and specified by a known measure. **"From One Wise, Aware"**: therefore they were made firm, and therefore they were detailed. It may also be said: The indication is to the verses of the Qur'an, which have been made firm in the hearts of the knowers, **"then detailed"**, their rulings upon the bodies of those who act. It was also said: **"made firm"** through the miracles, **"then detailed"** through the clear proofs. **"That you worship none but Allah"**, that is, that you do not associate anything in His worship, glorified is He, and devote worship exclusively to Him, mighty and majestic. **"Indeed I am a warner to you from Him"** of the punishment of shirk and its consequence, **"and a bringer of good news"** of the reward of monotheism and its benefit. It was also said: **"warner"** of the mighty things of His subjugation, **"and a bringer of good news"** of the subtle things of His union. **"And that you seek forgiveness from your Lord"**, ask Him, glorified is He, to cover you from looking at others, even your own actions and attributes. **"Then turn to Him"**, return by annihilation of the self in essence. It was also said: **"Seek forgiveness from your Lord"** from claims, and **"turn to Him"** from blameworthy passing thoughts. **"He will give you good enjoyment"** by granting you success in following the Law during the state of subsistence after annihilation. It is said: The good enjoyment is the purity of states, the brilliance of remembrances, the sweetness of thoughts, the manifestation of realities, the appearance of subtleties, joy in the good pleasure of Allah, the Exalted, and the pleasure of life by witnessing His lights, glorified is He. The complete enjoyment is the beloved witnessing his Beloved. How well has one said:

*My wish from this world is your meeting once; if I attain it, I have fulfilled every wish.*

**"Until a specified term"**, which is the time of your death. **"And He will give every person of merit"** through striving, effort, and sacrificing the self, **"his merit"** in ranks and nearness to Him, glorified is He. It is also said: **"He gives every person of merit"** in readiness, **"his merit"** in perfection. Abu 'Uthman was asked about the meaning of that and he said: He fulfils the hopes of one who thinks well of Him. **"But if you turn away"**, that is, you turn away from obeying the command and prohibition, **"then I fear for you the punishment of a great day"**, which is the day of return to Allah, the Exalted, on which the powerlessness of all else than Him becomes manifest, and the ugliness of disobeying what He commanded and the monstrousness of committing what He forbade become clear.

**"Behold, they fold their breasts"**, bending their chests over the blameworthy attributes within them, **"to hide from Him"**, the Exalted. This is due to their great ignorance of what is permissible for Him and what is not, glorified is His majesty. **"Even when they cover themselves with their garments, He knows what they conceal and what they reveal"** of sayings, actions, and all states. It was said: **"what they conceal"** of passing thoughts, **"and what they reveal"** of glances. It was said: **"what they conceal"** in their hearts, **"and what they reveal"** with their mouths. It was said: **"what they conceal"** at night, **"and what they reveal"** by day. The generalisation is preferable. Some people made the pronoun in "from Him" refer to the Messenger (ﷺ). You know that this is far off, since it is evident that the pronoun in "He knows" refers to Him, the Exalted. However, it has been mentioned in the secrets of the Qur'an that He, the Exalted, clothed the hearts of the truthful with the lights of His majesty, so they see with the eyes of their hearts what passes in the breasts of creatures of hidden things and passing thoughts, just as they see outward appearances with their outward eyes. It has come: "Beware of the discernment of the believer, for he looks with the light of Allah, the Exalted." On this basis, the pronoun in "He knows" may refer to the Messenger, peace be upon him. In any case, the verse was revealed concerning non-believers, as the outward meaning requires. It has already been stated to you that the matter, according to what was related from the scholar al-Habr, may Allah be pleased with him, is problematic.

Some of the people of spiritual taste said: According to this, the verse is an indication that those people did not reach the station of unification and did not realise the highest levels of monotheism. There is also obscurity in this, so reflect.

**"And there is no creature on earth but that its provision is upon Allah"**, that is, what it feeds upon, in body and in spirit. It is said: For each there is a provision upon Him, the Exalted, according to its capacity. So the provision of the outward is for bodies, the provision of witnessing is for spirits, the provision of union is for the secrets; the provision of awe is for the souls, the provision of longing is for the intellects, the provision of nearness is for the hearts. This is with regard to the human. As for the other animals, they also have a sensible provision and an intelligible provision, which Allah, the Exalted, knows. **"And He knows its place of rest and its place of storage."** The resting place of all is the loins of non-existence, and their storage is the wombs of coming into being. **"And He it is who created the heavens and the earth"** and what is in each **"in six days, and His throne was upon the water"**, that is, He was living and self-subsisting, as Ibn al-Kamal said.

It was said: The water is an indication of the hylic (*hayulaniyya*) prime matter. The meaning is: **"And His throne was"** before the creation of the heavens and the earth in essence, not in time, exalted above the matter, above it in rank. It was said: other than that. If you wish to apply it to the details of your own existence, the meaning, as it has been said, is: He created the heavens of the spiritual faculties and the earth of the body in the six months which are the least period of pregnancy, and His throne, which is the heart of the believer, was upon the water of the matter of the body, dominating over it, attached to it with the attachment of shaping and governing. **"That He may test you as to which of you is best in deed."** It was said: He made the goal of creation the manifestation of deeds, that is, We created that so that We may know the detailed knowledge which follows existence, upon which reward is based. **"Which of you is best in deed."**

**"And if We let man taste mercy from Us..."** and so on. The indication includes that it is fitting for the servant to be, in both ease and hardship, confident in his Lord, the Exalted, reliant upon Him, not veiled from Him by seeing the means, lest despair, ingratitude, insolence, and boasting over that come upon him, whether in existence or non-existence. If He grants him mercy, he thanks Him, first by seeing that it is from Him, glorified is He, with his heart; second, by using his limbs in what pleases Him and in acts of obedience and fulfilling His rights in them; and third, by letting his tongue speak praise and thanksgiving to Allah, the Exalted. By this, the thanks referred to in His words is realised: **"And few of My servants are truly thankful"** (Q. 34:13). To this, one has alluded who said:

*Blessings have benefited you from me in three ways: my hand, my tongue, and the hidden heart.*

By thanks, blessings increase, as the Exalted said: **"If you give thanks, I will surely increase you"** (Q. 14:7). It is reported from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face: When the extremities of blessings reach you, do not repel their furthest reaches by little thanks. Then, if He takes it away from him, let him be patient and not accuse Allah, the Exalted, of anything, for He, the Exalted, is most kind, most merciful to the servant, and most aware of his interest and most knowing. Then, if He restores it to him, he should not be insolent, deceived, or boastful over people because of it, for deception and boasting over what one does not own is a great ignorance. He, glorified is He, has indicated that among the dispositions of man is despair and ingratitude in hardship after mercy, and joy and boasting in prosperity after adversity.

**"Except those who are patient"** with Allah, the Exalted, in states of prosperity and hardship, in hardship and ease. Poverty and wealth, for example, are to them two mounts; they do not care which of them they ride. **"And did righteous deeds"**, whatever is good for them in all their states. **"For them is forgiveness"** for the sins of the self's self-assertion through despair, ingratitude, joy, and boasting. **"And a great reward"** from the reward of the manifestations of the attributes and actions and their gardens. And Allah, the Exalted, is the Protector of success.)

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 12:**

﴿So perhaps you are abandoning some of what is revealed to you﴾. That is, you abandon conveying some of what is revealed to you, namely what contradicts the opinion of the polytheists, out of fear of their rejection and their mockery of it. So the active participle (ism al-fa'il, the active participle) refers to the future, which is why it governs its object. And "perhaps" (la'alla) expresses hope (tarajji), which implies expectation (tawaqquu'). It does not follow that what is expected occurs, nor that its occurrence is more likely, since something that prevents it may exist. Therefore it is not objectionable that the expectation of abandoning the conveyance on his part (ﷺ) is something unbecoming to the station of prophethood, because what prevents it in him, peace and blessings be upon him, is his infallibility (ismah), like all the noble messengers, peace be upon them, against concealing the revelation that he was commanded to convey, betraying it, or abandoning it out of dissimulation (taqiyya, concealing one's true position out of fear). The purpose of such a statement is to incite him (ﷺ) and stir his motivation to fulfil the message. The same is said of every expectation similar to this one. It has been said: expectation sometimes belongs to the speaker, which is the original usage,
[p. 19]
because the performative meanings (al-ma'ani al-insha'iyya) subsist in him. Sometimes it belongs to the addressee, and sometimes to someone else connected to and associated with him. It is possible that the last of these is intended here, and the expectation is attributed to the disbelievers. The meaning would be that, since your effort in conveying to them what has been revealed to you has reached its limit, they expect from you that you will abandon the conveyance of part of it. It has also been said that "perhaps" (la'alla) here is not for hope but for distancing (tab'id), and it may be used in that sense, as the Arabs say: "Perhaps you will do such-and-such," to someone who cannot do it. So the meaning is: do not abandon. It has also been said that it is for rhetorical interrogation (al-istifham al-inkari), as in the hadith: "Perhaps we have hastened you?" Al-Samin and others preferred that it is for hope relative to the addressee, as you have just come to know. It is not permissible that the meaning be: "It is as if I see you will abandon some of what has been revealed to you, that which is burdensome to you, by My permission and revelation from Me, namely that He grants you dispensation regarding it, like ordering one person to confront ten, when they were commanded to confront one against two, and other such relaxations." For although this removes the difficulty, the statement of the Exalted after "they say" refutes it. Yes, it has been said: if what is meant is abandoning argument with the Qur'an in favour of combat, striking and spearing, it would be valid, because this surah is Meccan and was revealed before the command to fight. But in al-Kashshaf, after the statement "Know that," it says: if you reflect carefully, it will become clear to you that the foundation of this noble surah is the guidance of His Majesty, the Exalted, to His Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, regarding the manner of calling (to Islam) from its opening to its close, and regarding what befalls one who undertakes this lofty rank of hardships, and his endurance of what results from it in both abodes of rewards. It is not about consoling him, peace and blessings be upon him, for that does not fit the context. Consider the comprehensive conclusion, I mean His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And to Him the whole matter is returned, so worship Him and put your trust in Him﴾, and you will find it wondrous, and it distances this intention if we say that this is of the category of dispensation indicating consolation. So reflect upon it. The pronoun in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and distressed by it﴾ refers to "what is revealed," or to "part of it," and this is the apparent meaning according to Abu Hayyan. It has been said it refers to "the conveyance," or to "the denial." It has also been said it is ambiguous and is explained by "they say." The "wa" (and) is for coordination. ﴿and distressed﴾: it has been said it is coordinated with ﴿abandoning﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿your breast﴾ is its subject (fa'il). It is also permitted that the descriptive word be a predicate placed first, with "your breast" as the subject, and the sentence coordinated with ﴿abandoning﴾. It has been said that the "wa" must be for the circumstantial clause (hal), and the sentence after it is circumstantial, because this is an actual occurrence, not an anticipated one, so coordination is not valid. This has been criticised: if the constriction of his breast, peace and blessings be upon him, is taken in its apparent sense, it does not actually occur. Rather his noble breast is constricted by the hardships that befall him in conveying. The speaker deviated from the constriction of the attributive adjective (sifa mushabbaha, the adjective of resemblance denoting a stable quality) to "distressed" (ism al-fa'il) in order to show that constriction is something that befalls him, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, at times. Likewise, every sifa mushabbaha, when it is intended to denote occurrence, is changed into the active participle form, so one says of sayyid (lord), jawad (generous) and samin (fat) for example: sa'id, ja'id and sami (ones who become so). Upon this is the verse of a certain thief describing the prison and those imprisoned in it:

*In an abode where the base man grows fat, while the noble folk's pallor is plainly visible.*

The apparent meaning of the words of al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan) is that this is a regular pattern: every triliteral form built to denote stability and permanence, not in the pattern fa'il, is returned to it if the meaning of occurrence is intended, without needing to rely on transmitted usage. It has been said that the change is for the sake of agreement with "tarik" (abandoning), but this is not the case.

﴿lest they say: "Why has a treasure not been sent down to him?"﴾ That is, a large amount of wealth. They expressed it with "sent down" rather than "given," because their purpose was to challenge by the claim that this would be contrary to habit, since treasures are found in the earth and do not descend from the sky. It is possible that by "sending down" they meant giving without a customary cause, as the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) indicates: i.e., "Why has that not been given to him, so that his truthfulness would be established for us?"

﴿or an angel came with him﴾ to confirm him, so that we might confirm him. It is narrated that they said: "Make for us the mountains of Makkah into gold, or bring us angels who will bear witness to your prophethood, if you are a messenger," and so this was revealed. It is also narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that each of the two statements was made by a group.
[p. 20]
Then he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "I am not able to do that," and so this was revealed. It has been said the one who said each of them was Abdullah ibn Umayya al-Makhzumi. The way of reconciling this is known from what has passed more than once. The position of "that they say" is in the accusative or genitive. The original would be "out of dislike" or "out of fear" that they say, or "lest," or "because of" that they say. Because the statement occurred, they said: the imperfect verb is in the sense of the past, and the "an" (that) which is a verbal-source particle (masdariyya) is outside its normal requirement. They preferred the assumption of "dislike" over "fear" for this reason. It may also be intended, when assuming "fear," the fear that they would repeat this statement. Some chose that the meaning, in all of these, is "that they say something like their saying: 'Why has...' etc.," so that "an" remains in its normal function. Nothing objectionable arises.

﴿You are only a warner﴾: that is, nothing is incumbent upon you except warning with what has been revealed, without concern for what comes from them.

﴿And Allah is Guardian over all things﴾: that is, He is its sustainer and preserver, so He preserves your states and theirs. So put your trust in Him in all your affairs, for He will deal with them in a manner befitting their condition. Limiting the matter to the warner reaches the extreme of hitting the mark. It has been said this verse is abrogated, and it has been said it is muhkam (not abrogated).

The passage opens with *am* used as a disjunctive particle (*am al-munqati'ah*, "the disjunctive *am*"), which marks a change of subject. It shifts from the mention of their disregard for what is revealed, and their not being satisfied with its manifest miracles that testify to the truth of the claim, to the mention of something worse and greater that they commit. It is to be estimated as *bal* ("rather"), with the interrogative hamzah of denial, meaning: "Rather, do they say...?" Ibn al-Qushayri held that *am* is conjunctive, and the estimate is: "Are they content with what We have revealed to you, or do they say that it is not from God?" The first view is more apparent. Either way, the pronoun in (*iftarahu*, "he has fabricated it") refers to what has been revealed. Say (to them): if the matter is as you claim, ﴿then bring﴾ you also ﴿ten surahs like it﴾ in eloquence and excellence of composition. The word (*mithlihi*, "like it") is an adjective to (*suwar*, "surahs"). The apparent expectation would be that it agree with its noun in the plural, but it is used in the singular because the intention is the likeness of each one of them, not the likeness of the whole collection.

It has been said that (*mithl*, "like"), although singular, may or may not agree in number, so it may be applied to one or to many. It is treated as a verbal noun in origin, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Shall we believe in two humans like ourselves?﴾ It may also agree, as in His words: ﴿then they will not be the like of you﴾. It has also been said that here it is an adjective of a singular noun understood, meaning "the measure of ten surahs like it." It has also been said that it describes the ten as a whole, since they are speech and one single thing. Moreover, (*ʿashr*, "ten") is not in the form of a plural, so it is given the ruling of the singular, as in ﴿palm trees uprooted﴾.

His words ﴿fabricated﴾ (*muftarayat*) are another adjective of (*suwar*, "surahs"). It has been said that it is placed after the adjective of likeness to what is revealed, because that is the adjective that is the intended object of the challenge, since by it they are left unable to produce a counterpart. As for the adjective of fabrication, no purpose depends on it within the context of the challenge. It was mentioned in the manner of leniency and giving rein. Also, if the order were reversed, it might be thought that the intention was likeness to it in fabrication. The meaning is: ﴿bring ten surahs﴾ like it in eloquence, ﴿fabricated﴾ by yourselves, supposing that I fabricated it from my own self. For you are Arabs, eloquent and articulate, and the foundations of this are in you through practice of sermons and poetry, engaging with the methods of verse and prose, and the preservation of events and days, most completely.

Most scholars hold that this challenge occurred first, and when they were unable to meet it, He challenged them with ﴿a surah like it﴾, as the surah of al-Baqarah and Yunus speak of. Although this is later in recitation, it is earlier in revelation. It is not permissible to reverse this, since there is no sense in challenging with ten for one who has been unable to meet a challenge with one. Nor is it intended that they be made unable to produce ten surahs like ten specific ones from the Qur'an.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that the intended meaning is this, and he took the ten to be the surahs that had preceded this one up to this point. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that most of what he mentioned is Madani, whereas this surah, as far as I know, is Meccan. How then could a reference in Mecca be to what had not yet been revealed? He then said: "Perhaps this is not authentically attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both." Ibn ʿAtiyya held that this challenge occurred only after the challenge with a surah. This was also related from al-Mubarrad, who denied that this surah was revealed before those two surahs, and said: "Rather, the surah of Yunus was revealed first, then the surah of Hud was revealed."

Ibn al-Durays has transmitted this in his Fada'il al-Qur'an from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both.
