The reasoning behind it is that what occurred first was the challenge with a surah like it in eloquence, and including what it includes of reports of unseen matters, rulings and their like. When they were unable to do that, He commanded them to bring ten surahs like it in composition, even if they did not contain what it contains. Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, weakened this and said: it does not hold in every surah of the Qur'an. Suppose that the surah was earlier in revelation; yet since it was revealed in stages, it is possible that that verse came later than this one, and the earlier revelation of one surah over another does not contradict this. End of quote.

Al-Shihab commented on this, saying: his words "it does not hold" are without basis, because al-Mubarrad's intention was that it includes something of the seven types, and no part of the Qur'an is free of them. The claim that the revelation of that verse was later is contrary to the apparent sense, and such a thing is not said by opinion. He claimed that the truth is what al-Mubarrad said: that he, peace be upon him, first challenged them with a surah like it in composition and meaning, and then it was revealed, and he challenged them with ten surahs like it in composition, without restriction on meaning. The description of them as "fabricated" supports this. Some scholars supported al-Mubarrad's view by saying that the obligation in the verse of al-Baqarah was due to doubt, and only knowledge that they could not produce a complete likeness removes doubt. In this verse, the obligation is only due to their saying "he has fabricated it," so they were charged with something similar to what they had said. However, in the surah of Yunus, the matter is like the matter here, preceded by a report of their claim of fabrication, may God fight them. Moreover, they were charged only with something like what they were charged with in the verse of al-Baqarah. Furthermore, in his words "and doubt is not removed," etc., there is a clear objection.

Al-Allamah al-Tibi has a discourse here, which he claimed is what the context requires, but despite its little benefit, it has no basis for what he built upon it, as the author of al-Kashshaf made clear.

Moreover, al-Imam (al-Razi) reported that this verse has been cited as evidence that the inimitability of the Qur'an lies in its eloquence, not in its inclusion of unseen matters and the abundance of its sciences. For if it were so, His words "fabricated" would have no meaning. But if the aspect of inimitability is eloquence, then it is correct, because the eloquence of speech appears whether it is true or false. Al-Fadil al-Jalabi objected to this with a point based on neglect of the meaning of fabrication and invention. Yes, what was mentioned only indicates that it is correct that the aspect of inimitability is that, and it does not preclude the possibility that it is the unusual style, and its freedom from contradiction, as has been said.

﴿And call upon whomever you can﴾, meaning: seek help from whoever you are able to seek help from among your gods, which you claim provide you aid in everything you do and everything you leave, and the soothsayers to whose opinions you resort in calamities, so that they may bring you happiness in that matter.

﴿Other than God﴾ is connected to (*ud'u*, "call upon"), meaning: going beyond God, the Exalted. In it, according to what many have said, is an indication that no one can produce its like except God, mighty and majestic. ﴿If you are truthful﴾ in saying that I fabricated it, for that requires producing its like, and that in turn requires your capability to do so. The answer to (*in*, "if") is omitted, and what was mentioned before it indicates it.

﴿Then if they do not answer you﴾. The address here, according to what is narrated from al-Dahhak, is to those commanded to call upon whomever they can. The plural pronoun of the absent party refers back to "whom" (man), meaning: if those whom you call upon besides God, the Exalted, do not respond to you by assisting you and supporting you in opposing this (Qur'an), since they know their incapacity to do so and that their power falls too short to reach it. ﴿Then know that it was sent down with the knowledge of God﴾. That is, it was sent down only while being joined to His knowledge, the Exalted, and not to the knowledge of anyone else, as the word "that" (annama) requires, for it conveys restriction (hasr), like the kasra form (inna) according to the correct view. It is said that this is the meaning of the statement of the one who said: that is, joined with what none knows except God, the Exalted, and none besides Him is able to do.

Some have claimed that restriction is conveyed by the construction of annexation (idafa), as in the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿He does not reveal His unseen to anyone﴾, and that what is meant by "what none knows except Him, the Exalted" is the modalities and the distinctive features by which the inimitability (i'jaz, the miraculous unmatchability of the Qur'an) and the challenge (tahaddi, the divine challenge to produce its like) are established. He mentioned that none besides Him, glory be to Him, is able, as the context requires. Otherwise, what is mentioned in the noble structure is knowledge, not power. It was also said: that is because the negation of knowledge of a thing entails the negation of power over it, since no one can have power over what he does not know. The conditional clause falls within the scope of the saying. The use of the word of doubt (in the phrase "if") together with certainty about their non-response from the side of those they call upon is a mockery of them and a recording against them of the complete foolishness of their reason. The ordering of the command to know upon the mere fact of non-response is because it is preceded by the calling, which was preceded by their being rendered incapable and compelled. It is as if it were said: if they do not answer you when you turn to them after you have been compelled to that and your stratagems have failed and your excuses have been exhausted, then know, etc. Or it is because those whom they call upon to oppose this are, in their belief, stronger than them. So when their incapacity becomes manifest through their non-response, and even if that is before the manifestation of your own incapacity, their incapacity becomes more evident and clearer.

From the totality of what we have mentioned, it becomes clear that there is no difficulty in the verse. Among the things that cause wonder is the statement of Izz ibn Abd al-Salam in his Amali: "The ordering of this conditional, meaning the knowledge, upon that condition, meaning the non-response, is problematic; and likewise the saying of the Glorified: ﴿was sent down with the knowledge of God﴾ is also problematic, since the preposition (ba') cannot be causal, because knowledge is not the cause of its descent, nor can it be for accompaniment, since knowledge does not accompany its descent." He said that the answer is that what is meant by knowledge is only our knowledge, and it is attributed to Him, Mighty and Majestic, because it is created by Him, the Exalted. A parallel to this is what is in the saying of the Majestic, the Most High: ﴿nor do we conceal the testimony of God﴾, where testimony is attributed to God, the Glorified, in consideration that He, the Exalted, has legislated it. The Qur'an has descended with the proofs of the knowledge of the rulings of God, blessed is His name, so the signified is expressed by the signifier. The estimated sense is: ﴿then know that it was sent down﴾ accompanied by the spread of the knowledge of the rulings, which are the proofs. There is no doubt that it is fitting, when they are incapable of opposing it, that they should know that these verses are the proofs of the rulings of God, the Exalted. End of quotation. Would that I knew how this skilled scholar overlooked that clear exegesis! Perhaps, as it has been said: "from the intensity of manifestness comes concealment." ﴿And that there is no god but Him﴾. That is: know also that He, the Exalted, is the one exclusively entitled to divinity and its rulings, and that your gods are far removed from any rank of partnership with Him, the Exalted, in that.

﴿Will you then submit?﴾ That is: will you enter into Islam once no trace of doubt remains concerning its truth and the falsehood of the polytheism you are upon? This includes acceptance, first and foremost, that the Qur'an is from God, the Exalted; or it means: you will be submitters to the truth, which is that the Qur'an is from God, the Exalted, and you will abandon what you are upon of obstinacy and stubborn opposition. In the interrogative there is an emphatic command, because it carries the sense of request and an alert to the existence of the obligating cause and the removal of the impediment; for this reason the particle fa' (then) was brought. In the expression "submitting" (muslimun) rather than "you will submit" (tuslimun), there is confirmation of what the ordering of what was mentioned upon what precedes it requires, namely its obligation without delay. It was said: in that also is a despairing of them, that their gods could protect them from the punishment of God, exalted is His majesty and mighty is His authority. It is permissible that the pronoun in "for you" (lakum) refers to the Messenger, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. What supports this is that it came in another verse: ﴿if they do not answer you﴾ (Q 28:50). This is also narrated from Mujahid. The fitting form for the imperative "say" (qul) would have been the singular, but it was put in the plural for honor, and this is not restricted to the first-person pronoun, as al-Radi said. Among this is the verse: "And if you wish, women are forbidden other than you."

This sentence is not within the scope of the saying but is from God, the Exalted, as a judgment upon their incapacity, like the saying of the Glorified: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it﴾ (Q 2:24). He expressed it with "answering" as a hint that he, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, is in complete security concerning his affair, as if his command to them to produce its like is a call to them toward a matter he wants to occur. It is permissible that the pronoun refers to him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and to the believers, because they are followers of him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, in the command to the challenge. In this is a subtle indication that their duty is not to separate from him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and to stand with him in opposing the obstinate, as they used to do in jihad; and it is guidance that this is among the things that establish firmness in faith, and for this reason the consequence mentioned is placed upon it.

The knowledge commanded is that which is in the highest rank, as if the other degrees of knowledge were not knowledge at all. But this is not to indicate the lowliness of those degrees, rather the elevation of this rank. From this is known the secret of using the word of doubt together with certainty of non-response, for placing all the other degrees in the position of nonexistence entails placing the certainty of non-response in the position of doubt. It is permissible that the commanded matter is continuing upon what they are upon of knowledge. The meaning of "submitting" (muslimun) is sincere in Islam, or steadfast upon it. The discourse is of the category of strengthening and elevating toward the stations of certainty. Al-Jubba'i and others chose this interpretation of the verse, and Shaykh al-Islam mentioned that it is more fitting with what preceded of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and your breast is constricted by it﴾, and with what will come, God willing, of His saying, the Glorified: ﴿So do not be in doubt about it﴾ (Q 11:17), and more fitting with what follows it. It may also be supported by what we have pointed to, but it is not hidden that the discourse according to the first interpretation is consistent with what precedes it, because the plural pronoun in the earlier verse is for the disbelievers, and the pronoun in this one is a plural pronoun, so let it be for them as well; and because the disbelievers are the nearest of those mentioned, so returning the pronoun to them is more preferable; and because the second interpretation involves interpretations (ta'wilat) that are not needed in the first.

From here Abu Hayyan preferred it, and al-Zamakhshari approved it. Perhaps its supports are stronger than the supports of the latter, for whoever reflects; therefore we have placed it first. Even if it is said: when the exegesis comes from Mujahid, that is sufficient for you. And the word "alif-lam-mim" is written in the Mushaf, according to what al-Ajhuri said, without a nun. Zayd ibn Ali, may God be pleased with both of them, read "nazzala" (He sent down) with a fatha on the nun and the zay and with its doubling. In al-Bahr it is said that "ma" may be a verbal-masdar (meaning "that the sending down"), or a relative pronoun in the sense of "that which" (alladhi), meaning "that He who sent it down." The deletion of the object-referring pronoun in a construction like the one mentioned is common. The subject of "nazzala" is His pronoun, the Exalted. Some permitted that "ma" be a relative pronoun according to the reading of the majority as well, but that is unlikely by what is known in such constructions, that it is a relative pronoun; so understand.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 15:

﴿Whoever desires﴾ i.e., by their good deeds, outwardly, ﴿the life of this world and its adornment﴾ i.e., that which adorns and beautifies it: health, security, abundance of wealth and children, leadership, and other such things. The use of (kāna, "was") is to indicate continuity, i.e., whoever desires that in such a way that he hardly desires the Hereafter at all. ﴿We will pay them in full for their deeds therein﴾ i.e., We will deliver to them the rewards of their deeds in this world in full. So the statement contains an elision of a noun (ḥadhf muḍāf, "omission of a possessive term"), i.e., the rewards of their deeds. It has been said that "deeds" is used metaphorically for "rewards," and the words of Shaykh al-Islam point to this; but the first view is preferable. The verb (nuwaffi, "We pay in full") implies the meaning of nuwaṣṣilu (“We deliver”), which is why it takes ilā (“to”); otherwise it is among the verbs that take their object directly. It has also been said that it is a metaphor for that. Ṭalḥah ibn Maymūn read yuwaffi with the letter yā' (third person), with the verb attributed to God, may He be exalted. Zayd ibn ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with them both, read yuwafi with yā' and without shaddah, the imperfect of awfā. It is also read tuwaff with tā', in the passive voice, with ʿamāluhum in the nominative. In all these readings the verb is jussive, as the answer of the conditional, just as it is jussive in His words, glorified is He: ﴿Whoever desires the tillage of the Hereafter, We will increase for him in his tillage﴾. Al-Farrāʾ reported that kāna is superfluous (zāʾidah), and therefore the response is jussive. Abū Ḥayyān objected to this: if it were superfluous, the conditional verb would be yurīdu and it would be jussive. It was answered that he may have meant by its being superfluous that it is not necessary in meaning. Al-Ḥasan read nuwfi with lightening and the retention of the yā', and this is either according to the dialect of those who apocopate the defective verb by dropping the presumed vowel, as in the line:

Did not there come to you, while the news is being related...

or according to what is heard in Arabic speech when the conditional is in the past tense, regarding the non-jussiving of the apodosis. It is either because the particle, when it does not govern the nearby condition, is too weak to govern the distant apodosis, so it governs its place. It is reported from ʿAbd al-Qāhir that it does not govern it at all because of its weakness. The well-known two views among the grammarians regarding this are: that the apodosis is in the intention of being placed first, and that it is under the estimate of the fāʾ and the subject. This may be reduced to the latter. This is not specific to when the condition is with kāna according to the correct view, since it comes in other cases frequently, and among them:

And if a friend comes to him on a day of hunger, saying: "My wealth is not absent, nor is it forbidden."

﴿And they, therein, will not be deprived﴾ i.e., they will not be diminished. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in the genitive refers to "the life of this world." It has been said that it is more apt for it to refer to "the deeds," lest it be a repetition without benefit. This was refuted: its benefit is to convey from the outset that the absence of deprivation applies only in this world; had it not been mentioned, it could be imagined that it is absolute. Also, it is not impossible that it is for emphasis, and there is no harm in that. He expressed this by "deprivation" (bakhs), which is the diminishing of a right. For this reason al-Rāghib said: it is the diminishing of a thing in the manner of injustice. Yet they have no trace of right in what they were given, just as He expressed giving it as "payment in full" (tawfiyah), which is the giving of rights, although their deeds are far from being such as to merit that—as some verifiers said—by building the matter on the outward state and preserving the forms of the deeds, and in exaggerating the negation of diminishment, as if that were a diminishing of their rights, so it does not fall under the occurrence or issuance from the Generous at all. However, it should be known that this is not absolute; rather the matter depends on the will that proceeds according to the requirement of wisdom, as His words, glorified is He, express: ﴿Whoever desires the hasty life, We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We desire﴾.

Al-Naḥḥās reported in his Nāsikh from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that this verse abrogated the verse we are discussing. You know that there is no abrogation in reports, and perhaps this, if authentic, is to be understood as a loose usage.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 16:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to those mentioned, considered in terms of their continued pursuit of the desire for the worldly life; or in terms of their being paid their wages in it without any diminution; or in terms of both together. The sense of distance carried by it indicates the remoteness of their station in evil condition. ﴿Those for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter except the Fire﴾ because their aspirations were directed toward seizing the world, and their deeds were extended and confined to obtaining it; they achieved what follows from that and did not intend anything else by it. Therefore, it is inevitable that there is nothing for them in the Hereafter except the Fire and its everlasting punishment.

﴿And what they did therein is nullified﴾ that is, in the Hereafter, as is the apparent meaning. So the prepositional phrase is connected to ﴿nullified﴾, and (mā) may be either a verbal-source particle or a relative pronoun; that is, the nullification of their deed became manifest in the Hereafter, or (what they did) refers to the deeds that would have led to the otherworldly reward had they been done for the Hereafter. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the worldly life, in which case the prepositional phrase is connected to ﴿they did﴾ and (mā) remains as it is. The intended meaning of the nullification of the deeds is that they will not be recompensed for them, because they lack any standing due to the absence of sincerity, which is the condition for that. It has also been said: it means their being recompensed for them in this world.

﴿And false is what they used to do﴾

Abu Hayyan said: this is an emphasis of His saying, glorified is He, "was nullified", etc. The apparent meaning is that he took "what they used to do" to mean "what they did", and the falsity to mean lack of benefit, which returns to the meaning of nullification.

When some of them saw that a foundational statement is preferable to an emphatic one, they kept "what they used to do" on that meaning, and took the falsity of that to be its corruption in itself due to the lack of a condition of validity. He said: as if each of the two sentences is a cause for what precedes it, in the sense that "for them there is nothing in the Hereafter except the Fire" because of the nullification of their deeds and the non-occurrence of reward for them, because they are false and not as they should be. The better view is that of Abu al-Su'ud, may Allah have mercy on him, who took the falsity to mean corruption in itself, and "what they used to do" to mean their deeds in the course of obtaining worldly aims. Then he said: Because the first is by nature something that entails reward and recompense, and its absence is due to its not being accompanied by faith and correct intention, and because the second has no good aspect at all, he attached to the first the nullification which indicates the loss of its recompense, in the verbal form which indicates occurrence; and to the second the falsity which reveals that it is such that there is no benefit in it at all, in the nominal form which indicates that this is a necessary and established attribute of it. In the addition of "kāna" in the second but not the first, there is an allusion to the fact that the performance of righteous deeds by them, even if for a corrupt purpose, is not in continuity and permanence like the performance of the deeds which are the preliminaries of their base aims, end of quote.

In my opinion, it is possible, though remotely, that by "what they used to do" is meant what they persisted in of the desire for the worldly life, which is other than what they did of the deeds to which nullification was attributed. Applying such a term to desire is not objectionable, since it is among the actions of the heart. The reason for the use of "kāna" there is its agreement with what he indicated. In the sentence there is an explicit statement of the continuing nullification of that desire, and a description of its state after the description of the one who desires and the description of his deeds, the desire for the worldly life and its adornment. In any case, the apparent reading is that "false" is a predicate placed first and "what they used to do" is the subject. Al-Bahr permitted that "false" be a predicate after a predicate, with "what" raised by it as an agent. It was also read as "and nullified" in the verbal form, meaning its falsity became manifest, since it was known there that that and what it entails of worldly portions is nothing of benefit, or its worldly effect ceased, so it was nullified absolutely. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read "and false" in the accusative, and this is attributed to Asim; the author of al-Lawamih explained it as: "what" is a relative particle, "false" is an object of "they do". In it there is the fronting of the complement of "kāna", and concerning this, as with fronting the predicate, there is disagreement; the more correct view is that it is permissible, based on the apparent saying of the Exalted: "Are these the ones who used to worship you?" Whoever prohibits it interprets it otherwise. It is also permissible that it be accusative governed by "they do", with "what" as an indefinite particle serving as its qualifier, meaning "false, what falsity", and a parallel to this is the saying "what, despite its brevity, and for a matter Qasir cut off his nose". And it may be a verbal noun of the form fa'il, governed by an implied verb, with "what" a relative noun as its subject: that is, it became null a nullity which they used to do; and a parallel to this, used as an exception, is in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

Did you not see that I pledged to my Lord, and that I stood between the corner-post and the Station,
upon me is an oath that I will not revile any Muslim for the rest of my life, nor will (anything) come out of the mouth of false speech.

He meant: "nor will there come out of the mouth of false speech an emergence." According to al-Bahr, this involves governing the verbal noun which is a substitute for the verb in other than interrogative contexts, and this is the case here. The apparent view is that the verse concerns all disbelievers who perform righteousness not in the manner that it should be performed. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and others narrated from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that it was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians. Perhaps the intended meaning, as Ibn 'Atiyyah said, is that they were the cause of the revelation, so they enter into it, not that it is specific to them and no others enter it. al-Jubba'i said: it concerns the hypocrites who fought alongside the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and Allah made their share of that their portion in the spoils. But in this there is the point that this occurred after the Hijra, whereas the verse is Meccan. It has also been said: it concerns people of showing-off, to whom it is said if one of them recites the Qur'an: "You wanted it said: so-and-so is a reciter"; so it is said: "Go, for you have nothing with us." And similarly for others: the giver of charity, the one slain in jihad, and others who did deeds of righteousness not for the sake of Allah, the Exalted. Perhaps this is supported by what is related from Mu'awiyah when Abu Hurayrah narrated to him what contains that, and he wept and said: "Allah and His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, have spoken the truth: ﴿Whoever desires the worldly life and its adornment﴾ up to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and false is what they used to do﴾." On this basis, it is necessary to qualify His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿for them in the Hereafter there is nothing except the Fire﴾ by saying: for them, by reason of their ostentatious deeds, there is nothing except that. This is contrary to the apparent meaning, and the context requires that the verse concerns disbelievers in general and their righteousness, as we have said. From here it is well known that the disbeliever is given the reward of his deeds in this world in the form of widened provision, bodily health, abundance of children and the like, and for them there is no portion in the Hereafter. However, a group went to the view that the punishment of the Hereafter is lightened for him by these, and the case of Abu Talib supports this. Others went to the view that actions which depend on intention bring no benefit to the disbeliever in the Hereafter at all, for lack of its condition, since he was not among the people of intention because of his disbelief; and what brings him no benefit may still lighten his punishment. By this the apparent texts, some of which imply benefit in general and some of which imply none at all, may be reconciled. So reflect.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it, according to Majma' al-Bayan, is that when He, glorified is He, said: ﴿So will you be Muslims?﴾, it is as if someone said: if we show Islam for the safety of self and property, what will be the result? So it was said: ﴿Whoever desires the worldly life﴾, etc. Or it may be said that what came before includes the despair of the disbelievers that their gods could protect them from the might of Allah, mighty is His authority, as has passed, and some of the verifiers mentioned this. Thus it is not far-fetched that their hearing of that was a cause for their resolve to show Islam, or to perform some righteous deeds, thinking that these would protect and benefit them; so He explained to them the ruling on such a matter by His saying, glorified is He: "Whoever desires" etc. But you know that this requires claiming that this resolve was a matter of caution. In al-Bahr, in explaining the connection, it is said that when He, glorified is He, mentioned some of the states of the disbelievers in the Qur'an, He mentioned some of their worldly states and what they will come to in the Hereafter. Abu al-Su'ud expressed this in a manner which strengthens what he claimed about the suitability of the address in what preceded being to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and the believers. He said: What the sublime composition requires is that the intended meaning is disbelievers in general, such that those who disparage the Glorious Qur'an are included in them at the first level. For when He, mighty and majestic is He, commanded His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and the believers to increase in knowledge and certainty that the Qur'an is sent down with the knowledge of Allah, glorified is He, and that no power belongs to anyone other than Him, glorified is He, at all, and stirred them to steadfastness upon Islam and firmness in it when the impotence of the disbelievers and of what they invoke besides Allah, exalted is He, in opposing it became manifest, and it became clear that they have no standing at all, the situation required that He address some of their concerns which give the illusion that they have some standing, namely their attaining immediate portions and their enjoyment of worldly aims, and to show that this has nothing to do with indicating that. This He has explained in the most eloquent explanation. End of quote. It is not hidden that this can be established in a way that does not require introducing a hadith which makes the preceding address to him, peace and blessings be upon him, and the believers; so let it be understood.

In al-Ahkam, the verse was cited as evidence that what by nature is not done except for the sake of drawing near to Allah is not permissible to take a wage for, because wages are among the portions of this world; whoever takes a wage for it comes out of being an act of drawing near by the dictates of the Book and the Sunnah. Al-Kiya claimed that this is similar to His Prophet's saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Actions are only by intentions," and it indicates that whoever fasts in Ramadan without intending it as Ramadan does not count as Ramadan, and that whoever performs ablution for cooling down or cleanliness has no valid ablution. On this there is extensive disagreement, with what supports and opposes it, in its proper place.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 17 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Is one who is upon a clear proof (bayyina) from his Lord﴾ indicates the truth and the correct course in what he takes and what he leaves. Entry into Islam is included in this at the first level. Some scholars restricted it to this meaning, on the basis that it suits what follows. The root of *al-bayyina* (clear proof), as it has been said, is a clear indication, whether rational or sensory. It is also applied to evidence in general. Its *ha'* (the feminine ending) is for emphasis or for transfer (to the noun form). Although it has been said that it derives from *bana*, meaning "became clear and manifest," the notion of another party showing and clarifying something is taken into account in it. Some scholars derived it from the intensive form. The *tanwin* (indefinite ending) in it here is for magnification, meaning "a proof of great standing." What is meant by it is the Qur'an. In accordance with this, or with "the proof," the pronoun referring to it is mentioned in His words, glory be to Him: ﴿and there follows it﴾, meaning, comes after it, ﴿a witness﴾, a great one, who testifies that it is from Allah, exalted is His station. As al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said, this is *i'jaz* (inimitability) in its composition. The meaning of that being a follower of it is that it is an attribute of it that does not separate from it until Allah inherits the earth and whoever is upon it. So none of the creation, generation after generation, can produce its equal, even if they were to back one another.

Likewise the pronoun in (*minhu*, "from him"), which is connected to an omitted element that serves as a description of (*shahid*, "witness"). The meaning of it being "from him" is that it is not separate from him.

It is permitted that this pronoun refers back to the Lord, glory be to Him. The meaning of it being "from Him, exalted is He" is that it comes from His direction, glory be to Him, for testimony. On this basis, it is permissible that by the witness is meant the manifest miracles that appeared at the hand of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for they are among the witnesses that follow the Qur'an and come from Him, mighty and majestic. The matter of their following is evident. What is meant by the relative (*al-mawsul*, "the one who") is everyone who has the characteristic of that state among the believers.

It is reported from Abu al-'Aliya that it refers to the Prophet, peace be upon him. It is not hidden that His words, glory be to Him, coming later: (*ulaika*, "those"), etc., do not fit this except if it is taken as magnification. Also, the context, as you will know, if Allah wills, is to distinguish between the two groups: the believers and those who desire the life of this world. It is not to distinguish between them and the Prophet (ﷺ).

Abu Muslim and others interpreted *al-bayyina* as the rational proof, and *al-shahid* (the witness) as the Qur'an. The pronoun in *minhu* refers to Allah, exalted is He, and *min* is for origin (ibtida'iyya). Or the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, since it was mentioned earlier. In that case, *min* is either explanatory (bayaniyya) or partitive (tab'idiyya), on the basis that the whole Qur'an is not a witness. It is not for abstraction (tajrid), as al-Tibi imagined. So the verse contains an allusion to the two proofs, the rational and the transmitted (sam'i). The meaning of the second being a follower of the first, as has been said, is that it agrees with it and does not contradict it at all. From here they said: sound transmission does not contradict clear reason. For this reason, they interpreted the transmitted proof when its apparent meaning contradicts the rational proof. Perhaps in expressing the first by *al-bayyina*, whose usage in the speech of the Lawgiver (ﷺ) applies to two witnesses, and the second by *al-shahid*, there is an indication that the rational proof is stronger in indication than the transmitted proof. This is because the indication of the first is certain, whereas the indication of the second is generally conjectural, due to the well-known possibilities that prevent certainty. It may also be said that the expression of the second as *al-shahid* is because of its position as a follower (*al-tilw*, "reciting/following").

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, al-Dahhak, 'Ikrima, Abu Salih, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr that *al-bayyina* is the Qur'an, and *al-shahid* is Jibril, peace be upon him. In this reading, *yatlu* (recites) comes from *al-tilawa* (recitation), not from *al-tilw* (following). The pronoun in *minhu* refers to Allah, exalted is He. In a report from Mujahid, the witness is an angel who preserves the Qur'an. It is not meant in the common sense of "preservation," because, as Ibn Hajar said, that is specific to Jibril, peace be upon him. The pronoun in *minhu* is as in the previous interpretation, except if *yatlu* is from *al-tilw*, and the pronoun in the accusative refers to *al-bayyina*. It has been said that it refers to those upon it.

It is reported from al-Farra' that the witness is the Gospel. (*Yatluhu*, "follows it") and the pronoun in *minhu* are in the same pattern as what was reported from Mujahid, except that the pronoun in *yatluhu* refers to the Qur'an.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya that the witness is the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ). The lexicographers have mentioned this. Likewise, the angel is among its meanings. In this case, *yatlu* is from *al-tilawa* (recitation), the attribution is metaphorical, and its object is *al-bayyina*. The pronoun in *minhu* refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), on the basis that he is the one intended by the relative. *Min* is partitive. It has been said that the witness is his (ﷺ) image and his distinguishing features, because every sensible person who sees him knows that he, peace be upon him, is the Messenger of Allah.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: "There is no man from Quraysh except that a portion of the Qur'an was revealed concerning him." A man said to him: "What was revealed concerning you?" He said: "Do you not recite in Surah Hud: ﴿Is one who is upon a clear proof from his Lord﴾, etc.? 'One who is upon a clear proof from his Lord' is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and 'I am a witness from him'." Al-Minhal reported from 'Ubada ibn 'Abd Allah something similar. Ibn Mardawayh reported by another route from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: ﴿Is one who is upon a clear proof from his Lord﴾ is me, ﴿and there follows it a witness﴾ is 'Ali."

Al-Tabarsi reported something similar from one of the Ahl al-Bayt, may Allah be pleased with them. Some Shi'a clung to this in asserting that 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, is the successor of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is because Allah named him a witness, just as He named His Prophet, peace be upon him, a witness in His words, glory be to Him: ﴿Indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bearer of good news, and a warner﴾. The meaning of "witness" there is a witness over the community. This is supported by the conjunction of "a bearer of good news and a warner" with it. So his station, may Allah ennoble his face, among the community should be like the station of the Prophet, peace be upon him, among them. Since He informed, glory be to Him, that He "follows it," meaning, comes after it and will be after it, this indicates that he is its successor. But you know that this report is hardly sound. What is coming later in the verse, if Allah wills, refutes it. It is also contradicted by what Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* reported from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I said to my father, may Allah ennoble his face: 'The people claim that in the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿and there follows it a witness from Him﴾, you are the one who follows.' He said: 'I wish I were him, but he is the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ).'" Moreover, the presentation of this argument has a weakness and feebleness that reaches the utmost extent, as is not hidden from anyone with even a little discernment.

Abu Hayyan related that this witness is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. In it is what is in it.

In the coordination of *yatluhu* there are two possibilities. The first is that it is coordinated with what occurred as a description of *bayyina*. The second is that it is coordinated with the clause (*kana*, "was") and its subject. His words, glory be to Him: ﴿and before it, the Book of Moses﴾ are coordinated with (*shahid*, "witness"), and the pronoun in the genitive refers to it. The prepositional phrase has been placed between them. The apparent meaning is that it is connected to an omitted element that serves as a circumstantial description (*hal*) of the Book, meaning: ﴿and there follows it﴾ in confirmation ﴿the Book of Moses﴾ revealed ﴿before it﴾. The summary is: ﴿Is one who is upon a clear proof from his Lord﴾, and a witness from Him testifies to its truth, and another witness from before it, which is the Book of Moses. It has been said: the one that is mentioned later in revelation is mentioned first, because it is an inseparable attribute of it, and because of its antiquity in the description of following. This applies if the intended witness is inimitability, as some verifiers chose. It may be said that the delay in explaining the testimony of this witness after explaining the testimony of the first witness is because it is not as evident to the community as the testimony of the first. This also applies on a different assumption. The specification of the Book of Moses, peace be upon him, by mention is based on the non-intention of the Gospel in what preceded, because both religions agree that it is from Allah, exalted is He, unlike the Gospel, for the Jews disagree about it. So citing what establishes the proof against both groups is preferable.

Some scholars insisted that ﴿and before it, the Book of Moses﴾ is an independent sentence, not included within what precedes it. This is based on many of the previous possibilities regarding the witness.

Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi and others read (*kitaba*, "the Book") in the accusative, on the basis that it is coordinated with the object of *yatluhu*, or governed by an omitted verb, meaning: "and recites the Book of Moses." The first is preferable, because the default is no omission. In this reading, *yatlu* is from *al-tilawa*. The accusative pronoun refers to the Qur'an, the genitive refers to *man* (the one), and *min* is partitive, not abstractive. The meaning, according to what the *Kashshaf* implies: ﴿Is one who is upon a clear proof﴾ that the Qur'an is true and not fabricated. By it is meant the People of the Book, those who knew that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was upon the truth, and that his Book is the truth, because of what they found in the Torah. A witness from these people recites the Qur'an, and before the Qur'an the Book of Moses is recited. By this witness is meant what is meant in His words, glory be to Him: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to one like it﴾, and he is 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, may Allah be pleased with him. So in the verse there is praise of the People of the Book. He singled out from among them the follower of the two Books and their witness by mention, indicating his greater excellence and alerting that they are his followers in following the truth, even if they do not reach the rank of the witness. In His words, exalted is He: (*yatluhu*, "follows it") there is the bringing of the present state and an indication of the continuity of recitation. As has been said, it is in complete harmony with the speech.

﴿Imaman﴾ (as a leader), meaning, one who is followed in religion and taken as a model. In mentioning this attribute there is a clarification of the following of the Book, with what is not hidden of glorifying the status of what is followed. The tanwin in it is for magnification. Likewise in His words, glory be to Him: ﴿and mercy﴾, meaning a great blessing upon those to whom it was revealed and those after them until the Day of Resurrection, in terms of its enduring rulings, supported by the Mighty Qur'an. These two are circumstantial descriptions of the Book.

﴿Those﴾, meaning those described by that praiseworthy attribute, which is being upon a clear proof, ﴿believe in it﴾, meaning they affirm the Qur'an with true affirmation, according to what those true witnesses testify, which express its truth. They do not follow blindly any of the great authorities of religion. So the pronoun refers to the Qur'an. It has been said that it refers to the Book of Moses, peace be upon him, because it is closer, and that does not fit what follows, though it is not devoid of benefit. It has also been said that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿And whoever disbelieves in it﴾, meaning in the Qur'an, and does not take those true witnesses into account, and does not affirm them, ﴿of the factions﴾, meaning from the people of Makkah and those who formed alliances with them against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This was said by some. 'Abd al-Razzaq reported from Qatada that the factions are the disbelievers in general, for they formed alliances in disbelief. This was also reported from Ibn Jubayr. In a report of Abu al-Shaykh from Qatada, they are the Jews and Christians. Al-Suddi said: they are Quraysh. Muqatil said: they are the Banu Umayya, the Banu al-Mughira ibn 'Abd Allah al-Makhzumi, and the family of Abu Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah. ﴿Then the Fire is his appointed place﴾, meaning he will certainly arrive there, as His words, glory be to Him, state: ﴿They will have in the Hereafter nothing but the Fire﴾, and other verses. *Al-mawid* is the name of the place of promise, as in the words of Hassan:

*You led them to the basins of death in the morning,*
*so the Fire is their appointed place, and death meets them.*

The placement of hell as the promised place implies that he will suffer there torments beyond description, of many kinds. ﴿So be not in doubt about it﴾, that is, be not in doubt about the matter of the Qur'an and that it is from God Most High, after what the proofs have testified to and the virtue of those who hold fast to it has become apparent. Or it means: be not in doubt that hell is their promised place. Some have claimed that this is the more evident meaning, but it is not so. In any case, if the address is general, addressed to whoever is fit for it, then the purpose is to urge correct reflection that removes doubt. If the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), then it is a clarification, since he is not a place for doubt, and it is an allusion to those who doubted. His (ﷺ) being forbidden from it does not imply that it occurred or was expected from him (ﷺ).

As-Sulami, Abu Raja, Abu al-Khattab as-Sadusi and al-Hasan read ﴿مُرْيَةٍ﴾ (*miryah*) with a *ḍammah* on the *mīm*. This is the dialect of Asad and Tamim. The *kasrah* (*mirryah*, with *kasrah* on the *mīm*) is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz.

﴿Indeed, it is the truth from your Lord﴾, that is, the one that causes you doubt in your religion and your worldly affairs, ﴿but most of the people do not believe﴾.

This is either because their insight is deficient and their thinking is disordered, or because of their arrogance and obstinacy. And "the people" (*an-nās*), as narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, means the people of Makkah. The author of *al-Fayyān* said: it means all the disbelievers. That is the end of this.

As for the hamzah (الهمزة) in ﴿أفَمَن﴾ (*afaman*): it has been said that it is for affirmation (*taqrīr*), and ﴿مَن﴾ (*man*) is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), with the predicate omitted, meaning: "Is it then one who is in this state like one who desires the life of this world and its adornment?" The omission of the counterpart of the hamzah is common. Abu Hayyan chose this view. What the words of az-Zamakhshari imply, and perhaps this is the better view, is contrary to it, since he said: the meaning is "Is one who desires the life of this world like one who is upon clear proof?", that is, they do not follow them or come near them in rank, and so on to the end of what he said. The summary of this in *al-Kashf* is that the *fāʾ* (فاء) is conjunctive, indicating sequence, and it calls for what it conjoins with, which is indicated by God's words ﴿whoever desires...﴾ (*man kāna*), etc. So the estimate is: "Is then the one who desires the life of this world, taking it as a relative clause, like the one who is upon clear proof from his Lord?" The predicate is omitted, indicated by the *fāʾ*, meaning: they follow them or draw near to them. The interrogation is for denial, which conveys that there is no closeness between the two groups, let alone similarity. For this reason it is more eloquent than something like God's words ﴿Is one who is a believer like one who is a sinner?﴾.

As for it being a conjunction with His words ﴿whoever desires the life of this world﴾, there is no basis for that, because it would become a conjunction of a sentence, and it would not indicate denial of similarity. Nor is there any sense in estimating the interrogative in the first clause, since the conditional and its response do not carry denial. End of quote. This follows one of the two schools of the grammarians regarding such a construction.

It is known from what has been established that the verse is connected to His words ﴿whoever...﴾ (*man kāna*), etc. According to Shaykh al-Islam, its thrust is also to encourage what was mentioned: belief in the Qur'an, monotheism and Islam. Aṭ-Ṭabarsī claimed that it is connected to God's words ﴿Say: "Then bring ten surahs like it"﴾, and that the meaning is: if they do not bring that, then say to them: "Is one who is upon clear proof (*afaman kāna ʿalā bayyinah*)?" And he has no proof of that.

[p. 30]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 18:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾. This means he attributes to Him what does not befit Him, like their saying: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." Exalted is Allah far above that, a great exaltation. It also includes their saying about their gods: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾. The purpose of the verse is to censure those disbelievers, that along with their disbelief in the signs of Allah, they are fabricators against Him, glorified is He. It is also possible that it serves another kind of proof that the Qur'an is not fabricated, for whoever knows the condition of one who fabricates against Allah, glorified is He, knows how he commits it. It is also possible that it is a fair statement (al-kalam al-munsif, a statement that concedes a point to the opponent), meaning: no one is more unjust than me if I say of what is not the speech of Allah, Exalted is He, that it is His speech, as you claim, or [no one is more unjust] than you, if you deny that His speech, glorified is He, is His speech while it is established that it is the speech of the Majestic, the Exalted. In this there is a great threat and intimidation that is not hidden. In my view, it is also possible, if what precedes concerns the believers among the People of the Book, that this refers to describing the condition of their disbelievers who attributed to Him, glorified is He, what He did not send down, from the distorted text they fabricated, and who denied that He, glorified is He, sent down the Qur'an or the description of the Prophet (ﷺ). In any case, the purpose is the negation that someone could be more unjust than that, or equal in injustice, as has been stated before.

﴿Those﴾, that is, those described with the extreme injustice, which is fabrication, ﴿will be presented﴾ inasmuch as they are described by this, ﴿before their Lord﴾, that is, their true Owner and the One who disposes of them as He wills. In this there is, as has been said, an indication of the falsity of their view in taking lords besides Him, glorified and exalted is He. Some scholars took the statement to involve an omitted mudaf (a noun that is the first term of an annexation, such as "the affairs of" before a noun), meaning: their deeds are presented, or they took it as the use of metaphor (majaz). According to what has been indicated, there is no need for that, because their being presented in that respect and under that title is a presentation of their deeds in a more emphatic way, for the presentation of the doer with his deed is more dreadful than the presentation of his deed while he is absent. The apparent meaning is that there is no omission in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿before their Lord﴾, and whoever stops at ﴿Allah﴾ should consider it.

It has been said that there is an omitted mudaf, meaning: before the angels of their Lord and the prophets of their Lord. These are the ones meant by "the witnesses" in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and the witnesses will say﴾. Interpreting them as the angels in general is what is reported from Mujahid, and interpreting them as the guardian angels is what is reported from Ibn Jurayj, peace be upon them. It has been said that they are the angels, the prophets, and the believers. It has been said that they are their limbs. From Muqatil and Qatadah it is reported that they are all the people of the place of standing (on the Day of Judgment). It is the plural of shahid in the sense of hadir (present), like sahib and as-hab, based on the permissibility of pluralizing fa'il into af'al, or the plural of shahid in its meaning, like sharif and ashraf, meaning: those present at the presentation or at the place of standing on the Day of Resurrection will say: ﴿These are the ones who lied against their Lord﴾. It is possible that this is a testimony identifying the one from whom the lie proceeded, as if its occurrence is a clear matter that does not need testimony. What needs testimony is only that, and for this reason they did not say "these lied" without the relative pronoun. It is also possible that it is a censure of them for that shameful deed, not a testimony against them, as is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: "says" rather than "testifies," and as a preparation for what follows from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Surely the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: because of the fabrication mentioned. The apparent meaning is that this is part of the speech of the witnesses according to both possibilities, and what al-Bukhari and Muslim reported supports it, and a great many others, from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Allah, Exalted is He, will bring the believer near until He places His covering over him and conceals him from the people, and makes him confess his sins, and says to him: Do you know the sin of such-and-such? Do you know the sin of such-and-such? He says: My Lord, I know. Until, when He has made him confess his sins and he sees in himself that he is ruined, He says: I have concealed them for you in the world, and I forgive them for you today. Then he is given the book of his good deeds. As for the disbelievers and the hypocrites, [the witnesses] say: ﴿These are the ones who lied against their Lord. Surely the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾."

He permitted, according to the first possibility, that it be part of the speech of Allah, Exalted is He. In that case, it is permissible that the wrongdoers mean those who include the wrongdoers by fabrication and the wrongdoers in other than that, and the former are included in it primarily. This is supported by what Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Maymun ibn Mihran, who said: Indeed a man prays and curses himself in his recitation, saying: ﴿Surely the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾, while he is a wrongdoer.

Perhaps that is permissible according to the second possibility as well. In any case, ﴿these are the ones who﴾ is a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate). The possibility that ﴿these﴾ is the mubtada' and ﴿who﴾ is a tabi' (follower, an element grammatically dependent on the head word) of it, and the sentence ﴿Surely the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ is its khabar, is also possible. The apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun, meaning: upon them, to censure them by the derivation of the wrongdoing, along with an indication of the cause of the ruling, as you see. As for the sentence ﴿and the witnesses will say﴾, it has been said that it is a resumptive sentence (mustanfa'ah, a new sentence not grammatically linked to what precedes), as if a questioner asked, upon hearing that they will be presented before their Lord: what will happen then? So it was answered by what has been mentioned. It has been said, and this is the apparent view, that it is coordinated with the sentence ﴿they will be presented﴾, in the sense: those will be presented, and the witnesses will say concerning them, or their witnesses and those present at their presentation will say: ﴿these﴾, etc. It seems that this clarification shows that it is linked in the estimation to the mubtada' in the way that the coordinated sentence is linked to it. It has been said that the demonstrative noun, standing in the position of the pronoun for contempt, is sufficient as a link. So reflect.

[Page 31]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 19:

﴿Those who bar⁠﴾ meaning: all those who are able to bar [others] from it, or who engage in barring ﴿from the way of Allah﴾, meaning His upright religion. The application of this designation to it, like "the straight path," is metaphorical (majaz).

﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾ meaning: they seek to find deviation in it. The intent is that they describe it as crooked, while it is the furthest thing from crookedness. The application of "seeking" to "describing" is a metaphor, using the cause for the effect (min ityaq al-sabab ala al-musabbab). It is also possible that the speech contains an elision of a modifier (hadhf mudaf), meaning: they seek for its people to deviate from it and apostatize. It has been said that the meaning is: they seek it [i.e., the way] in a state of crookedness, and ʿiwajan (crooked) is in the accusative as a direct object (maf'ul bihi). It has also been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and is interpreted as "those who make it crooked" (mu'awwajin).

﴿and they, in the Hereafter, they are disbelievers﴾ meaning: and the situation is that they do not believe in the Hereafter. The repetition of the pronoun serves to emphasize their disbelief and to restrict it to them, since it functions as a separating pronoun (fasl), which conveys restriction and a kind of emphasis. The restriction is claimed (ikhtisas idde'a'i), as hyperbole concerning their disbelief in the Hereafter, as if the disbelief of others in it were not disbelief in comparison with theirs. It has also been said that the repetition is for emphasis, and the fronting of "in the Hereafter" is for specification (takhsis). The better view is that its fronting is for the rhyme endings (ru'us al-ayy).

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 11, verse 20:

﴿Those﴾ are the ones described with what necessitates destruction. ﴿They could not escape﴾ Allah the Exalted, unable to save themselves from His seizure if He willed it.

[Page 32]

﴿on earth﴾, despite its vastness, even if they fled from it in every direction. Some have taken "the earth" as a metaphor for the world. ﴿And they had no protectors besides Allah﴾ who could defend them from His punishment. But He delayed this for a wisdom that required it. The word "min" (from) is extra, for the purpose of comprehensively negating. The word ﴿protectors﴾ (*awliya'*) is in the plural either in view of the individual disbelievers, as if it were said: "No one among them had any protector," or in view of the multiplicity of what they used to invoke besides Allah the Exalted. In that case, this is an explanation of the condition of their gods, showing that they had fallen from the rank of protection.

﴿Their punishment will be doubled﴾ is a resumed sentence in which He explains what will be theirs and what will befall them. He claimed that it contains the wisdom of delaying the seizure. Some claimed that it is part of the words of the witnesses, but that is a supplication and it is nothing.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Ya'qub read *yudda'afu* (it is doubled), with the emphatic form (*bi-l-tashdid*), ﴿they were not able to hear﴾. That is, they found hearing the truth which the Messenger ﷺ brought burdensome and extremely repugnant, to the point that it was as if they were unable to hear it. This is like the saying of one who says: "The lover cannot bear to hear the words of the blamer." So in the expression there is an explicit, subordinate metaphor (*isti'arah tasrihiyyah tab'iyyah*). There is no objection to considering a comprehensive metaphor (*isti'arah tamthiliyyah*) instead, even if that view is held. In sum, the verse does not refute the Mu'tazilah, nor Ahl al-Sunnah, because the latter do not deny ability altogether, even though they deny that the servant creates anything at all. It seems that because the ugliness of their condition in not submitting to the Qur'an, whose way of reception is hearing, is greater than their refusal to accept the other signs that are tied to sight, He, glorified is He, emphasized the negation of the former for them, as far as you have understood, and in the latter He was content with negating sight. So He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿and they could not see﴾, that is, they were blind to the signs of Allah the Exalted, spread out in the souls and the horizons. It seems that the sentence is an answer to an implied question about the cause of the doubling of the punishment, as if it were said: "What is it that made them deserve that doubling?" And it is answered: "Because they hated the truth with the utmost hatred, found its hearing burdensome in the greatest degree, and were blind to the signs of the Sovereign, the Exalted."

This is not troubled by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Whoever comes with an evil deed, he will not be recompensed except with its like, and they will not be wronged﴾, on the basis that what is meant by "its like" is what the evil deed requires of punishment with Allah the Exalted. Perhaps what they did of evil deeds requires that doubling, so that doubling is the like, just as the like of the evil of disbelief is abiding forever in the Fire. It was also said: the doubling is for their fabrication and lying against their Lord, their obstruction from the way of Allah the Exalted, their seeking to make it crooked, and their disbelief in the Hereafter, as indicated by the attribution of the doubling of punishment to these people described with those qualities. By this he combined what is here with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, and so on. It is likely that the causation expressed by the sentence on this view is because that is the root principle of all their ugly acts and sins.

Some claimed that the doubling is to preserve the basis, for otherwise it would be removed and no punishment would remain, due to habituation through a long duration. In this there is what there is. It was also said that the sentence is an explanation of what was negated regarding the protection of the gods, for what does not hear and does not see is far removed from protection. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿is doubled﴾, etc., is an intervening digression between the two, rebuking them from the outset with the evil of their end. In this there is that it contradicts the context and entails disjointing the pronouns.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that *ma* (in *ma kanu yastati'una*) be a temporal verbal (*masdariyyah zarfiyyah*) particle, meaning: their punishment is doubled for the duration of their ability to hear and see. The meaning is that the punishment and its doubling is perpetual for them and continuing. Al-Farra' permitted that it be a verbal particle with the preposition removed from it, as the preposition is removed from *an* and *anna*. In this there is a distance, both in wording and in meaning.

﴿Those﴾: the ones described by those ugly traits.

﴿who have lost their souls﴾ by trading the worship of God, exalted is His majesty, for the worship of the gods. It was also said: they lost because they exchanged guidance for misguidance and the Hereafter for this world, and what they had gained through that exchange, the worldly enjoyments of life and leadership, was lost to them.

In al-Bahr (Al-Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan), it is said that this is by omission of a mudaf (the noun elided from an idafa construction), i.e., they lost the happiness of their souls and their comfort, for their souls remain tormented.

[Page 33]

It was objected that keeping it on its apparent meaning is better, because remaining in torment is no true remaining. ﴿And what they used to fabricate has vanished from them﴾ of the gods and their intercession.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 22:

﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter they are the greatest losers.﴾ That is, no one is more evident in loss, or greater in loss, than them. Here af'al (the elative form, "more/most") expresses excess, either in quantity or in quality. Defining the predicate with the definite article of genus (lam al-jins) serves to convey restriction (hasr). If (hum) is taken as a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl, "separating pronoun"), it conveys emphasis on exclusivity. If it is taken as a subject (mubtada'), with what follows it as its predicate, and the whole sentence as the predicate of inna, it conveys emphasis on the ruling.

Regarding (la jaram) there are several opinions. In al-Bahr, citing al-Zajjaj, la is a negative particle and its negated object is omitted, meaning, for example: their deeds will not benefit them. Jaram is a past-tense verb meaning "earned" (kasaba), as one says: jaramat al-dhanb, "she earned the sin," when she committed it. The poet said:

"We set his head upon a palm trunk, for what his hands earned (jaramat), and we did not transgress."

What follows it is its object, and its subject is what the context indicates, meaning: that earned for them the greater or more evident loss. This is reported from al-Azhari. It is also reported from Sibawayh that la is a negative particle, as reported from al-Zajjaj, and jaram is a past-tense verb meaning "is right/true" (haqqa), and what follows is its subject, as if it were said: that deed will not benefit them, it is true that (anna-hum fi al-akhirah) etc.

Abu Hayyan mentioned that the view of Sibawayh, and likewise al-Khalil, is that the whole of (la jaram) means "truly," and what follows it is raised by it as its subject. It was also said: la is a superfluous particle (silah) and jaram is a verb meaning "earned" or "is right." From al-Kisa'i: la is a negative particle and jaram is its noun, built with it on fatḥah, like la rajul. The meaning is "no opposition and no prevention." Evidently the predicate in this view is omitted, and the preposition has been dropped from anna, to be estimated according to what the meaning requires. It was also said: jaram is the noun of la, and its meaning is severance, from jaramtu al-shay', "I cut the thing," meaning: there is no severance, since the greater loss of theirs is established; that is, this does not cease at any time, so the opposite would be the case.

Al-Sirafi reported from al-Zajjaj that (la jaram) originally meant "do not let them enter into jaram," i.e. sin, like his sin, meaning he caused him to enter into sin. Then its usage became frequent until it came to mean "there is no alternative (la budda)." This meaning is also reported from al-Farra'. In al-Bahr it is stated that jaram is upon it the noun of la. It was also said: jaram means "falsehood," either because it is so laid down for it, or because it means "earned," and falsehood needs it. From here (la jaram) is interpreted as "truly," since truth is the opposite of falsehood, and "no falsehood" becomes an oath, like "no lie" in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I am the Prophet, there is no lie."

In al-Qamus it is stated that one says: la jaram, la dha jaram, la an dha jaram, la 'an dha jaram, la jaruma (like karuma), and la juram with a ḍammah, meaning "there is no alternative," or "truly," or "without doubt." This is its original usage, then it became frequent until it transformed into the meaning of an oath, so for this reason it is answered with the lam, and one says: la jaram la'atiyannaka. End of quotation. There is in this a disagreement with what al-Sirafi reported from al-Zajjaj. As for what he mentioned about la jaruma (like karuma), some reported it from Abu 'Amr regarding this verse. And "la dha juram" was related by al-Farra' from Bani 'Amir. He also related la juram with a ḍammah from some Arabs. But al-Shihab said: there is hesitation regarding the establishment of this dialect in the eloquent speech of the Arabs, and jaram in it may be a noun or a passive verb whose vowel was lightened for ease of pronunciation. Some have reported la dhu jaram, la 'an jaram, and la jar, with the mim dropped due to frequency of use, just as the fa' was dropped from sawfa for this reason, in their saying: saw tara.

Evidently the intervening particles between la and jaram are superfluous, and the statement of some indicates this. It was related without la jaram: "anta anta fa'alta dhaka" (it is you who did that). Perhaps the intended meaning is that your being the doer does not need to be described as la haram. So let that be reviewed. And God Most High guides you.

Then, when God Most High had mentioned the path of the disbelievers, their deeds, and clarified their final destiny and what is theirs, He began to explain the state of their opposites, namely the believers, and to show what is theirs of praiseworthy outcomes, as a completion of what preceded concerning the praiseworthy qualities of the believers, mentioned collectively in His saying, glory be to Him:
Page 34
﴿Is one who has a clear proof from his Lord﴾ and so on, so that the stark difference between the two in state and outcome may become evident. So the Mighty One, the Speaker, said:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 23:

﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ i.e., affirmed (ṣaddaqū) everything that must be affirmed of the Qur'an and other than it. This does not happen except through hearing the truth and witnessing the signs, those on the horizons and those within themselves, and reflecting upon them. Or the meaning is: they performed belief (al-īmān) and were characterized by it, as in the saying "so-and-so gives and withholds." ﴿And did righteous deeds﴾ i.e., righteous deeds (al-a'māl al-ṣāliḥāt). Perhaps what is meant by them includes encouragement to follow the path of God, Mighty and Majestic, and the like, in contrast to what the disbelievers' party is upon. ﴿And humbled themselves before their Lord﴾ i.e., they were at peace with Him, glorified be He, and submitted to Him in humility (khashaʿū). The root of ikhbāt (humbling oneself) is descending into the khabt, which is the low-lying part of the land; then it was applied to the tranquility of the soul and humility, as a metaphor of the intelligible by the sensible, and then it became literal for it. From this comes the word khabīt (with the letter tā', meaning "base" or "vile"). It is said that the tā' is a substitution for the thā' (ث) in khabīth. ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise; therein they will abide forever.﴾ "Abide" (khālidūn) means remaining eternally. The intent is not to restrict eternal abiding to them, because the disobedient among the believers enter Paradise according to the People of Truth and abide therein. Perhaps whoever claims this intends by negating eternal abiding from the disobedient to limit it to the first part (of the verse), as has been said regarding it in what you will hear, God willing.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 24:**

﴿The likeness of the two groups﴾ mentioned, the believers and the disbelievers, i.e., their astonishing state. The root of *mathal* (likeness, parable) is like *mithl* (equivalent, counterpart). It was then borrowed for a saying whose manner of presentation is compared to its source, and it is used only for what is strange. It became a customary figurative usage, and from here it is borrowed for a story, a condition, or an astonishing attribute.

﴿Like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing﴾, i.e., like the state of one who combines blindness and deafness, and one who combines sight and hearing. There are then two comparisons. The first is the comparison of the state of the disbelievers, described as blind and deaf to the signs of Allah the Exalted, with the state of one created blind and deaf, to whom neither speech nor gesture is of benefit. The second is the comparison of the state of those who believed and did righteous deeds, who benefited by their hearing and their sight, guided to Paradise and turning away from what they had been floundering in, the misguidance of disbelief and the darkness, with the state of one who is seeing and hearing, who is guided by lights in the darkness and who gains the spoils of warning and good tidings, attaining the goal. The conjunction (*'atf*) serves to treat the difference of attributes as the difference of essences, as in his saying:

*Alas for Ziyaba, for the morning tiller, then the one who gains, then the one who returns.*

It is also possible that there are multiple comparisons, by considering the state of each of the two groups, the disbelieving group and the believing group, as compared to two states: that is, he likened the disbelieving group to the blind and also likened them to the deaf, and he likened the believing group to the seeing and also likened them to the hearing. It may also be considered that each of the two groups is divided into two kinds, so one kind of the disbelievers is likened to the blind and another kind of them to the deaf, and one kind of the believers is likened to the seeing and another kind of them to the hearing. This has been judged unlikely, since dividing the disbelievers into those likened to the first and those likened to the second, and likewise the believers, is not intended at all, on the evidence of its parallels in other verses, such as his saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And they are not equal, the blind and the seeing﴾, and his saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has sealed their hearts﴾, regarding the pure disbelievers, and his saying, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind﴾, regarding the hypocrites. The verse, in light of its possible meanings, has some resemblance in general to the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*As if the hearts of birds, moist and dry, beside their nests, are dates and a decayed fig-stalk.*

So reflect upon it. The comparison may also be considered a *tamthili* (representational or composite) comparison, by abstracting from the state of the first group, in their deafness and blindness mentioned above, and their falling, because of that, into the doubled punishment and the loss beyond which there is no loss, a form abstracted from one who has lost the two faculties of sight and hearing (page 35), so that he stumbles in his path, falls into the pits of destruction, and does not find a way to his goal. And it abstracts from the state of the second group, in their use of their faculties in the signs of Allah the Exalted as they ought to be used, and their success in the abode of eternity, a form compared to a form abstracted from one who has sight and hearing and uses them in his affairs, so he is guided to his path and attains his aim. It is not hidden that this is contrary to the apparent meaning. Perhaps the most apparent of the possibilities is what was indicated at first, and the speech is of the type of *laff wa nashr* (wrapping and unfolding, i.e., a figure in which several items are mentioned together and then each is matched to its counterpart). The *laff* is either *taqdiri* (implied), if it is considered in regard to the two groups, since it is in effect the disbelievers and the believers; or *tahqiqi* (explicit), if it is considered in regard to what is indicated by his saying, exalted is He: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ and so on, and his saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾, the verse. The matter of the *nashr* (unfolding) is evident. The antithesis (*tibaq*) between the blind and the seeing, and between the deaf and the hearing, is not hidden. The disbelievers' part was placed first. It is said that this is in consideration of what preceded, and because the context is for explaining their state. The blind was placed before the deaf because it is more manifest and more widely known as a bad condition than the other.

In *al-Bahr* (*Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit* by Abu Hayyan): the reason the structure did not come as "like the blind and the seeing, and the deaf and the hearing" is so that each of the two opposites would follow its opposite directly. For when He mentioned the closing of the eye, He followed it with the closing of hearing, and when He mentioned the opening of sight, He followed it with the opening of hearing. This is the method of antithesis and is more complete in its inimitability. God willing, a parallel to this will come later in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Indeed, for you there is that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked﴾ ﴿and that you will not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun﴾. Then, the apparent meaning of what has preceded is that the speech is on the ellipsis of a *mudaf* (a noun in a construct phrase that is omitted), and the object of the preposition is governed by the particle *ka* ("like"), and the prepositional phrase is attached to an omitted element which occurs as a predicate of *mathal* (likeness).

It is also permitted that the particle *ka* itself be the predicate of a subject, and its meaning would be the meaning of "likeness," and there is no need to posit an omitted *mudaf*; that is, the likeness of the two groups is the likeness of the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing. ﴿Are the two equal?﴾ meaning the two groups mentioned. The interrogation is denunciatory, a rebuke, according to what has been said, because of what preceded regarding the denial of similarity in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Is one who is upon clear evidence from his Lord﴾, and so on. (*Mathalan*) meaning "in state" or "in attribute," and it is in the accusative as a *tamyiz muhawwal 'an al-fa'il* (a specification transferred from the subject); the original would be "Are the two equal in their likeness?"

Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted that it be a *hal* (circumstantial accusative), though this is far-fetched. ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ meaning: Do you doubt the non-equality and the disparity between them, or are you heedless of it so that you do not remember it by reflecting on what has been set forth for you of the parable? So the hamza is for the denunciatory interrogation, and it applies to both conjoined items together. Or: Do you hear this, and then do not remember? In that case the denunciation applies to the non-remembrance after the realization of what necessitates its existence, which is the parable struck. That is: Will you not then do the remembering, or will you not reason? The meaning of denouncing non-remembrance is considering it improbable from those addressed, and that it is something that cannot be the case. It is not of the type of the denunciation in ﴿Is one who is upon clear evidence from his Lord﴾ and ﴿Are the two equal?﴾, for that is for negating similarity and negating equality.

Then, He, exalted is He, began to mention the stories of the prophets who called to Allah the Exalted and to explain their states with their peoples, so that the Prophet (ﷺ) would increase in striving in the call and in bearing what he suffered from the obstinate opponents. So the Mighty One, the Speaker, said:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 25:**

﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people﴾. The *waw* is *ibtida'iyyah* (introductory), and the *lam* falls in the answer to an omitted oath (*qasam*). Its letter is estimated to be a *ya'* rather than a *waw*, although the *waw* is the more common usage, so that two *waws* do not come together. Some scholars estimate it as a *waw* and do not mind this.

Noah, according to the well-known account, is the son of Lamech, son of Methuselah, son of Idris ('alayhi al-salam), and he was the first prophet sent after him. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: he ('alayhi al-salam) was sent at the age of forty, and he remained calling his people for what Allah the Exalted related as a thousand years minus fifty years.
