He lived after the Flood for sixty years, and his lifespan was one thousand and fifty years. Muqatil said: he was sent when he was one hundred years old. It was also said: when he was fifty, and it was said: when he was two hundred and fifty. He stayed calling his people for what the Glorified related, and he lived after the Flood for two hundred and fifty years, so his lifespan was one thousand four hundred and fifty years.

[Page 36]

﴿Indeed, I am to you a warner﴾ is read with *kasra* (*inni*) on the basis of intending speech, meaning: "so he said" or "saying."

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it with *fatha* (*anna*), on the basis of an omitted preposition, meaning: "accompanied by that statement," which is "Indeed, I am to you a warner." When the preposition is attached, it takes *fatha* as the word *kāna* does (*kāna* in Arabic is a verb). The meaning with *kasra* is as in your saying: "Indeed Zayd is like a lion," on the basis that *kāna* is a compound and is not a particle in its own right. There is no shift from the third person to the second person in this, contrary to Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi). Perhaps the restriction to mentioning his ('alayhi al-salam) being a warner is because they did not seize the spoils of his good tidings ('alayhi al-salam), ﴿a clear one﴾. That is, one who makes clear to you the causes of punishment and the way of deliverance from it.

﴿That you worship none but Allah﴾. That is, on the basis that you worship none but Allah, with (أنْ) taken as a *masdariyyah* (a particle that turns the following verb into a verbal noun) and the yā' connected to *arsalnā* ("We sent"). The (لا) is *nāhiyah* (prohibitive), meaning: We sent him while he was bringing a prohibition of them from *ishrāk* (associating partners with Allah). But a phrase intervenes between them, explaining some of his attributes, so that it would be more readily accepted. He did not say that at the beginning of the surah, lest it be like separating the tree from its bark. It is also permitted for (أنَّ) and what follows it to be in the sense of a verbal noun, as the object of *mubīn* ("clarifying"), meaning: clarifying the prohibition of *ishrāk*. It is also permitted for (أنَّ) to be *mufassirah* (explanatory), connected to *arsalnā*, or to *nadhīr* ("warner"), or to *mubīn*, meaning: We sent him with something, or a warner with something, or a clarifier of something, namely ﴿that you worship none but Allah﴾. However, it has been said: the warning in this is not apparent. This is on the reading with the kasra mentioned above. As for the reading with the fatḥa, (لا) and so on is a *badal* (substitution) for ("Indeed I am to you") and so on. The word "saying" is to be understood after (أنْ), so the meaning is: We sent him with his saying, "Indeed I am to you a warner," and with his saying "do not worship," so it is a *badal al-baʿḍ* (partial substitution) or *badal al-kull* (total substitution), for emphasis, and the claim that (أنَّ) is the entire warning itself. It is also permissible not to supply the word "saying", in which case *badal al-ishtimāl* (substitution by inclusion) is more apparent. Whoever claims that it is so in every case, since there is no connection between them of part and whole, has overlooked that, on the supposition of the word "saying", his statement, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a painful day﴾, the cause for which the prohibition is given, is among what is said, and it is a specific warning; so that will be a part of it or the whole, by way of claim. The apparent meaning of "the day" is the Day of Resurrection, though it is permitted that it be the day of the Flood. Describing it as *alīm*, meaning *mu'lim* (painful), is a *isnād majāzī* (figurative attribution), because the one who causes pain is Allah, exalted is He; the time-period is placed in the position of the agent itself, because the act occurs in it much, so it is made as if the act occurred from it. Likewise the punishment is described by that in more than one place in the Mighty Qur'an, and it is possible to consider it here too. The genitive has been made by proximity (*jiwār*), and the aspect of figurative usage then is that the attribute of a thing is made for the strength of its being qualified by it, as if it had designated it, so what is attributed to the agent is attributed to it. The parallel to that in both aspects is "its day is fasting" and "its grandfather's fortune prospered." It may be said: describing punishment as causing pain is a customary literal usage (*ḥaqīqah ʿurfiyyah*), and such a thing is considered an agent in the language; so one says, "The punishment pained him," without any figurative usage. It has been said: this statement, and what is similar to it in meaning, is among what is related in more than one verse, because it did not come from him, peace be upon him, only once, but he repeated it throughout his long period, as is indicated by the statement of His exalted saying, relating about him: ﴿My Lord, I have called my people night and day﴾, and the verses that follow. It is joined to the act of sending that accompanies it, or to the supposed saying after it, their answer, which interrupts concerning the circumstances of the believers who followed him after the "[those] who said" with the connective *fa* of consequence. Then He, exalted is He, said:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 27:**

﴿So the chiefs (al-mala') among those of his people who disbelieved said﴾. That is, the nobles among them. As many have said, the word is from the expression "so-and-so is *mali'* (full) with such-and-such," when he is capable of it, because they are "filled" with the management and handling of affairs. Or it is because they are *mutamali'un*, that is, they support and help one another. Or it is because they fill hearts with awe, eyes with beauty, and hands with gifts. Or it is because they are filled with sound opinions and sound judgments. This is on the understanding that *al-mala'* is intransitive and also transitive.

[Page 37]

He described them as disbelievers in order to censure them and to record this against them from the very beginning. It does not mean that some of their nobles were not disbelievers.

﴿We see you only as a human being like us﴾. They meant: you are only a human being like us, and there is no distinction in you that singles you out from among us with prophethood. Had that been the case, we would have seen it. This does not mean that it is impossible but that we do not see it. The same applies to ﴿And we see none following you except those who are our lowest, immature in judgment﴾. Both verbs are from seeing with the eye, and *basharan* (as a human being) and *ittaba'aka* (following you) are two circumstantial clauses (hal) referring to the object. In the second, *qad* is understood, or not, according to the difference of opinion. It is also possible that both are from seeing with the heart, which is the more apparent sense. In that case they are the second object. The judgment (ra'y) in the first then relates to the likeness (mithliyya), not to humanity alone.

From the Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari) it is understood that the verse has two possible meanings. The first is that they intended an insinuation that they are more deserving of prophethood, as if they said: Suppose you are like us in excellence and distinction through abundance of wealth and status; why then have you been singled out for prophethood over us? The second is that they meant he should be an angel and not a human being. This was criticized as containing a hidden Mu'tazili tendency. Al-'Allama al-Tibi explained this, but it was disputed. In al-Kashf it is said that their words "like us" are an explanation to establish humanity, and their words "and we see none following you" are an argument that they are weak-minded and have no discernment, so they considered it possible that the Messenger could be a human being. Their later words, "And we see in you no superiority over us," are a record that the call to prophethood is false, since he (peace be upon him) and the lowly are placed in the same category, in a style which indicates that they are the most deficient of humankind in excellence, let alone in rising. There is no hidden Mu'tazili meaning in this speech, and the context does not reject it. End.

In al-Intisaf it is said: it is possible that they intended both meanings together, as if they said: it is due to the Messenger that he be an angel and not a human being, and you are a human being. And if it were permissible for the Messenger to be a human being, then we are more deserving of the mission than you. The first intention is supported by his words in the reply: "Nor do I say that I am an angel" (11:31). The second intention is supported by "And we see in you no superiority over us" and what follows. It appears that their aim was nothing more than to establish that he (peace be upon him) is like them and that there is in him no distinction from which prophethood, the obligation of obedience and following would result. Perhaps their words "and we see none following you" and so on are an answer to what might be objected to them: that he (peace be upon him) is not like them, since those who were guided to follow him did so. So they said: the following of those who follow you does not distinguish you, so it does not oblige us to follow you, since he who follows you is one [of whom it is said] ﴿except those who are our lowest﴾, that is, our most despised and our least. The word is the plural of *arhal*. The usual and more analogical plural for such a word, when its plural is wanted, is the sound masculine plural, as in *al-akhsirun*, the plural of *akhsar*. But here it is broken, because by dominant usage it has come to function as a noun. For this reason the lexicon makes *al-radhl* and *al-arhal* synonyms, meaning the base and the vile. Its functioning as a noun means that the described noun is hardly ever mentioned with it, as in *al-abtah* and *al-abraq*.

It is also permitted that it is the plural of *arhal* as the plural of *radhl*, so it is a plural of a plural. A parallel is *akalib* and *aklub*, from *kalb*. That it is the plural of *radhl* is contrary to analogy. They did not say "except our *arahil*" in order to exaggerate their contempt for them. They despised them only because of their poverty, for since they knew only the outward aspect of the worldly life, the more noble in their eyes was he who had the greater share of it, and the lowly was he who was deprived of it. They did not understand that the world in all its parts does not weigh the wing of a gnat in the sight of God Most High, and that true bliss is the bliss of the Hereafter, and the noble is the one who attains it, and the lowly the one who is deprived of it. There are many people of this ignorance in this age; may God the Glorified protect us from the abasement and deprivation in which they are. According to some reports, those people were weavers, cobblers and cuppers. By their words ﴿at first sight﴾ they meant its outward sense, that which is without deep reflection. "Judgment" (ra'y) is from the sight of thought and contemplation. It was said that it is from sight with the eye, but this is not right.

It is also permitted that *al-badi* means *al-awwal* (the first). On the first reading it is from *al-bud* (appearance), and on the second from *al-bad'* (beginning). The *ya'* is substituted for a *hamza* because of the kasra before it. Abu 'Amr and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read it this way. Its being in the accusative under both readings is by way of a time adverb (zarfiyya) for *ittaba'aka* (they followed you), meaning: they followed you in the outward (or first) of their opinion. They did not reflect and did not verify. Had they done so, they would not have followed you. Their purpose in this is to exaggerate the disregard of that following. Some made this the cause of the despising, but this is nothing. It was also said that the meaning is: they followed you at the first of their opinion, or its outward aspect, but they were not with you inwardly.

This connection was objected to, on the grounds that what precedes *illa* (except) does not govern what follows it unless it is either the thing excepted from (mustathnan minhu), as in *ma qama illa Zaydan al-qawm* (no one stood except Zayd, the people), or an exception (mustathna), as in *ja'a al-qawm illa Zaydan* (the people came except Zayd), or a follower of the thing excepted from, as in *ma ja'ani ahadun illa Zaydun khayrun min 'Amr* (no one came to me except that Zayd is better than 'Amr). But *badi al-ra'y* is none of these three in "at first sight." It was answered that this is excused in the case of an adverb, because more latitude is allowed in it than in other things. The question of the adverbial function was also raised, since *fa'il* is not originally an adverb. Makki said: *fa'il* could be an adverb just as *fa'il* can, like *qarib* and *malin*, because it is annexed to *al-ra'y*, and it is often annexed to a verbal noun which may be put in the accusative as an adverb, as in *jahda ra'yi annaka muntaliq* (my utmost opinion is that you are departing).

Al-Zamakhshari said, and others followed him, that the original is "the time of the occurrence of the first of their affair, or the time of the occurrence of the outward of their opinion." This was deleted and the annexed noun was put in its place. Perhaps the supposition of "time" is so that it may stand for the adverb and be in the accusative as an adverb. The consideration of "occurrence" is based on the view that the active participle does not stand for the adverb and take the accusative, whereas the verbal noun often does. They mentioned it to indicate that it includes the meaning of occurrence in both of its senses, and therefore this is permissible in it. Their intention is not that it is elided, since there is no need for that in meaning on either explanation. What they mentioned here, that among the adjectives only *fa'il*... no, that only *fa'il* stands for the adverb, is among the strange observations, as al-Shihab said. However, it was corrected by rejecting it, since *fa'il* frequently functions as an adverb just as *fa'il* does, as in *kharij al-dar* (outside the house), *batin al-amr* (the inner matter), *zahiruhu* (its outward aspect), and other things that are common in their speech.

It was also said that the adverb is connected to *lana-raka* (we see you), meaning: we do not see you at the first of our judgment or in what appears of you. It was said it is connected to *la-arhalina* (our lowest), meaning: they are lowly at first glance or in outward appearance, because their baseness is manifest and needs no deep reflection.

It was said that it is an adjective of *basharan* (a human being). It was said it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of Noah in *ittaba'aka*, meaning: while you are one whose judgment is exposed, with no sound discernment in you. It was said it is in the accusative as a vocative address to Noah (peace be upon him), meaning: O one whose judgment is at first sight, that is, what is in your mind of judgment is apparent to everyone. It was said it is a verbal noun on the pattern *fa'il*, in the accusative as an absolute object, and that what precedes governs it, on the supposition of an adverbial function.

﴿And we see in you no superiority over us﴾. This is addressed to him (peace be upon him) and to all his followers together, by way of predominance of the masculine, meaning: we do not see for you and for your followers ﴿any superiority over us﴾, that is, any excess that would qualify you to be followed by us. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that this was explained as excess in creation and character, and it was related from some that it was explained as abundance of possession and sovereignty. Perhaps what we have mentioned is better. It seems their intention was to deny seeing any superiority after following, that is, we do not see in you and in them after following any excellence over us that we should follow. Otherwise, they had already denied his superiority (peace be upon him) at first in their words "we see you," and they declared that his followers, and God forbid, are lowly, and this necessarily entails denying that they have any superiority over them. It was also said that this is an emphasis on what was understood at first. It was said that the address is to his followers (peace be upon him) only, and so it is a shift (iltifat), meaning: we see for you no honor over us in that following, so that we may agree with you in it. The "superiority" is taken as bounty and kindness in both possibilities of the address. This is on the basis that the intention of the chiefs in their reply to him (peace be upon him), when he called them to what he called them to, was: we will not follow you nor abandon what we are upon for your saying, because you are a human being like us, and there is nothing in you that calls for your prophethood and for your being the Messenger of God Most High to us by this. Your followers are lowly ones who followed you without reflection or verification. So their following does not show that there is in you something that calls for it which is hidden from us. Also, you are not one who bestows bounty upon us, so that your bounty would be a reason for us to agree with you whatever you are, nor are your followers people of bounty over us, so that we should agree with them even though they are lowly, out of regard for the right of bounty. For a person may agree with the lowly because of his bounty and not mind that he is lowly, and this is among the things that pass through the mind, except that there is something in the heart about it.

﴿Rather, we think you are liars﴾, all of you together, since their speech is one and your call is one. Or it means you, in your claim to prophethood, and them, in their confirmation of you. It was said: they limited themselves to *zann* (supposition) to avoid attributing to themselves rash assertion, just as they expressed what they expressed at first, with an allusion, from the beginning, to the opinion of the followers, and with a courteous deference to him (peace be upon him) through the way of opinions, in the manner of fairness.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 28**

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause (*istiʾnāf bayānī*, a clause that answers an implied question). ﴿O my people, tell me﴾, i.e., inform me. In it is an allusion to the feebleness of their opinion mentioned above. ﴿If I am upon a clear proof﴾, a manifest argument, ﴿from my Lord﴾, and a witness who testifies to me of the soundness of my claim, ﴿and He has given me mercy from Him﴾, which is prophethood, as related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both. He also permitted that the mercy is the proof itself, mentioned to indicate that, although it is a proof from Allah, it is also a great mercy and blessing from Him, glorified is He.

The reason for the singular pronoun in His words ﴿then it was made obscure to you﴾, i.e., it was concealed, is evident on this reading. If by it prophethood is meant, then by "the proof" is meant the evidence indicating its soundness, so the singular is used because each of the two is intended. Or the pronoun refers to the proof, and the mention of only the proof suffices, because the concealment of the proof entails the concealment of the one claiming it. On this reading, the clause ﴿and He has given me mercy﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (*muʿtaraḍah*), or the pronoun refers to the mercy. In the speech there is an implied element, i.e., "I concealed the mercy after concealing the proof and what indicates it," and it was omitted for brevity. It was said that it is understood in meaning without being stated, or that the omitted element is "it was made obscure," which is not mentioned after the word "proof" and is omitted for brevity. In this there is an implied clause before the evidence.

Most of the Seven canonical readers (*al-sabʿah*) read ﴿fa-ʿamiyat﴾ with a fatḥah on the ʿayn and a light mīm, in the active voice. It derives from ʿamā, the opposite of sight, and what is meant here is concealment, metaphorically. One says "a blind proof" just as one says "a seeing (*mubṣirah*) one" for a clear one. In the speech there is an implicit metaphor (*istiʿārah tabaʿiyyah*), in that he likened the concealment of the proof to blindness, since each prevents one from reaching the goals. Then the verb was formed on this basis, as is not hidden from you. He also permitted that there is an allegorical metaphor (*istiʿārah tamthīliyyah*), in that he likened the one who is not guided by the proof, because it is hidden from him, to one who traverses a desert whose paths he does not know and follows a blind guide in it.

It was said that the speech is an inversion (*qalb*), and the original is ﴿fa-ʿamītum ʿanhā﴾ (you became blind to it), as the Arabs say: "I put the cap on my head," and from it is the poet's verse:

*You see the bull in it, its head entering the shade.*

And His words, glorified is He: ﴿So do not think that Allah will fail His promise to His messengers﴾. Abū Ḥayyān objected to this, saying that inversion, according to our companions, is never permitted except in cases of necessity. The verse of the poet is not an example of it, but rather of extension in the use of the adverbial. Likewise the verse is not an example of it either, because *akhlafa* takes two objects, and its derived form does too. You may attribute it to either of them as you wish. Moreover, if what was mentioned were an inversion, the construction would take *ʿan* rather than *ʿalā*. Do you not see that you say "I became blind to such-and-such" (*ʿamītu ʿan kadhā*) and do not say "I became blind upon such-and-such" (*ʿamītu ʿalā kadhā*)?

Al-Aʿmash related from Wathhāb "wa-ʿamiyat" with a light waw. Ubayy, al-Sulamī, al-Ḥasan and others read ﴿so He made it obscure to you﴾, with the verb attributed to Allah, the Exalted. It was also read with explicit mention of Him. The apparent meaning of this is in agreement with the Sunnis (*ahl al-sunnah*), who hold that both good and evil come from Him. For this reason al-Zamakhsharī interpreted it away, to preserve his creed. ﴿Shall we compel you to it?﴾, i.e., shall we force you to be guided by it? This is the answer to ﴿arayitum﴾ and takes the place of the answer to the condition.

[p. 40]

In al-Baḥr (*al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*) it is stated that the clause is in the position of the second object of the verb, and its first object is "the proof," understood. The answer to the condition is omitted, and it is indicated by ﴿arayitum﴾, i.e., "if I am..." etc., "then inform me." Where two object pronouns are combined and the more definite one is placed first, and the second-person pronoun is more definite than the third-person pronoun, the second may be joined (*waṣl*) or separated (*faṣl*). Thus outside the Qur'an one may say *anulzimukum iyyāhā*. This is the view of Ibn Mālik in *al-Tashīl*, and some agreed with him. Ibn Abī al-Rabīʿ said that joining is obligatory in such cases. Sībawayh's statement in *al-Kitāb* supports this: "When the two objects to which the verb of the agent extends are one addressed and one absent, and you begin with the addressed before the absent, the sign of the absent is the one that does not take its place as the independent pronoun. This is like *aʿṭaytukahu* (I gave it to you) and *aʿṭākahu* (he gave it to you). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Shall we compel you to it?﴾. So this is like that, since you began with the addressed before the absent." End of quotation. If the absent were placed first, separation is obligatory according to the sound view, so one says *anulzimuhā iyyākum*.

Some permitted joining and cited the saying of ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him: *arāhumunī* (he showed them to me), and he did not say *arāhum iyyāya*. The full discussion of this belongs in its proper place. The waw was brought in to complete the *mīm* of plurality. It is reported from Abū ʿAmr that he made the first *mīm* quiescent for lightness, and this is permitted according to al-Farrāʾ. Al-Zajjāj said: the Basran grammarians agreed that it is not permitted to make the case-ending vowel (*ḥarakat al-iʿrāb*, the final vowel marking grammatical case) quiescent except in poetic necessity, as in the poet's saying:

*So today I drink, not carrying sin from God, nor being an uninvited guest.*

And his saying:

*A mourner informs us of the death of a lord, over whom fingers are cut off from grief.*

As for what is reported from Abū ʿAmr about quiescence, the narrator did not record it accurately from him. Sībawayh related from him that he used to lighten the vowel and make it brief (*ikhtilās*), and this is the truth. Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned something similar and said: explicit quiescence is a solecism (*laḥn*) according to al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, and the expert Basran grammarians. In the reading of Ubayy: ﴿Shall we compel you to it?﴾ with the phrase *min shaṭri anfusinā* (from the side of our selves). It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he read *min shaṭri qulūbinā*, i.e., from its quarter and direction (*min tilqāʾihā wa-jihatihā*). In al-Baḥr it is stated that this is by way of explanation, not as Qur'an, since it contradicts the consonantal text of the codex (*sawād al-muṣḥaf*).

﴿And you are averse to it﴾, i.e., you do not choose it nor reflect upon it. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). Al-Samīn said: it is either a circumstance of the agent or of one of the two objects. It was preferred that it is a circumstance of the addressees' pronoun, and the prepositional phrase was placed first for the sake of the verse-endings (*fawāṣil*). The essence of the answer is: "Inform me: if I am upon a proof whose indication of the soundness of my claim is manifest, but it is hidden from you and not accepted by you, can we compel you to accept it while you turn away from it and do not reflect upon it?" That would not be so, as Shaykh al-Islam explained it. Then he said: its apparent sense indicates that it issued from him, peace be upon him, by way of expressing despair of compelling them and refraining from disputing with them, like His words ﴿and my counsel will not benefit you﴾ etc. But it is to be understood that his intention, peace be upon him, was to turn them away from turning aside from it and to urge them to reflect upon it, by directing the denial indicated by the interrogative hamza to compulsion while they are averse, not to compulsion absolutely.

Our master Saʿdī Jalabī said: the meaning of compulsion here is coercion by killing or the like, not mere obligation, since it is what has in fact occurred. Let this be understood.

He also permitted that by "the proof" is meant the rational proof (*dalīl al-ʿaql*), which is the criterion of excellence. By it individuals of humankind are distinguished from one another, by it honour before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is attached, and by it selection for messengership is made. Holding to it and steadfastness upon it are by being upon it. By its concealment from the disbelievers is meant their failure to perceive that he, peace be upon him, is upon it. By mercy is meant prophethood, whose exclusivity to him, peace be upon him, among them they denied. The meaning is: you claimed that the office of prophethood is attained only by one who has a virtue over all other people, entailing his being singled out for it rather than them. Inform me: if I am distinguished over you by an added excellence and the possession of a virtue from my Lord, and He has given me, in accordance with it, prophethood from Him, so that proof was hidden from you; you did not perceive or attain it, and you did not know my possession of it and my being upon it until now, so that you thought I am like you. While it is established in itself, shall we compel you to accept my prophethood, which follows from them, while you are averse to that?

[p. 41]

It was then said: the interrogation is for the purpose of inducing acknowledgment, and this is most suitable to the situation of disputation. In that case his speech, peace be upon him, is a reply to their doubt, which they embedded in the course of their statement, that he is a human whose utmost status is to be like them, without any superiority over them, and a cutting off of the root of their feeble opinions. End of quotation.

In it: that the meaning of *anulzimukumuhā* is "we compel you to accept my prophethood, which follows from it," is not evident. Moreover, there is room for consideration regarding the matter of "following," as is not hidden. Perhaps his bringing in the condition in the manner he did is by way of accommodation to the listeners' terms, and the attribution of the compelling to the plural pronoun is either for honour, or in consideration that those who follow him, peace be upon him, share that with him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 29:

﴿O my people﴾. He addressed them thus to show gentleness toward them and to draw them on gently. ﴿I do not ask of you any wealth for it﴾, i.e., for the conveying (tabligh) understood from what came before. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the warning (inzar), to singling out God, may He be glorified, in worship, and it has been said that it refers to calling to monotheism (tawhid), and it has been said other than that. All these sayings are close in meaning, meaning: I do not ask of you, in return for that, ﴿wealth﴾ that you would pay to me after your faith, nor a reward for myself in exchange for your guidance. ﴿My reward is only from God﴾, for He, may He be glorified, will reward me for that in the Hereafter, and it is inevitable according to His promise, which is not broken. So by "reward" is meant the reward for conveying the message. It is permissible that what is meant is the reward for obedience in general, and that this is included in it as a primary inclusion. In expressing "wealth" first and "reward" second there is what is not hidden of the superiority of what is with God, may He be exalted, over what is with them. ﴿And I will not drive away those who have believed﴾. It has been said: this is a response to what they hinted at with their saying ﴿And we see not those who follow you except the lowest among us﴾, namely that if the nobles followed him they would agree with them, and that following the poor prevents them from that, as they stated in their saying ﴿Shall we believe in you when the lowest follow you?﴾. So that was a request from them to drive those away and a condition of their faith in him, peace be upon him, on that, out of disdain for being grouped together with them in one row, end of quote. What is related from Ibn Jurayj is that they said to him: O Noah, if you wish that we follow you, then drive these away; otherwise we will not be content that we and they be equal in the matter. This is like what the Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the poor companions (may Allah be pleased with them): Drive these away from you, and we will follow you, for we are ashamed to sit with them in your assembly. So this is a response to what is not mentioned in the noble text, but there is in it a kind of allusion to it. It was read as (bi-ṭāridin) with tanwin. Al-Zamakhshari said: "according to the original", meaning that the active participle, when it has the sense of the present or future, its original form is to govern and not be made genitive. This is the apparent sense of Sibawayh's words. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying: it may be said that the original is the genitive construction, since it is subject to two resemblances: one of them is its resemblance to the imperfect verb, which is resemblance to something other than its kind, and the other is its resemblance to nouns when they take the genitive construction, and attaching it to its own kind is more fitting than attaching it to something other than its kind, end of quote. It may be said, however, that the priority of attaching it to nouns is only valid if the genitive construction in nouns is the original, and it is not so.

﴿Indeed they are meeting their Lord﴾. This is a reason for refraining from driving them away, as if it were said: I will not drive them away nor distance them from my assembly, because they are among the people of nearness, those brought near and successful with God, Exalted is He; and the understanding of success comes through the help of the context, otherwise meeting God is for the successful and others alike. Or it means that they are meeting their Lord, so they will dispute with their driver before Him, and He will punish him for what he did. Whoever takes it to mean that they are, in this world, affirming the meeting with their Lord, certain of it, knowing that they will surely meet Him, so how could I drive them away, has gone against the apparent sense. Moreover, this affirmation is among the consequences of faith. It has also been said that the meaning is: they will meet Him, and He will recompense them for what is in their hearts of sound and firm faith, as has become clear to me; or otherwise, contrary to that, by which you know them from the outward judgment of their affairs at first glance without deep reflection. And what is upon me that I should split open their hearts and learn the secret of that from them, so that I drive them away if the matter is as you claim? In this there is, along with its being based on the premise that the request to drive them away was due to their lack of sincerity and not to considering them lowly, a matter whose state is too clear to be hidden, which is refuted by the certainty of the wrath of God, Exalted is He, being consequent upon driving them away, as will come, God willing.

﴿But I see you as a people who act ignorantly﴾. That is, in every respect in which one should have knowledge, and this includes their ignorance of their station with God, Exalted is He, and of the harm that results from driving them away, and of the feebleness of their opinion in asking for that and in making their faith conditional upon it, and other than that. The choice of the verbal form indicates renewal and continuity, and he used "see" in agreement with their own expression. It is permissible that "ignorance" here means wrongdoing toward another and doing what burdens him, not the blameworthy sense of lack of knowledge, and this is a common meaning, as in his saying:

Ala la yajhalanna ahadun alayna fanajhalu fawqa jahli al-jahilina
(Let no one act ignorantly toward us, lest we act ignorantly beyond the ignorance of the ignorant.)

That is: but I see you as a people who behave foolishly toward the believers by ascribing to them baseness.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 30:

﴿And O my people, who would protect me from Allah?﴾ That is, who would shield me from Him, the Exalted, and ward off the descent of His wrath upon me? The interrogative is for denial: that is, no one would help me against that if I were to drive them away and distance them from me, when they hold such a station and nearness with Him, the Exalted. And in the speech there is what is not hidden of the gravity of the matter of driving them away. ﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾ That is, will you persist in the ignorance you are in, so that you do not take heed of what has been mentioned of their condition, until you know that what you do is far removed from what is right? It has been said: because this reason is independent in a particular way, clearly indicating the obligation to refrain from driving them away, it was set apart from the preceding reasoning and introduced with "O my people."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 31 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And I do not say to you, "With me are the treasuries of Allah"﴾. This begins—according to what many have said—the refutation of the doubts they raised, in detail. This is from the kind of "scattered exposition" (al-nashr al-mushawwash), relying on the listener's knowledge. Something has intervened between their doubts and their answer—according to what al-'Allamah al-Tibi said—because it is an introduction and preparation for the answer. He explained it by saying that his words, ﴿O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord and He has given me mercy from Himself﴾, are an affirmation of his prophethood—meaning, "What I have told you, ﴿that I am to you a clear warner, that you worship none but Allah﴾, is only upon clear evidence affirming my prophethood and the soundness of my call. But it has been hidden from you and blinded to you, to the point that you raised those feeble doubts. Despite that, my concern in what I claim is nothing but guidance. And I do not seek wealth such that I would cling to the wealthy among you and drive away the poor, while you are ignorant of this meaning, in that you say, 'Drive away the poor.' And Allah, glory be to Him, did not send me except to encourage the seeking of the Hereafter and the renunciation of this world. So who will help me if I oppose what I have brought?" Then he proceeded with what he proceeded with. In al-Kashf: his words ﴿O my people, tell me﴾ up to the verse are a general answer to all the doubts, together with the expression that they do not return, in what they throw out, to even minimal reflection. His words ﴿And O my people, I do not ask you﴾ are a completion of the expression and an urging toward what he included of enticement toward what is with him. His words "I am not one who drives away" are an explicit answer to what they implied in their words ﴿And we see none follow you except those who are our lowly ones﴾, of the baseness of the followers, and that, had it not been for their position, following would have been possible—a display of firmness in what he is upon—and that what he brings and issues forth is from a proof from Allah, the Exalted, which suffices him; "and how could he abandon the clear truth for the muddled falsehood?" Then he proceeded to the detailed answer with his words ﴿And I do not say﴾ etc., and this is better than what al-Tibi mentioned. They took this as a reply to their words ﴿And we do not see for you﴾ etc., as if he were saying: my not being followed and my being denied, if it is for your denial of me of the excess of wealth and standing, then I have not claimed that, nor have I said to you that the treasuries of Allah's provision and its possession are with me, such that you dispute with me over it and deny it. Rather, what came from me was the claim of messengership supported by miracles. Perhaps his answer, upon him be peace, concerning that is from the perspective that it is what is meant by it, and what follows from the answer about it, from the perspective that it was also meant for his followers, upon him be peace. And making it an answer to their words ﴿We see you only as a human like us﴾, as al-Tabarsi permitted, is nothing; and taking the treasuries as what we have pointed to is the reliable interpretation.
Page 43
Al-Jubba'i and Abu Muslim said: the intended meaning of them is the capabilities of Allah, the Exalted—i.e., "I do not say to you, when I claim prophethood, that with me are the capabilities of Allah, so that I do what I wish, give what I wish, and withhold what I wish." This is nothing. Similar to it—rather more calamitous and bitter—is the saying of Ibn al-Anbari: the intended meaning of them is the unseen things of Allah, the Exalted, and what is hidden from creation. Ibn al-Khazin made this clause a conjunction with "I do not ask you" etc., and the meaning according to him is: "I do not ask you for wealth in return for it, and I do not say to you, 'With me are the treasuries of Allah which nothing exhausts, so that I call you to follow me for them, to give you from them.'" ﴿Nor do I know the unseen﴾ is conjoined with "with me are the treasuries of Allah," the thing said by the saying, and he mentioned with it the negation, although conjoining to the negated saying is also negated, without an negative particle being mentioned with it—to emphasize the earlier negation and to remind of it, and to remove the possibility that he would not say this whole group. So it does not preclude that one of them be said: that is, "Nor do I say that I know the unseen, so that you deny me as an improbability." And what I mentioned of the claim of prophethood and the warning of punishment is only by revelation and information from Allah, the Exalted, supported by evidence; and the unseen is what has not been revealed and for which no proof stands. Perhaps he, upon him be peace, did not negate the saying of knowledge of the unseen in the manner he did in the earlier and later parts, as an exaggeration in negating this attribute, of which none besides Allah, the Exalted, has any share at all. It is also permissible to conjoin it to "I say": that is, "I do not say to you that, nor claim knowledge of the unseen in my saying, 'I am a clear warner, I fear for you the punishment of a painful day,' so that you hasten to denial and improbability." It is said: it is conjoined to this or that, except that the meaning is "I do not know the unseen until I know that these followed me at first sight without insight and firm conviction"—and his condition is not hidden. It was objected against the first that it is not suitable to the context. Then it is said: "The apparent is that when he claimed prophethood, they asked him about the unseen matters, and said to him, 'If you are truthful, inform us of them.' So he said, 'I claim prophethood by a sign from my Lord, and I know the unseen only by His informing, glory be to Him.' It is not necessary that this be mentioned in the noble composition, just as the request to drive them away is so, ended." In it: the claim of the absence of suitability is not as it should be; and also it is not hidden that there is no indication showing that it is an answer to what was not mentioned. As for the request to drive them away, the contempt is an indication of it in general, and some of the early scholars have explicitly said so, and the like of this is not said from opinion. ﴿Nor do I say, "I am an angel"﴾: a reply to their words ﴿We see you only as a human like us﴾, i.e., I do not say, to promote what I claim of prophethood, "I am an angel," so that you say that to me and deny me. For humanity is not among the impediments of prophethood, but rather among its foundations—meaning, as it has been said: you have taken the loss of these three matters as a pretext for denying me, while the truth is that I do not claim any of that, nor anything connected to any of them. What I claim is connected to the virtues by which the measures of humans differ. It is said: he meant by this, "I do not say: I am a spiritual being, uncreated from male and female, but rather I am only a human like you, so there is no sense in your objecting to me with your saying, 'We see you only as a human like us.'" In both views, there is no evidence in it that the angels are superior to the prophets, peace be upon them, contrary to one who cited it for that and made this a separate statement not a reply to what they had said previously—which has no basis. So reflect.

﴿Nor do I say to those whom your eyes despise﴾: i.e., you belittle them. The original is "tazhri" with a *ta'*, but it was changed to a *dal* due to the assimilation of the *zay* in voicing, since the *ta'* is among the voiceless letters. The root of *izdira'* is disparagement; it is said: *izdarahu* when he disparaged him. The expression with the present tense is for continuity or for relating the situation, since the disparagement has occurred. Ascribing it to the eyes is a metaphor for emphasis, in one opinion, in that it is ascribed to the sense from which the disparagement of anyone cannot be imagined; as if one who does not perceive that nonetheless perceives it. And as an alert that they belittled them at first sight, and by what they witnessed of their shabby condition and scarcity of means, without reflection and contemplation of their meanings and perfections. The return pronoun of the relative clause is omitted, as we have indicated. The *lam* is for the purpose, not for conveying, since otherwise it would have said afterward "yu'tikum" — i.e., "I do not say, out of accommodation to you and yielding to your desire regarding those whom you have deemed lowly and despised for their poverty among the believers,"

﴿"Allah will never give them good"﴾ in this world or in the Hereafter; so perhaps Allah, glory be to Him, will give them the good of both abodes.

﴿Allah knows best what is in their souls﴾: of what they prepare themselves with for receiving that. And in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim: of faith. In it is a justification for conjoining the negation of this saying—which is not something the disbelievers deny, nor something they imagine proceeding from him, upon him be peace, either primarily or by implication—to the negation of those other sayings which are what they deny and imagine proceeding from him, upon him be peace. That is because both negations are a rejection of their false analogy which they held to earlier; for they supposed that prophethood entails the aforementioned matters: claiming angelhood, knowledge of the unseen, and possessing treasuries; and that finding their places and seizing their spoils is not the habit of the lowly. So he, upon him be peace, answered by negating all of that. It is as if he said: I do not say that the existence of those things is among the requirements of prophethood, nor that the absence of wealth and standing is among the barriers to good. He, upon him be peace, limited himself to negating the mentioned saying, although he was certain that Allah, glory be to Him, would give them great good in both abodes, and that they were in firm certainty in faith—following the ways of fairness with the people, and being content with contradicting their words, and guiding them to the path of guidance: that what is fitting for everyone is not to pronounce a judgment except on what he knows with certainty, and to build his affairs on manifest evidence, and not to gamble on what he has no clear proof for. End. And you know that he, upon him be peace, did pronounce with certainty the success of these people in his words ﴿And I am not one to drive away those who believe; indeed they will meet their Lord﴾, on the basis that they are the ones intended by "those who believe," and that what is meant by their meeting their Lord is that they are brought near in the presence of holiness, as one of many has said. Likewise the ruling if the meaning of the relative is whoever is characterized by the attribute of the relative clause in general, since they enter it primarily—because what is asked, explicitly or implicitly, is their driving away. Perhaps the decision at one time and its absence at another is due to what the context requires. That, and that in the disbelievers having supposed that reaching the place of prophethood and seizing its spoils is not the habit of the lowly is a hidden matter, despite the claim that they hinted, with their words ﴿And we see none follow you﴾ etc., which is the likely basis for that supposition, toward requesting their driving away and making their faith dependent on him, upon him be peace, out of disdain for being aligned with them in a single row.

In al-Bahr: the meaning of ﴿And I do not say to those who﴾ etc. is: your belittling them does not diminish their reward with Allah, the Exalted, nor void their wages, and I do not judge them with any of this; rather the judgment in that belongs to the One who knows what is in their souls, and He will recompense them for it. It is said: this is a rejection of their words ﴿And we see none follow you﴾ etc., in the sense: I do not judge concerning them that they will have no good, because you suppose their inner states are not like their outer ones—"Allah knows best what is in their souls." End. And what is in it is not hidden.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi that he interpreted "good" as faith, i.e., "I do not say to those whom your eyes despise that Allah will never give them faith." This was questioned: the apparent meaning is that the relative refers to those followers who were considered lowly, and they are believers in his view; so there is no sense in negating the saying that Allah, the Exalted, has given them faith, to comply with them and yield to their desire.

It was answered: what is meant by this faith is the reliable kind that does not disappear at all, as the expression of it as "good" indicates. They had only attributed to them following at first sight, and meant by that that they believed with a faith that has no stability; and that would be made a rejection of that saying. And "will never give them" is taken to mean "what He has given them"; so it is as if they said: they followed you and believed in you without reflection, and such faith is liable to vanish; they will not persist in it and will apostatize. So he, upon him be peace, rejected them by saying: I do not judge concerning those that Allah, the Exalted, has not given them an enduring faith, and that they will apostatize as you claim. His words, upon him be peace, "Allah knows best what is in their souls," would be a committing of the judgment on that to Allah, the Exalted; or an indication of the grandeur of what Allah, the Exalted, has given them of faith, as one says "Allah the Exalted"

I know best what Zayd suffers from ʿAmr when that which he suffers from him is a great matter that cannot be described. So it is as if it were said: their faith is of great worth and lofty standing, so how can I say that Allah, exalted is He, will not grant them lasting faith? In this there is so much strained and forced reasoning that Allah alone knows it best.

He understood the relative pronoun (alladhina) as referring to people who are extremely despised, other than those [of whom Noah had been speaking], and who had not yet believed. That is: I do not say to those whom your eyes look down upon, and who have not yet believed, that Allah will not grant them success in faith, given that they are in a state of extreme shabbiness of condition and lowliness, which you claim to be an obstacle to good. Allah knows best what is in their souls, by which they become fit to receive the bestowal of success upon them; and this is the basis for that, not the outward conditions, of which I do not speak. ﴿Indeed I, then﴾, that is, if I said that, ﴿am surely of the wrongdoers﴾, by diminishing their rank and reducing their rights, or of those who wrong themselves by that. In this there is an allusion that they are wrongdoers in their looking down upon them and despising them.

It is also possible that "if I said" refers to some of what was mentioned: possessing the treasuries, claiming knowledge of the unseen, being an angel, and denying that Allah, exalted is He, has given those people good. And since these people, because of their great ignorance, need to have it explained to them, as with the earlier statements, that they would thereby be included in the company of the wrongdoers.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 32:

﴿They said: "O Nuh, you have argued with us﴾, i.e., you disputed with us and contended with us. Its root is from jadaltu al-habl (جَدَلْتُ الحَبْلَ), meaning I tightly twisted the rope, and from it comes al-jadil (the twisted cord). Jadaltu al-bina' (جَدَلْتُ البِناءَ) means I made the building firm, and a "durut majdulah" (دِرْعٌ مَجْدُولَةٌ) is a tightly woven coat of mail. Al-ajdal (الأجْدَلُ) is the falcon, the one of firm build, and al-mijdal (المِجْدَلُ) is a palace of firm construction. Contention was called jidal (جِدالًا) because the two disputants seem to twist each of them the other away from his opinion. It has also been said: the original meaning of jidal is wrestling and throwing one's companion down onto al-jadalah (الجَدالَةِ), which is hard ground.

﴿So you have multiplied our argument﴾: this is coordinated (عُطِفَ) with what precedes it, in the sense that you began to dispute with us and prolonged it, or you brought one kind of disputation and then followed it with other kinds. So the fa' (فَ) retains its literal sense, and there is no need to interpret "jadaltana" as "aradta jidalana" (you intended to dispute with us), as the majority said regarding His words, exalted is He: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾. A parallel is "jadala fulan fa-akthara" (so-and-so disputed and multiplied it). Some scholars took the whole of this to be a metaphor (kinayah) for persistence and continuation.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "jadalana" (جَدَلَنا), which, as Ibn Jinni said, is a noun with the meaning of jidal. When he (peace be upon him) overcame them with proof and displayed before them what silenced them, their stratagems were exhausted and their pleas failed them, and they said: ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with, of the punishment hastened﴾. It is also permissible that what is meant by this is the punishment indicated in His words: ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a painful day﴾, on the basis that "the day" does not refer to the Day of Resurrection. "Ma" (مَا) is a relative pronoun, and its returning pronoun is omitted, i.e., "with that which you threaten us with," and in al-Bahr it reads "ta'iduna-hu" (تَعِدْناهُ). It is also permissible that it be a verbal-masdar particle (مَصْدَرِيَّةً), but this involves a degree of artificiality. ﴿If you are among the truthful﴾: in your judgment that the punishment will overtake us if we do not believe in you.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 33:

﴿He said: "Only Allah will bring it upon you, if He wills"﴾. That is, that matter is not up to me, nor is it within my power; rather, it belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, whom you have disbelieved in and whose command you have disobeyed. He will bring it upon you, sooner or later, if His will, which follows wisdom, becomes attached to it. In this there is, as has been said, what is not hidden of making the promised punishment appear terrifying. It is as if it were said: bringing it about is a matter outside the sphere of human powers, and only Allah, exalted is He, does it.

In the use of the glorious, all-comprehensive Name there is emphasis on that terrifying effect. ﴿And you cannot escape﴾, by which He, glory be to Him and exalted, is meant, being unable to repel the punishment or flee from it. The "bi" (ba') is extra, for emphasis, and the nominal sentence indicates continuity; what is meant is the continuation and emphasis of the negation, not the negation of continuity and emphasis. There are similar examples of this.

[Page 46]

**"And my counsel will not benefit you"** (﴿ولا يَنْفَعُكم نُصْحِي﴾). *Nuṣḥ* (sincere counsel) is seeking out a statement or an action that contains good, and it is a comprehensive word. It was also said that it is informing people of the places of error so that they may avoid them, and of the paths of right guidance so that they may follow them. It derives from the expression *naṣaḥtu lahu al-wudd*, meaning "I purified the affection for him," i.e. I made it pure. *Nāṣiḥ al-ʿasal* is its purest part (honey). Or it derives from the expression *naṣaḥtu al-jild*, "I sewed the hide," and *al-nāṣiḥ* is the tailor, while *al-niṣāḥ* is the thread.

ʿIsā ibn ʿUmar al-Thaqafī read *(naṣḥī)* with a fatḥah on the nūn, and it is a verbal noun (maṣdar). According to the reading of the majority, as Abū Ḥayyān said, it may be a verbal noun like *al-shukr* (gratitude), and it may be a noun (ism).

**"If I desire to counsel you"** (﴿إنْ أرَدْتُ أنْ أنْصَحَ﴾). Here "if" (*in*) is a conditional (*sharṭ*) whose apodosis (*jawāb*) has been omitted, because what precedes it indicates it. It is not its apodosis, because of the impossibility of placing the apodosis before the condition, according to the most correct view held by the Basran grammarians. That is: "If you desire that I counsel you, my counsel will not benefit you." The whole sentence is evidence for the apodosis of His, glory be to Him, statement: ﴿إنْ كانَ اللَّهُ يُرِيدُ أنْ يُغْوِيَكُمْ﴾ ("If God desires to lead you astray"). The estimate is: "If God desires to lead you astray, then if I desire to counsel you, my counsel will not benefit you." They regarded the verse as belonging to the category of a conditional clause interposed upon a conditional clause (*iʿtirāḍ al-sharṭ ʿalā al-sharṭ*).

In the commentary on *al-Tashīl* by Ibn ʿAqīl, it is stated that when two conditions follow one another, for example in your saying: "If you come to me, if I promise you, I will do you good," the apodosis belongs to the first, and it suffices without the apodosis of the second. Ibn Mālik claimed that the second condition restricts the first in the manner of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), so that it is as if it were said in the example: "If you come to me while I am promising you, I will do you good." The correct view on this question is that the apodosis belongs to the first, and the apodosis of the second is omitted because of the indication of the second condition and its apodosis. So when you say: "If you enter the house, if you speak to Zayd, if he comes to you, then you are free," then "you are free" is the apodosis of "if you enter the house," and it together with its apodosis indicates the apodosis of "if you speak to him," and "if you speak to him" with its apodosis indicates the apodosis of "if he comes." The indication of the apodosis is an apodosis in meaning, and the apodosis comes later, so the third condition is placed first, and likewise the second. It is as if it were said: "If he comes, then if you speak, then if you enter, then you are free." So he is not freed unless this sequence occurs: his coming, then your speaking, then your entering. This is the doctrine of al-Shāfiʿī, may God have mercy on him.

Al-Jaṣṣāṣ mentioned that there is a difference of opinion on this between Muḥammad and Abū Yūsuf, may God Most High have mercy on them both, and it is not the doctrine of Imam al-Shāfiʿī alone.

Some jurists said: the apodosis belongs to the last, and the last condition with its apodosis is the apodosis of the second, and the second condition with its apodosis is the apodosis of the first. According to this, he is not freed until these occur in this order: entering, then speaking, then coming. Some of them said: when they are combined, manumission occurs without any order. This applies when the successive conditions are without a conjunction. If it is joined with *aw* (or), then the apodosis belongs to one of them without specification, as in: "If you come to me or if you honour Zayd, I will do you good." If it is joined with *wa* (and), then the apodosis belongs to both. If it is joined with *fa* (then), the apodosis belongs to the second, and it with its apodosis is the apodosis of the first, so the *fa* is taken out of the category of conjunction.

Ibn Hishām claimed that there is a question about whether the verse belongs to this category. He said: this is because two conditions do not follow one another with an apodosis after them, as in what you have heard of the examples, and as in the saying of the poet:

*If you call on us for help, if you are terrified,*
*you will find from us strongholds of honour, which generosity adorns.*

Here no apodosis is mentioned, but what is in meaning the apodosis of the first precedes the two conditions. So it should be estimated at its side, and the original would be: "If I desire to counsel you, then my counsel will not benefit you, if God desires to lead you astray." Or the apodosis should be estimated after the two, and then, after that, a precedence should be estimated to the side of the first condition, which has no basis. End of quotation.

Al-Jalāl al-Suyūṭī said that a treatise was composed on this question, and he included it in his gloss on *al-Mughnī* in a fine manner. It is not hidden from you that what is estimated is equivalent in force to what is stated, and that the common usage in the succession of two conditions without a conjunction is that the apodosis comes after them, according to what is heard, so it is estimated in this way and its judgment applies to it.

The discussion of what has preceded includes two different conditions, one of which is the apodosis of the other. The later in mention has been made earlier in meaning, according to what is customary in this question. According to al-Zamakhsharī, as has been said, it is a single restricted conditional, since "will not benefit you" has been made the indication of the apodosis of "if God desires" (﴿إنْ كانَ اللَّهُ يُرِيدُ﴾), and "if I desire" has been made a restriction of that, like the example "If you do me good, I will do you good, if I am able." So reflect.

The discussion is connected with their saying: ﴿قَدْ جادَلْتَنا فَأكْثَرْتَ جِدالَنا﴾ ("You have disputed with us and multiplied our disputation"). It proceeded from him, peace be upon him, as a demonstration of his inability to turn them back from the error they were in, by means of proofs and clear evidences, because of the extreme of their persistence in obstinacy. It also served as notice that what came before from him was only by way of counsel to them and compassion for them, and that he spared no effort in guiding them to the truth and directing them to its clear path. But this will not benefit them when God, glory be to Him, desires to lead them astray. The negation of the benefit of counsel is restricted by His desire, although that desire is certainly realized, to indicate that this counsel accompanies the desire and the concern for it, and to realize the contrast between this and what corresponds to it, namely the desire of God, Most High, to lead them astray.

He limited himself in this to the mere desire of leading astray, not the act of leading astray itself, by not saying "if God leads you astray," as an exaggeration in showing the overwhelming power of His majesty, glory be to Him. For this indicates that his counsel, accompanied by concern for it, will not profit them at the mere desire of God, Most High, to lead them astray, so how much less when that is realized and created in them. The addition of *kāna* (was) is to indicate that God's desire precedes in time just as it precedes in rank, and to indicate its renewal and continuation.

Before this statement he placed what relates to their saying: ﴿فَأْتِنا بِما تَعِدُنا﴾ ("So bring us what you promise us"), from His statement: ﴿إنَّما يَأْتِيكم بِهِ اللَّهُ إنْ شاءَ﴾ ("Only God will bring it to you, if He wills"), as a reply to them from the very beginning, and as a recording against them of the descent of the punishment, together with the connection of the answer to the question. This is what our master Shaykh al-Islam said.

Then, "if I desire" (*in aradtu*), if it is kept in the future sense, does not contradict his having counselled them in the past. It was also said that it is a concession to them for the sake of strengthening the argument, because they claimed that what he did was not counsel, since if it were counsel it would have been accepted from him. The *lām* in "to you" (*lakum*) is not for emphasis, as might be thought, because the verb is transitive by itself, as in the saying:

*I counselled the sons of ʿAwf, but they did not accept my messenger,*
*and my messages did not succeed with them.*

This is because al-Ṣiḥāḥ says that it is more eloquent with the *lām*.

In the verse there is evidence that God's desire may be related to leading astray, and that acting contrary to His desire, glory be to Him, is impossible. Otherwise the conditional statement, which indicates that the apodosis necessarily follows the condition, would not be true. The Muʿtazilah fell into confusion over it and differed in its interpretation. It was said: ﴿يُغْوِيَكُمْ﴾ means "destroy you," from *ghawā al-faṣīl* when a suckling calf is bloated from excessive drinking of milk and so perishes. Al-Farrāʾ and others narrated the use of *al-ghawy* in the sense of destruction, but Makkī denied it.

It was also said: leading astray is a metaphor for its punishment, that is, "if God desires to punish your leading the creation astray and misguiding them."

It was also said: the people of Noah believed that God, Most High, desired to lead them astray, so he, peace be upon him, presented that as a matter of astonishment and denial, meaning: "My counsel will not benefit you if the matter is as you claim."

It was also said: he called the abandonment of compelling them, and leaving them to their own affairs, "leading astray" as a metaphor.

It was also said: *in* is a negation, meaning "God did not desire to lead you astray," and the negation of that is evidence of the negation of leading astray. In that case "my counsel will not benefit you" and what follows is a statement from him, peace be upon him, to them, and a consolation for himself concerning them, because he saw their persistence and their continuation in disbelief. But it is not hidden what this involves of contradicting the apparent meaning known in usage, and of committing what should not be committed in the speech of the Mighty King.

Some people objected to the argument that a conditional statement does not indicate that the condition occurs or is possible, so the argument is not complete and there is no need for interpretation or for debate. It was answered that the context rejects this, since there is no benefit in merely supposing it. If they wish to reduce it to an exceptive syllogism (*qiyās istithnāʾī*), then either the antecedent is affirmed, which is what is sought, or the negation of the consequent is affirmed, which contradicts the reality, since the benefit is not achieved.

In sum, the verse is very clear in support of what the People of the Sunnah held, and God, glory be to Him, is the Giver of success. ﴿هُوَ رَبُّكُمْ﴾ ("He is your Lord"), that is, your Creator and the Owner of your affairs, ﴿وإلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ ("and to Him you will be returned"), so that He will surely requite you for your deeds.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 35:

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "It means Nuh, peace be upon him." That is, "Rather, do the people of Nuh say that Nuh invented what he brought, attributing it to Allah, Mighty and Majestic?" (Say), O Nuh, ﴿"If I have invented it"﴾ by mere supposition,
[p. 48]
﴿"then upon me is my crime."﴾ That is, its consequence. It is either with an elided modifier (muda), or a metonymy of the cause for the effect (tajawwuz bi-al-sabab 'an al-musabbab). The crime (al-ijram) was explained as the earning of sin, and it is the verbal noun of ajram, and it came in a rare form (ala qillat jurm). Among its examples is the poet's words:

"An outcast of his clan and a hostage to sin, for what my hand committed and my tongue uttered."

It was read (ajrami) with a fathah on the hamzah, which, as al-Nahhas said, is the plural of jurm (sin). Al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam raised a difficulty about the conditional clause (al-shartiyyah), since the supposed invention here is in the past tense, while the conditional is by the consensus (ijma') of the Arabic grammarians purely for the future (al-istiqbal). He answered that what is meant, as Ibn al-Siraj said, is: "If it is established that I invented it, then upon me is my crime," in accordance with what has been said about the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿"If I had said it, You would have known it"﴾ ﴿"and I am innocent of what you commit"﴾, that is, of your crime in attributing the invention to me. It has been said: the original is "If I invented it, then upon me is the punishment for my invention," but that is an impossible supposition. "And I am innocent of your inventing," that is, of your ascribing to me the invention. He turned away from that for the sake of incorporation (idmaj), since they are criminals, and the matter is reversed. The particle (ma) was taken as a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), rather than a relative pronoun (mawsulah), because the relative pronoun would require the awkward deletion of its returning pronoun, and because that is what fits his words "ijrami" earlier. What Ibn 'Abbas's statement implies, that the verse is part of the story of Nuh, peace be upon him, and concerns him, is the apparent meaning, and it is the view of the majority. From Muqatil it is reported that it concerns the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, with the polytheists of Makkah, that is: "Rather, do the polytheists of Makkah say that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, invented the report of Nuh?" It has been said: it seems that it was placed within the course of the story when a portion of it is being narrated, in order to verify its reality, to affirm its occurrence, and to excite the listeners to hear it, especially since he had recounted a part of it concerning what took place between him, peace be upon him, and his people by way of disputation, while a separate part remained concerning their punishment. It is not hidden that this view is far-fetched, even if it is justified in the manner that it is. In al-Kashshaf it is said: that its being about the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, is more apparent and more fitting than its being part of the story of Nuh, peace be upon him, because ﴿"Or do they say, 'He has invented it'?"﴾ is like a repetition of His, glory be to Him, words: ﴿"Or do they say, 'He has invented it'?"﴾, indicating complete obstinacy, and that such a thing, after the telling of the story in this inimitable style, is not fitting to be ascribed to invention. So it came as an increase of denial upon denial, as if it were said: "Rather, even with this clarification, do they still say 'he invented it'?" This is like the parenthetical insertion of His, glory be to Him, words in Surat al-Ankabut: ﴿"And if you deny, then peoples before you have denied"﴾, which explained the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, according to one of the two views. End of quotation. I do not regard it as reliable.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 36:

﴿And it was revealed to Noah: "Indeed, none of your people will believe except those who have already believed."﴾ This is a declaration to him, peace be upon him, that they will not believe, and an announcement that no one remains among them whose faith can be expected. Ishaq ibn Bishr and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Noah, peace be upon him, used to strike [people] and then wrap himself in felt, and he would be placed in his house, and they would think that he had died. Then he would come out and call them [to faith]. It happened that a man came to him with his son, and he was leaning on a staff. [The man] said: "O my son, look at this old man, let him not deceive you." [The son] said: "O father, let me have the staff." So he took the staff and said: "Set me on the ground." So he set him down, and [the son] walked toward him and struck him, wounding him with a severe wound on his head, and the blood flowed. Noah, peace be upon him, said: "My Lord, You see what Your servants do to me. If You have any need of Your servants, then guide them. And if it is otherwise, then grant me patience until You judge, and You are the best of judges." Then God Most High revealed to him and made him despair of the faith of his people, and informed him that there remained, in the loins of men and the wombs of women, no believer. And He, glorified is He, said: "O Noah, indeed he will not believe," and so on.

As for the meaning of "those who have already believed," it has been said: it refers to those who persisted in faith, and persistence carries the ruling of coming into being, which is why if someone swears he will not wear this garment while he is wearing it, and he does not take it off immediately, he is considered to have broken the oath. It has also been said: the meaning is "except those who have prepared themselves for faith and from whom faith is expected," and the apparent meaning is not intended, for otherwise the meaning would be "except those who have believed, for they will believe." It has been objected to this view that, along with its remoteness,

[page 49]

it implies that some of the people will believe after this, which contradicts His despairing him of their faith. It may be said that the intended meaning is the apparent one, and the exception is in the manner of the exception in His saying, "and that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed," according to what many have said. Thus the statement conveys despair in its most complete and eloquent form, meaning: none of your people will newly bring about faith and attain it afterward, except those who have already brought it about and attained it before. This is impossible, because it involves attaining what is already attained and bringing about what is already brought about. So the bringing about of faith and its attainment afterward is something that does not occur at all. In the Shihabi glosses it is said: if it were said that the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), and that the meaning is "no one will believe after that except these," that would be an eloquent meaning, so reflect upon it. Abu al-Barham recited "wa-awha" in the active voice, and "annahu" with a kasra on the hamza, according to the Basran grammarians by assuming an implied verb of saying, and according to the Kufan grammarians by treating "awha" as "qala" (said). Those who permit the obligation of what cannot be borne (taklif bima la yutaq) have used this verse as evidence.

﴿So do not grieve over what they have been doing.﴾ That is: do not take on distress and do not grieve over what they were engaged in of denial, mockery, and harm during this long period, for the time of retribution against them has arrived.

﴿And construct the ark under Our eyes﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "so do not grieve" (فَلا تَبْتَئِسْ). It was said that the imperative is for obligation (wujub), since there is no way to preserve the soul from drowning except by it, so it is obligatory just as preserving the soul is obligatory. It was also said that it is for permissibility (ibahah), but this is nothing. The definite article in "al-fulk" (the ark) is either generic (lil-jins) or referential (lil-ʿahd), on the basis that it had been revealed to him, peace be upon him, beforehand that God, glorified is He, would destroy them by drowning and would save him and those with him by means of something he would make by God's command, having such-and-such characteristics and such-and-such a name. The bāʾ (ba) is for accompaniment (mulabasah), and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥal) relative to the subject. "Eyes" (aʿyun) is literally the organ, and this is used figuratively (tamthil), as if God, glorified is He, has eyes that watch over him from the transgression of the disbelievers and from deviation in the craft. The plural is for emphasis (mubalaghah). It has departed from its meaning of paucity through its being in construct form, as it was said, and it is meant to denote abundance; in this case it strengthens the emphatic sense. Some claimed that "eyes" means "watchers" (ruqaba'), and that in this there is one of the most eloquent types of tajrid (abstraction), namely that they derive from a thing itself another like it in its attribute, for emphasis on its perfection, as Abu ʿAli recited:

"The sons of Marwan unjustly spilled our blood,
and in God, if they do not act justly, is a just judge."

Here, from the Essence of the All-Preserver (al-Muhaymin), a group of watchers has been abstracted, while He, glorified is He, is Himself the Watcher. It was also said that the association with the eye is a kinaya (metonymy) for protection, and the association with "eyes" in the plural is a kinaya for the perfection of protection and the intensity of it. A parallel to this is "spreading the hand" and "spreading both hands": the former is a kinaya for generosity, and the latter for intensifying it. It was also permitted that the intended meaning is complete protection, by way of majaz mursal (metonymy of the general sense), since protection is among the necessary consequences of the organ. It was also said: what is meant by "Our eyes" is Our angels, whom We have made as eyes over the places of your protection and assistance; the plural in this case is on its literal sense, not for emphasis. It is understood from the practice of some of them that this is among the mutashabih (ambiguous verses), and discussion of this is well known. In al-Durr al-Manthur, under the explanation of this verse, al-Bayhaqi related on the authority of Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah who said: "Whatever God, blessed and exalted is He, has described Himself with in His Book, its recitation is its explanation; it is not for anyone to explain it in Arabic or in Persian." Abu Talhah ibn Musarrif recited "bi-aʿyunnā" (بَأعْيُنّا) with idgham (assimilation of the two nūns), and "wa-wahyinā ilayka kayfa taṣnaʿuhā wa-taʿlīminā" (ووَحْيِنا إلَيْكَ كَيْفَ تَصْنَعُها وتَعْلِيمِنا), meaning: by Our revelation to you of how to make it, and by Our teaching. Isḥaq ibn Bishr and Ibn ʿAsakir related on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he, peace be upon him, did not know how to make the ark, so God, exalted is He, revealed to him: "Make its head like the head of a rooster, its breast like the breast of a bird, and its tail like the tail of a rooster; make for it doors in its side, and fasten it with dusur (planks/nails)." He was commanded to coat it with pitch, and there was no pitch on the earth, so God, exalted is He, caused a spring of pitch to gush forth for him, where he carved it, boiling in a bubbling until it coated it. In this report it is also said that God, exalted is He, sent Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, who taught him its craft. It was also said: the angels, peace be upon them, were teaching him.

[Page 50]

﴿And do not address Me concerning those who have done wrong﴾, meaning: do not argue with Me about them, and do not call upon Me to ward off punishment from them. In this there is an emphasis that is not present if it had been said, "And do not call upon Me concerning them." Since it contains what hints at what it entails, he confirmed the reason, saying: ﴿indeed they are to be drowned﴾, meaning: they are decreed to be drowned, the decree has already passed and the pen has dried, so there is no way to avert it. The apparent meaning is that the relative term (al-mawsul, "those who") refers to whoever of his people did not believe, absolutely. It was also said that what is meant is his wife and his son Kanaʿan, but this is nothing.

*Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 38:*

﴿And he was constructing the ark﴾. This is a narration of a past situation, to bring its wondrous form to mind.

It has been said: its implied sense is "and he took up, or set about, constructing the ark."
