According to what is narrated from Qatadah, Ikrimah and al-Kalbi, it was made of sajwood (*saj*), which he planted himself and did not cut until it reached a length of four hundred cubits (*dhira'*), the cubit being measured to the shoulder, over forty years, according to what is narrated from Sulayman al-Farisi. It has also been said that he left it to grow for twenty years. It has been said that he remained a hundred years planting, cutting and drying it. Amr ibn al-Harith said: he did not plant it, but rather cut it from Mount Lebanon.

From Ibn Abbas it is narrated that it was made of shimshad wood, and that he cut it from Mount Lebanon. It has also been said that it is mentioned in the Torah (*Tawrah*) that it was made of pine. It is narrated that Sam, Ham and Yafith (Japheth) used to carve with him. In another narration, peace be upon him, there were also people with him whom he had hired to carve. It is mentioned that its length was three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height above the sky thirty.

Ibn Jarir and others narrated from al-Hasan that he said: its length was one thousand two hundred cubits and its width six hundred cubits, and he made a door for it in its middle. Its construction was completed, according to what is narrated from Mujahid, in three years.

From Ka'b al-Ahbar: forty years. It has also been said: sixty years; it has been said: a hundred years; and it has been said: four hundred years. There is disagreement as to the place where he built it. It has been said: in Kufa; it has been said: in India; it has been said: in the land of al-Jazirah; and it has been said: in the land of Syria. The vessel of the reports, in establishing the matter, in my view, is not fit to be ridden in, since it is not free of defect. So the proper course for one who does not incline toward excess is to believe that peace be upon him made the ark as God the Exalted related in His Book, and not to delve into the measure of its length, width and height, what wood he made it of, how long he took to complete its work, or other matters which the Book did not explain and the authentic Sunnah did not clarify.

This is on the expression "he was constructing" (*yasna'*), as has been said, in keeping with the continuity understood from the clause in the accusative of circumstance (*hal*) referring to his pronoun, namely God the Exalted's words: ﴿And whenever a company of his people passed by him, they mocked him﴾, that is, they ridiculed him for his construction of the ship. This was either because they did not know it, nor how it was to be used, so they marvelled at it and mocked him. What supports their not knowing it is what is narrated from Ibn Abbas: that when God the Exalted said to him, "Construct the ark," he said, "O Lord, what is the ark?" He said, "A house of wood that moves upon the surface of the water." He said, "O Lord, and where is the water?" He said, "Indeed I am, over what I will, Powerful." Or it was because he, peace be upon him, was building it in a desert far from water, and they would laugh and say, "O Noah, you have become a carpenter after you were a prophet." This is based on the assumption that the ship was known among them. What supports this is what Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim narrated and graded as sound, and al-Dhahabi graded as weak, from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Noah had remained among his people a thousand years less fifty years, calling them, until at the end of his time he planted a tree, and it grew tall and spread in every direction. Then he cut it and began to shape it into a ship. They would see him and ask him, and he would say, 'I am making it a ship.' They would mock him and say, 'You are making a ship on dry land? How will it sail?' He would say, 'You will soon know.'" The hadith...

And most of them, as Ibn Atiyyah said, hold that they had never seen a ship at all, nor did one exist at that time. It is mentioned in the books of the earliest matters (*al-awwaliyyat*) that Noah, peace be upon him, was the first to make a ship. The truth is that there is no certainty about this.

"*Kull*" (every, whenever) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and "*ma*" is a temporal verbal (*masdariyyah*) particle, meaning: every time of passing, and the governing element for it is its response, which is "they mocked."

God the Glorified's words: ﴿He said, "If you mock us, then indeed we mock you"﴾ is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), as if a questioner asked, "What did Noah, peace be upon him, do when they reached this extent of mockery?" And it was said: he said, "If you mock us for this work and for taking up the means of deliverance from the punishment, then indeed we mock you for your turning away from averting it through faith and obedience, and for your persistence in disbelief and sins, and your exposing yourselves to the causes of the descent of God the Exalted's wrath, of which your mocking us and your ridiculing us is part." The word "mocking" is applied to them in its literal sense, and to him, peace be upon him, by way of mutual correspondence (*mushakalah*), since such mockery does not befit the prophets, peace be upon them. Some interpreted it as "making someone appear foolish," which is a metaphor, since it is a cause of mockery, so "mockery" is used and its cause is meant.

It has also been said that his mockery was for their recompense, being of the same kind as their conduct, and so it is not reprehensible, and there is no need to resort to a sense contrary to the apparent meaning. The plural pronoun in "*minna*" (from us) is either because their mockery of him, peace be upon him, was also mockery of the believers, or because they used to mock them as well, but he contented himself with mentioning their mockery of him, peace be upon him. For this reason, all of them were subject to recompense in the words "we mock you," so the speech is balanced on both sides.

The comparison in God the Glorified's words, ﴿as you mock﴾, is either in mere certainty and occurrence, or in the recurrence and repetition, as they mocked, company after company. It has been said: there is no objection to taking the apparent meaning, and there is no harm in that, since it concerns recompense. From here some have said that the verse is evidence for the permissibility of responding to the likes of the ignorant and the foolish with the same kind of act, and God the Exalted's words support this: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾; ﴿and the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾; ﴿and if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾, and so on. The apparent meaning is that both acts are occurring in the present.

Ibn Jurayj said: the meaning is, "If you mock us in this world, then we will mock you in the Hereafter." It has also been said: in this world, at the time of drowning, and in the Hereafter, at the time of burning. Al-Tabarsi said: what is meant by "we mock you" according to this is "we will repay you for your mockery," or "we will gloat over you at your drowning and your burning." In this there is some obscurity. He also allowed that the governing element of "*kullama*" (whenever) may be "he said," which is the response, and the clause "they mocked" may be an attribute of "a company," or a substitute for "passed by" as a substitute of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*), since their passing was for mockery. So the fact that mockery is not the same as passing, nor a kind of it, does no harm. Abu Hayyan considered that this rules out the substitution, but this is not so. On this permission it follows that this statement was repeated by him, peace be upon him, and this is evident. As for the parsing, it has been said: there was no repetition, rather he answered them with it on some occasions. It is preferred on the ground that the purpose is to show the extreme of their harm to him, peace be upon him, and his endurance of their hurt, not his hastening to answer whenever (*kullama*) there occurred from them what hurt him of speech. It may be said that there is in this an indication that, after he despaired of their faith, he no longer cared about provoking them, and for this reason he threatened them with an eloquent threat in his words:

*[Page 51]*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 39:

﴿So you will soon know who will receive a punishment that will disgrace him﴾, that is, expose him, or humiliate him, or destroy him; these statements are close in meaning. The punishment intended here is drowning. ﴿And there will descend upon him﴾, descending as a due debt descends when it is due, ﴿a lasting punishment﴾, that is, a constant one, which is the punishment of the Fire. And (who) (man) refers to them. It is a relative pronoun in the position of the object of knowing (ʿilm), and here it means recognition (maʿrifa), so it transitively takes one object.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya permitted that what is meant is knowing (ʿilm) in its transitive form taking two objects, but he restricted it to one. Abu Hayyan (in al-Bahr) criticized him, saying that it is not permissible to omit the second object by restriction, because its original form is the predicate of a subject, and not by abbreviation here, because there is no evidence for its omission.

Page 52

It was also said: (man) is an interrogative, the subject, and the clause after it is the predicate; the subject-predicate clause is suspended from it, serving in place of the object or the two objects. It was said: Since the basis of their mockery was their considering him foolish in undertaking the grave hardships to avert what hardly falls under soundness in their view, namely the flood, and in bearing the hardships of building the ship, and they regarded this as a punishment, it was said, after their considering him foolish: ﴿So you will soon know﴾ etc., meaning: what I am undertaking does not involve a punishment that will befall me. ﴿So you will soon know who will be punished﴾. Knowledge has indeed reached its target after their considering him foolish, end quote. This is evident if the mockery attributed to him, peace be upon him, is understood as considering him foolish.

It may perhaps be applied even if the mockery is taken in its apparent sense, with slight effort; so understand. The description of the punishment as disgracing is because mockery and derision customarily entail shame and disgrace. The mention of the lasting punishment descending is for the sake of exaggeration in the threat. There is in this much figurative language that is not hidden. Restricting it to the due debt and expressing the first with "coming" is the utmost eloquence. Al-Zahrawi reported that it was also read as yaḥull with a damma on the ḥa'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 40 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Until, when Our command came﴾: a limit (ghayah) for His words, glorified is He, ﴿he was building the ark﴾. The word *hatta* (until) is either a preposition (jarr) attached to it, and *idha* (when) is merely a temporal adverb, or it is an inceptive (ibtida'iyya) particle, introducing a conditional sentence (shart) and its response (jawab), and the clause has no grammatical position (mahall) in the i'rab (grammatical analysis). The circumstantial phrase (hal) of what occurred in between has already been pointed out. The word *amr* (command) is either the singular of *awamir* (commands), meaning the command to board the ship, or to let the water gush forth, or to the clouds to send down rain, or to the angels, peace be upon them, to act upon what is intended, or the like. Or it is the singular of *umur* (affairs), meaning the matter, namely the descent of the punishment upon them. ﴿And the tannur boiled over﴾: that is, water gushed out of it and rose up violently, just as a cooking pot boils over when it bubbles, and there is in this a metaphor (isti'ara) that is not hidden. The *tannur* (oven) here is, according to the majority, the bread oven. According to what is narrated from al-Hasan and Mujahid, it was an oven belonging to Hawwa' (Eve), in which she baked bread, and then it came to Nuh, peace be upon him, and it was made of stone. It was also said that it is an oven in Kufa, at the place of its mosque, on the right of one who enters from the side facing the Gate of Kinda, and this is reported in a narration from Ali, may Allah honour his face. It was also said: an oven in India; it was said: at the spring (ayn) of Warda, in the land of the Jazira al-Umariyya or in the land of Sham. It was also said: the intended meaning is not a specific oven but the genus, and the meaning is that water boiled over from the ovens. In this there is a wondrous power that is not hidden. There is no contradiction between this and His words, glorified is He: ﴿and We caused the earth to gush forth with springs﴾, since it is possible that the gushing (tafjir) was other than the boiling (fawaran), so the boiling was for the oven and the gushing for the earth. Or the intended meaning of the earth is the places of the ovens. Its morphological form (wazn) is *taf'ul* from *nur* (light/fire), and its original form was *tanuwur*, so the first waw was changed to a hamza because it was vowelled with a damma, then it was deleted for ease, then the nun was doubled as a substitute for what was deleted. This was transmitted from Tha'lab. Abu Ali al-Farisi said: its form is *fa'ul*. It was also said: according to this, it is a foreign word (a'jami) with no derivation, and its root is *tanara*, and there is no nun before a ra' in the speech of the Arabs. *Narjis* (narcissus) is also arabicized. The well-known view is that it is among the words in which the Arabic and the foreign languages agree, like *al-sabun* (soap) and *al-sammur* (sable). It is reported from Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and al-Zuhri that *al-tannur* here means the surface of the earth. From Qatada it is reported that it means the most elevated place of it, that is its highest and loftiest part. Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and others narrated from Ali, may Allah honour his face, that it means the dawn breaking (tanwir al-subh). The apparent meaning is that it was not used in the foreign language with these last meanings. He also allowed that the boiling of the tannur may be a metaphor for the appearance of the punishment and the intensity of the terror, and this is like what came in the report, *hamiya al-watis* (the furnace has become hot), as a metaphor for the intensity of war. There is not much difference in meaning between the two sentences, and it is a good meaning, far from what the reports have brought. ﴿We said: carry in it﴾: that is, in the ship. He made the pronoun feminine because it refers to the ship (safina). The sentence is either a resumption (isti'naf) or the response (jawab) of *idha*. ﴿Of every﴾: *ayy* (any) of every kind of animals that benefits those who are saved from drowning and their offspring afterwards, and the custom had not been that they be created without a male and female.

*Page 53*

The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa-l-majrur) is connected to *ihmil* (carry), or to an omitted word that stands as a circumstantial phrase (hal) of its object, namely His words, glorified is He: ﴿two of each pair﴾. *Zawjayn* (two) is the dual of *zawj* (pair/mate), and what is meant by it is the one paired with another of its kind, so the male is a mate (zawj) for the female just as she is a mate for him. It may be applied to both of them together, but this is not the intended meaning, for otherwise it would follow that he should carry four of every kind. So that this is not intended, it was described by His words, may He be exalted: ﴿two﴾. The essential meaning is: carry a male and a female of every kind of animal. The majority read *min kull zawjayn* with the genitive construction (idafa), so *ithnayn* according to this is the object of *ihmil*, and *min kullin zawjayn* is a circumstantial phrase of it. If it were postponed, it would be an attribute (sifa) of it, that is: carry two of each pair, that is a kind male and a kind female. It was also said: *min* is redundant (za'ida), and what follows it is the object of *ihmil*, and *ithnayn* is an attribute (na't) of *zawjayn*, based on the permissibility of the redundant *min* in an affirmative sentence (mujab). Then what we mentioned in the explanation of the generality is what some scholars inclined to, and some included the insects and birds in it. It is mentioned that it is reported that he, peace be upon him, made three decks (butun) for the ship. He carried in the lowest deck the wild beasts, the predators and the insects. In the middle deck he carried the animals and livestock, and he and those with him boarded the uppermost deck, together with what they needed of provisions. He also carried with him the body of Adam, peace be upon him, and placed it as a partition between the men and the women. This carrying was by a bequest from him, peace be upon him, which his descendants inherited until it reached Nuh, peace be upon him. What contradicts this division is what is reported: that the lowest tier was for the wild animals, the middle for food, and the uppermost for him, peace be upon him, and for those who believed. Some scholars went to excess in the generality and included what is not of the genus of animals, and it is supported by what Ishaq ibn Bishr and others narrated from Ali, may Allah honour his face, in a raised (marfu') report: "that Nuh, peace be upon him, carried with him in the ship from all kinds of trees." And by what Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: Nuh, peace be upon him, was commanded to carry with him from every pair two, so he carried from dates the *ajwa* and the *lawn*.

Al-Nasa'i narrated from Anas ibn Malik that Shaytan disputed with Nuh, peace be upon him, over a vine stalk. He said: "This is mine." Nuh said: "It is mine." They agreed that Nuh would have a third of it and Shaytan two-thirds of it. One does not usually rely on reports of this kind when they are examined closely. Among what was carried with them in the ship is what Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The people of the ship were troubled by the mouse, so the lion sneezed, and from its nostrils came out two cats, a male and a female, and they ate the mice, except what Allah, may He be exalted, willed to remain of them. They were also troubled by the filth of the people of the ship, so the elephant sneezed, and from its nostrils came out two pigs, a male and a female, and they ate the filth of the people of the ship. In the narration of al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul*, and Ibn Jarir and others, from him: Nuh, peace be upon him, complained to Allah, may He be exalted, about the mice gnawing the ropes of the ship. Allah revealed to him, so he wiped the forehead of the lion and two cats came out. He complained about dung in the ship, so He, glorified is He, revealed to him, and he wiped the tail of the elephant and two pigs came out, and they ate the dung.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the chain of Zayd ibn Aslam from his father, in a raised report: "The people of the ship complained about the mouse, saying: 'The little rat (fuwaysiqa) ruins our food and our goods.' So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed to the lion, and it sneezed, and the cat came out of it, and the mouse hid from it." The pig is not mentioned in it, and what is understood from it, with what it contains, is that the cat was not present at the carrying. Among those who were first is that the cat and the pig did not exist. Some reports contradict this: Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih who said: When Allah, may He be exalted, commanded Nuh, peace be upon him, to carry, he said: "How shall I deal with the lion and the cow? How shall I deal with the she-goat and the wolf? How shall I deal with the pigeon and the cat?" Allah, may He be exalted, said: "Who put enmity between them?" He said: "You, my Lord." He said: "Then I will bring them together so that they do not harm one another." What lies between this and the first division is not hidden either. The reports about the lion also differ. In one report, his companions, peace be upon him, said: "How can we be at ease when the lion is with us?" So Allah, may He be exalted, afflicted it with fever, and that was the first fever that descended to the earth. In another report, it used to harm them in the ship, so fever was cast upon it so that it would occupy itself with itself. In another, that when he, peace be upon him, was commanded to carry, he said: "My Lord, how about the lion and the elephant?" He, glorified is He, said to him: "I will cast fever upon both of them, and it is heavy." In another, from Abu Ubayda, that when he, peace be upon him, was commanded to carry, he could not carry the lion until fever was cast upon it, so he carried it and brought it in. It is not hidden that some of these indicate that the casting of the fever was before entering, and some that it was after. What makes casting fever unnecessary afterwards is the repelling of the harm of joining it with the human, as He joined together some of what has passed with others. Perhaps the repelling of harm by fever rather than by joining is, if it is correct, a wisdom, but it is not apparent to us. Some reports indicate that with him, peace be upon him, in the ship were some jinn, and in some of them that Iblis, may the curse be upon him, was also there.

From Ibn Abbas: when Allah, may He be exalted, wished to make the donkey enter the ship, Nuh took hold of the donkey's ears and Iblis took hold of its tail. Nuh pulled it and Iblis pulled it. Nuh, peace be upon him, said: "Enter, Satan," and the donkey entered and Iblis entered with it. When the ship set sail, he sat at its stern singing. Nuh said to him: "Woe to you! Who gave you permission?" He said: "You did." He said: "When?" He said: "When you said to the donkey: 'Enter, Satan,' so I entered with your permission." In another narration from him: Nuh, peace be upon him, said to the donkey: "Woe to you, enter, even if Satan is with you." It was a word that passed upon his tongue, so Satan entered with him.

Ibn Asakir narrated from Ata that the accursed one came to board the ship, and Nuh, peace be upon him, pushed him away. He said: "O Nuh, I have been reprieved, and you have no way over me." So he knew that he was truthful, and he ordered him to sit upon the rattan (khayzuran) of the ship. Its outward meaning contradicts what is narrated from Ibn Abbas. They differed as to how the animals were gathered although they were scattered across the regions of the earth. It was said: they sensed the punishment, so they gathered together. From al-Zuhri: Allah, may He be exalted, sent a wind which brought to him from every pair two of the birds, the predators, the wild animals and the cattle.

From Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with them both: Allah, may He be exalted, sent Jibril, peace be upon him, who gathered them, and he began to strike the pairs with his hands, so his right hand would fall upon the male and his left upon the female, and he would bring them into the ship, until he had brought in the number that Allah, may He be exalted, had commanded. Ishaq ibn Bishr and others narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit that a female goat (ma'iza) disobeyed him, peace be upon him, so he pushed her by her tail, and therefore it was broken, and her private parts appeared. A ewe passed by and entered, so he wiped its tail and covered its private parts.

In the books of reports there are many of these narrations, from which wonder is required. As for me, I believe only that Allah, whose power is exalted, created the female goat and the ewe from before in the form they have today, and that He, glorified is He, did not create the cat from the lion, although it resembles it in form, nor the pig from the elephant, although there is some resemblance between them, as we witnessed in the year the elephant came to Baghdad. Had the elephant been required to eat dung, it would have been more pleasing to the people of the ship than the addition of a pig to it. And more pleasing to them than all of that is that there be no one in the ship except themselves, or that there be one animal from whose sneezing there would be created for them what they want of animals and what they need afterwards.

What the heart inclines to is that the Flood was not a general one, as some have held, and that he, peace be upon him, was not commanded to carry what the custom has been for its generation from the putrefaction of the earth, such as mice and insects. Rather he was commanded to carry what he and those with him would need when they were saved from drowning, lest they lose it and undertake the hardship of bringing it from the regions the drowning had not reached. So it is as if it were said: "We said: carry in it of everything you need when you are saved, two of each pair." And if we say that the drowning was general, we also say: he, peace be upon him, was not charged with carrying anything of what comes into being from putrefaction, but was charged with carrying what reproduces from among the animals for the benefit of the survival of the species. And the ship was in such a condition that

*Page 55*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 40 (part 2 of 2):

It is customary, or the miracle and power of Allah, Exalted is He, is too great to be constrained by that. Even if it is said that the generality [of the command to load the animals] is meant in a way that leaves some mountains [standing], it is permissible to say: he, peace be upon him, carried only what has no escape [from the flood] and whose loss would harm his community. And if it is said that the generality is absolute, and that he, peace be upon him, carried into the ship only what the ship could customarily accommodate, of what he needed, so that his companions would not be distressed by the total loss of it, as human nature requires, and that whatever was beyond that drowned, nevertheless Allah, whose power is exalted, created a counterpart of what had drowned afterwards, in the same manner in which He had done before. That is not strange from One whose command is between the Kaf and the Nun (the divine word kun, "Be"), may His majesty be exalted and His dominion be great.

That said, the reason he mentioned that [the loading of the animals] before his family and the rest of the believers is said to be: because he was engaged in the loading that was commanded, since it requires him, peace be upon him, to be personally involved in distinguishing one kind from another and specifying the pairs. As for humans, they enter the ship by their own choice, so the meaning of "loading" is lighter in their case. Or it is because that [kind of animal] is loaded through the direct handling of humans, and they enter it only after he has loaded them. It is also possible that the precedence [of mentioning the animals] was to preserve the noble arrangement of the text from being scattered. Whatever the case, His words, glorified is He: ﴿and your family﴾ are coordinated with "two of each pair" or with "two". The intended meaning of "his family", according to what is in some reports, is his believing wife and his sons from her, who were Sam, peace be upon him, the father of the Arabs (its original form, according to al-Bakri, is with the letter shin marked with a dot), and Ham, the father of the Sudanese. It is said that he [Ham] had intercourse with his wife in the ship, so Nuh, peace be upon him, prayed that his seed be altered, and it was altered. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported this via the chain from Ibn Jurayj from Abu Salih. And Yafith, on the pattern of Sahib, who is the father of the Turks, and Ya'juj and Ma'juj. And the wife of each of them. Except for those against whom the word had already gone forth, that they are among the drowned because of their wrongdoing. This is in His words, glorified is He: ﴿And do not address Me concerning those who have wronged﴾, [and so on to the end of] the verse. The intended meaning is another wife of his, called Wa'ila with an unmarked ('ayn) letter, and in one report Wali'a, and his son from her, Kan'an, whose name, it is said, was Yam, and this is his title among the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab, the Jews and Christians). Both of them were disbelievers. In this there is an indication that it is permissible for prophets, peace be upon them, to marry disbelieving women, unlike our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), because of His words, exalted is He: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful for you﴾ [and so on to the end of] the verse.

The exception may be considered connected if "family" is taken to mean those family members who were of the same faith, and it may be considered disconnected if it is taken to mean those related by kinship. The validity of the exception is sufficiently assured by the fact that it is known upon reviewing their circumstances and examining their deeds. The particle ʿalā ("upon") is used because what precedes is harmful to them, just as the particle lām ("for") is used for what is beneficial, in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And certainly Our word had preceded for Our servants, the messengers﴾, and His words, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward from Us has preceded﴾. ﴿And whoever believed﴾ is coordinated with "family", meaning "and the believers from other than them". The singular form "those" [in "those among them"] is for the aforementioned exception. The use of the singular form in "believed" [in the phrase "whoever believed"] to preserve the word "whoever" (man) indicates fewness, as His words, exalted is He, make clear: ﴿And none believed with him except a few﴾.

It is said that they were seven: his wife, his three sons, and their three wives. This was narrated from Qatadah, al-Hakam ibn Utbah, Ibn Jurayj, and Muhammad ibn Ka'b. But the coordination of ﴿and whoever believed﴾ with "family" refutes this, unless "family" is taken to mean the wife, for this meaning is established. However, it is said that this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and the exception according to it is also disconnected. It is reported from Ibn Ishaq that they were ten: five men and five women. And also from him that they were twenty with Nuh, peace be upon him, half of them men and the other half their women. It is said that they were seventy-eight, half of them males and half of them females. It is said that they were eighty men and eighty women. And it is said: and it is said. The sound report, however, is that they were seventy-nine: his wife, his three sons, their wives, and seventy-two men and a woman from other than them, from the Banu Shith (Seth). The consideration of "togetherness" (ma'iyyah) in faith is to indicate togetherness in the place of settlement of faith and salvation.

(And he said) that is, Nuh, peace be upon him, said to those with him from the believers, as His words, exalted is He, indicate: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

Page 56

It is said that the pronoun refers to Allah, Exalted is He. But in this there is the problem that if it were so, the appropriate wording would have been "Indeed, your Lord..." etc. Perhaps this view [is meant to be read] after the mention of what he was commanded to load into the ship of the pairs, as if it were said: so he loaded the pairs as he was commanded, or he brought them into the ship.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 41:

And he said to the believers, ﴿Embark therein﴾. That is, "Settle in it." He made this a kind of riding, because the ship in the water is like a mount on land. In this there is a subordinate metaphor (istiʿara tabaʿiyya), in that the act of being in it is likened to riding. It has been said that it is an implicit metaphor (istiʿara makniyya), and that the use of the preposition "in" (fi) is due to considering the act of settling. Otherwise the verb is transitive by itself, and this is the view of al-Qadi al-Baydawi. It has also been said that the verb takes the preposition because it implies the meaning of "enter" (ud-khulu). It has been said that its implied sense is "ride the water in it," and it has been said that "in" (fi) is extra, for emphasis. The first view seems better. Some of the researchers said: riding (rukub) is being above something that moves, and it is transitive by itself. Its use with "in" is not because what is commanded is their being inside its hollow rather than above it, as some thought. The most apparent reports say that he (peace be upon him) and those with him rode on top of it. Rather, the use of "in" is to observe the sense of place and location within the ship.

The reason for this is that the meaning of riding is being above something that has motion, either by its own will, like an animal, or by external force, like a ship, a wheel, and the like. When it is used of the first kind, it retains the original sense, and one says "I rode the horse," and on this is the verse, ﴿And the horses, mules and donkeys, that you may ride them﴾. When it is used of the second kind, it hints at the place of the object with the word "in," and one says "I rode in the ship," and on this is the noble verse, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Then when they board the ship﴾ and ﴿until, when they boarded the ship, he tore it﴾. End of quotation. Its apparent meaning is that riding here is literal, but some stated that it is not literal.

Al-Raghib said: riding originally means a person being on the back of an animal, and it may be used of a ship. In this there is an emphasis on what some have stated.

(In the name of Allah) is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of ﴿Embark﴾, and the ba' is for accompaniment (mulabasa). Since the accompaniment of the name of Allah, mighty is His name, is by mentioning it, they said: the meaning is "Embark, naming Allah." They also permitted that the circumstantial clause be implied, and that this [phrase] be its governed element, standing in its place. For this reason they called it a circumstantial clause. The original is: "Embark, saying, ﴿In the name of Allah is its course and its mooring﴾." The words "its course" (majraha) and "its mooring" (murساha) are in the accusative as adverbs of time, meaning the time of its sailing and its anchoring, on the basis that they are nouns of time, or they are verbal nouns in the mim form meaning "sailing" and "anchoring." A governed element (mudaf) is implied, namely "time," as in your saying, "I came to you at the rising of the star," where the implied meaning is "at the time of its rising." However, when the governed element is deleted, the governing element (mudaf ilayh) takes its place and takes its case, and this is common with verbal nouns. It is also permitted that the two be nouns of place, with their accusative governed by the "settled" (istiqrar) that the preposition and its object relate to, or by "saying." It is not permitted that they be governed by "embark," since the meaning is not "embark at the time of sailing and anchoring, or in their place." Rather the meaning is "seeking blessing" or "saying in them." The view that they are in the accusative absolutely has been criticized on the grounds that they are limited, and a limited place necessarily requires "in." Some permit the accusative in such cases because of the vagueness it contains. They also permitted their being in the nominative as subjects of the adverbial element (zarf), because it relies on the one with the circumstance, or that they are a subject and a conjunct, and "in the name of Allah" is the predicate, or the predicate is omitted, its implied sense being "they are realized," or similar, and it is a complement for them. The clause is either a declarative clause, disconnected from what precedes it because the two differ in being informational and imperative, on the basis that Noah (peace be upon him) commanded them to embark on the ship, then informed them that its sailing and anchoring are in the name of Allah, the Exalted, or that its sailing and anchoring by His name, the Exalted, are realized, with no doubt about them. In this there is an encouragement to embark and a removal of whatever fear of drowning or the like might stir in their hearts. It is reported from al-Dahhak that when he (peace be upon him) wanted to set it sailing, he would say, "In the name of Allah," and it would sail, and when he wanted to anchor it, he would say, "In the name of Allah," and it would anchor.

[p. 57]

Or it is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the ship, meaning: "Embark therein, sailing and anchoring, in the name of Allah." This is an implied circumstance, since there is no sailing or anchoring at the time of embarking. So it has been said. It was criticized in al-Taqrib on the grounds that a circumstance is implied only when it is a single word, like "sailing," whereas if it is a clause, it is not, because the meaning of "embark" and "its sailing" is "in the name of Allah," and this is the actual state at the time of embarking. End of quotation. The author of al-Kashf answered this by saying there is no difference between His saying, ﴿Enter them, abiding forever﴾, and the saying of one who says, "Enter them while you are immortal," regarding not being simultaneous and the return to the implied circumstance. Thus what we are discussing is the same. It was objected to this answer that the intent of that speaker is that their sailing is treated as a single word, as in "I spoke to him, mouth to mouth," and that this is a forced reading without need. This is also not accepted in the example cited, and that is only in the saying of one who says, "I spoke to him, face to face." End of quotation. It seems that the intent of the author of al-Taqrib was not clear to him. They mentioned that the difference between a circumstance that is a single word and one that is a clause is that the second requires actual realization and involvement in itself, and it may suggest that it occurs before the governing element and continues with it, as when you say, "He came to me while he was riding," for it requires that he was involved in riding and continued upon it. This contradicts it being expected, and at least it is not good to interpret it that way when a single-word reading is easy. So understand.

It is also permitted that it be an implied circumstance from the subject of "embark." It has been objected that there is no returning pronoun to the one with the circumstance, and that the pronoun of "in the name of Allah" refers to the subject, and the implied sense "so its sailing with you or by you is in the name of Allah" is a forced reading.

The claim that al-Radi mentioned that a nominal circumstantial clause may sometimes lack both linking elements when the connection is clear, as in "I went out, Zayd is at the door," is not valid, because what he mentioned is weak in Arabic grammar, so it should not be relied upon. Yes, a nominal clause must have the waw in it. The claim that an implied circumstance can never be a clause absolutely: each of these two is within the realm of prohibition, as is not hidden.

It is also permitted that the noun be superfluous (muqhamman), as in the verse of Labid:

"Stand up and speak of what you both know,
and do not scratch a face or shave the hair,
until the year, then the greeting of peace upon you both,
and whoever weeps a full year has made his excuse."

And by Allah is meant its sailing and its anchoring, that is, by His power, or by His command, or by His permission. This is either implied or a meaning is intended. Some restricted this permission to the case where "naming" or "saying" is not implied, since the meaning does not become clear then. Both implied readings work, and the single-clause and double-clause readings both apply, and likewise the implied time and place according to one opinion. The attribution is metaphorical, of the type: "His day is fasting," and "a righteous road."

And [the reader] ﴿majraha wa mursaha﴾ with a fatha on the mim, as verbal nouns, or time nouns, or place nouns, on the basis that they derive from the triliteral roots "jara" and "rasa." Mujahid read ﴿mujriha wa mursiha﴾ in the active participle form, and Abu al-Baqa' interpreted them as adjectives of the Divine Name. It was objected to this: if the active participle's genitive construction has the sense of the future, it is indefinite, and it is not valid to describe a definite noun with it. So the correct view is that they are in apposition. The claim that the intent of the grammarian is the semantic adjective, not the grammatical adjective, so that it does not contradict apposition, is far-fetched. But al-Khalil said that a genitive construction that is not pure may sometimes be made pure and thus definite, except for the attributive adjective (al-sifa al-mushabbaha), whose genitive construction is never made pure and so is not definite. Rusuww means firmness and steadiness, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"So I restrained a soul at that moment, free-born,
it stays firm when the coward's soul rises up."

﴿Indeed my Lord is All-Forgiving, All-Merciful﴾. It has been said: the clause is a new sentence explaining the cause. That is: were it not for His forgiveness of your transgressions and His mercy upon you, your faith would not have saved you from this calamity. In this there is an indication that their salvation was not by merit, because they were believers, but purely by the mercy and forgiveness of Allah, the Exalted, according to what the People of the Sunna hold. Its being a cause for "embark" is rejected on the grounds of lack of relevance,

[p. 58]

so something is supplied that makes the speech sound, such as: "Comply with this command so that He may save you from destruction by His forgiveness and mercy." Or it is said: ﴿Embark therein﴾ remembering Allah, the Exalted, and do not fear drowning because of whatever shortcomings may have occurred from you, for Allah, His majesty is great, is Forgiving of sins and transgressions, and Merciful to His servants. Some made it a cause by considering what it contains of an allusion to salvation, so it is as if it were said: "Embark, so that Allah, glorified is He, may save you."

**[Commentary of al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah Hud (11), verse 42]**

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And it was sailing with them through waves like mountains﴾. He allowed three possibilities regarding it. The first is that it is a new (resumptive) sentence (mustaʾnaf). The second is that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun concealed in *bismillah* (in the name of God), meaning: their sailing was established (*bismillah*) while it was sailing. The third is that it is a circumstantial clause from something omitted that the context indicates, meaning: they boarded it sailing. Here the elided fa' is for coordination. *Bihim* (with them) is connected to *tajri* (it sails) or to something omitted, meaning: "accompanied." The present tense is used to narrate a past situation. There is no sense in making it circumstantial from the concealed pronoun in the first circumstantial clause, as is not hidden.

*Al-mawj* (waves) is what rises from the water when it churns; its singular is *mawjah*. ﴿Like mountains﴾ is in the position of a descriptive clause (sifah) for *mawj*, meaning: in high waves, varying in height, piled up. It was said: it sailed with them in such waves, while there remained above the water six cubits of it. This sailing was questioned in light of what is reported, that the water was a vault between heaven and earth and that the ship was sailing inside it like a fish. It was answered that this report has no soundness, and reason nearly rejects it. Yes, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Asakir and ʿAbd ibn Humayd transmitted through the route of Mujahid, from ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, who said: "The water rose above the top of every mountain by fifteen cubits." Even granting the soundness of what was mentioned, this sailing was at the beginning of the matter, before the affair grew severe, as His saying, glorified is He, indicates: ﴿And Noah called out to his son﴾, etc., for that is only conceivable before the connection between the ship and the land was cut. For then it is possible for what passed between Noah, upon him be peace, and his son to occur: the discussion, the invitation to the ship, and the reply of seeking refuge in the mountain.

Some verifying scholars said: this call was before boarding the ship, and the *waw* (and) does not indicate sequence. It is reported from ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, that he read *ibnuha* (her son), so that the feminine pronoun refers to his wife. In attributing him to her there is an indication that he was her stepson (rabib), because attributing him to the mother while the father is mentioned is contrary to the apparent sense, though they permitted it. It was justified on the ground that he was attributed to her because he was an unbeliever like her. As for what is said, that he was of illegitimate birth, based on His saying, glorified is He: ﴿but they betrayed them both﴾, this is the committing of a great sin beyond measure, for God, exalted is He, has purified the prophets, upon them be peace, of even what is less than that of deficiency by far. So God forbid, and again God forbid, that they be pointed to with a finger of reproach. The intended meaning of "betrayal" is betrayal in religion. Attributing this view to al-Hasan and Mujahid, as al-Tabarsi claimed, is a plain lie.

Muhammad ibn ʿAli and ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, may God be pleased with them all, read *ibnah* (her son) with an open *ha'* and without an alif, relying on the alif in place of it. It is a dialect form, as Ibn ʿAtiyyah said, and from that is his saying:

*Will you not lead with her a sheep, so that she eats it, or that you sell him in some of the markets?*

It was said: this is weak in Arabic, until some of them restricted it to poetic necessity. The pronoun also refers to the mother.

Ibn ʿAbbas read *ibnah* with a sukun on the ha'. According to what Ibn ʿAtiyyah and Abu al-Fadl al-Razzi said, it is the dialect of the Azd, for they make the pronoun ha' of the masculine silent, and from it is his saying: *My two lean camels yearn for him, two sleepless ones.* It was said: it is the dialect of Banu Kilab and ʿUqayl. Among the grammarians are those who restrict this sukun to poetic necessity, and they recite:

*And I drink water, though no thirst for it is in me, except because its springs are the flood of its valley.*

al-Suddi read *ibnahuma* (their two sons) with an alif and a silent ha', and this was explained as a form of the vocative of lament (nudbah). It was questioned on the ground that the grammarians stated that the particle of calling is not omitted in the lament. It was answered that this is a narration, and what they forbade is in the lament itself, not in its narration. From Ibn ʿAtiyyah: *abnaha* (with a fathah on the hamzat al-qat' which is for calling). In this there is that the lament does not call with the hamzah, and that the transmission is with the wasl (connecting) in it, and calling with the hamzah did not occur in the Qur'an. The view of lament is far-fetched, since it does not suit the invitation to the ship afterwards, as is not hidden. If it were said that *abnaha* in this reading is also the object of *nada* (called out), as in the other readings, and the alif is for lengthening, and the silent ha' is the pronoun ha' in some dialects, there would be no objection from the point of view of meaning, and this is evident. Yes, the saying of that depends on hearing it in such a case; and once it is established, in my view the reading is certainly to be explained that way, if it is sound.

The majority read *ibnahu* (his son) with an annexation to the pronoun of Noah. They joined the ha' with a waw, and this is the eloquent (fasih) usage. The tanwin of *Nuhin* is kasrah according to the majority, to avoid the meeting of two sukuns. Waki' read it with a dammah, following the vowel of the case ending (iʿrab).

Abu Hatim said: it is a bad dialect, not known.

*And he was in a place apart* (maʿzil): that is, a place where he isolated himself from his father, his brothers and those of his people who believed. The intended meaning of being far from them is either physical or figurative, and its essence is opposition to them in religion. So *maʿzil* with a kasrah is the name of the place of isolation, and that may be literal or figurative, and it may be a name of time. When it is with a fathah, it is a verbal noun. It was said: the intended meaning of "he was in a place apart" is that he had separated from the unbelievers, having isolated himself from them, and Noah, upon him be peace, thought that he wished to part from them, and for this reason he invited him to the ship. It was said: he called to him because he was feigning faith, so he thought he was a believer. This was chosen by many verifying scholars, such as al-Maturidi and others. It was said: he knew that he was an unbeliever up to that time, but upon him be peace thought that at the sight of those terrors, and when the flood reached the highest point, he would turn back from what he was upon and accept faith. It was said: he did not decide that he was included in the exception, because he was like one whose case is unclear, so the compassion of fatherhood moved him to call out: "O my son" (*ya bunayya*), with a fathah on the ya' which is the final letter of the word, relying on the fathah in place of the alif that replaces the ya' of attribution in His saying "ya bunaya." It was said: it was dropped because it met a silent letter, the silent ra' after it. The first view is supported by the fact that it was read this way where no silent letter follows.

Some people said: there is weakness in it, according to what Yunus related of the weakness of "ya abi" and "ya ummi," with the alif omitted and the fathah standing in for it.

The majority read with a kasrah, restricting it to the ya' of attribution. It was said: it was dropped because two sukuns met, as was said of the alif. His calling him with the diminutive is of the category of tenderness and compassion, and a father often calls his son in this way. ﴿Ride with us﴾, i.e., in the ship. And because it is definite, and to indicate the narrowness of the situation, since the choking (jarid) prevented the recited verse (qarid), and since the being-with (maiyyah) suffices without mention of it, the word "with" was not mentioned, and boarding was stated without qualification. The lightening of the ba' and its assimilation into the mim are two seven readings. The reason for assimilation is closeness in point of articulation. ﴿And do not be with the disbelievers﴾ is an emphasis of the command, and it is a prohibition against living with the disbelievers and entering into their crowd, and a certainty that entering among them necessitates drowning, by the demonstrative method.

[p. 60]

"He said, 'I will betake myself to a mountain that will protect me from the water.'" That is, I will join myself to a mountain among the mountains. It was also said that he meant Mount Tur Zeita. "It will protect me" means it will guard me by its height from the water, so that it does not reach me. He said this assuming that it was like other waters in the usual seasons of floods, from which one may protect oneself by climbing to a high place. He was ignorant of the fact that this flood was meant to destroy the disbelievers, so it would certainly overtake them even if they were on the summits of mountains.

(He said), making the true state of affairs clear to him and turning him away from that impossible notion: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah.﴾ This is a negation of the genus of protector, which encompasses the negation of all its instances, both in essence and in attribute, for the sake of emphasis in denying that the mountain could be a protector. He added "today" to draw attention to the fact that this day is not like other days in which events occur and usual calamities befall, from which one may escape by resorting to some ordinary means. In place of the water, he expressed the matter as "the command of Allah," meaning His punishment, which was alluded to earlier by His words, glorified is He: ﴿until when Our command came.﴾ This serves to magnify its importance and to convey its terrifying nature, to alert his son to his error in calling it water and in imagining that it was like other waters from which one escapes by fleeing to familiar refuges, and as a reason for the aforementioned negation, for the command of Allah, glorified is He, cannot be overcome, and His punishment cannot be repelled. It also serves as a preface to restricting protection to the presence of Allah, exalted is His protection, through the exception, as if it were said: "There is no protector from the command of Allah, exalted is He, except Him, exalted is He." The phrase ﴿except for whom He has mercy﴾ was used to magnify His exalted majesty, and to indicate that His mercy is the cause of protection, since His mercy precedes His wrath. All of this is for the complete care of him, peace be upon him, in securing what he sought, namely the salvation of his son, by explaining the gravity of the calamity, cutting off his vain hopes, turning his reins away from excusing himself with what will not avail him at all, and guiding him to seek refuge in the true Refuge, exalted is His sanctuary. For this reason, the apparent answer that would be expected, namely "the mountain will not protect you from it," was set aside. This is what some of the verifiers have mentioned, and it is one of the possible interpretations of the verse, and the strongest of them.

The second interpretation: "protector" (ʿāṣim) is in the form of a nisba (attributive adjective, meaning "possessor of"), and the relative pronoun refers to the one who is shown mercy. That is, there is no one possessing protection, i.e., no one protected, except whom Allah has shown mercy. This is supported by the reading ﴿except whom He has shown mercy﴾ in the passive voice. Al-Zamakhshari, in al-Kashshaf, objected to this by saying that fāʿil in the sense of nisba is rare. It was answered that he meant its rarity in itself, which is disputed, but in relation to the attribute, it is not harmful.

The third interpretation: "protector" is taken in its literal sense, and "whom He has mercy on" means "one who is shown mercy," and the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ, i.e., not connected to the preceding), not connected (muttaṣil), as in the first two interpretations. That is, there is no protector from the command of Allah, but whomever Allah has shown mercy is protected. It was objected to this that such a disjunctive exception is rare, because in reality it is a separate sentence that differs from the first not only in negation and affirmation but also in nominal and verbal form. The most common usage of it is like "The people came to me except a donkey."

The fourth interpretation: "protector" (ʿāṣim) means "protected" (maʿṣūm), like dāfiq meaning madfūq (poured), and fātin meaning maftūn (enchanted), in the verse of the poet:

*Slow in standing, sweet in speech,*
*My heart has become enchanted by him.*

"Whom He has shown mercy" means "the merciful one" (rāḥim), and the exception is also disjunctive. That is: there is no one protected except the Merciful, in the sense that "but the Merciful protects whom He wills."

The fifth interpretation: the discourse is based on an implied place, and the exception is connected. That is: there is no protector except the place of one whom Allah has shown mercy, among the believers, which is the ark. It was said: this is a good interpretation, containing a contrast with his words ﴿it will protect me﴾, and it is the preferred one after the first. The word "protector" in this case is literal, but its attribution to the place is metaphorical. It was also said that it is a metonymy (majāz mursal) for the place of refuge, and the meaning is: there is no place of refuge except the place of one whom Allah has shown mercy. It has been claimed that this is the most preferred of all, because it came as an answer to his words ﴿I will betake myself to a mountain﴾, etc. But this is not accepted.

The sixth interpretation is what the author of al-Kashshaf put forward, which is that the meaning is: there is no one protected except the place of one whom Allah has shown mercy, and what is intended by it is the protection of the one within it, through metonymy (kināya). For when the ark is protected, the one in it is protected.

The seventh interpretation: the exception is an emptied exception (mufarragh), and the meaning is: there is no protector today, of anyone or for anyone, except whom Allah has shown mercy, or for whom Allah, glorified is He, has shown mercy. Some of them counted this among the closest interpretations, and I do not think you would prefer any other interpretation to the first, which is the one he chose.

According to what Abu Hayyan said, the apparent meaning is that the predicate of lā (there is no) is omitted, because it is known, that is: there is no protector present. Most Hijazis use omission in such constructions, but the Banu Tamim were committed to omitting it there.

"Today" (al-yawm) would be in the accusative, governed by an implied verb indicated by "protector" (ʿāṣim), that is: there is no protector who protects today, and the prepositional phrase is connected to that verb. He prohibited that "today" be accusative governed by the noun of lā, and that the prepositional phrase be connected to it, because then it would have to be indeclinable and without tanwīn (nunation) due to its length. (Note: this refers to the grammatical argument that a noun governed by lā with a lengthy complement would be treated as the nominal form.)

Al-Hawfi permitted that "today" be connected to an implied element that serves as the predicate of lā, and the prepositional phrase is connected to that implied element as well. He also permitted that it be connected to an implied element which is the predicate, with "today" in the position of a qualifier (naʿt) for "protector." Abu al-Baqa rejected the predicate function of "today" on the grounds that it is a time adverb, and a time adverb cannot be a predicate about bodies (juththa). He maintained that it is an object of "from the command of Allah," and that the predicate is the prepositional phrase. Abu Hayyan rejected the permissibility of its being a qualifier, on the grounds that a time adverb cannot be a qualifier for bodies, just as it cannot be a predicate about them.

﴿And the wave came between them.﴾ That is, between Noah, peace be upon him, and his son, so that the exchange of words between them was cut off. It was said: they were exchanging words, and before the exchange was complete, a great wave came, and he was riding a horse that had become arrogant and self-admiring, so it engulfed him and his horse. In the verse here there is nothing except the affirmation of the barrier. As for his, peace be upon him, knowledge of his son's drowning, it did not occur until afterwards.

Al-Farra' said: "between them" means between the son of Noah, peace be upon him, and the mountain. Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated this from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazza. Abu al-Su'ud criticized this by saying that the statement of the Exalted, ﴿so he was among the drowned﴾, follows only from the wave coming between him, peace be upon him, and his son, not between him and the mountain, because the mountain is far from being a protector, even if no wave came between him and the refuge he sought. It was answered that the consequence does not contradict this, because what is meant is "so he was among the drowned" without delay. Or it is based on his assumption that the water would not reach him. The verse also indicates a drowning that befell the disbelievers in the most eloquent manner, as if that were a matter of certain occurrence that needs no explanation. The use of "was" (kāna) rather than "became" (ṣāra) in the phrase ﴿he was among the drowned﴾ is an emphasis on his being one of them.

[p. 62]

﴿And it was said: O earth, swallow﴾ (i.e., absorb). The word is used metaphorically from the swallowing of food by an animal, to indicate that this [absorption] was not like the ordinary gradual drying. Restricting *bal'* (swallowing) to what is eaten is the well-known view of the lexicographers. Al-Layth said: "It is said: *balaʿa al-māʾ* (he swallowed the water) when he drank it," which clearly shows that it is not restricted to what is eaten. Al-Sayyid [al-Sharif al-Jurjani] mentioned that this usage is figurative. Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Wahb ibn Munabbih that *bal'* in the sense of *ibtilaʿ* (swallowing) is an Abyssinian (Habashi) usage. Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, from his father, that in the sense of drinking it is an Indian usage.

﴿your water﴾, i.e., the water on your surface from the flood. It is referred to as "water" after having been referred to earlier as "the command of God," because the context is one of diminution and reduction, not one of magnification and awe.

﴿And, O sky, cease﴾, i.e., withhold from sending rain. It is said: *aqlaʿat al-samāʾ* (the sky ceased) when its rain stopped, and *aqlaʿat al-ḥummā* (the fever broke) when it subsided. It is apparent that the rain had not stopped until the sky was addressed as it was. Whether the gushing of the water had continued until the earth was addressed as it was, or not, I have not seen anything about it, and the verse is not explicit on either matter.

﴿And the water subsided﴾, i.e., decreased. It is said: *ghāḍahu* (he diminished it) when he reduced it, and all its meanings return to this.

The statement of al-Jawhari, "*ghāḍa al-māʾ* (the water subsided) when it became little and receded, and *ghīḍa al-māʾ* (the water was made to subside), meaning that this was done to it," does not contradict this, for little is itself a form of decrease. The interpretation of this as decrease is transmitted from Mujahid.

﴿And the matter was decided﴾, i.e., what God had promised Noah, peace be upon him, was accomplished: the destruction of the disbelievers of his people and the deliverance of him and his believing family. It is also permitted that the meaning is "the matter was completed."

﴿And it came to rest﴾, i.e., settled. It is said: *istawā ʿalā al-sarīr* (he sat upright upon the throne) when he settled upon it.

﴿upon al-Judi﴾ — with the *yāʾ* doubled. Al-Aʿmash and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read it with the *yāʾ* single, and both are dialectal forms, as Ibn ʿAṭiyya said. It is a mountain near Mosul, or in Syria, or in Amul, pronounced with a long vowel and a *ḍamma* on the *mīm*. The well-known [view]

[p. 63]

It has come in some reports that the mountains were lofty at that time, and [the Judi] was humble before God, may His majesty be exalted. So God honoured it by the settling of the ship upon it, for whoever is humble before God, He raises. The settling of the ship upon it was on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ. Ahmad and others transmitted from Abu Hurayra that he said: "The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, passed by some Jews who were fasting on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ, and he said: 'What is this fast?' It was said: 'This is the day on which God, exalted is He, delivered Moses, peace be upon him, and the Children of Israel from drowning, and Pharaoh drowned.' And this is the day on which the ship settled upon al-Judi, so Noah and Moses, peace be upon them both, fasted it in gratitude to God, exalted is He." The Prophet ﷺ said: "I have more right to Moses, peace be upon him, and more right to fasting this day," so he fasted it and commanded his companions to fast.

Al-Isfahani in *al-Targhib* transmitted from him, may God be pleased with him, that it is also the day on which ʿIsā, peace be upon him, was born, and that fasting it equals a year of accepted worship. Riding [of the ship] by Noah, peace be upon him, was, as transmitted from Qatada, on the tenth of Rajab.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn ʿAbd al-Ghafur, from his father, in a report traced to the Prophet, that he, peace be upon him, boarded on the first day of Rajab, fasted, and those with him fasted. The ship sailed with them for six months, and this reached Muharram; the ship came to rest on al-Judi on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ. Noah, peace be upon him, fasted, and he commanded all those with him from the beasts and animals, and they fasted in gratitude to God.

It is said in some reports that the ship circled the whole earth with them, and did not enter the Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram), but it did circle it seven times. It is also said that the Black Stone was hidden in Mount Abu Qubays, and that the House [the Kaʿba] was raised to heaven. In a report of Ibn ʿAsakir from Mujahid, nothing of the water entered the Ḥaram. The apparent implication of this is that there was no concealment, just as there was no raising. In my view, the report that both [occurred] is hardly authentic, and even if it were authentic, I do not see the secret of raising [the House] without the stone, or hiding the stone without the House. Rather, in my view, there is hesitation about the raising of the House absolutely, though I am one who does not hesitate that God is over all things powerful.

﴿And it was said: Away with the wrongdoing people!﴾, i.e., destruction for them. The *lām* is connected to the verbal noun (*bu'd*). It has been said that it is connected to *qīla* (it was said), and the meaning is "it was said for their sake: away," but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. The mention of the description of wrongdoing indicates its causal role in the destruction, and serves to recall what preceded in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And do not address Me concerning those who did wrong﴾. There is no hiding what this verse indicates regarding the generality of the destruction of the disbelievers. Other verses and many reports bear witness to this. Indeed, there is in it, even taken at face value, a clear indication of the generality of the destruction of all upon the earth except the people of the ship. Ubayd ibn ʿUmayr transmitted that among those struck by the flood was a woman with a child; she placed him on her chest, and when the water reached her, she placed him on her shoulder; when the water reached her, she placed him on her hands. God, exalted is He, said: "Had I shown mercy to anyone on the earth, I would have shown mercy to her, but the word has been fulfilled from Me."

Some have claimed that not one of the disbelievers was saved except ʿŪj ibn ʿŪq, and the water reached only his knee. The reason for his survival was that Noah, peace be upon him, needed teak wood, but it was not possible for him to transport it, so ʿŪj carried it from Syria to him, peace be upon him, and God, exalted is He, saved him from drowning for that. The apparent sense of al-Qamus implies his survival, for it mentions ʿŪj ibn ʿŪq (with both vowelled with *ḍamma*), a man who was born in the dwelling of Adam, peace be upon him, and lived until the time of Moses, peace be upon him. But the truth is that not one of the disbelievers was saved at all. The report about ʿŪj is transmitted by Hayyan ibn Bayyan, so do not be inclined to accept it. Nor is the drowning of children who had no sin a difficulty, since it is merely a cause of death in relation to them. And what harm is there in causing the death of one who has no sin? At every moment God, exalted is He, causes the death of countless such [people]. He, may His majesty be exalted, is the True Owner and the Absolute Disposer; He does what He wills and decrees what He desires.

There is no need, in answering this, to resort to what Ishaq ibn Bishr and Ibn ʿAsakir transmitted from ʿAbd Allah ibn Ziyad ibn Samʿan, from men whom he named, that God sterilized their men forty years before the flood and sterilized their women, so they did not bear children for forty years from the time Noah, peace be upon him, called upon them, until the youngest reached puberty, and the proof was established against them; then He sent down the sky upon them with the flood. This is because of its weakness, and because of the contradiction between it and the report mentioned just above, and because it would leave [the destruction of] the animals not in the ship unexplained. It has come from Jaʿfar al-Sadiq, may God be pleased with him, that when Noah, peace be upon him, carried those he carried in the ship, the cattle, the wild animals, and the predators saw the punishment, so they began to lick his foot, peace be upon him, saying: "Carry us with you." He would say: "I have only been commanded to carry two of every kind," and he did not carry them.

Likewise, there is no need to answer that God destroyed those children because He knew, may His majesty be exalted, what they would have done. This is like what is said about the question of admitting the children of the disbelievers into Hellfire on the Day of Resurrection according to the view of one who holds it, for it has its own difficulties. In sum, causing living beings to die by any cause whatsoever, whether suddenly or gradually, is not something objectionable, and He is not questioned about it.

Know that this noble verse has reached the highest levels of inimitability (*iʿjāz*) and has humbled the most eloquent of the Arabs, forcing their foreheads to the ground. It combines beauties that the scope of exposition cannot contain, and it was, among the spearheads of eloquence, like the spearhead of the spear. It is narrated that the disbelievers of Quraysh intended to produce a rival to the Qur'an. They devoted themselves to the finest wheat bread, lamb meat, and pure wine for forty days, so that their minds might be clear. When they set about what they intended and heard this verse, some of them said to others: "This speech does not resemble the speech of created beings," so they abandoned what they had undertaken and dispersed. It is also narrated that Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, who, as in al-Qamus, was eloquent and articulate, indeed it was said that he was the most eloquent man of his time, wanted to produce a rival to the Qur'an. He composed speech, arranged it in sections, and named them *suwar* (chapters). One day he passed by a boy reciting them in a school. He turned back, erased what he had done, and said: "I bear witness that this cannot be matched ever, and it is not the speech of humans."

It is not hidden that this does not imply that the rest of the verses of the glorious Qur'an are not inimitable, since the limit of inimitability is the level that humans are unable to reach, and it is certainly beyond their power. It comprises two things. The first is the highest extremity of eloquence, that is, what eloquence reaches and whose surpassing cannot be conceived. The second is what approaches that extremity, that is, the lofty levels from which human faculties also fall short. The meaning of the inimitability of all the verses of the Glorious Book is that they are all of the kind that human faculties fall short of matching, whether they belong to the first category or the second. Therefore, their variation in eloquence does no harm. This is what the scholars of this discipline have said. Some Persians recited about this:

*Dar bayān wa dar faṣāḥat kī būd ham-sangī-e sukhan / wa rajīh guyanda būd chūn Ḥāfiẓ wa chūn Aṣmaʿī*
In exposition and in eloquence, who was a match for speech? Who could be preferred, like Ḥāfiẓ or like al-Aṣmaʿī?

*Dur-e kalām-e Īzad bī-chūn ki waḥy-e manzilast / ki bi-wad tā yadan chūn qīla: yā arḍu ub-laʿī*
How incomparable is the pearl of the Word of God, which is a revealed scripture, for it [is such] that the hand ... as it was said: "O earth, swallow."

Some masters of perfection have expounded some of the excellences of this verse, and they left aside much that the describers could hardly describe. There is no harm in mentioning some of what has been said, for the benefit of the ignorant and as a reminder to the heedless virtuous. We say: Al-ʿAllāma al-Sakkākī mentioned that consideration of it is from four aspects: from the aspect of *bayān* (figurative expression), from the aspect of *ʿilm al-maʿānī* (the science of meanings), and these two are the sources of rhetoric (*balāgha*); from the aspect of semantic eloquence (*faṣāḥa maʿnawiyya*); and from the aspect of verbal eloquence (*faṣāḥa lafẓiyya*).

As for consideration of it from the aspect of the science of *bayān*, which is the examination of what it contains of metaphor (*majāz*), figurative transfer (*isticāra*), and metonymy (*kināya*), and what is connected to these, such as the indicator (*qarīna*), the nurturing (*tarshīḥ*), and allusion (*taʿrīḍ*): He, glorious is His dominion, when He wished to express the meaning, "We wished to return what gushed from the earth to its belly, so it returned; and to cut off the flood of the sky, so it ceased; and to make the water that descended from the sky subside, so it subsided; and to decide the matter of Noah, peace be upon him, which is the completion of what We had promised concerning the drowning of his people, so it was decided; and to settle the ship upon al-Judi, so it settled; and to leave the wrongdoers drowned," He, glorious is He, built the speech upon the likening of what is meant to one commanded who cannot disobey, given the perfect majesty of the commander, and the likening of the bringing-into-being of what is willed to a decisive and binding command that takes effect in the occurrence of what is intended, depicting His, glorious is He, immense power, and that these great bodies of the heavens and the earth are subject to His will in bringing into being and annihilation, and to His will in change and alteration.

[p. 64]

as if they were intelligent, discerning beings who truly knew Him, may He be exalted, with the knowledge that it is obligatory to submit to His command and to yield to His judgment. Striving to fulfil His will became incumbent upon them, and they conceived of the greatness of His power, so His awe grew in their souls and spread its pavilion across the courtyards of their hearts. Thus, as His signal, may He be glorified, appears to them, the one signalled to is at once ready; and as His command, may His majesty be exalted, reaches them, the one commanded is at once carrying it out. There is no receiving His signal except by executing and submitting, and no receiving His command except by obeying and complying. Then, upon the combination of these two comparisons, He built the composition of the speech, so He, may He be exalted and sublime, said: ﴿It was said﴾. This is a metaphor (majāz) for "willed," by way of mentioning the effect and meaning the cause, since the will is a cause for the occurrence of speech in general. The indicator (qarīna) of this metaphor is the addressing of inanimate objects, namely ﴿O earth﴾ and ﴿O sky﴾, since it is valid for the meaning to be the occurrence of something related to inanimate objects, while speech cannot validly be directed to them. Then He, glorified, said, as you see: ﴿O earth﴾ and ﴿O sky﴾, addressing them both by way of metaphor (istiʿāra) for the aforementioned resemblance. The apparent meaning is that he intended that there is here an implicit metaphor (istiʿāra bil-kināya), in that he mentioned the comparandum, namely the sky and the earth, while the intended meaning is the occurrence of a matter, and he intended the comparans, namely the one commanded, described as one from whom disobedience cannot proceed, by way of claim, with the indicator being the attribution of address to them and the entry of the vocative particle upon them. These two are among the distinctive features of the obedient one commanded, and this would be an imaginative representation (takhyīl).

It may be said that he intended that the metaphor here is an explicit subsidiary metaphor (istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya tabaʿiyya) in the particle of address, on the basis of likening the connection of the will to what is willed with the connection of the address and the call to the one addressed. But this is not correct, for this comparison is not good as a primary one, but only as a consequence of the first comparison. So how can it be made the root of what follows from it! Moreover, his saying "for the aforementioned resemblance" repels this interpretation. Then he borrowed, for the submersion of water into the earth, the word "swallowing" (balʿ), which is the action of drawing in what is eaten, because of the resemblance between them, namely going to a hidden resting place.

In the Kashshāf, [al-Zamakhshari] made "swallowing" a metaphor for the earth's absorbing (nashf) the water, and this is preferable, for absorbing indicates a drawing in of the earth's parts toward what is upon it, like swallowing in relation to an animal. Also, absorbing is the action of the earth, while submersion is the action of the water, with antithesis between the two actions being transitive. Then he borrowed "water" for "food" by way of implicit metaphor, likening it to food, because the earth is strengthened by water in producing crops and trees, as the eater is strengthened by food. The indicator of the metaphor is the word ﴿swallow﴾, because it is set for use with food and not with water.

It is not hidden from you that if the school of the early scholars (salaf) regarding metaphor is considered, then ﴿swallow﴾ is an explicit metaphor, and yet, according to the wording, it serves as an indicator for an implicit metaphor in "water," in the manner they stated regarding ﴿they break the covenant of God﴾. As for if his [al-Zamakhshari's] school is considered, then "swallowing" should remain in its literal sense, like "growing" in "the spring made the herbage grow," which is distant; or it should be made a metaphor for a supposed matter, as in "the situation spoke," in which case it entails the view of subsidiary metaphor, as is well known. He, may He be exalted, commanded by way of metaphor for the second comparison, and he addressed in the command as a supporting elaboration (tarshīḥ) for the metaphor of the vocative.

The summary is that in the word ﴿swallow﴾, considered in its essence, there is a metaphor for the submersion of water; considered in its form, namely that it is the form of a command, there is another metaphor for the bringing about of what is willed; and considered as a command addressed to someone, it is a supporting elaboration for the implicit metaphor in the one called, since its indicator is the vocative. Whatever exceeds the indicator of the implicit metaphor serves as an elaboration of it. As for making the vocative an explicit subsidiary metaphor so that the address of the commander becomes an elaboration of it, you already know what is wrong with it. Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿your water﴾, attributing the water to the earth by way of metaphor, likening the connection of the water to the earth to the connection of ownership to the owner. He chose the pronoun of address for the sake of elaboration.
