The gist of this is that there is a linguistic metaphor in the attributive construction, which indicates royal possession, and for this reason he made the address an elaboration of this metaphor, insofar as the address indicates the earth's suitability for being owned. Therefore what is said, that the metaphor is rational (ʿaqlī) and the expression is diverted from its apparent meaning, is nothing.

Then he chose, for the cessation of the rain, "clearing up" (iqlāʿ), which is the agent's abandoning of the action, because of the resemblance between them in the absence of what was from the rain or from the action. So in ﴿clear up﴾ there is a metaphor in its essence, and likewise in its form as well, and it is based on likening the bringing about of what is willed to a decisive, binding command. The address in it is also an elaboration of the metaphor of the vocative, and the gist is that the discussion regarding it is like what passed regarding ﴿swallow﴾. Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And the water was diminished, and the matter was decided, and it came to rest upon al-Judi, and it was said: "Away with the wrongdoing people!"﴾. He did not explicitly state who diminished the water, nor who decided the matter and made the ship level, and He said ﴿Away﴾, just as He did not explicitly state the speaker of ﴿O earth﴾ and ﴿O sky﴾ at the beginning of the verse, following the same method in each of these, by way of implicit reference (kināya). For those great matters proceed only from one possessing a power that cannot be contained, an irresistible Subduer who cannot be overcome. So there is no room for the thought to arise that another, whose greatness is exalted, is the speaker of ﴿O earth﴾ and ﴿O sky﴾, or that there is one who diminishes what was diminished or decides a matter like that awesome one, or that the making level of the ship and its settling is by the making level of another.

The gist is that when an action is specifically assigned to a particular agent, it is consequently appropriate to omit mention of that agent, and to build the verb for its object, or to mention what is the effect of that action in the active-voice form and attribute it to that object. This becomes an implicit reference to restricting the attribute, which is the action, to the thing it qualifies. This is better than what has been said regarding the framing of the implicit reference here: that the omission of the agent and the building of the verb for the object are among the necessary implications of knowing the action and its being specific to the agency of that action. So he mentioned the necessary implication, and meant what it necessarily implies. The reason is that ﴿it came to rest﴾ is not in the passive voice, like ﴿it was said﴾ and ﴿was diminished﴾.

Then, may He be exalted, concluded the speech with a reference, as an admonition to those who follow the path of that people in denying the messengers, peace be upon them, wronging themselves and nothing else. This was a concluding statement to show the place of wrath and the grounds for their deserving it, and that the rising of the flood and that awesome scene occurred only because of their wrongdoing, as is indicated by the supplication for destruction after their destruction, and by the description of them as wrongdoers together with attaching the judgment to that description. Some have stated that distance (buʿd) in its original sense is the opposite of nearness, and is with regard to place, occurring in the perceptible, and may be used in the intelligible, as in ﴿they have strayed far astray﴾. Its use for destruction is a metaphor. Nāṣir al-Dīn said: it is said "baʿuda buʿdan" with a damma and then a sukūn, and "baʿada baʿadan" with a fatha, when one goes far away, a distant going, such that there is no hope of his return. Then it was borrowed for destruction and restricted to the invocation of evil. In the Qāmūs no distinction is made between the two verbal forms in the two meanings, where it says: "al-buʿd" is well known, and "al-mawt" and their verbs are like "karuma" and "fariḥa," "buʿdan" and "baʿadan." So understand.

Some have claimed that the earth and the sky were given the faculty of understanding by which they comprehend the command, and therefore what was said was said to them literally, and that the one who said "Away" was Noah, peace be upon him, and those believers with him. It is not hidden that this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and there is no report on which reliance can be placed regarding it. The discussion according to the first view is more eloquent.

As for the consideration of these verses from the standpoint of the science of meanings (ʿilm al-maʿānī), which is the examination of the function of each word in them and the purpose of each advancement and delay among their clauses: He chose "yā" (O) over the rest of its sisters because it is the most frequently used, and because it indicates the distance of the one called, which the situation of displaying greatness and manifesting the dignity of might and majesty requires, namely making the one called distant, which indicates contempt toward him. He did not say "yā arḍi" with a kasra, because the attribution to Himself, may His majesty be exalted, requires honouring the earth and giving it dignity, so it was left out to avoid diminishing this. He did not say "yā ayyatuhā al-arḍu," although this is common in calling generic nouns, aiming at brevity and avoiding the effort of an alerting expression, which indicates heedlessness, unsuitable for that station. The words "earth" and "sky" were chosen over their other names, such as "the one that carries" and "the grey one," or "the one that shades" and "the green one," because they are more concise, more frequent in use, and more complete in correspondence, for the opposition between them is well known through these two names. The word ﴿swallow﴾ was chosen over ﴿ibtaliʿi﴾, because it is more concise and more harmonious with ﴿clear up﴾, for if the hamza of the connective is counted, they are equal in the number of letters, and if not, they are close in that respect; this is unlike ﴿ibtaliʿi﴾.

It has been said: "your water" was used in the singular rather than the plural, because the plural contains an appearance of abundance, which the station of displaying majesty rejects. This is also the reason for using the singular for "earth" and "sky." Why did He not say ﴿swallow﴾ without an object? So that its omission would not imply what is not intended, namely generalizing the swallowing to the mountains, the hills, the seas, and all the still waters, out of regard for the station of the awesome majesty of the commander and the perfect submission of the one commanded. Since it was known that what is intended is the swallowing of water alone, it was known that what is meant by ﴿clear up﴾ is the withholding of the sky from releasing water. So the complement of ﴿clear up﴾ was not mentioned, for brevity and to avoid superfluous padding that is not needed. This is the reason for omitting mention of the fulfilment of the command after the command: He did not say, "It was said: O earth, swallow! and it swallowed; and O sky, clear up! and it cleared up," because the station of majesty and the perfection of submission dispenses with mentioning that, which might suggest the possibility of disobedience. ﴿Ghīḍa﴾ was chosen over ﴿ghuyyiḍa﴾ with the doubled letter, because it is more concise.

[Page 65 marker not part of translation; see below]

Then the sentence "the water" refers to water other than the water of the flood from the sky, and likewise "the matter" refers to something other than the command of Noah; it is the fulfilment of what was promised. This is for the purpose of brevity and of dispensing, through the definite article, with that, because it is either a substitute for the genitive noun, as is the view of the Kufans, or because it serves the function of the attributive construction in indicating the known referent. ﴿Istawat﴾ was chosen over ﴿suwwiyat﴾, meaning "was set level," although the former is more suitable with its sisters, which are in the passive voice, out of regard for the fact that the verb corresponding to settling, namely sailing, is attributed to the ship in the active voice, in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and it sailed with them﴾. Moreover, ﴿istawat﴾ is more concise than ﴿suwwiyat﴾. The verbal noun ﴿buʿdan﴾ was chosen over ﴿li-yabʿud al-qawm﴾, seeking to emphasize the meaning of the verb through the verbal noun while being concise in expression; ﴿buʿdan﴾ alone takes the place of ﴿li-yabʿudū buʿdan﴾, with an additional benefit, namely indicating that they deserve destruction, through the use of the preposition lām. The unrestricted use of "wrongdoing" without its qualifiers, in a context of emphasis, conveys the inclusion of every kind, so their wronging of themselves is included in it, to add further alertness to the abhorrence of the evil of their choice in denying, insofar as their denial of the messengers is a wrong against themselves, because its harm returns to them. This is the consideration from the standpoint of the composition of the words.

As for the standpoint of the arrangement of the clauses: He placed the vocative before the command, so it was said: ﴿O earth, swallow﴾ and ﴿O sky, clear up﴾, rather than saying: "Swallow, O earth! and clear up, O sky!" This follows what is required in the case of one who is truly commanded, namely placing the alerting before the command, so that the command following it may settle in the very soul of the one called, with that purpose in view, as an elaboration of the implicit metaphor in earth and sky. Then he placed the command to the earth before the command to the sky, because the earth is the origin, given that the beginning of the flood was from it, when its oven first boiled over. Then His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿was diminished﴾ was made to follow the command to the earth and the sky, because it is connected to the story of the water and its seizing of their skirts. Do you not see that the original sentence was: "It was said: O earth, swallow your water," and so it swallowed its water; "and O sky, clear up," ceasing to release the water, and so it ceased releasing it; ﴿and the water was diminished﴾, the water that had descended from the sky, and so it diminished.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 44 (part 3 of 3):

He restricted the water to that which gushed forth, although the verse is unrestricted, because the earth's swallowing of its water was understood from His words, glorified be He: ﴿O earth, swallow your water﴾.

He objected that if "the water specific to the earth" is meant as what lies on its surface, then it includes both the earthly and the heavenly kinds, and if it is meant as what sprang forth from it, then the wording does not indicate this in any way. For this reason al-Zamakhshari (Mahmud al-Zamakhshari) took "the water" in its unrestricted sense, and his statement implied that ﴿the water was made to subside﴾ is a report of the accomplishment of the command in His words, glorified be He: ﴿O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold﴾. The meaning, then, is that they were told this, they obeyed the command, and the water decreased.

Al-Tibi (Sharaf al-Din al-Tibi) preferred what al-Sakkaki (Abu Ya'qub al-Sakkaki) held, claiming that the meaning of ghayd (subsiding) in that case is what al-Jawhari (Isma'il al-Jawhari) stated. According to him, this differs from the meaning mentioned by al-Zamakhshari. He said: the attribution of the water to the earth, since it serves as tarshih (an elaboration of the metaphor, i.e., a supporting detail that keeps the metaphor alive) for the isti'arah (metaphor), likening its connection to it to the connection of ownership to the owner, and for this reason the second-person address was used, requires the exclusion of all other waters except that by which the earth became prepared for the address, as a obedient subordinate. This is the known meaning in His words, exalted be He: ﴿and the oven boiled over﴾. By this consideration, there arises a deep continuity in forgetting the simile and the tarshih. If the attribution were taken in other than this way, it would be like tajrid (stripping the metaphor of its supporting elements), and how great the difference between them is. Moreover, if it were taken in generality,
[Page 67]
it would necessitate that His swallowing encompass all the waters entirely, since the command came from a station of greatness, as you have learned from the words of al-Sakkaki. But this is not so. Al-Kashf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary, al-Kashshaf) criticized him, saying that this is a claim without evidence, and a rejection of an oath, since there is no known referent. The apparent meaning is the water that is upon the surface of the earth, and this does not contradict the tarshih or the attribution of ownership. Then, the apparent meaning of likening the water to nourishment is that the attribution should be taken as the attribution of nourishment to what is nourished, in terms of benefit, strengthening, and becoming a part of it. Its being owned or otherwise is not considered in this. As for generality, it is both desired and achieved under both interpretations, since water is confined to the earthly and the heavenly kinds. You have said that both have been exhausted, from His words, exalted be He: ﴿then it swallowed﴾, and His words, exalted be He: ﴿and it was made to subside﴾. There is no doubt that the water we have is other than the water of the Flood.

This being said, the interpretation of al-Zamakhshari is the one that fits. Do you not see His words, majestic and exalted be He: ﴿and the waters met﴾, meaning the earthly and the heavenly waters? Here, the two waters were mentioned earlier, in His words, glorified be He: ﴿your water, and O sky﴾, because its supposition refers to the sending of the water according to their claim. So when it is said ﴿and the water was made to subside﴾, it inevitably refers back to the two, since they were mentioned earlier. Then, if it is made to follow only from "withhold" (aqli'i), it would not be good to conjoin it to the root of the story, namely ﴿and it was said: O earth, swallow﴾. How could that be, when choosing this interpretation indicates that the Flood's character as a flood has ceased, because the decrease of water is other than its complete removal, and that the inner parts of the earth did not remain in the state of strong upwelling they had been in, but returned to the desired equilibrium? There is absolutely no such meaning in the restriction to subsiding. End of quotation.

Al-Tabarsi (Abu 'Ali al-Tabarsi) claimed that the Imams of the House, may Allah be pleased with them, agreed that the attributed water is that which gushed forth and boiled over, and that it is precisely that which was swallowed and subsided, and nothing else; and that the water of the sky became seas and rivers.

Ibn 'Asakir (Abu al-Qasim Ibn 'Asakir) narrated, through the chain of al-Kalbi (Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi), from Ibn 'Abbas, what supports this. This is clearly contrary to what the words of al-Sakkaki require, and there is much doubt about its soundness.

Then, He, exalted be He, followed the subsiding of the water with what is the primary purpose of the story, which is His words, exalted be His majesty: ﴿and the matter was decided﴾. Then He followed the mention of the purpose with the account of the ship, because it came later in existence. Then the story was concluded with the allusion you have come to know.

This is all a consideration of the verse from the aspect of eloquence (balagha). As for its consideration from the aspect of semantic fluency (fasaha ma'nawiyya), it is, as you see, a subtle arrangement of meanings and an expression of them, condensed and clarified, with no complexity that trips up the mind in seeking the intended meaning, nor any twisting of the path for the seeker. Rather, if you test yourself upon hearing it, you will find that its words race ahead of its meanings and its meanings race ahead of its words. No word in it reaches your ear without its meaning reaching your heart even sooner.

As for its consideration from the aspect of verbal fluency (fasaha lafziyya), its words, as you see, are Arabic, in common use, following sound rules, free from dissonance, far from ugliness, sweet to the sweetest, smooth to the smoothest. Each of them is like water in its purity, like honey in its sweetness, and like the breeze in its gentleness. May the bounty of the Revelation of Allah, exalted be He, be praised for what its verses have gathered. Despite the varied descriptions of its beauty by those who describe it, time would end while it still has what has not been described. What has been mentioned in explaining the excellences of this verse, in comparison with what it contains, is but a drop from a reservoir and a flower from a garden.

Ibn Abi al-Isba' (Zaki al-Din Ibn Abi al-Isba') mentioned that it contains twenty types of badi' (rhetorical embellishment), although it consists of only seventeen words. These are: the complete paronomasia (al-munasaba al-tamma) in ﴿ibla'i﴾ and ﴿aqli'i﴾; the metaphor (isti'ara) in both; the antithesis (tibaq) between the earth and the sky; the majaz (figurative usage) in ﴿O sky﴾, since the literal meaning would be "O rain of the sky"; the allusion (ishara) in ﴿and the water was made to subside﴾, for it expresses many meanings, since water does not subside until the rain of the sky ceases and the earth swallows what comes out of it, so that what is upon the surface of the earth decreases; the ridf (sequence/implication, i.e., a word following another in meaning) in ﴿and it came to rest﴾; the tamthil (illustrative simile) in ﴿and the matter was decided﴾; the ta'lil (aetiological reasoning, giving a cause) since the subsiding of the water is the cause of the settling; the correctness of the taqsim (division), since it covered all the divisions of the water in its state of decrease; the ihtiras (precautionary qualification) in the supplication, lest it be supposed that the drowning, by its generality, included one who did not deserve destruction, since His justice prevents Him from invoking destruction upon one who does not deserve it; the goodness of the nasaq (sequence) and the harmony of wording with meaning; the brevity (ijaz), since He, glorified be He, related the story comprehensively in the briefest expression; the tasmih (embedding of the beginning's meaning in the end, so the beginning indicates the ending); the tahdhib (refinement), since its individual words are described with attributes of beauty; the beauty of clarity (husn al-bayan), in that the listener does not hesitate in grasping the meaning of the speech nor is anything in it obscure to him; the tamkin (firm placement), since the closing rhyme (fasila) is settled in its place and at rest in its position; and the insijam (harmony).

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti (Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti), after quoting this from Ibn Abi al-Isba', added the objection, and others added many other things, but these, like the words of Ibn Abi al-Isba', have all been pointed at with the finger of objection.

Our shaykh 'Ala' al-Din, may Allah elevate his rank in the highest of the 'Illiyyun, composed a treatise on this noble verse, in which he gathered what had appeared to him and what he had come to know of its excellences. These reached one hundred and fifty excellences. I sought this treatise in order to mention some of its subtleties, but I did not find it, and it seems the flood of events has drowned it. Perhaps what we have quoted contains a remedy for deficiency. And Allah, exalted be He, is the Granter of success to what is right, and with Him is the knowledge of the Book.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 45:

﴿And Noah called out to his Lord﴾. That is, he intended this, as shown by the fact that Allah's words that follow are linked to it with *fa'* (so, then): ﴿so he said, "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family"﴾. It has also been said that the calling out is in its literal sense, and that the *fa'* (of linking) is used because detail ordinarily follows summary. ﴿And indeed Your promise is true﴾. That is, indeed Your promise of that, or every promise You make, is not subject to failure. Thus the specific promise in question is included in it, by primary inclusion.

﴿And You are the most just of judges﴾, because You are the most knowing of them and the most just of them. It has been mentioned that when the elative form *af'al* (the comparative/superlative form) is derived from something that does not admit comparison or increase, its meaning must be taken in a sense that suits the meaning of that non-comparable attribute. Al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam said in his *Amali*: "This and similar expressions, such as *arham al-rahimin* (most merciful of the merciful) and *ahsan al-khaliqin* (best of the creators), are problematic, because *af'al* is only annexed to its own kind, and here that is not the case, since creating (*khalq*) from Allah, exalted is He, means bringing into existence (*ijad*), while creating from others means acquiring (*kasb*), and these two are distinct, according to the well-known view of the Ash'arites." And mercy from Allah, exalted is He, is acceptable if it is understood as will (*irada*) or treated as a metaphor by comparison (*majaz al-tashbih*). If, however, it is meant as the bringing into existence of the act of mercy, it is also problematic, since there is no originator other than Him, exalted is He. Al-Amidi answered that it means "the greatest of those who are called by this name." This was objected to on the ground that it makes comparison apply to something other than that for which the word was coined, and this suits the view of the Mu'tazilah. So reflect on this.

It has also been said that the meaning here is: You are more wise than those who possess judgment, on the basis that *al-hakim* (judge) derived from *al-hukm* is like *al-dari'* (one who wears armour) derived from *al-dir' (armour)*. This was objected to on the ground that the pattern is not analogical (*qiyasi*), that *hakim* in the sense of *hakim* (wise) has not been heard, and that *af'al* cannot be formed from it, because it does not follow the verb. One does not say *alban* or *atmar* from a person, since there is no verb with that meaning. The answer that it has become common in their speech, so it is permitted, is a weak (*marjuh*) possibility. The answer that it belongs to the category of *ahnaka al-shatayn* (one who has the strongest grip on the two jaws) does not avoid artificiality, as stated in *al-Kashf*. It has been countered that for "wisdom" there is a triliteral verb, *hakama*, and the elative of a triliteral verb is analogical. Moreover, *ihtanaka al-jarad* (the locust consumed everything), *alban*, and *atmar* have been heard, so at best it would be from a non-triliteral verb, and what is wrong with that is not hidden. Some have interpreted it on this basis as "the most knowing of them in wisdom," as in their saying *aball* from *abal* meaning "knowing," and *ahdhaq* (the most skilled) in the affair of camels.

Whatever the case, this calling out by him, peace be upon him, flows with appeal for compassion and a graceful seeking of means toward One whom he knew to have been a benefactor and bestower of favour in his affair, both at the beginning and at the end. It is in the manner of the supplication of Job, peace be upon him: ﴿When he called out to his Lord: "Harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful"﴾. Accordingly, this would have been before the drowning, and the *waw* (and) does not require sequential order. It has also been said that the calling out came after the drowning, and that its purpose was to inquire about the reason his son was not saved, given the prior promise of Allah, exalted is He, to save his family, and his son was one of them. The full discussion of this will come shortly, if Allah, exalted is He, wills.

[p. 69]

**﴿He said﴾** is a resumptive, explanatory construction (*istiʾnaf bayani*: a new clause answering an implied question), as if it were said: "What did his Lord, glorified is He, say to him when He called him with that?" So it is said: **He said: ﴿O Noah, indeed he is not of your family﴾**, meaning he is not of them at all, because the basis of being "of the family" is religious kinship, and it is severed by disbelief. There is no connection between a Muslim and a disbeliever. For this reason they did not inherit from one another. They have also said that the kinship of religion is closer than the kinship of blood, as Abu Firas indicated in his saying:

*The affection of Salman for him was a kinship,*
*while there was no blood tie between Noah and his son.*

Or, ﴿he is not of your family﴾ means those whom you were commanded to carry in the ark, since he is excluded from them by the exception. This is related from Ibn Jarir and ʿIkrima, while the first view is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. According to both views, he is not among those who were promised deliverance. It seems that since Noah's supplication, peace be upon him, was based on the assumption that Kanaan was of his family, and since it recalled the promise of Allah, exalted is His remembrance, He first negated that he was of them. Then He gave the reason for his not being of them, by way of confirmatory resumption (*istiʾnaf tahqiqi*), with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed he is an unrighteous deed﴾. Its original form is "indeed he is one of corrupt deed" (*dhu ʿamal fasid*), and the word *dhu* (possessor of) was dropped for intensification (*mubalagha*), by making him the very essence of his deed because of his constant persistence in it. The noun is not to be understood as elided, because then the intended intensification would be lost. A similar construction occurs in al-Khansaʾ's elegy for her brother Sakhr:

*Is the mother of a young camel, longing over a colt,*
*whose sighs are aided by the groaning of the calf-teat?*

*She grazes as long as she grazes, until she remembers,*
*and then she is nothing but advance and retreat.*

*On a day more painful when Sakhr parted from me,*
*and life has both sweetness and bitterness.*

The word *ṣāliḥ* (righteous) was replaced by *ghayr ṣāliḥ* (not righteous), either because *fāsid* (corrupt) is sometimes applied to what has become corrupt though it is by nature suited to righteousness, so it is not an explicit term for what is purely corrupt, like injustices; or to hint that the deliverance of those who were saved was only because of their righteousness.

Al-Kisaʾi and Yaʿqub recited (*innahu ʿamala ghayra ṣāliḥin*) in the past-tense form of the verb with *ghayr* in the accusative. This is the recitation of ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, Ibn ʿAbbas, Anas, and ʿAʾisha. She and Umm Salama narrated it from the Prophet ﷺ. The original is "he did a deed that was not righteous," and it was also recited thus, as related from ʿIkrima. Thus the qualified noun is omitted and its adjective takes its place. This is common and regular when the meaning is clear and no ambiguity remains. Some have criticized this reading here, saying that the Arabs hardly say "a deed not righteous" (*ʿamalun ghayru ṣāliḥin*) but rather "he did a deed not righteous." This is not a valid objection. This recitation supports the view that the pronoun *innahu* in the first reading refers to Noah's son, because in it the pronoun certainly refers to him. Thus the view that in the first reading the pronoun refers to his abandoning the boarding with them and his staying behind from them, meaning that this abandonment is a deed not righteous, becomes weak, because it is contrary to the apparent sense in itself, as is not hidden. Similar to this is the view that the pronoun refers to Noah's calling, peace be upon him, meaning that this calling of yours is a deed not righteous. In that case the sentence would cease to be an explanation of what preceded, the benefit of that would be lost, and the discourse would not be on one course. However, there is a report from Ibn ʿAbbas that supports this. Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from him that he said: "The wives of the prophets, peace be upon them, do not commit adultery." The meaning of the verse is: "Your asking Me, O Noah, is a deed not righteous, which I do not approve for you."

In the narration of Ibn Jarir from him: "Your asking about what you have no knowledge of is a deed not righteous." Perhaps this is not established from this report, because the apparent sense of the first narration is that he made the pronoun refer to the request and not to Noah's son, because attributing adultery to one to whom it is not attributable is implied. He, may Allah be pleased with him, is too exalted to be unaware that this dreaded consequence does not follow.

Then, since Noah's supplication, peace be upon him, was based on Kanaan being of his family, and this was negated and verified by explaining its cause, He made a consequence of this the prohibition of asking for his deliverance. But the prohibition came in a general form that includes what was mentioned, including it primarily. So He said, glorified is He: **﴿So do not ask Me﴾**, meaning: when you come to know the clear state of affairs, then do not request from Me **﴿what you have no knowledge of﴾**, meaning a request about which you do not know with certainty that its fulfilment is right and in accordance with wisdom, on the assumption that *mā* refers to the thing asked, which is the object of the verb "ask." Or, a request about which you do not know that it is right, on the assumption that *mā* refers to the verbal noun, which is an absolute object (*mafʿul mutlaq*). Then the prohibition is explicitly directed at both what is known to be corrupt and what is of uncertain state. This is what Shaykh al-Islam stated. He also allowed that **﴿what you have no knowledge of﴾** means that you do not know whether it is right or wrong, and this is the view taken by al-Qadi. Then the prohibition applies to what is of uncertain state, and what is known to be corrupt is understood from it by a stronger inference. In either case it is general and includes what we are concerned with, as we have mentioned. The calling was called asking because it implies asking, even if not explicitly stated, as is not hidden. With this, according to what is related from Abu ʿAli, the phrase is either connected to what the mentioned knowledge indicates, even if it does not govern it, as in the saying:

*I raised him until he grew up,*
*and my reward for it was that I be beaten with a stick.*

Or it is connected to what is settled in that, and the discussion of what comes later is the same, God willing.

The verse makes clear that his calling, peace be upon him, was not an inquiry about the cause of his son's non-deliverance while the cause of deliverance was certain in his view, as al-Qadi allowed, on the basis that it was after the drowning. Rather, it was a supplication from him, peace be upon him, for his son's deliverance when the waves came between them, and he did not yet know of his destruction. Either by bringing him near the ark through the clashing of the waves, for example, or by bringing the ark near him. It was said: or by delivering him by another means. But the recalling of the promise in the supplication rejects this, for it is specific to deliverance in the ark. Mere interposition of a wave does not necessitate destruction, much less knowledge of it, since it is evident that Allah could preserve him by His mercy, and He had promised him the deliverance of his family. He did not believe that there was an obstacle in him to being included among them, because of hypocrisy and not openly declaring disbelief. This is because such a view requires, in wording, the assumption of an elision and a connection, and in meaning, that the prohibition against inquiring about what one does not know is not in accordance with wisdom, since not knowing a thing is a motive for inquiring about it, not for abandoning it.

It was also said: the asking about the reason for non-deliverance is, with what it contains of boldness, and a semblance of objection, since it became clear to him, peace be upon him, that his son was among those excepted by destruction. This is not sound, for how could it be, when that calling of his is one that drips with supplication for compassion?

It was also said: the prohibition is only against asking about what one has no need of, either because it does not concern him, or because the indications about his condition were already established, not asking for guidance. So there is no harm then in the words of al-Qadi. But this is, as you see, not right. A perfumer cannot repair what time has spoiled. The truth is that this request concerned deliverance, and it occurred before the drowning was certain, at the sight of its approach. He did not know of his disbelief at that time, for he had not openly declared it. Otherwise he would not have supplicated for him, nor would He have forbidden him to do so. The words **﴿and do not be with the disbelievers﴾** do not indicate that he was a disbeliever in his view. Rather, it is a prohibition against entering their company, and a definite statement that doing so necessitates drowning, in the demonstrative manner, as we have stated before. It seems that Noah, peace be upon him, understood his son's argument as not being obstinate opposition and stubbornness, because of the dominance of love and his distraction from giving reflection its due. Therefore he made the request he made, and was rebuked that a man in his position, guiding and bearing the burdens of the call for so long a period, should not have been confused about the speech of one seeking guidance and the speech of a stubborn opponent. This returns to abandoning the more excellent course, which is what is meant by His saying, glorified is He: **﴿I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant﴾**.

Shaykh al-Islam mentioned that his withdrawal, with his intention of seeking refuge in the mountain, is not an explicit proof of persistence in disbelief, because it is evident that it is possible that this was due to his ignorance that deliverance is confined to the ark, and his supposition that the mountain also functions in that way. Or it was due to disliking being confined in the ark. Rather, his saying **﴿I will take refuge in a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾**, after Noah had said to him **﴿and do not be with the disbelievers﴾**, perhaps gave Noah, peace be upon him, hope regarding his faith, since he did not say "I will be with them," or "we will take refuge," or "it will protect us." Singling himself out with the attribution of the two mentioned actions perhaps indicates his separation from the disbelievers, his withdrawal from them, and his compliance with some of what Noah, peace be upon him, had commanded him. However, if Noah, peace be upon him, had carefully considered his condition and investigated his states in everything he did and left undone, he would not have been confused as to whether he was not a believer and whether he was excepted from his family. That is why it was said to him: **"Indeed I admonish you"**, and so on. This clearly shows that the focus of the reproach was his confusion, as we have mentioned. This is the view of al-Zamakhshari, who said: Allah, exalted is He, had presented to him, peace be upon him, the promise of delivering his family, with the exception of those against whom the word had already gone forth. He was obliged to believe that among the whole group there were those who deserved punishment because they were not righteous, and that not all of them would be saved. And he should not have had any doubt, when his son was near drowning, that he was among those excepted, not among those who were excepted from. So he was rebuked for becoming confused about what should not have been confused. It seems he meant that the exception indicated that the consideration that matters is righteousness, not kinship. So he should have made that the primary principle and examined the family for its presence, and considered them all equal in deserving punishment except those whose righteousness and faith were known. He should not have made being of the family the primary principle, so that he asked for his deliverance while doubting his faith. Thus he fell short in what was incumbent upon him, to some degree of shortfall. The men of firm resolve are held accountable for even the smallest things, and the good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near.

Ibn al-Munir did not accept that this was a rebuke. He said: "In al-Zamakhshari's words there is something that indicates that he believes Noah, peace be upon him, did something that required ascribing ignorance to him and rebuking him for it. But the matter is not as he imagined." Then he said: "We shall clarify that the truth in the verse is far removed from its literal wording, while clearing Noah, peace be upon him, of what al-Zamakhshari supposed was attributed to him. We say: when Noah, peace be upon him, was promised the deliverance of his family, except those against whom the word had already gone forth, and he had not been informed of his son's condition nor had knowledge of the inner reality of his affair, but rather believed by outward appearance that he was a believer, he remained holding to the general wording of the family, which was established, and no certainty of his son's disbelief opposed it, to the point that he would leave the family and enter the excepted. So he asked Allah, exalted is He, about him on that basis. Then He made clear to him that he was in His knowledge among the excepted, and that he himself had no knowledge of this. Therefore he asked about him. This is a case in which giving an excuse is more fitting than considering it a rebuke. For Noah, peace be upon him, is not charged by Allah, exalted is He, with knowledge of what He has kept to Himself as unseen. As for His saying, glorified is He, **'I admonish you'**, and so on, the meaning is a prohibition against the occurrence of the request in the future, after He had informed him of the inner reality of his affair, and that if he asked in the future, he would be among the ignorant. The purpose of this is to present what keeps him, peace be upon him, on the course of infallibility. An admonition does not require that a sin has occurred. Rather, its aim is that no sin should occur in the future. That is why Noah, peace be upon him, complied with it and sought refuge in Allah, glorified is He, that there should occur from him what he was forbidden, as His saying, glorified is He, indicates:"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 47:

﴿He said: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge."﴾ Its being false is not hidden from what I know, and it is very much contrary to the apparent meaning. It has come from al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad that he said: "It has reached me that Noah, upon him be peace, wept for forty days over the words God Most High addressed to him." Ahmad related in al-Zuhd from Wuhayb ibn al-Ward al-Hadrami that he said: "When God Most High rebuked Noah concerning his son, and sent down to him ﴿I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant﴾, he wept for three hundred years, until there was under his eyes something like a stream from the weeping."

Al-Wahidi claimed that the request was before the drowning and with knowledge of his disbelief, because Noah, upon him be peace, did not know that his asking his Lord for the salvation of his son was forbidden to him while he persisted in disbelief, until God Most High informed him of that. He objected that if he was aware of his disbelief, along with the explicit statement that among his family there are those who deserve punishment, then seeking deliverance would be one of the reprehensible things; so reflect. According to what we have established, the apparent meaning is that his saying "My Lord" and so on is a repentance for what he had done, upon him be peace. And "mā" here is also an expression either for the thing asked or for the asking, i.e., "I seek refuge in You that I ask You hereafter for a thing whose attainment I do not know to be in accordance with wisdom, or a request whose correctness I do not know, whether it is known to be corrupt or its status is unclear, or I do not know whether it is correct or not correct." He did not say "I seek refuge in You from it" or "from that," for the sake of emphasis in repentance and to show eagerness and vigor in it, and seeking blessing by mentioning what God Most High taught him. This is more eloquent than saying "I repent to You of asking You," because it indicates that this is a dreadful, forbidden matter from which there is no escape except by seeking refuge in God Most High, and that his power, upon him be peace, falls short of being saved from hardships except by that, as in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim; and the possibility that it contains a rejection and denial, like the saying of Moses, upon him be peace, in the Baqarah ﴿I seek refuge in God that I should be among the ignorant﴾, which hardly passes through the mind of any of the ignorant.

Furthermore, in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud there is "Indeed it is an unrighteous deed" (inna-hu 'amalun ghayru salih) "that you ask Me." He preferred by this that the pronoun in "innahu" in the widely transmitted reading refers to the call that includes the request. Ibn Kathir read ﴿fa-la tas'alanna﴾ with a fatha on the lam and a shaddah on the nun with fatha, and this is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. Likewise Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it, except that they kasra'd the nun, on the basis that its original form is "tas'alunI," so the nun of protection was deleted because of the gathering of nuns, and the shaddah nun was given a kasra for the following ya', then the ya' was deleted, being satisfied with the kasra. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and Zayd ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with them both, read it likewise, except that they retained the ya' after the nun; its matter is evident. Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Mulaykah read "tu'alanI" without hamza, from sa'ala yas'alu, so both are interchangeable, and this is a widespread dialect. The rest of the seven read with a hamza, with the lam sukun, a kasra on the nun and its lightening; Warsh and Abu 'Amr retained the ya' in continuous reading, and the rest omitted it. ﴿And if You do not forgive me﴾ what came from me of the aforementioned request, ﴿and have mercy on me﴾ by accepting my repentance, ﴿I shall be among the losers﴾ in deeds, as a consequence of that. The delay in mentioning this after the report of the command given to the earth and the sky and what follows it, although its proper place would be to be mentioned right after His, glorified is He, saying ﴿so he was among the drowned﴾, as occurred in reality, as you know, since the call was for seeking deliverance before knowledge of the destruction. It has been said: so that it would be in the style of the story of the cow in its surah, indicating that this meaning stands independently in purpose, because of the subtleties in it, such as making kinship of religion overwhelm kinship by lineage, and that one should not proceed in fundamental religious matters except after certainty. This was criticized by pointing out the difference between what is here and what is there according to one who has a heart; and what is mentioned about making kinship of religion overwhelm kinship by lineage, etc., is not lost even on the assumption that the discourse is arranged according to the order of occurrence.

Some verifiers chose that this is because mentioning this call, as you see, requires what came before as an answer, which requires mentioning his repentance, upon him be peace, which leads to mentioning its acceptance within the command to his descent from the ark, upon him be peace, with peace and the abundant blessings upon him and upon the believers, as will come, God willing. There is no doubt that these meanings are so intertwined, one holding onto the other's waistband, that the noble verses containing them hardly separate them from one another, and that this is only with the completion of the story, and that is only with the completion of the flood. Therefore the situation necessarily required mentioning its completion before this call, and it occurs at the mention of Canaan being among the drowned. Because of this subtlety the excellence of the eloquent concision increased. There is also another benefit in it, namely the explicit statement of his destruction from the very beginning; if the call had been mentioned after ﴿so he was among the drowned﴾, one might have supposed at first, until the statement ﴿indeed he is not of your family etc.﴾ came, that he would be saved by his supplication, so his destruction was stated explicitly. Then he related the story in a manner that silenced the eloquent orators, then he addressed what occurred in the midst of that between Noah, upon him be peace, and the Lord of Majesty, may His wisdom be exalted and His word be high. Then, after his repentance, upon him be peace, he mentioned its acceptance in His saying, mighty and majestic:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 48:

﴿It was said: "O Noah, descend"﴾, etc. This is in the most eloquent style. The verb is in the passive form (buniya al-fi'l li-ma lam yusammi fa'iluhu), because it is evident that the one who says it is Allah, exalted is He. It was also said that the speaker is the angels, peace be upon them. "Hubut" means descent. It was said: that is, descend from the ark. It was also said: from the mountain to the earth. This is because it is narrated that the ark came to rest on al-Judi on the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah. Those with him stayed there
[p. 73]
for a month. Then it was said to him: "Descend." So he descended to the land of Mosul and built near the mountain a village called "the Village of the Eighty," the number of those who were in the ark. In another narration from Ibn Abbas, each of them built a house, and so it was called "the Market of the Eighty."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: When the ark came to rest on al-Judi, Noah, peace be upon him, remained as long as Allah willed. Then he was given permission to descend, and he descended onto the mountain. He called the raven and said: "Bring me news of the earth." So it went down to the earth, where the drowned of Noah's people were, and it alighted on a carcass of theirs. It was slow in returning, so he cursed it. He then called the dove, and it landed on his palm. He said: "Descend and bring me news of the earth." So it descended, and after a short while it came back shaking its feathers with its beak, and said: "Descend, for the earth has produced growth." Noah said: "May Allah bless you and the house that shelters you, and make you beloved to people. Had it not been that people would overpower you, I would have asked Allah, glorified is He, to make your head of gold." In my view, the apparent meaning is that the descent is from al-Judi, on which the ark came to rest, to the earth. There is nothing in the context that requires it to be after the settling without any delay, such that one would say that what is beneath the mountain was then submerged in water. The expression "descent" in this sense is most clear. Perhaps the intended meaning of "the ark" here is the place of boarding. The report of the dove and the raven has spread throughout the regions, and storytellers have become obsessed with it. Allah knows best its authenticity, though the stronger assumption is that it is not authentic. Likewise, the report of the Village of the Eighty in the land of Mosul is well known: when it became too cramped for them, they moved to Babylon and built it.

Ibn Asakir narrated from Ka'b al-Ahbar that he said: The first wall built upon the face of the earth after the Flood was the wall of Harran, then Damascus, then Babylon.

It was read as "ihbut" with a damma on the ba' (i.e., the imperative of hubut with a different vowel). ﴿With peace﴾, meaning: accompanied by safety from what you dislike, coming from "us" (min-na), that is, from our side. It may also be that "peace" means greeting and salutation, that is, being greeted by us. ﴿And blessings upon you﴾, meaning: abundant goods that grow in your offspring and in what sustains your livelihood and theirs, of various kinds of provision. Or it means "blessed upon you," that is, one who is invoked for blessing, such that it is said: "May Allah bless you." This suits the meaning of peace as greeting, so it is like His saying: "Peace be upon you, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings." The root of barakah, as al-Raghib said, is the chest of a camel. It is said: "The camel knelt (baraka al-ba'ir)" when it laid down its chest. Permanence is implied in it, which is why a retained body of water is called a birkah (pool). Barakah is the establishment of divine goodness in a thing, named so because goodness becomes firmly established in it as water is established in a pool.

Since divine goodness flows in a manner that is neither perceived nor counted, anything in which an unperceived increase is observed is called blessed (mubarak) and having barakah. Because of what this indicates of permanence, and because it is not perceived, the word tabaraka is used exclusively of Allah, exalted is He, as has been said. In al-Kashshaf: everything that is established and remains has knelt (baraka), and the kneeling of a camel is taken from it. Then "al-barak" in the sense of the chest is from the second meaning, since it is more evident as the instrument of kneeling. Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya narrated from al-Kisa'i that he recited "wa-barakatun" in the singular. In the verse, according to both readings, there is the device of al-ihtiba' (interlocking), since it omits from the second part what was mentioned in the first, and mentions in it what was omitted from the first. The implied meaning is: "peace from us upon you and blessings," or "and a blessing from us upon you." This is from Him, exalted is He, an announcement and glad tidings of the acceptance of his repentance, peace be upon him, and his deliverance from loss, together with an indication of the earth's return to its former state of producing vegetation and other things.

﴿And upon nations﴾, arising ﴿from those with you﴾, branching out from them. Here "min" (from) is for beginning (ibtida'iyyah), and the intended meaning is the believing nations that multiply from those with him until the Day of Resurrection. The intended meaning of "those with him" is his descendants, by the use of the general term to mean the specific, based on what has been said: that no one else had offspring. Thus all people, according to this view, are from the descendants of Noah, peace be upon him. For this reason he, peace be upon him, is called the Second Adam and the Lesser Adam. This is cited as evidence by His saying:
[p. 75]
﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾. It may be said that "min" remains general, based on what most exegetes hold: that descent is not restricted to his children, but that those with him also have surviving descendants. The discussion of those who cited the former argument will come, Allah willing.

As for His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And nations﴾ in the nominative case, which according to al-Zamakhshari is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause ﴿We will grant them enjoyment﴾ is its attribute, and the predicate is omitted, meaning: "and among them are nations." This is permissible because of what preceded it as an indication. For the mention of the blessed nations that branch from them in indefinite form indicates that some of those who branch from them are not upon their attribute. The meaning is that not all who branch from them share in the peace and blessings; rather, among them are nations who enjoy worldly life, ﴿then there will touch them from Us a painful punishment﴾, in this world or in the Hereafter or in both.

Abu Hayyan permitted that "umam" be a subject whose attribute is omitted, and that attribute is what permits beginning with an indefinite noun. The estimate is "and nations from them," and the clause ﴿We will grant them enjoyment﴾ is the predicate, as they say: "Ghee is a manwan for a dirham." It may also be a subject with no attribute implied, and the predicate is also ﴿We will grant them enjoyment﴾. What permits the beginning with an indefinite noun is that the place is one of specification. This is like the words of the poet:

When she weeps from behind her, she turns to him with one side and another side, to us unchanged.

As for al-Qurtubi's statement that "umam" is raised in the sense of "and there shall be nations," if he meant it as an interpretation of meaning, it is good; but if he meant it as grammatical analysis (i'rab), it is not well-made, because this is not one of the positions where "yakunu" (there is/shall be) is implied. Al-Akhfash said: this is like when you say: "I spoke to Zayd, and Amr is sitting," which may be a coordinated construction, or the waw may be for the circumstantial state (hal), and the clause here is a presumed circumstantial clause, because at the time of the command to descend those nations did not yet exist.

Abu al-Baqa said: "umam" is coordinated with the pronoun in "ihbut" (descend), and the estimate is: "Descend, you and nations," and the separation between them suffices to dispense with emphasis. "We will grant them enjoyment" is an attribute of "umam." In this there is an issue: those who were with Noah in the ark were all believers, because of His saying: ﴿and those who believed﴾, and they were not two groups of disbelievers and believers, such that the disbelievers would be commanded to descend with him. Unless it is held that among those believers there were some whom Allah, glorified is He, knew would disbelieve after the descent, so He informed about them the state to which they would come. But this is distant.

He permitted that "min" in ﴿those with you﴾ be explanatory (bayaniyyah), meaning: "and upon nations who are those with you." They are called "nations" because they are factions gathered together and separate groups, or because all nations branched from them, so they are nations figuratively. In this case the nations referred to in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and nations We will grant them enjoyment﴾ are some of the nations that branched from them, namely the disbelieving nations that multiply from them until the Day of Resurrection.

In al-Kashshaf it is said that the correct view is the first. It was said: because it corresponds to His saying: ﴿and nations We will grant them enjoyment﴾, and because it is more comprehensive, and because "min" for beginning is especially more frequent in indefinite contexts, and for the subtle point of including those who arise among those greeted with peace, and of excluding those granted enjoyment from them, which indicates what He expressly stated in His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is one whose deed is not righteous﴾. For this subtle point "from them" was omitted in the second, and the peace of Noah, peace be upon him, was relied upon instead of the peace of the believers of his people, because the Prophet is the leader of his community, and this honour and his unity with him, peace be upon him, suffice for them. Therefore it is not meant that the explanatory reading is preferable, lest it follow that those who are not greeted with peace are included. Moreover, the word "nations" in its usage for those with him, under either consideration, carries no grandeur, because calling a small group "a community" is not fitting, let alone "nations." There is no exaggeration in this context, so one does not depart from the literal meaning. And if it is taken as in His saying: ﴿Indeed Abraham was a nation﴾, it would not suit the magnification of Noah, peace be upon him. It has been mentioned that, on the explanatory reading, the matter of the believing nations arising from those with him, peace be upon him, remains vague, without any mention of it or indication of it, unless it is said: since the intended meaning of "those with you" is the believers, it is known that those who share with them the attribute of faith are like them in what preceded. Yes, it has been said that in the indication of the mentioned term upon the omitted predicate according to that view there is some obscurity, because the mentioned "min" is explanatory, while the omitted one is partitive or for beginning. Perhaps this may be answered by insisting that there is no omission at all, as is one of the views we mentioned just above. So reflect upon all that has been mentioned.

The transmitted position is that the nations in both places are not restricted to specific believers and similarly specific disbelievers. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Muhammad al-Qurazi who said: Included in that peace and blessings is every believing man and woman until the Day of Resurrection, and included in that enjoyment and painful punishment is every disbelieving man and woman until the Day of Resurrection. Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Hasan that he said concerning the verse: Allah, exalted is He, has always taken for us our portion and our share, and remembered us in a way we do not remember ourselves. Whenever a nation perished, He created us in the loins of those whom He saves by His kindness, until He made us the best nation brought forth for mankind.

It was also said: the nations who were granted enjoyment are the people of Hud, Salih, Lut and Shu'ayb, peace be upon them, and by the punishment is meant what befell them. Some have exaggerated the generality of "nations" in the first place, making it include all the animals that were with him, peace be upon him, since Allah, exalted is He, placed blessing in them. But this is nothing, as is not hidden.

Here is a subtle point: in this verse one letter has been repeated many times with extreme lightness, whereas the letter ra' is not repeated like it in the words of the poet:

The grave of Harb in an empty place, and near the grave of Harb there is no grave (qabr)...

And despite what you see in it of extreme heaviness and difficulty of pronunciation, to Allah, exalted is He, belongs the majesty of revelation; how abundant are its subtleties.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 49 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the story of Noah (peace be upon him). It is used with the distal demonstrative because the story is past, so it is treated as far away. It is possible that the distal form was used to indicate the lofty rank of the story. It was also said that the reference is to the verses of the Qur'an, but this is not the correct view. The word is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence. His statement, glory be to Him, ﴿from the news of the unseen﴾ means some of its reports that carry importance. That these are only "some of that" is understood in light of the fact that, because of the long passage of time, the details were no longer known to anyone but God, to the extent that the Magians, it is said, reject them entirely. It was also said that their being from the unseen applies to people other than the People of the Book. Many scholars have mentioned that the unseen is of two kinds: that to which no created being's knowledge relates at all, which is the absolute unseen (al-ghayb al-mutlaq), and that to which the knowledge of a specific created being does not relate, which is the unseen relative to that created being (al-ghayb al-mudaf). This second kind is what the jurists mean when they speak of declaring a ruler who claims knowledge of the unseen to be a disbeliever. His statement, glory be to Him, ﴿We reveal it﴾ is a second predicate for ﴿those﴾, and the pronoun in it refers to the story, meaning revealed ﴿to you﴾. Or the predicate is ﴿from the news of﴾, and ﴿we reveal it﴾ is related to it. The purpose of placing it first is to negate that the knowledge of this was obtained through soothsaying or learned from others. The use of the present tense is to narrate a past situation vividly. Alternatively, ﴿from the news of﴾ is the predicate, and this phrase (﴿we reveal it﴾) is in the position of a circumstantial clause relating to ﴿news﴾. The purpose of mentioning that it is revealed is to compel his people (may God's peace and blessings be upon him) to affirm his prophethood, and to warn them against what befell those who denied.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Neither you nor your people knew it before this﴾ is another predicate, meaning it was unknown to you and to your people. ﴿Before this﴾ refers to the revelation to you, which is known from what has passed. It was also said that it means the time, and it was also said that it means the knowledge acquired through revelation.

In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, the reading is: ﴿before this, the Qur'an﴾. It is possible that the phrase is a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in ﴿we reveal it﴾, or to the kaf in ﴿to you﴾, meaning: neither you nor your people had knowledge of it. The mention of the people alongside him (may God's peace and blessings be upon him) is by way of escalation, as you would say: "This matter is not known to Zayd, nor to the people of his town," since if the many of them do not know it, how would one of them know it? It is known that he had not mixed with others.

﴿So be patient﴾ is a consequence of the revelation, or of the knowledge derived from it, which is indicated by what has preceded. ﴿Before this﴾ means: since We have revealed it to you and you have come to know it by this, then be patient through the hardships of conveying the message and the harm from your people, just as Noah (peace be upon him) was patient through the various afflictions you have heard about during this lengthy period. It was also said that this refers back to His statement: ﴿perhaps you will abandon part of what is revealed to you﴾, and so on. ﴿Indeed the final outcome﴾ is victory in this world and success in the Hereafter, ﴿belongs to the righteous﴾, as you have heard in the case of Noah and his people. It was said that this is a justification for the command to be patient and a consolation to him (may God's peace and blessings be upon him). By piety is meant its first degree, though it was permitted that it means its third degree, which in that sense includes patience, so it is as if it were said: "Be patient, for the final outcome belongs to the patient."

It was also said that the verse is a summary of what preceded and an explanation of the wisdom in revealing that story, namely guiding him (may God's peace and blessings be upon him) and warning his people who denied him. And God knows best.

* * *

Among the allusive (ishari) readings of these verses: ﴿Perhaps you will abandon part of what is revealed to you﴾, and so on. Since it is the nature of human beings that a speaker loses enthusiasm when he finds no receptive place for his words, and his chest is constrained by that, He, exalted is His majesty, stirred the enthusiasm of His Prophet (may God's peace and blessings be upon him) through this noble verse which was sent down to him. He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿You are only a warner﴾. Warning is never free of one of two benefits: lifting the veil from those who are granted success, and establishing the proof against those who are forsaken. ﴿And God is over all things a Guardian﴾, so all guidance belongs to Him. ﴿Whoever desires﴾ by his deed, which outwardly is one of the deeds of the Hereafter, ﴿the life of this world﴾, such as status and praise, ﴿We will pay them their deeds in full﴾, meaning their recompense in this world if We wish. ﴿And they will not be deprived therein﴾, meaning they will not have anything diminished from it. ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is in the Hereafter nothing but the Fire﴾, so that their hearts are tormented by the worldly veils. ﴿And what they did therein is nullified﴾, of acts of righteousness, so they gain nothing from them. And there came the hadith: "Actions are only by intentions, and every person will have only what he intended," and so on. ﴿Is one who is upon clear evidence from his Lord﴾, meaning certainty based on rational or intuitive, unveiling-based proof, ﴿and there follows him a witness from Him﴾, which is the Qur'an confirming that. Here it is shown that rational proofs are supported by the textual Qur'anic verses. Unveiling (kashf) is judged to be sound when the revealed texts bear witness to it and agree with it. For this reason they said: every unveiling that contradicts what came from God, exalted is He, is not valid. ﴿And before it was the Book of Moses﴾, meaning that the proof follows the Book of Moses before this Book, in the state of being ﴿a guide﴾ to be followed in the verification of matters ﴿and a mercy﴾ for whoever is guided by it. This is one interpretation of the verse mentioned by some of them, though we have already mentioned the possibilities in it. They also mentioned that the purpose is to show the great distance between the rank of one who desires the life of this world and the rank of one who is upon clear evidence from his Lord.

The Sufis, may their secrets be sanctified, gave various expressions about the clear evidence (bayyinah). Ruwaym said: it is elevation above the hearts and judgment over the unseen. The leader of the sect (Junayd) said: it is a reality supported by the apparent knowledge (of the Shari'ah). It was also said other than that. And from Abu Bakr ibn Tahir: whoever is upon clear evidence from his Lord, his limbs are devoted to acts of obedience and to what agrees with God's will, his tongue is occupied with remembrance and proclaiming God's blessings and favors, his heart is illuminated by the lights of success and the radiance of realization, and his secret and spirit witness the Truth at all times. He knows what appears from the hidden unseen. His vision is certainty without doubt, and his judgment over creation is like the judgment of the Truth. He speaks only the truth and sees only the Truth, because he is absorbed in it, so how could he see anything else? ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God?﴾, and so on. Some of them made it an allusion to those who affirm existence for other than Him, glory be to Him, who are the people of multiplicity and veils. They interpreted ﴿the witnesses﴾ as the monotheists who do not witness in the abode anything other than Him, glory be to Him, as a dwelling place.

Some people reversed the matter and made it a refutation of the people of unity (ahl al-wahdah), who say that everything you see with your eye or conceive with your mind is God, glory be to Him, in the sense that the disbelief of the Christians is faith in relation to Him. But the people of God, exalted is He, are too far removed from saying this, according to what its outward meaning suggests. Among them are those who made it indicate the state of one who claims to be a friend of God, exalted is He, who adorns himself with the garb of the masters and speaks their words, while inwardly he is more immoral than a monkey and more ignorant than the donkey of Tawmah. ﴿The likeness of the two groups is like the blind and the deaf and the seeing and the hearing﴾. It was said: "the seeing" is one who observes what is intended by it and what happens to him and against him at all times. "The hearing" is one who hears what is addressed to him of reproach, discipline, urging, and encouragement, and is never heedless of the address in any state. It was also said: "the seeing" is one who looks at things with the eye of the Truth, so he denies nothing and is not amazed at anything. "The hearing" is one who hears from the Truth and distinguishes inspiration from whispering. It was also said: "the seeing" is one who witnesses His acts by the knowledge of certainty, His attributes by the eye of certainty, and His essence by the truth of certainty. So the absent things are present to him, and the hidden things are unveiled to him. "The hearing" is one who hears from the calls of knowledge by the Shari'ah, then from the inspirations of recognition by its measure, then he is unveiled by an address from the Truth in secret. It was also said: "the hearing" is one who hears only the speech of his Beloved, and "the seeing" is one who sees only the lights of Him, so he is in their radiance by night and day. To this points the saying of one of them:

"O Layla, from your face is the sun of forenoon, and the darkness is only in the air.
People are in the darkness of their night, while we are in the brightness from your face."

Each of "the blind" and "the deaf" was interpreted by the opposite of what "the seeing" and "the hearing" were interpreted by. His statement, glory be to Him, ﴿Are the two equal?﴾ means that they are not equal, because of the opposition and the vast distance between them, to the extent that their fires cannot see each other. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned from the story of Noah (peace be upon him) with his people what contains guidance, warning, and admonition beyond which there is no more. ﴿The chiefs of those who disbelieved among his people said﴾, meaning the nobles, who were engrossed in the affairs of this world and who were veiled by what they were in from the Truth: ﴿We see you only as a human like us﴾, because they stood at the limit of reason mixed with illusion, so they did not see for anyone a station beyond what they had reached, and they did not perceive the station of prophethood and its meaning. ﴿And we see none following you except those who are our lowest in judgment at first glance﴾. They described them this way because of their poverty, since they knew only the outward appearance of the life of this world, and they did not know that nobility lies in perfection, not in wealth.

﴿And we see in you no superiority over us﴾, nor any precedence that qualifies you for what you claim, ﴿but we think you are liars﴾, so there is no prophethood for you, and they have no knowledge. ﴿He said: O my people, have you considered: if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾, which obliges you to submit to it, ﴿and He has given me mercy﴾, a special guidance of unveiling, exalted above the level of proof, ﴿from Him﴾, above the level of your minds, from the God-given knowledge and the station of prophethood. (But it has been hidden from you) because you are veiled by the outward from the inward, and by creation from the Reality. ﴿Shall we compel you to it while you are averse to it?﴾, meaning you do not turn toward it. It is as if he (peace be upon him) meant that compulsion to it is not possible along with aversion. But if you wish to receive it, then purify your souls and abandon your denial until the effect of the light of desire appears upon you, and then accept it. In this there is an indication that the one who denies cannot receive an outpouring from the people of God, and he will hardly benefit from them as long as he is in denial, and whoever does not believe does not benefit.

﴿And O my people, I do not ask you for wealth for it﴾, meaning I have no aspiration for any of your wealth, by which you thought nobility is attained. ﴿My reward is only from God﴾, so He will reward me with what is better and more lasting. ﴿And I will not drive away those who believed; indeed they will meet their Lord﴾, meaning they are the ones held in nearness to Him, exalted is He. They are the doves of the towers of the kingdom (malakut) and the falcons of the ascending stairs of might (jabarut). ﴿But I see you as a people who are ignorant﴾, you act foolishly toward them and harm them. ﴿And O my people, who would support me against God if I drove them away?﴾, as you wish, while they are in that station. ﴿Will you not then be reminded?﴾, so that you may recognize that seeking to drive them away is misguidance. In this there is an indication that turning away from the poor believers leads to the wrath of the Lord of the worlds.

Abu Uthman said: In the verse, "I am not one who turns away from those who have turned toward God, exalted is He. Whoever turns truly toward God, exalted is He, God turns toward him. And whoever turns away from one toward whom God has turned has turned away from God, glory be to Him." ﴿And I do not say to you that with me are the treasuries of God﴾, and so on, meaning: I do not claim superiority by abundance of wealth, nor by knowledge of the unseen, nor by being an angel, so that you would deny my superiority on account of lacking these things and on account of humanity being incompatible with what I am upon. ﴿Nor do I say to those﴾ whom you look down upon with contempt, ﴿that God will never give them any good﴾, as you say, since good for me is what is with God, exalted is He, not wealth. ﴿God knows best what is in their souls﴾ of good, more than I and more than you do, and He knows their measure and their worth. ﴿Indeed I would then be﴾, meaning if I said that, ﴿among the wrongdoers﴾ like you. ﴿And construct the ark under Our eyes﴾. It was said: this contains an allusion to the eye of unification (ayn al-jam'), which is referred to in the hadith: "My servant does not cease to draw near to Me through voluntary acts," and so on.

And it was said: that is, be within Our care and protection, and do not be in regard to your work and your reliance upon it. For whoever looks to other than Me is veiled by it from Me. Some of them said: that is, let go of your own planning, and do what you are doing of your actions with regard to Our witnessing, not with regard to your own witnessing or that of any of My creatures. It was also said: that is, make the ark, but do not rely on it, for you are within Our eyes, under Our care and guardianship. If you rely on the ark, you will be left to it and will fall from Our eyes. ﴿And do not address Me concerning those who have done wrong; indeed, they are to be drowned.﴾ In this there is an indication of the tenderness of his heart, peace be upon him, after bearing their harshness and harm, and such is the way of the truthful (al-siddiqun). The discourse in the rest of the verse is clear. It is not hidden that it is obligatory to believe in its apparent meaning and to affirm the occurrence of the Flood as God, glorified is He, has related it, and denying that is manifest disbelief (kufr). However, some of the masters have mentioned that after believing in that, it is possible to entertain an interpretation according to which it is the portion of the Sufi from the verse. This is by interpreting the ark as the sacred law (shari'ah) of Noah, by which he and those who believed with him were saved, and the Flood as the overwhelming of the sea of hayula (prime matter) and the destruction of whoever has not stripped himself of it by following a prophet and purifying the soul, as came in the addresses of Idris, peace be upon him, to his own soul, the meaning of which is: indeed this world is a sea filled with water; if you take a ship that you ride when the body is ruined, you will be saved from it to your world, and otherwise you will drown in it and perish. On this basis it may be said: the meaning of ﴿and he was making the ark﴾ is that he takes a sacred law made of the planks of good deeds and the nails (dusur) of knowledge, by which deeds are arranged and firmly established. ﴿And whenever a company of his people passed by him, they mocked him﴾ as is witnessed among the libertines (ahl al-khala'a), who ride the back of desire, mocking those who observe the law and are bound by the fetters of obedience. ﴿He said: If you mock us﴾ in your ignorance, ﴿then we will mock you﴾ when the baseness of your end becomes apparent, ﴿as you mock﴾. ﴿Then you will come to know﴾ at that time ﴿who will receive a punishment that disgraces him﴾ in this world, through the arrival of what does not suit his aim and desire, ﴿and upon him will descend a lasting punishment﴾ in the Hereafter, through the overwhelming of the fires of deprivation and the appearance of the dark forms of vices. ﴿Until when Our command came﴾ to destroy his nation, ﴿and the oven boiled over﴾ through the overwhelming of corrupt humours and excessive moistures over the innate heat, and the force of the nature of the water of hayula over the fire of the animal spirit. Or ﴿Our command﴾ is to their spiritual destruction, ﴿and the oven boiled over﴾ through the overwhelming of the water of the desire of nature over the heart and its drowning in the sea of corporeal hayula. ﴿We said: Load therein of every kind two of each pair﴾, that is, of every category, two of each species, whose specific and generic forms remain when individuals perish.

The meaning of their being carried in it is His knowledge of their survival together with the survival of human spirits, for His knowledge is a part of the ship composed of knowledge and action. Thus their being known is their being carried, and His knowing them is His bearing them within it. (And your family) and whoever is connected to you in your course from your relatives, ﴿except him against whom the word has already gone forth﴾, that is, the judgment of his destruction in eternity because of his disbelief, ﴿and those who believe﴾ from your nation, ﴿and said: Embark therein; in the name of God is its course and its anchoring﴾, that is, in the name of God the Greatest, which is the existence of every perfect gnostic from among the individuals of the human species: the running of its rulings and their circulation in the sea of the corporeal world, and their establishment, and their rulings, as you see in the running of every law and its rulings through the existence of the perfect one from among those who are attributed to it. ﴿Indeed my Lord is Forgiving﴾ of the dark forms of your bodily souls and the sins of the garments of nature that destroy you and drown you in its sea, and that is through following the law. ﴿Merciful﴾ through adding the knowledge-bestowals, the unveilings, and the luminous forms by which He saves you. ﴿And it sails with them through waves﴾ from the sea of corporeal nature, ﴿like mountains﴾, which block the sight and prevent movement, and they are not troubled by that, being protected from any of that wave striking them. This running occurs to the wayfarer at the beginning of his affair, and had he not been protected by adhering to the ship of the law, he would have perished.

[Page 79]
