Perhaps in the verse, according to this, there is a figurative extension (taghlib). ﴿And Noah called out to his son﴾, the one veiled by reason mixed with illusion (wahm), ﴿and he was apart﴾ from that veil, from religion and the law, ﴿O my son, embark with us﴾, that is, enter into our religion, ﴿and do not be with the disbelievers﴾, the veiled, the destroyed by the waves of the desire of the soul, drowned in the sea of nature. ﴿He said: I will betake myself to a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾, that is, I will seek refuge in the brain and seek protection in the intellect shining there, so that it may protect me from the overwhelming of the sea of hayula, and I will not drown in it. ﴿He said: There is no protector today from the command of God, except for him upon whom He has mercy﴾, and He is God, who has shown mercy to the people of monotheism (tawhid) and poured upon them from the showers of His kindness what enabled them to know His true religion. ﴿And the wave came between them﴾, that is, the wave of the desire of the soul and the overwhelming of the water of the sea of nature, and he was veiled from the Truth. ﴿So he was among the drowned﴾ in the corporeal sea of hayula. It was also said: from the side of the Truth, through the tongue of the law, to the earth of nature: ﴿O earth, swallow your water﴾, and stand at the limit of moderation; and to the heaven of reason, veiled by habit and sense, mixed with illusion, clouded by the cloud of desire: ﴿and O heaven, withhold﴾ from supplying the earth. ﴿And the water subsided﴾, that is, the water of the force of corporeal nature and the supply of moisture that veils the light of the Truth and prevents true life. ﴿And the matter was decided﴾ by the salvation of those who were saved and the destruction of those who perished. ﴿And it came to rest﴾, that is, the ship of his law, ﴿upon al-Judi﴾, which is the mountain of the existence of Noah. ﴿And it was said: Away with the wrongdoing people﴾, who worshipped desire instead of the Truth and placed nature in the place of the law. ﴿And Noah called to his Lord﴾, etc. The discourse in this manner is clear in it. ﴿It was said: O Noah, descend﴾ from the place of gathering and the summit of the station of guardianship (wilayah), and immersion in tawhid to the station of detail and the legislation of prophethood, by returning to creation and witnessing multiplicity within the unity, without nullifying the levels. (With peace from Us), that is, safety from being veiled by multiplicity, ﴿and blessings﴾ from the codifying of the laws of the sacred law, ﴿upon you and upon nations﴾ arising ﴿from those who are with you﴾ in your religion until the end of time. (And nations) that is, and there will arise from those who are with you nations: ﴿We will grant them enjoyment﴾ in this world, ﴿then there will touch them from Us﴾ in the afterlife ﴿a painful punishment﴾, by their being burned with the fire of the traces and being tormented by the dark forms.

This is what was said. Then he mentioned that if you wish to apply it to what is within the souls, you take Noah to be your spirit, and the ark to be your perfection in knowledge and action by which your salvation comes at the flood of the sea of hayula, and the oven to be the oven of the body, and its boiling over to be the overwhelming of foreign moisture and corrupt humours, and what it indicated, ﴿of every kind two﴾, to be the armies of the animal faculties and nature, and the birds of the spiritual faculties. You interpret what came in the story of the three sons and the wife: Ham as the heart, Shem as the theoretical intellect, Japheth as the practical intellect; the wife as the soul at rest; the other son as the illusion (wahm); the other wife as corporeal nature from which illusion is generated; the mountain as the brain; its settling upon al-Judi and its descent as like the descent of Jesus, peace be upon him, at the end of time. End of quotation. Whoever looks with the eye of fairness does not rely except on the apparent meaning of the story, and has no need for this interpretation, and suffices with what it indicated: that when lineage is not adorned with righteousness, it is drowned in the sea of nonexistence.

So what benefit is lineage from Hashim, when the soul is from Bahila?

And from the fact that one should seek out supplication diligently and not let compassion distract him from that to other than what has been mentioned. The verse is explicit regarding the disbelief of the people of Noah, peace be upon him, whom God, exalted is He, drowned. In the texts of the Fusus al-Hikam (Nusus al-Hukm) of the Greatest Shaykh, may God sanctify his secret, there is what is explicit regarding their faith and their salvation from punishment on the Day of Resurrection, and that is a matter we do not understand from the Book or the Sunnah. ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows.﴾ And God, exalted is He, is the Guide to the straight path.

**[Page 80]**

﴿And to ʿĀd﴾ is connected to an omitted verb coordinated with His statement, glorified is He, ﴿We sent﴾ in the account of Noah. It is the governing verb (*nāṣib*, the word that puts the following term in the accusative) of His statement, exalted is He, ﴿their brother﴾. That is, "And We sent to ʿĀd their brother," i.e., one of them by lineage, as in their saying "O brother of the Arabs." The prepositional phrase was placed first so that the pronoun would refer back to it. It has also been said that ﴿to ʿĀd their brother﴾ is coordinated with His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Noah to his people﴾, which is in the accusative, with the prepositional phrase coordinated with the prepositional phrase. This is coordination with two complements of a single governing word, and it is not one of the disputed questions. Yet the first view is closer, as in *al-Baḥr* (*al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*), because of the long separation by many clauses between the coordinated words.

His statement, glorified is He, ﴿Hūd﴾ is an explicative apposition (*ʿaṭf al-bayān*, a noun that clarifies the preceding noun) to ﴿their brother﴾. It has been permitted that it be a substitute (*badal*) for it. He, peace be upon him, was a paternal cousin of the father of ʿĀd, and he was sent to them from among them so that this would be more persuasive for them to follow him.

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause (*istiʾnāf bayānī*, a new clause answering an implied question), since his being sent, peace be upon him, naturally raises the question of what he said to them and called them to. It is as if it were said: "What did he say to them when he was sent to them?" So it was said: "He said." ﴿O my people﴾: he addressed them with this to win their hearts. Ibn Muḥaysin read *yā qawmu* with a *ḍamma*, and this is a dialect form for the vocative with a suffixed *yāʾ*, related by Sibawayh and others.

﴿Worship Allah﴾, i.e., Him alone. They were polytheists who worshipped idols. What indicates that this is the intended meaning is His statement, exalted is He, ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾, for it is a resumptive clause functioning as an explanation of the worship commanded, and as a justification for the command to it. It is as if it were said: "Single Him out in worship and do not associate anything with Him, for you have no god other than Him, glorified is He." Moreover, worship is not counted when it is combined with associating partners. Therefore the command to worship Him entails the command to single Him out in it.

﴿Other than Him﴾ with the nominative is an attributive adjective (*ṣifa*) to ﴿god﴾ according to its position (*maḥall*), since it is the subject (*fāʿil*) of the adverbial phrase (*ẓarf*, here the implied predicate "for you"), because it relies on the negation. Al-Kisāʾī read it in the genitive, treating it as an adjective following the wording of the noun it modifies.

﴿You are not﴾: you are not, by making divinity belong to other than Him, exalted is He, as al-Ḥasan said, or by your saying that Allah, exalted is He, commanded us to worship idols, ﴿except fabricators﴾ against Him, exalted is He high above that with great exaltedness.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 51:

﴿O my people, I do not ask you for any wealth in return for it; my reward is only from the One who originated me.﴾ Every messenger addressed his people with this statement, to remove any suspicion they might entertain and to make the admonition purely sincere, for admonition that is mixed with worldly greed has no effect. The use of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is for magnification, and making the relative clause (silah) the act of "fitr" (originating), which is bringing into existence and innovating, is because it is further removed from being attributed to their partners. ( ﴿And if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say, "Allah."﴾ ) Together with this being the foremost of the blessings flowing from the presence of Allah the Exalted, which necessitate gratitude, a gratitude that can only be realized by acting in accordance with the prevailing requirement of His command, glorified is He, while turning away from worldly aims, of which reward is one. Perhaps there is in this an indication that he, peace be upon him, was free of need for their reward, which he only desired in order to be assisted by it in managing his affairs and sustaining his livelihood, [and that this is] with Allah the Exalted, who brought him into existence after he was not, and undertook to provide for him as He undertook to provide for all the other creatures He brought into existence, such as the animals. ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ That is: will you be heedless of this, so that you do not comprehend the admonition of one who seeks no reward for it except from Allah the Exalted? Nothing negates suspicion more than this, so that you would submit to what he calls you to; or else you are ignorant of everything, so that you do not understand anything at all, for the matter is one that should not be hidden from any sensible person.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 52:**

﴿And O my people, seek forgiveness from your Lord﴾ for shirk (associating partners with Allah), ﴿then turn in repentance to Him﴾. That is, return to Him, exalted is He, through obedience. Or it means: repent to Him, glorified is He, and make your repentance sincere and remain steadfast in it. It has been said: istighfar (seeking forgiveness) is a kinayah (allusion by implication) for faith (iman), because it is among its concomitants (rawadif). Since faith in Allah, glorified is He, does not by lexical meaning require disbelief in other than Him, it has been said that the sense is: ﴿then turn in repentance﴾ as if it were said: believe in Him, then turn in repentance to Him, exalted is He, from worshipping other than Him. This was objected to: His, glorified is He, saying (Worship Allah) indicates that worship is exclusively for Him. So if (seek forgiveness) is taken in the sense mentioned, it adds no benefit beyond what is linked to it, although it was possible to link it to the first (i.e., to the first command). Taking a word in other than its apparent sense, with little benefit, is something that must be avoided in the speech of Allah, the Inimitable. It has also been said: what is meant by istighfar is repentance from shirk, and what is meant by repentance is repentance from what proceeded from them other than shirk. [Page 81] This was also objected to, on the grounds that faith erases what came before it. It has been said: what is meant by the first is seeking forgiveness through faith, and by the second, seeking nearness to Him, glorified is He, through repentance from shirk. This was objected to, on the grounds that the nearness mentioned is never separated from seeking forgiveness through faith, because it is one of its necessary consequences, so it cannot come after it, as the particle (then) indicates. It has been said: [and it has been said]. Some of the discussion on this has already preceded at the beginning of the surah.

﴿He will send the sky﴾, that is, the rain, as in the saying of the poet:

When the rain falls upon the land of a people, we pasture it, even if they are angry.

﴿upon you in abundance﴾, abundant in flow and continuous, without harm. So mif'al (the intensive pattern) is for emphasis, as in mi'tar and miqdam.

﴿And He will increase you in strength upon your strength﴾, that is, honour added to your honour, or along with your honour. This returns to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He will aid you with wealth and sons﴾, because worldly honour is by these. It is reported from al-Dahhak that quwwah (strength) was explained as fertility (khisb), and from Ikrimah that it was explained as the child of a child. It has been said: what is meant by it is physical strength. He, peace be upon him, encouraged them with abundant rain and increased strength, because they were people of crops, gardens and buildings. It has been said: Allah, exalted is He, withheld rain from them and made the wombs of their women barren for three years, so Hud (peace be upon him) promised them, on condition of seeking forgiveness and repentance, abundant rains and multiplied strength through procreation. It has been said: the first strength is in faith, and the second in bodies, meaning: He will increase you in strength of faith along with the strength of your bodies. ﴿And do not turn away﴾, that is, do not turn away from what I have called you to. ﴿as sinners﴾, persisting in what you are upon of sin. It has been said: as sinners by turning away, and this is a forced interpretation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 11, verse 53:

﴿They said: "O Hud, you have brought us no clear proof"﴾, that is, no evident argument indicating the truth of your claim. They said this because of their extreme obstinacy, or because of the severity of their blindness to the truth and their failure to reflect on the signs. Thus they believed that what he brought was not a sign, when in fact it was one. Otherwise, he and the other prophets, peace be upon them, brought manifest proofs and striking miracles, even if he does not specify some of them for us. As in the report: "There is no prophet except that he was given of the signs what mankind believed in because of its like." ﴿And we shall not abandon our gods﴾, that is, we shall not abandon their worship, ﴿on your word﴾, that is, because of your word alone, unsupported by proof. Here "ʿan" (on, from) indicates causation, as was said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except for a promise he had made to him﴾. This is what the statement of Ibn ʿAtiyya and others points to. Accordingly, the prepositional phrase is connected to ﴿abandon﴾ (*bi-tarikī*).

Some verifying scholars held that it is connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the pronoun concealed within it, meaning "returning" (*sadirīn*). This is from *al-sadr* (the return), the opposite of *al-warad* (the arrival at water), in the sense of returning from the water. The use of *al-sadr* and *al-warad* as a metaphor (*kinaya*) for action and management has become common in their speech, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"How greatly the age needs one who takes charge of the arrival and the departure."

That is, one who manages affairs with the soundness of his judgment. The term *al-sadr* alone may be used for this, since it implies *al-warad*, so they say: "He only issues from his opinion." The meaning here, then, is: "We shall not abandon our gods while acting upon your word." The negation in this case applies to both the restriction and the restricted together, since they neither abandon their gods nor act upon his word, peace be upon him. It was also said that *sadirīn* means "turning away," and it is a restriction of the negation, meaning: our abandoning the worship of our gods has been negated while we are turning away ﴿from your word﴾. In this case it is a response to his saying: ﴿Do not turn away﴾. Some scholars regarded the intention of this as implicit meaning (*tadmin*), not as an omitted connection, by the indication of ("ʿan"). They regarded it as a metaphor, as you have learned. The statement of al-Zamakhshari is clear on this, as the *Kashshaf* reveals. ﴿And we are not believers in you﴾, that is, we do not confirm what you have brought, or whatever you bring and leave, and this includes that. They exaggerated in refusing to respond, and so they denied the evidence for his prophethood, peace be upon him.

Then they said, emphasizing that, ﴿and we shall not abandon﴾, and so on. Then they repeated what the preceding discourse had indicated, namely their non-belief, through the nominal sentence together with the added *bāʾ*. The fronting of the subject, which conveys emphasis, indicates that no hope can be placed in them in any way. There is in this, of despair, what it contains.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 11, verses 54–55:**

﴿We say only that some of our gods have afflicted you with evil.﴾ That is, it has struck you, from *'arawahu* (it befell him), and its origin is *i'tarahu*, meaning "he intended his *'ura*," i.e., his place and his side. ﴿Some of our gods with evil﴾: by it they meant, may God fight them, madness. The *ba'* (bi) is for transitivity (*ta'diyah*). The indefiniteness of *su'* (evil) has been said to be for diminution (*li-l-taqlil*), as if they did not exaggerate in their insolence, as the attribution of this to *some* of their gods and not all of them indicates. It has also been said to be for magnification (*li-l-taktheer*), an indication that what he said could only come from one who has been struck by great evil, an exaggeration of his departure from the rule of reason. Some have mentioned it as a glorification of the matter of their gods, and that *some* of them have such influence as they have. The clause is the object of the saying, and *illa* (except) is a *laghw* (idle particle), because the exception is *mufarragh* (emptied, i.e., without an explicit excepted element). Its original form is: "we say a saying except our saying this," so the excepted element (*mustathna minhu*) was omitted, and the excepted saying was omitted, and its content (*maqul*) was placed in its position. Alternatively, *i'tarak* itself is the excepted element, because its wording (*lafz*) is intended, so there is no need to posit a saying after *illa*, and it is not a case in which the clause is the excepted element. The meaning of this is that some of our gods have corrupted your intellect, because you revile them, turn people away from their worship, and reduce them from the rank of divinity by what you have said before: ﴿You have no god other than Him; you are only fabricators﴾. Their purpose in this, as has been said, is to explain the cause of what came from Hud, peace be upon him, after they mentioned their non-regard for his words, peace be upon him. It has also been said that it confirms what they said earlier: ﴿We will not abandon our gods on your word﴾, etc.

﴿Nor are we going to believe you﴾, etc. Their belief that he, peace be upon him, was as they claimed (and far be it from him), necessitates that they do not count his words as significant, and that they regard them as among the superstitions, let alone believe in them and act upon their requirements. They mean: we do not believe your speech except as the nonsense that cannot bear truth, issuing from madmen, so how could we believe in it and act upon its implications? They pursued the path of opposition and obstinacy in an ascending order from bad to worse. They first said that he had not brought a clear proof, although what he brought might be a proof in itself even if its indication of the intended meaning was not clear. Second, they refused to comply with his words, peace be upon him, by saying: ﴿We will not abandon our gods on your word﴾, although that could have been achieved by their believing him in what he said. Then they denied that they believed him, peace be upon him, by saying: ﴿Nor are we going to believe you﴾, although his speech, peace be upon him, was of the kind that accepts belief. Then they denied even that level when they said what they said. May God fight them: ﴿How are they deluded?﴾ End of quotation.

There is room for discussion in this, and perhaps the placing of this clause without a conjunction, unlike the first two clauses, supports the view that it was not brought for emphasis like them. Yes, its inclusion is for establishing what was said earlier, which is hardly deniable, so reflect.

﴿He said: "I call God to witness, and you bear witness that I am quit of what you associate﴾ ﴿with Him﴾ (*min dunihi*), that is, of what you take as a partner, while He, glory be to Him, has not taken it as a partner and has not sent down any authority concerning it. Here *ma* is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*), and ﴿with Him﴾ is connected to *tushrikun* (you associate), not a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of its agent. That is: you associate, going beyond God, Exalted is He, in this ruling, since there is no benefit in restricting it to Him. It is also permitted that it be a verbal noun (*masdariyyah*), meaning: from your associating. Al-Zamakhshari permitted both possibilities, saying: that is, from your associating gods other than Him, or from what you associate with Him as gods other than Him. The question of the connection of the preposition in both is one. The estimation of "gods" is to clarify the meaning and to indicate that the object is intended by the drive of the speech. The adverbial phrase cannot be a qualifier of it in both readings, because its explanation (*bayan*) is achieved in both by the same means as we mentioned in explaining the first, and that only holds if the mentioned element is connected, and the meaning is not "gods other than God" according to that interpretation. Al-Tibi has something that differs from this, but it is not sound. And *inni bari'* (I am quit) is in dispute between the two verbs before it. Sometimes the two transitive or intransitive verbs dispute over a noun that is suitable for both to govern, as you say: "I gave and I granted Amr a dirham," just as an intransitive and a transitive verb dispute, such as "stood" and "I struck Zayd."

He, peace be upon him, has answered their shameful claim, which is based on the belief that their gods harm and benefit, with this. In that is an indication of his greater trust in God, Exalted is He, his complete reliance on Him, and His protection of him. He established this by manifesting reliance on the One who suffices him against their harm, in His saying: ﴿

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 56:

﴿Indeed, I have put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord.﴾ In this is a rational proof (ta'lil) for the negation of their harm, in the following manner: you, even if you leave no bowstring unstrung and exert your utmost effort in opposing me, cannot do anything of what you intend against me. For I am reliant upon Allah, the Exalted, confident in His protection, and He is my Owner and your Owner. Nothing proceeds from you, and no affliction befalls me, except by His will. The past tense is used because it is more indicative of the performative (inshа') sense, which suits the situation. Then, he (peace be upon him) demonstrated their inability to harm him, alongside his trust in Him, glorified is He, by saying: ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock.﴾ That is, He is its Owner, capable over it, directing it as He wills, with no creature defying Him, glorified is He. The forelock (nasiyah) is the front of the head, and it is also applied to the hair growing upon it. The use of "seizing by the forelock" to denote power and dominance is metaphorical or metonymic. In al-Bahr it is stated that it has become a convention for power over an animal. The Arabs used to cut the forelock of a captive they had spared as a sign that he had come under their control and been seized by the forelock. His saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾ is included within the proof, and it is an image (tamthil) and a metaphor (isti'arah), since He, the Exalted, is aware of the affairs of His servants, rewards and punishes them, and is sufficient for whoever holds fast to Him, like one who stands upon the highway, guards it, and repels the harm of travellers along it. It is like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾. It has also been said that its meaning is: indeed, your return is to Him, the Exalted, for recompense and the decisive judgment, but the first is likelier. In al-Kashshaf: in His saying ﴿Indeed, I have put my trust in Allah﴾ and the verse, there are subtleties whose contemplation will dazzle you, from the excellence of the reasoning, and what it implies: that whoever relies upon Him does not care for the terror of what befalls him. Then the progression to reversing the threat with His saying ﴿my Lord and your Lord﴾: how then could one who clings to the threshold of servitude be harmed, and one who turns away be saved? What this implies of the obligation of relying upon Him, glorified is He, when this is so; and its reinforcement by His saying ﴿There is no creature﴾ up to the completion of the image, for His power over the one who turns away is more manifest than His compassion toward the one who turns toward Him, contrary to the first attribute. And what it contains of depicting His lordship and power, the Exalted, and depicting the humiliation of the worshipped beings before the force of His dominion, whatever they may be. And concluding with what conveys both purposes definitively is sufficiency for the one to whom He is entrusted and disgrace for the one who turns away from His remembrance and turns his back, based on the meaning that He, glorified is He, is upon truth and justice; no one who holds fast to Him is lost before Him, and no wrongdoer escapes Him. And in His saying "my Lord" (rabbi) without repeating "and your Lord" (wa-Rabbukum) as in the first, there is a subtle secret: after the meaning has been brought to brevity, free from superfluity, it indicates an increase in His particularity to him, and that He is the Lord of all by right, while being his Lord alone by honour and kindness.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 57:

﴿But if you turn away﴾, meaning "you turn away" (تَتَوَلَّوْا). It is a present-tense verb (mudari', present tense) from which one of the two tā' has been elided, and it is construed this way because of the requirement of the phrase "I have conveyed to you" (أبْلَغْتُكم) that precedes it. Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that it be a past-tense verb (ماضيًا). In the speech there is an iltifat (shift in address), and its beauty is not evident; for this reason, whoever took it as past tense supposed a different reading, "then say: I have conveyed to you," but there is no need for that. What supports this is the reading of al-A'raj and 'Isa al-Thaqafi, (تُوَلُّوا) with a ḍammah on the tā' and the lām, the present tense of tawalla. The meaning is: "if you persist in what you were upon of turning away and aversion," because that occurred from them, and so it is not suitable for the conditional (shart, conditional clause). He also permitted that it remain on its apparent sense, by taking it to refer to the turning away that occurred after he had argued with them. The apparent view is that the pronoun refers to the people of Hud, and the address is with them, and this is part of the sentences spoken before. Al-Tibrizi said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, and this is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab). The speech has moved from the first discourse to reporting about those present in the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ). It is as if it were said: inform them about the story of the people of Hud, and call them to faith in Allah, lest there befall them what befell the people of Hud (peace be upon him), ﴿But if you turn away﴾, then say to them, "I have indeed conveyed," and so on. This is far-fetched, as is not hidden.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿then I have conveyed to you that with which I was sent to you﴾, it is the evidence for the apodosis (jawab al-shart, the answer to the conditional). That is: if you turn away, I am not blamed for any failure in conveying, for what I was sent with has reached you, but you refused anything except denying the message and opposing the Messenger. It was said: the estimate is "if you turn away, then there is no great concern of mine regarding you, for my innocence has been established by the conveying, and you are the ones guilty of aversion from faith." It was also said: it is a jaza' (apodosis) by consideration of its necessary meaning, while the future meaning is considered by its manifestation; that is, there is no negligence on my part, and no excuse for you. It was also said: it is a jaza' by consideration of the report, for just as the connection of meaning is intended, the connection of the report is intended, as in ﴿Whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾, according to what has passed. All of this is because the conveying occurred before their turning away, and the apodosis is future relative to the time of the condition.

Abu Hayyan claimed that its validity as an answer is because in conveying his message to them there is included what will befall them of the total punishment; it is as if it were said: "if you turn away, you will be uprooted by punishment." What indicates this is the declarative clause, which is the words of the Exalted: ﴿and my Lord will bring after you another people﴾. In this there is an evident objection. This, as more than one has said, is a resumptive new clause (isti'naf, resumption) with a threat to them, that Allah the Exalted will destroy them and bring other people in their dwellings and their wealth. According to some, it is an isti'naf nahwi (grammatical resumption), based on the permissibility of beginning it with the wāw.

Al-Tibi said: what is meant by this is that the clause is not included in the conditional sentence as an apodosis, but rather is an independent clause coordinated with the conditional sentence. This is contrary to the apparent sense of the expression, and according to it, it is ordered after the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is upon a straight path﴾, and the meaning is that He, upon justice, will take vengeance upon you and destroy you. Al-Jalabi said: I see no obstacle to taking it as a bayani (explanatory) resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani) answering what follows from the turning away, and this is the apparent view, as if it were said: "What will be done to them if they turn away?" It was said: "He will bring after them," and so on. Some have objected that the bayani resumption is not joined with the wāw. He also permitted that it be a coordination (ʿaṭf) on the apodosis, but on what follows the fā' (fa'), because it is the apodosis in reality, and the fā' is a linking particle for it. The entry of the fā' upon the present-tense verb here is because it is a follower (tābi') in which there is leniency.

It was also said: its estimate is "then say: He will bring after them," and so on. Ḥafṣ, by the transmission of Hubayra, read (يَسْتَخْلِفْ) with a jazm (apocopated jussive), and this is a coordination on the place of the apodotic clause with the fā', as if it were said: "But if you turn away, He will excuse me and destroy you, and bring in your place other people." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that this jazm be a sukūn (quiescence) to avoid a succession of vowels. ʿAbdullah (ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him) read likewise, and read with a jazm the words of the Exalted: ﴿and you will not harm Him at all﴾. It was said: whoever made the first jazm also made this jazm, because it is coordinated upon it, and this is the apparent view. The meaning is: you will not harm Him by your destruction at all, that is, His dominion will not be diminished and His affair will not be disordered. What supports this is what has been narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he read "and you will not diminish Him at all" (ولا تَنْقُصُونَهُ شَيْئًا), and he put "shay'an" in the accusative as a absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) for "tadurrūn," that is, "any harm," because it does not take two objects. Some made it a second object explaining it, by what takes two objects, because of the transmitted reading. Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that the meaning be: you are not able, if He destroys you, to harm Him with anything, nor to avenge yourselves upon Him, nor do you oppose His action with anything that harms Him, exalted is He far above that by a great exaltation. The first is more evident. Some estimated the turning away in place of the destruction, that is: "nor will you harm Him by your turning away with any harm at all," because that is impossible for Him, glory be to Him. ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Guardian over all things﴾, that is, a watchful one who encompasses things in knowledge; so your deeds are not hidden from Him, and He does not neglect your being held to account. Thus ḥifẓ (guardianship) is a kināyah (metonymy) for requital. It is also permissible that al-Ḥafīẓ mean al-Ḥāfiẓ in the sense of the dominating ruler, that is, He, glory be to Him, is a guardian who has dominion over all things, and it is part of His nature that nothing can harm Him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 58:

﴿When Our command came﴾, i.e., Our punishment descended, on the understanding that "command" (amr) is the singular of "affairs" (umur). It has been said: or "that which was commanded." The expression of it in this manner, attributed to a pronoun of His, may He be exalted in majesty, and of its descent by "coming," contains what is not hidden of magnification and awe-inspiring terror.

He also permitted that it be the singular of "commands" (awamir), meaning: "Our command came with the punishment." The statement is literal if what is meant is the command of the angels, peace be upon them. It is also permissible that this be a metaphor for occurrence, by way of illustration. ﴿We saved Hud and those who believed with him﴾. It has been said they were four thousand; and it has been said three thousand. Perhaps the victory for the Prophets, peace be upon them, was not permitted to the believers at that time, so this does not contradict what was previously transmitted, that he, peace be upon him, was alone. For this reason, his facing the vast multitude was counted as a miracle for him (ﷺ). However, this requires evidence, such as the claim of his being alone apart from them at the time of the dispute. In the Shihabi marginal notes, it is stated that there is no obstacle to this by considering two states and two times, so reflect. The apparent view is that what took place in the dispute was only at the beginning of the call, and the coming of the command was much later, and the faith of those who believed was in between, so the contradiction is removed. (By a great) mercy (from Us), which is the faith with which We bestowed favour upon them.

This was narrated from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned it, and because some of them sensed in it a whiff of Mu'tazilism, it was not given consideration. There is no harm in taking mercy to mean grace, so that it indicates this was by the sheer grace of God Most High, since it is for Him, glorified be He, to punish the obedient just as it is for Him, exalted be He, to reward the disobedient. The first prepositional phrase, "by a mercy," is connected to "We saved," and this is the apparent view held by many commentators.

Abu Hayyan permitted that it be connected to "believed," meaning: their faith in God Most High and His Messenger, peace be upon him, is by a mercy from God Most High, since He enabled them to it. Perhaps the ordering of the salvation after the descent is by consideration of what it included of punishing the disbelievers, so he has stated the salvation explicitly for emphasis, and ordered the other by consideration of its being the purpose of it as an indication. It is also permissible that "li-ma" be for mere "time" (lil-hin): ﴿and We saved them from a harsh punishment﴾, a repetition to explain what they were saved from, which was the wind that carried the howdah, demolished the dwellings, entered the noses of God's enemies and came out of their posteriors, cutting them into pieces. Or the intended meaning of this salvation is salvation from the punishment of the Hereafter, and of the first, salvation from the punishment of this world. The first was preferred because it is more suited to the requirement of the context. Its summary is that the first is information that the faith to which they were granted success became the cause of their salvation. The second is that this salvation was from a punishment, i.e., a punishment indicating the perfection of favour and an incitement to faith. It is in no way from the style of "Zayd pleased me and his generosity," as al-Allama al-Tibi supposed.

It has been objected to the second that their salvation from the punishment of the Hereafter is not at the time of the descent of punishment in this world, nor caused by it, unless it is answered that it is coordinated with the qualifier and the qualified, as was said concerning His saying, glorified be He: ﴿they cannot delay an hour nor advance﴾. It has been said: there is no concealing what is in it of artificiality without need, because what is suitable to the expression in the past tense, indicating its certainty as if it had occurred, is that by this consideration it be taken as occurring at the time of the descent, metaphorically; or the meaning is: We decreed this, and what will be for them became clear, because this world is a model of the Hereafter. In any case, the intended meaning of the harshness of the punishment is its severity. It may be said, on the first possibility, regarding the description of the punishment that was by the wind, with harshness, which is the opposite of the gentleness that is the attribute of the wind, there is what is not hidden of subtlety; and in it also is a fitting correspondence to their condition, for they were harsh and severe.

I'll translate this passage now, following the instructions for transliteration, honorifics, and Qur'anic quotations.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 59:**

﴿And those were ʿĀd﴾. The demonstrative has been made feminine in agreement with the tribe, as has been said. So the demonstrative refers to what is in the mind, and the form used is that for the distant, either to belittle them or to place them in the position of the distant because of their non-existence. Or the demonstrative refers to their graves and places of destruction, and in that case the demonstrative is for a distant, perceptible object, and the predication is metaphorical, or it is of the type of ellipsis (majaz al-hadhf), meaning: "those are the graves of ʿĀd." It is also permitted that it be by way of the omission of "the people of those ʿĀd," and the sentence is a subject and predicate. The intended purpose is to urge reflection upon them and admonition by their conditions.

As for His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿They denied the signs of their Lord﴾ etc., it is a resumptive statement recounting some of their abominations, meaning: they disbelieved in the signs of their Lord, with which He strengthened His messenger who called to Him and by which He indicated his truthfulness, and they rejected them, and they said: ﴿O Hud, you have not brought us any clear proof﴾. Or they denied His signs, glorified be He, in the horizons and in the selves, which indicate Him, exalted be He, as Hud, peace be upon him, said to them.

It is also permitted that by them be meant the signs which Hud and the other messengers, peace and blessings be upon them, brought, and the plural "the messengers" that comes later according to one opinion agrees with this. The verb "jahada" is transitive with the preposition bi (in) by treating it as analogous to "kafara," because that is what is meant, or by implying its meaning, just as "kafara" is used in the manner of "jahada," so it is transitive without a preposition, as in His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿Indeed, ʿĀd disbelieved in their Lord﴾. It has been said: "kafara," like "shakara," is transitive both directly and with bi. The apparent sense of the words of al-Qamus is that "jahada" is likewise.

﴿And they disobeyed His messengers﴾. It has been said: the intended meaning of "the messengers" is Hud, peace be upon him, and the messengers who were with him before him. This is contrary to the apparent meaning. It has also been said: the intended meaning is Hud, peace be upon him, and all the messengers before him, sent to their nations before and after him, peace be upon him, on the basis that his disobedience, peace be upon him, and likewise the disobedience of every messenger, is equivalent to the disobedience of all the messengers, because all of them agree upon monotheism, so disobedience to one is disobedience to all in it. Or on the basis that every messenger before had commanded the people to obey the messengers and to believe in them if they encountered them, but they did not comply with that command.

﴿And they followed the command of every tyrant﴾ who is exalted above accepting the truth. Al-Kalbi said: he is the one who kills in anger and punishes for disobedience.

Al-Zajjaj said: he is the one who compels people to what he wills. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned that he is the one great in himself, arrogant towards the servants.

Page 87

﴿Obstinate (ʿanid)﴾, meaning: rebellious, from ʿanada, with the vowel of the nun in three forms: ʿandan with sukun, ʿanadan with fatha, and ʿunūdan with a damma on the ʿayn, when he transgresses and exceeds the limit in disobedience. Al-Raghib explained it as "self-admiring with what he has," and al-Jawhari as "one who opposes the truth and rejects it while knowing it," and likewise ʿānada. The latter is applied to the camel that strays from the path and deviates from the right course; its plural is ʿunnad, like rākiʿ and rukkaʿ, and the plural of ʿanīd is ʿunud, like raghīf and rughuf. It has been said that ʿunūd means ʿanīd.

Some have claimed that one says "baʿīrun ʿunūd" (a camel that strays) and does not say "ʿanīd," and the first is pluralized as ʿanadah and the second as ʿunud. Another view is that ʿunūd is one who deviates from the physical path, and ʿanīd is one who deviates from the path in judgment; both are from ʿanada. Its original meaning, it has been said, is "he withdrew to one side," because ʿanad with a fatha on the nun means a side; one says "he walks in the middle, not on the side (ʿanadan)," and from it comes the adverb ʿinda ("with/at"). The word ʿind is also used for a direction, with three vowel forms.

This ruling is not like the two preceding rulings of denying the signs and disobeying the messengers in covering each and every individual among them, for following a command is one of the judgments of the lowly and not of the leaders. It has been said: it is similar in covering, and the intended meaning of "command" is the matter (al-shaʾn), and "every tyrant obstinate" refers to whoever has this attribute among people, not to specific persons of ʿĀd who are characterized by it. The intended meaning of following the command is adhering to it or being content with it in the most complete manner, and this reverts to the attribution, meaning that each of them attributed himself with the attribute of every obstinate tyrant. The clear artifice in this is not hidden, and one may claim generality without needing to resort to such a thing. The intended meaning, as preceded, is that they disobeyed the one who called them to the path of guidance and obeyed the one who drove them to the abysses of perdition.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 60:

﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse﴾ meaning, expulsion (*i'bad*) from mercy and from every good. That is, the curse was made to cling to them. He expressed this by "following" (*al-tab'iyyah*) for emphasis (*al-mubalaghah*), as though the curse never leaves them, however they turn, but rather revolves with them wherever they turn. Or it is because it befell them in the company of their followers. It was also said that the statement is figurative (*al-tamthil*), making the curse like a person who follows another in order to push him into a pit ahead of him. The plural pronoun refers to 'Ad in general, as is the apparent meaning.

It is also permissible that it refers to those among them who followed the tyrants, and the state of a people whose tyrants are ahead of them is that the people of the Fire are ahead of them and the curse and destruction are behind them. From the cursing of these it is known, according to what has been said, that the cursing of others, namely those they followed, is by a stronger argument. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection﴾ meaning, they were also followed on the Day of Resurrection by a curse, which is the everlasting punishment of the Fire. This is omitted because the first mention indicates it, and to signal that each of the two curses is a distinct type, not joined in one phrase such as "they were followed in this world and on the Day of Resurrection by a curse." A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And write for us in this world a good, and in the Hereafter﴾. He used "the Day of Resurrection" here instead of "the Hereafter" for the awe (*al-tahwil*) that the context requires.

﴿Indeed, 'Ad disbelieved in their Lord﴾ meaning, they disbelieved in their Lord, or they disbelieved His blessing and did not thank Him by believing, or they denied Him. ﴿Indeed, distance be for 'Ad﴾ is a supplication against them for destruction, although they are already destroyed in the fullest sense, recording against them that they deserve this and are worthy of it. In the supplication for survival and deserving it, one says "may so-and-so not be distant," and this is frequent in Arabic speech. From it is his saying:

*May my people not be distant from me, those who are the poison of enemies and the bane of the hostile.*

It is also permissible that it is a supplication with cursing, as in al-Qamus: "al-bu'd and al-bi'ad: cursing." The lam is for clarification (*lam al-bayan*), as in their saying "suqyan laka" (watering to you). It was said that it indicates deserving (*lil-istihqaq*), but this is not the case. The repetition of the particle of alerting and the repetition of 'Ad are for emphasis in depicting their condition as dreadful and urging reflection on their story. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the people of Hud﴾ is an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*) to "'Ad," and its benefit is to indicate that 'Ad were two groups: the first 'Ad and the second 'Ad. The second is the 'Ad of Iram according to one opinion. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned in his discussion of Surah al-Fajr that the descendants of 'Ad ibn 'Aws ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh were called 'Ad, as the descendants of Banu Hashim are called Hashim. Then the earliest of them were called the first 'Ad, and Iram is a name for them after their grandfather, and those after them were called the last 'Ad. He recited for Ibn al-Raqiyyat:

*An ancient glory, whose first builder reached 'Ad, and before them Iram.*

This is perhaps the most accurate according to the transmission, with an allusion that their deserving of distance was because of what happened between them and Hud, peace be upon him, and they were his people. This is not for removing ambiguity, since there is no ambiguity that this 'Ad is none other than the people of Hud, peace be upon him, given the explicit naming of him and its repetition in the story. It was said that it was mentioned to add further emphasis by specifying them, along with what that entails of harmony with the verse-endings (*fawasil al-ayy*).

[p. 88]

And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him." The discussion of this is like the discussion of its earlier parallel just above. Most readers (qurra') prohibit the diptote form (sarf) of "Thamud," taking it as the name of the tribe. Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read it with sarf, taking it to mean the people as a group.

﴿He produced you from the earth﴾, that is, He began your creation from it, since it is the first material, and Adam, the origin of mankind, was created from it. It was also said that the speech omits a modifier, meaning "He produced your father," and it was said that "min" means "fi" ("in"), but this is nothing. The intended meaning is restriction (hasr), as the words of some eminent scholars suggest, as if the people, because they did not give Allah His due, believed that the one who does this is other than Him, or Him together with another. So they were addressed in the manner of qasr al-qalb (restriction that corrects a false belief) or qasr al-ifrad (restriction that excludes a partner). There is also the possibility that they believed one of the two matters to be true in reality, not merely figuratively (tanzil). That would require the claim that they were naturalists (tabi'iyyah) or dualists (thanawiyyah). Otherwise, the idolaters, even though they worshipped other beings alongside Him, do not believe that any other being has created them in any way at all. Deriving the restriction, as has been said, comes from placing the agent in a fronted position (ma'nawi). It was also said that it is drawn from the context: since He restricted divinity to Himself, that entails restricting creation to Him as well. So the statement of what they were created from, after the statement that He alone is the Creator, implies this. Reflect on this. It seems that whoever holds the restriction here also holds it in His words, Glorified is He: ﴿and He settled you in it﴾, because of the conjunction and because it is coordinated after the fronting is considered. So it does not extend to what follows it, and there is no benefit in committing to that. That is, He is the One who made you its builders and its inhabitants. The form istaf'ala is then used with the meaning of af'ala. It is said: "a'martuhu al-ard" and "istamartuhu" when you make him its cultivator and entrust him with its cultivation. Al-Raghib and many exegetes took this view. Zayd ibn Aslam said the meaning is that He commanded you to cultivate what you need: building dwellings, digging rivers, planting trees, and other things. In this case the sin (s) of istamara is for requesting (talab). Al-Kiya also took this view, and used the verse as evidence that cultivating the earth is obligatory on account of this request. In al-Kashshaf it is divided into: obligatory, such as building necessary bridges and the congregational mosque; recommended, such as building mosques; permissible, such as building houses; and forbidden, such as building taverns, and buildings erected for showing off or from unlawful wealth, such as the buildings of many oppressors. An objection was raised against al-Kiya: there was no real request here, but the making of them dependent on this, together with His empowering them to do it and inspiring them how to build, takes the place of a request. Al-Dahhak said the meaning is: He made you long-lived in it and let you remain, and one of them would live a long time, to the extent that some of them lived a thousand years. It is well known that the verb is from al-'umr, meaning the duration of life, with shadda (doubling), and from al-'imara, the opposite of ruin (kharab), with takhfif (single consonant). So taking it from al-'umr involves a figurative extension (tajawwuz).

It is related from Mujahid that istamara is from al-'umra, with a damma and a sukun, and is a maqsur (short-vowelled) form. It means, as al-Raghib said, a gift in which you give someone something for the duration of your life or his life. The meaning is: He gave you it and nurtured you, that is, He granted you that for as long as you are alive. Then He, Glorified is He, inherits it from you. Or the meaning is: He made you people who dwell in your homes in it, because when a man inherits his house from one who came before him, it is as if he gave him its use, since he lives in it for his lifetime and then leaves it to someone else.

﴿So seek His forgiveness, then turn to Him in repentance﴾: this is a consequence of what was mentioned before, since the kinds of His kindness that were mentioned call for seeking forgiveness and repentance, Glorified is He. His words ﴿Indeed my Lord is near﴾ mean near in mercy, in accordance with His words, Glorified is He: ﴿Indeed the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾, and the Qur'an explains some of itself by other parts. ﴿Responsive﴾ to whoever calls on Him and asks Him. This adds clarification of what necessitates that. The first is the moving cause (illa ba'itha), and this is the final cause (illa ghayyiyya). How subtle the fronting and the delay are! Some have stated that "near" looks to "repent" and "responsive" looks to "seek forgiveness," as if it were said: return to Allah, for He, Glorified is He, is ﴿near﴾ to you, nearer than the jugular vein, so ask Him for forgiveness, for He, Majestic and Exalted is He, is ﴿responsive﴾ to those who ask. This view is not without elegance.

[Page 89]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 62:

﴿They said, "O Salih, you were among us a man of hope"﴾ meaning, among us, ﴿مَرْجُوًّا (marjuwwan)﴾ meaning virtuous and good, whom we would put ahead of all of us, according to what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "mashuran" means we hoped that you would be a leader who fills the place of the great ones. Kaʿb said: they hoped he would become king after their king, because he was of noble descent and wealth.

Muqatil said: they hoped he would return to their religion, since he disliked their idols and turned away from their religion. ﴿قَبْلَ هَذا (qabla hadha)﴾ means: of what I have undertaken of the call to monotheism and abandoning the worship of the gods. So when we heard from you what we heard, our hope in you was cut off. It was also said: they hoped he would enter their religion after his call to the truth, then their hope was cut off. The phrase -فَقَبْلَ هَذا- means "before this time," not "before the call he had undertaken."

Al-Naqqash related from some of them that (مَرْجُوًّا) means "despised" (ḥaqīran). It seems he first explained it as "delayed," not cared for and not regarded with concern, and then he meant it in that sense. Otherwise, مَرْجُوًّا in the sense of "despised" has not come in the speech of the Arabs. Their statement ﴿أتَنْهانا أنْ نَعْبُدَ ما يَعْبُدُ آباؤُنا (Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped?)﴾ came as a threat and an expression of disgust at that statement from him. The expression -بِيَعْبُدُ- (ya'budu) is used to convey a past state. Talha read (مَرْجُؤًا) with a long vowel and a hamza.

﴿وإنَّنا لَفي شَكٍّ مِمّا تَدْعُونا إلَيْهِ (Indeed we are in doubt about what you call us to)﴾ of monotheism, abandoning the worship of the gods, and other things such as seeking forgiveness and repentance, ﴿مُرِيبٍ (disquieting)﴾. It is an active participle (ism fa'il) from the transitive verb "arabahu," used when it causes him to fall into ریبة (ribah), which is unease of the soul and the absence of tranquility through certainty. Or it is from the intransitive "arāba al-rajulu," when he is one who has ribah. The attribution in both cases is figurative (majaz), but there is a difference between them, as some of the researchers said: the first is transferred from the entities to the meaning, and the second is transferred from the possessor of doubt to the doubt, as you say "shiʿru shāʿir" (the poetry of a poet). On the first reading, it is attribution to the cause, because the existence of doubt is the cause of the doubter's casting doubt, and without it he would not be able to cast doubt.

The tanwin in (مُرِيبٍ) and in (شَكٍّ) is for emphasis (tafkhim). (وإنَّنا) is with three nuns. It is said also: إنّا with two nuns, and both are dialects of Quraysh.

Al-Farrāʾ said: whoever says إنَّنا keeps the letter in its original form, because the pronoun of the speakers, -نا-, is added so that three nuns come together. Whoever says إنّا finds their joining burdensome, so he drops the third and keeps the first two.

Abu Hayyan preferred that the deleted letter is the second nun, not the third, because deleting the third would be a mutilation of the word, since only one quiescent letter would remain from it, whereas deleting the second leaves two letters after it visibly. Moreover, the deletion of the second nun of إنَّ is known with non-first-person pronouns, but the deletion of the nun of -نا- is not known. And there is no doubt that resorting to what is known is preferable to resorting to what is not known.

He said, ﴿O my people, have you considered?﴾ (that is, tell me) ﴿if I am upon clear evidence﴾ (a manifest proof, a decisive argument and insight) ﴿from my Lord﴾ (my Owner and the One who manages my affairs), ﴿and He has given me from Him﴾ (from before Him, glorified is He) ﴿mercy﴾ (prophethood). This is from the equitable speech and the gradual leading-on (istidraj), since it is not conceivable from him, peace be upon him, that there is doubt regarding what falls within the scope of ﴿in﴾ (inna), whose original function is to express the speaker's doubt. ﴿Then who will help me against Allah﴾ (that is, who will prevent me from His punishment). In the statement there is an implied genitive construction (mudaf muqaddar), and "support" (al-nusrah) is used in one of its necessary implications. Alternatively, the verb is implicitly containing the meaning of "prevent," which is why it is transitive with "min" (from). The shift to the explicit mention (of Allah) is for the increase of awe. The fa' (then) is for the sequence of denying any helper, based on what preceded of his being upon clear evidence and the giving of mercy, on the assumption of disobedience, as indicated by His saying: ﴿if I disobey Him﴾ (that is, in being lenient in conveying the message, in forbidding association with Him, the Exalted, and in complying with you in what you desire). For disobedience on the part of one of such a condition is more remote, the accountability for it is more binding, and the denial of His support is more inclusive.

﴿Then you would not increase me﴾ (by your following me, that is, you would not benefit me, since there is no basic loss in me that you could increase) ﴿except in loss﴾ (that is, except that you make me a loser by voiding my deeds and exposing me to the wrath of Allah, the Exalted). Or: ﴿Then you would not increase me﴾ by what you say except that I would attribute to you loss and say to you: "Indeed, you are losers," rather than following you.

This was narrated from al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl. The subject in the first interpretation is they, and the object is implied; in the second, it is the reverse. The tafʿil form (the intensive/causative verbal pattern) often denotes attribution, as in fasaqtahu (I attributed wickedness to him) and fajartahu (I attributed immorality to him). The increase is in its meaning, and the fa' (then) is for the sequence of the absence of increase upon the absence of a helper, which is understood from denying him on the assumption of disobedience, along with the realization of what negates it: his being upon clear evidence from his Lord and the granting of prophethood to him.

It was narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the meaning is: ﴿Then you would not increase me except﴾ in harm regarding your own loss. Thus the statement involves an omitted genitive construction. From Mujahid: "You increase nothing by your argument from the worship of your fathers except loss." He attributed the increase to himself because they gave him that, and he had asked them to believe. Ibn Atiyyah said: the meaning is, "You do not give me, in what I require of you of faith, anything except a loss to yourselves." He attributed the increase to himself in that he requires their statements and is responsible for their oaths, just as you say to one you advise: "I want good for you, and you want evil for me," whereas the clear form would have been, "and you want harm," but since you were wanting good, and what that entails is good, it is proper to attribute the increase to yourself. It was also said: the meaning is, "You do not increase me except in my causing you loss, since whenever you increase in denying me, your loss increases." These are opinions, as you see.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 64:

﴿And O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah﴾. The idafah (genitive construction) is for honour and to draw attention to the fact that she is distinguished from all others of her kind in both character and creation. ﴿A sign for you﴾: a miracle (mu'jizah) indicating the truth of my claim to prophethood. It is a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier, a state-description) of ﴿she-camel of Allah﴾, and the governing element is the meaning of the verb contained in the demonstrative (ism al-ishārah).

It has also been said that the meaning is one of drawing attention. The apparent reading is that it is a ḥāl that establishes a new meaning (ḥāl mu'assisah). It is permitted that it be a ḥāl that emphasises (mu'akkidah), as in ﴿this is your father, affectionate﴾, since the idafah indicates that she is a sign. And ﴿for you﴾ (lakum), as in al-Bahr and elsewhere, is a ḥāl of it, and it is placed before it because it is indefinite; had it been placed after, it would have been a ṣifah (adjective) of it. It was objected that a ḥāl coming from a ḥāl is something no grammarian has maintained, because a ḥāl describes the state of the agent or the object, and a ḥāl is neither of these. It was answered that it is in the sense of the object, because of the demonstrative, since it is identical with the thing pointed to, which is an object in meaning; and the difficulty in this is not hidden. It has also been said: the better view is to say that this ḥāl is an adjective in meaning, but the grammarians did not parse it as an adjective because of a principle they agreed upon, namely prohibiting the placing of what they call a follower (tābi') before the thing it follows (matbū'). So the saying "the ḥāl describes the state" is restricted to other than this ḥāl. It was objected that this and similar answers do not close the door of objection, because the objector denied that any grammarian has held that a ḥāl may come from a ḥāl, and what was mentioned does not establish that view, which is evident. Yes, it may be said that the restriction of Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari, who are both among those who studied Arabic, to this kind of parsing suffices for the purpose in the fullest way; and by "dependence" in his speech al-Zamakhshari meant semantic dependence, not grammatical dependence, so there is no contradiction in it; this is a discussion that does no harm.

It has also been said: ﴿for you﴾ (lakum) is a ḥāl of ﴿she-camel﴾ (nāqah), and ﴿a sign﴾ (āyah) is a ḥāl of the pronoun in it, so they are interlocked (mutadākhilah). The meaning of the camel belonging to the addressees is that she is beneficial to them and specific to them, she and her benefits; so it is not objected that the very essence of the camel has no specificity to them, rather what is specific is that she is a sign for them. It has also been said: ﴿for you﴾ is a ḥāl of the pronoun in ﴿a sign﴾, because it has the sense of a derived noun (mushtaqq). The more apparent view is that ﴿for you﴾ explains to whom she is a sign. It is permitted that ﴿she-camel﴾ be a badal (substitute) or an 'atf bayan (explicative apposition) of the demonstrative, with ﴿for you﴾ as its predicate, and ﴿a sign﴾ a ḥāl of the concealed pronoun in it.

﴿So leave her﴾: let her be ﴿to eat in the land of Allah﴾, so there is no burden of her upkeep upon you. The verb is jussive (majzūm) because it occurs in the answer to an imperative. It has been read in the nominative (marfū') as a resumption (istinaf) or as a ḥāl, as in al-Bahr. The understood meaning of eating is its literal sense; but it has been said that in the verse there is an elliptical sense, i.e. she eats and drinks. It is also permitted that it be a metaphor for nourishment in general, and the context is evidence for this.

﴿And do not touch her with harm﴾: that is, with anything of it, let alone hamstringing or killing. The prohibition here is of the same type as the prohibition in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not approach the property of the orphan﴾, etc.

﴿Then a near punishment will seize you﴾ for that: imminent, which will not delay beyond your touching her with harm except briefly, and that is three days; then it will fall upon you. It has been said: by describing it as near he meant that it is in this world. To the first view went more than one of the exegetes, and the report was from a revelation from Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 65:

﴿So they hamstrung her﴾, i.e., they disobeyed what they had been commanded and hamstrung her. As for ʿuqr (hamstringing, i.e., cutting a limb that affects the self), it has been said that it is cutting off a limb that has an effect on the living being.

Al-Raghib said: It is said, "I hamstrung the camel" when you slaughtered it (naḥr), and it also comes in the sense of wounding, as in the Qamus. He attributed the hamstringing to all of them, although the one who did it was one of them, namely Qiddar (on the pattern of Hammam) according to one view. He is called "the red one of Thamud," and he is used as a proverbial example of ill omen, because they were pleased with his action. It has also been reported that they all shared her meat. Then Salih, peace be upon him, said to them: ﴿Enjoy yourselves﴾, i.e., live.

﴿in your homes﴾, i.e., your land. Lands are called diyar (dwellings) because one moves about (yuda ru) in them, i.e., one acts and conducts affairs in them. It is said: Diyar Bakr for their lands. The Arabs who live around Mecca say: "We are from the Arabs of the dar," meaning from the Arabs of the town (balad). Al-Zamakhshari went this way. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is the plural of dara, like sahah and sahin and suh, and from it is the saying of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt praising ʿAbd Allah ibn Judʿan:

For him there is a caller in Mecca, loud and clear, and another above his dara calling out.

It is also possible that the whole dwelling-place of a tribe is called a dar. The word dar is also applied to the world, and some have interpreted it that way here. Al-Tabarsi interpreted tamatto (enjoyment) as taking pleasure, i.e., take pleasure in what you desire. ﴿for three days﴾, then the punishment will seize you. It is said that when they hamstrung the she-camel, her young one climbed the mountain and cried out three cries, and Salih, peace be upon him, said: "For every cry there is a term of one day." The beginning of the days, according to some reports, is Wednesday. It is also related that he, peace be upon him, told them: "Tomorrow your faces will become yellow, the day after tomorrow red, and on the third day black; the punishment will overtake you in the morning." It happened as he said. ﴿That﴾ is a reference to what is indicated by the command to enjoy yourselves for three days, after which the punishment descends; the distance implied in it is for magnification. ﴿is a promise not to be denied﴾, i.e., not denied in it. The preposition is elided and the object becomes a direct object by extension (tawassu'), because the pronoun cannot be put in the accusative as an adverb of place, and a preposition does not govern after its deletion. They call this elision and connection (al-hadhf wal-iysal), and it is common in their speech; it occurs with nouns, like mushtarak, and with verbs, as in his saying:

And a day we witnessed, safe and inhabited, few besides the thrusts of the spears are its gifts.

Or ﴿not to be denied﴾ is figurative, as if the promiser said to him: "Will you keep your word to me?" If he keeps it, he confirms it; otherwise he denies it. Here there is an implicit metaphor (istiʿara makniyya takhyiliyya). It has also been said: it is a metonymic figure (majaz mursal), by taking ﴿maktub﴾ to mean false and different; or it is a promise that is not a lie, with ﴿maktub﴾ being a verbal noun on the pattern of maf'ul, like majlud and maʿqul, meaning ʿaql and jald. It has been heard from them in this sense, but it is rare. And the exaggeration in calling that a promise, in the sense of mockery, is not hidden.

﴿When Our command came﴾, meaning Our punishment, or We commanded its descent. There is in this, as is not hidden, a magnifying of the matter. ﴿We saved Salih and those who believed with him﴾: the phrase ﴿with him﴾ is connected either to ﴿saved﴾ or to ﴿believed﴾. ﴿By a mercy from Us﴾, meaning by means of it, or while being enveloped by it. In the tanwin (nunation) and the description there are two kinds of magnification. ﴿And from the disgrace of that day﴾, meaning: We saved them from the disgrace of that day, which is the destruction by the Cry. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We saved them from a harsh punishment﴾, in the sense that We saved them, and that salvation was from the disgrace of that day. It is also permitted that what is meant is: ﴿And We saved them from the humiliation and disgrace of the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning from its punishment. Thus this verse is like the verse in Hud, exactly the same.

Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying it is not good, because no preceding clause mentioned the Day of Resurrection so that the tanwin would be a substitute for it. What is mentioned is only ﴿When Our command came﴾, so it should be estimated as "the day when Our command came," and this is good. The answer that the indicator may be non-verbal, as it is here, is open to scrutiny. It was also said: the indicator is His statement, exalted is He, earlier: "a harsh punishment," and there is in this what there is. It was also said: the waw is extra (ziyadah, superfluous), so that "min" is connected to the mentioned "saved," but this is not permitted according to the Basran grammarians, because they do not hold that the waw is added; therefore they require here a connection to an omitted element, which is coordinated with what preceded.

Talhah and Aban read ﴿And from disgrace﴾ with tanwin and with the accusative of "yawma'idhin" (that day) as an adverbial (zarfiyyah) object, functioning as a complement of "disgrace." It is reported from Nafi' and al-Kisa'i that they both read with the genitive construction and with a fatha on "yawma," because it is annexed to "idh," which is indeclinable (ghayr mutamakkin). This is like the fatha on "hin" in the words of al-Nabigha:

"At (the time) when you reproached white hair for youth, you said: 'Would that I were sound,' while greyness was restraining (me)."

﴿Indeed your Lord﴾ is an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿He is the Strong, the Mighty﴾, meaning: the one able over everything, and the one overpowering over it at every time. Within this falls the saving and the destruction on that day.

﴿And those who did wrong were seized by the Cry﴾. The people of Salih are meant. He shifted from the pronoun to the explicit noun to record their wrongdoing against them and to signal that wrongdoing as the cause for the descent of the punishment upon them. ﴿The Cry﴾, that is, the cry of Jibril (Gabriel), or a cry from the heaven in which there is every thunderbolt and every terrifying sound. According to al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit by Abu Hayyan), it is on the pattern of fa'lah, indicating a single instance of ṣiyah (shouting). It is said: ṣaha yaṣīḥu when he calls out with strength. The root of this, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, is the splitting of the sound, from their saying: inṣāḥa al-khashab aw al-thawb (the wood or the cloth split), when it cracked and a sound was heard from it; and ṣayḥ al-thawb is likewise. The Cry may also be used to express terror. In al-A'raf (7:78) it is stated: ﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾. It was said: perhaps it occurred right after the Cry, which was followed by the agitation of the air. The discussion of this has already been presented by us. ﴿So they became in their homes﴾, that is, their dwellings and their residences; it was also said: their lands. ﴿Prostrate﴾, lifeless and motionless, dead, not moving. The full discussion of this, in meaning and in grammatical analysis (i'rab), has already passed.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 68:

﴿As though they had never dwelt in it﴾. That is, as though they had never lived ﴿in it﴾, that is, in their dwellings. It has been said that the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), meaning: they became (jāthimīn, "lying prostrate", "lifeless") resembling those who never existed and never stood in any place at all. ﴿Indeed, Thamud﴾: the noun was placed in the position of a pronoun for the sake of added clarification. Ḥafṣ and Ḥamzah prevented it from taking tanwīn (nunation, i.e. the ending -un) by considering it the name of a tribe, while most of the Seven Readers (al-sab'ah, the seven canonical reciters) gave it tanwīn by considering it the name of a living group, as we mentioned just above. It has also been said that it is treated as the name of the great ancestor, meaning that the intended referent is the first father, who is a ṣarf (declinable) noun. In that case, a modifier is understood, such as "offspring" (naslin), "children" (awlādin), or the like.

Page 93

It has also been said that it was given tanwīn in view of its original form, even though what is intended here is the tribe. ﴿They disbelieved in their Lord﴾: He explicitly stated their disbelief, although it was already known from what preceded regarding their circumstances, in order to condemn their state and to give the reason why they deserved the invocation against them of distance and destruction in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Away with Thamud!﴾. Al-Kisa'i read it, alone, with tanwīn only. The discussion of the explanation of their story has already been given in the fullest manner.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 69:**

﴿And certainly Our messengers came to Ibrahim﴾. They were the angels. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that they were twelve angels.

al-Suddi said: they were eleven, in the form of youths of the utmost beauty and radiance. The author of al-Fayyan relates that they were ten, among them Jibril (Gabriel). al-Dahhak said: nine. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: eight. al-Mawardi relates that they were four, but he did not name them.

It has come in a report from Uthman ibn Muhsin that they were Jibril, Israfil, Mika'il and Rafa'il, peace be upon them. In a report from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr, they were three, only the first three. Muqatil said: Jibril, Mika'il and the Angel of Death, peace be upon them. Some scholars chose to limit it to saying they were three, because that is the least that the plural indicates, and there is nothing to rely on for more than that. The coming (of the messengers) is attributed to them, not the sending, because they were not sent to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, but to the people of Lut, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have been sent to the people of Lut﴾. They came to him only with the purpose of glad tidings.

It has been said: since the aim of this noble surah is to mention the conduct of the earlier nations with the messengers sent to them, and the descent of punishment upon them, and not all of Ibrahim's people were struck by the punishment, but only a particular group of the people of Lut, (the surah has adopted) a style different from the consistent pattern preceding it in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to 'Ad, their brother Hud﴾, ﴿And to Thamud, their brother Salih﴾; then it returned to that pattern where it says: ﴿And to Madyan, their brother Shu'ayb﴾.

The "ba'" in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿with glad tidings﴾, indicates accompaniment, meaning: accompanied by glad tidings. By it is meant, it has been said, the glad tidings in general, which include the glad tidings of a son from Sarah, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Ishaq﴾, the verse, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy﴾, and so on. It also (includes) glad tidings of the absence of harm to him, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when the fear had left Ibrahim and the good news had come to him﴾, since the argument is clearly a consequence of the coming of the glad tidings. The first glad tidings were, it is said, from Mika'il, and the second from Israfil, peace be upon them both. It has also been said that by them is meant the glad tidings of the destruction of the people of Lut, peace be upon him, for the destruction of wrongdoers is among the most excellent things with which a believer may be given glad tidings.

It is objected that his, peace be upon him, argument concerning them contradicts this. al-Zamakhshari inclined to hold that they were glad tidings of a son, and that this is what is meant by "glad tidings" in what follows. He gave as the reason for this preference in al-Kashf (the work of al-Zamakhshari's commentary's glossing) his saying: because it is the more fitting of the general sense, and because of His saying, glorified is He, in al-Dhariyat: ﴿And they gave him the good news of a knowing boy﴾. Then he said after it: ﴿What is your business, O messengers?﴾. Then he said: As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when the fear had left Ibrahim﴾, and so on. Although it is possible that there were two glad tidings, so that each place is understood as referring to one of them, this is contrary to the apparent meaning. End of quotation.

Since the report of the coming of the messengers, peace be upon them, is likely to prompt the listener's question, "What did they say?", the answer is: ﴿They said: Peace﴾, that is, "We greet you with peace" or "We greet you, a greeting of peace." So it (the word "salaman") is in the accusative by a verb omitted, and the sentence is the object of "said". Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may also be that the object of "they said" is according to the meaning of what they said, not a quotation of their exact words.

This was related from Mujahid and al-Suddi, and for this reason the verb "said" governs it. This is like saying to a man who has said, "There is no god but Allah": "You have spoken truly and sincerely."

It has also been said that the accusative (in "salaman") is governed by "they said", because of what it contains of the sense of mentioning, as if it were said: "They mentioned peace." ﴿He said: Peace﴾, that is, "Upon you is peace," or "Peace be upon you." The beginning of a sentence with an indefinite noun of this type is permissible, as established in grammar. He, peace be upon him, greeted them with a better greeting than theirs, because his was a nominal sentence, which indicates permanence and stability, and so it is more emphatic. The original meaning of "salam" is safety from what harms.
