Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "silm" in the second instance without an alif, with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam. It is said to be a dialect form of "salam", like "hirm" and "haram". From it is the verse:

*"We passed by, and we said: 'Peace!' so he greeted, as the clouds, shining, were covered with lightning."*

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is possible that "silm" means the opposite of war. It has been explained that when they refused to take his food, and he feared them, he said it, meaning: "I am at peace, not at war, for they did not eat the food of anyone between whom and themselves there was war." It has been objected that this implies that his saying was after the food was brought, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So he did not delay﴾, and so on, is clear in contradicting that.

al-Zamakhshari mentioned in al-Kashshaf that Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam in both places, and this contradicts what is transmitted in the books of recitations (qira'at). Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "qala salaman" with the accusative, as the first. And it is related from him that he read it with the nominative in both places. ﴿So he did not delay﴾, that is, Ibrahim, peace be upon him, did not hesitate.

﴿In bringing a roasted calf﴾, that is, in his bringing it, or about his bringing it. The "ma" is negative, and the pronoun in "labitha" refers to Ibrahim. The "an ja'a" is by the supposition of a preposition governing the verb, and the deletion of the preposition before "an" is common. Ibn al-'Arabi relates that "an" means "until." It has also been said that "an" and what follows it is the subject of "labitha", meaning: "its coming was not delayed." This is related from al-Farra', and Abu Hayyan preferred it.

It has been said: "ma" is a verbal (masdari) particle and the verbal noun is the subject, or it is a relative noun meaning "that," similarly, and "an ja'a" is by the omission of a modifying word, meaning "the amount," and this is the predicate: meaning, "so his delaying it was the amount of its coming," or "that which delayed him was the amount of its coming." This is nothing.

"Ijl" is the young of a cow. It is called "hasil" and "khabsh" in the dialect of the people of al-Sarah. The "ba'" in it indicates transitivity or accompaniment. "Hanidh" is the fat one whose fat drips, from "hanadhtu al-faras", when you make a horse sweat, as if its fat were like a blanket upon it, or as if what flows from it were the sweat of an animal covered with a blanket for sweat. al-Suddi restricted "hanidh" to "fat" in his interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with a fat calf﴾. It has also been said it is roasted on hot stones in a trench. This came in a report from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah, and in a report from Mujahid it is interpreted as cooked.

He, peace be upon him, brought a calf because his wealth was cattle, and that is the finest of what they have. It was his habit, peace be upon him, to honour the guest, and for this reason he hastened the hospitality. This is part of the etiquette of hospitality, for it involves giving care to the guest's affair. In his bringing the whole calf, although by apparent reckoning part of it would have sufficed for them, there is evidence that it is part of good manners to bring the guest more than he will eat.

It has been disputed whether this calf was prepared before their arrival, or was prepared after they came. There are two views. Abu Hayyan chose the first, because of the indication of speed in bringing it. The author (of this commentary) prefers the second, because it shows greater care and is more eloquent in honouring them. Speed is not an explicit proof of the first view, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 70:

﴿But when he saw their hands not reaching toward it﴾ is a metonymy (kināya) meaning that they did not stretch their hands toward it, and this implies that they did not eat. It has also been said that the negation is itself the metonymy, based on a report that they were pricking the meat with arrows (qidāḥ) in their hands. But this is not right. There is some doubt about the soundness of this report, since such pricking is most like frivolous play, and the angels, peace be upon them, are too exalted for such a thing.

As for "saw" (ra'ā), it has been said that it is cognitive (ʿilmiyya), so that the clause ﴿not reaching﴾ is the second object. The apparent reading, however, is that it is visual (baṣariyya), and the clause is in the place of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). In this there is evidence that part of the etiquette of hospitality is to look at the guest to see whether he eats or not. However, they mentioned that this should be done with sidelong glances and stealth, not by fixing the gaze, because fixing the gaze makes the guest feel he is falling short in eating. That is, [Lot's/Abraham's] seeing that from them.

﴿He disliked them﴾, that is, he recoiled from them. ﴿And he sensed﴾, that is, he perceived and grasped. It has been said that he concealed (aḍmara) within himself, from their direction, ﴿fear﴾ (khīfa), that is, dread. Its root is the state a person is in because of fear. Perhaps its mention is for emphasis, since he perceived this although he did not know them beforehand and did not know what sort of people they were. This is indicated by what is in al-Dhariyat in His words, glorified is He, reporting about him: ﴿He said, "Peace." "A people unknown."﴾ [that they were angels]. He thought that they had been sent for the punishment of his people because of a matter that God had disapproved of. ﴿They said﴾ when they saw the effect of that upon him, peace be upon him, or God informed them of it, or after he had said to them what is in al-Hijr: ﴿Indeed, we are fearful of you.﴾ The apparent meaning of this is that there was a speech in actuality, not in potential, as is a possibility in it, as you will see, God willing. It is also permitted that this was because they knew that his knowledge, peace be upon him, that they were angels necessitated fear, since they do not descend except with punishment.

It has also been said that God gave the angels, absolutely, a kind of knowledge that He did not give to others, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿They know what you do.﴾ And in the Sahih [of al-Bukhari]: "The angels said: 'My Lord, this servant of Yours intends to commit an evil deed'," the hadith. This is a view that the angels know the inner matters of the heart.

But there are sound reports that clearly contradict this. The verse and the mentioned report are not fit as evidence for this claim. The attribution of speech to them apparently means that all of them said ﴿Do not fear﴾, though it is possible that the speaker was some of them, since the action of some is often attributed to all in such cases. The apparent meaning of His words, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, we have been sent﴾ is that it is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf) in the sense of giving the reason for the prohibition mentioned, just as His words, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, We give you good news﴾ is a resumptive clause in the same way. Their being sent to another people makes him safe from fear, that is, ﴿We have been sent﴾ with punishment ﴿to the people of Lot﴾ specifically. From what we have mentioned it is known that he, peace be upon him, sensed that they were angels, and this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. It may be supported by their words: ﴿Do not fear. Indeed, we have been sent﴾, for, as is not hidden from anyone with even a little taste, this is only said to someone who recognized them but did not know for what purpose they had been sent, and so he feared. Also, the denial indicated by "disliked them" (nakirahum) is not the same as the denial indicated by what is in al-Dhariyat, so there is no difficulty in the denial being there before the food was brought and here after it.

The root of denial (inkār) is the opposite of recognition (ʿirfān). "Nakartu," "ankartu," and "istankartu" have the same meaning. It has been said that ankara is used for what is not perceived by the senses (of meanings), and nakara for what is perceived by sight. Among examples is the poet's words:

"She disowned me, and what she disowned of the events was nothing but the grey hair and the baldness."

He meant by the first, as has been said, "she denied my affection." Al-Raghib said that the root of this is that something arrives upon the heart which it cannot conceive, and that is a kind of ignorance, and by this the verse is explained. Some differentiated between what is here and what occurred in al-Dhariyat, saying that the first refers to their state when he brought the calf forward to them, while the second relates to themselves and has no connection to seeing that they did not eat. Rather, it happened at his seeing them, because they were not of the kind of people he was accustomed to. This requires assuming an omitted modifier (ḥadhf al-muḍāf) or observing a respect (mulāḥaẓat al-ḥaythiyya). The objection to what we have presented is that it involves the use of a figurative expression (majāz), but perhaps the matter here is easy.

Some have gone to the view that he, peace be upon him, did not know they were angels until they said to him: ﴿Do not fear. Indeed, we have been sent.﴾ Perhaps the reason for his fear of them was that they had not partaken of his food, so he thought they intended him harm, since the custom at that time was like that. He, peace be upon him, was staying at an outlying part of the land, separate from his people. This is a report from Ibn ʿAbbas, which Ishaq ibn Bishr and Ibn ʿAsakir transmitted through the chain of Juwaybir from al-Ḍaḥḥāk from him. It has also been said that the cause of his fear was that they entered without permission and at an improper time.

Al-ʿAllama al-Ṭībī said: The truth is that the fear arose only from the combination of their being unknown and their refusing food, as is known from the verses that came in this story. Also, if he had recognized them as angels, he would not have placed food before them or urged them to eat first. They moved to their words: ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to the people of Lot﴾ so that it would be comprehensive of the meanings, such that the intended sense is also understood from it. End of quote.

In this there is an allusion to a refutation of al-Zamakhshari. His speech varied regarding the cause of the fear: at one time he attributed it to his recognition that they were angels, and at another time to their not having refused his food. Perhaps by that recognition he meant recognition after the food was brought. What al-Ṭībī mentioned, that if he had recognized them as angels he would not have brought food, etc., is not a damaging objection, since it is possible he feared them after the food was brought at first, because they did not refuse it, and then after discerning that they were angels he feared them because they were angels sent for punishment. Al-Zamakhshari related one of the two fears in one place and the other in another place.

Some verifiers said: The explanation that they were angels is the correct one, so that His words, glorified is He: ﴿Do not be afraid. Indeed, We give you good news of a knowing boy﴾ fit together with what precedes it. For if the fear were because they were of an unfamiliar appearance, or something similar, the reason given by His words, exalted is He: ("Indeed, We give you good news") would not be appropriate. It is only a reason for the prohibition against fear, from the fact that they were angels sent for punishment. It is as if they said: "Do not be afraid. Indeed, We give you good news of a knowing boy," and "Indeed, we have been sent to the people of Lot." So the Qur'an, in its concision, mentioned one of the two reasons in one place and the other in the other place. There is no doubt that in al-Hijr there is brevity, through folding up the account of the exchange of words, and the hurrying with the roasted calf, and their not refusing his food. This is because the purpose of recounting the story there is to encourage and warn, so that one may take lessons from the condition of Abraham, peace be upon him, and what he received of good news and honor, and the condition of the people of Lot, peace be upon him, and what they were afflicted with of evil and blame. Do you not see His words, glorified is He: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ up to His words, exalted and high is He: ﴿concerning the guests of Abraham﴾? So it limited itself to what serves that purpose. As for in this surah, it was brought for the guidance on which the noble surah is built, together with the incorporation of consolation and the refutation of what they had accused him, peace and blessings be upon him, of, the fabrication. In each part of the story there is what fills these aims, so it was related in its proper form. In the surah of al-Dhariyat it is for the last two purposes only, so there is brought what serves that. So there is no fault in your seeing brevity, in that you may transfer to it from the expanded account what completes the speech after you know the point of the brevity. This is one of the distinctive features of the noble Book of God. End of quote. It is not without merit. In it there is the view that the clause ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to the people of Lot﴾ is a resumptive clause in the place of a reason, as is the apparent reading.

Shaykh al-Islam, may mercy be upon him, said: The apparent reading is what has been mentioned, except that it is not so. For His words, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Then what is your business, O messengers?" They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a criminal people"﴾ are clear that they said this in answer to his question, peace be upon him, and He has summarized the speech, being content with that. End of quote.

It is objected that this does not necessarily prevent taking it according to the apparent reading, since it is possible that they said that as a reason for the prohibition against fear. However, even if what is meant is the sending with punishment for the people of Lot, peace be upon him, it is vague and was not presented in a way that makes clear what kind of punishment it was, whether it was annihilation or not. So he, peace be upon him, asked to clarify this, as if he said: "O messengers to the people of Lot, what is this great matter with which you have been sent?" They answered him with what contains an explanation of that, together with an indication of the cause for the descent of that matter upon them, which is their saying: ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to a people who are criminals﴾ ﴿except the family of Lot. Indeed, we will save them all﴾, and so on. The understanding of the punishment of annihilation for the people of Lot, peace be upon him, from this is clear, and likewise the indication of the cause.

[Page 97]

The sum is that the question in that verse is about the matter (khaṭb), which is basically a great affair in which much discourse occurs, and by asking about it is meant the clarification of a matter he, peace be upon him, had not known from their speech before. This is either because it was not known from them, or because he was preoccupied and not fully attentive, so that he, peace be upon him, could know it from them. In his address to them, peace be upon them, by the title of messengers, there is something that supports the priority of their words "Indeed, we have been sent" over this question. But it was omitted there, relying on what is here. There is no novelty in omitting from the later what relies on the earlier. The fact that al-Hijr and al-Dhariyat come after Hud in recitation is not in dispute. Their coming later in revelation is what Ibn Durays related in Fada'il al-Qur'an from Muhammad ibn ʿAbdullah ibn Abi Jaʿfar al-Razi, from ʿUmar ibn Harun, from ʿUthman ibn ʿAṭa' al-Khurasani, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas. He mentioned that all of them were revealed at Makkah, that between Hud and al-Hijr there is one surah, and between al-Hijr and al-Dhariyat there are thirteen surahs. So let this point be considered.

From the words of some it is understood that he, peace be upon him, did not verify that they were angels until after Gabriel, peace be upon him, touched the calf with his wing, whereupon it got up and ran until it reached its mother, and then he recognized them and felt safe from them. I do not find the soundness of this report verified. What I incline to is that he, peace be upon him, recognized them before that, and that his fear of them, because they were angels, was that he did not know for what purpose they had descended. And for one who knows the condition of Abraham, peace be upon him, it is far-fetched to say that he feared strangers and that the fear reached the point where ﴿he said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you"﴾, especially if we say that those he feared were three, and that he, peace be upon him, was not in an outlying part of the land but among his companions, or was there but among his servants and youths. ﴿And his wife﴾ was Sarah, daughter of Haran ibn Nahur, and she was his cousin, ﴿standing﴾ in service, as Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid. Their women did not veil, especially the old women among them, and she, may Allah be pleased with her, was an old woman. Wahb said: She was standing behind the curtain, listening to their conversation. Some took from this that the covering of women was obligatory. The apparent reading is that it was not so, since the verse of the hijab came later. It is possible to say that standing behind the curtain was incidental. From Ibn Ishaq it is related that she was standing praying. Al-Mubarrad said: She was standing apart from the child, which is contrary to the well-known usage. Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Mughira that he said: In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, "and his wife was standing while he was sitting." In the Kashshaf, instead of "and he was sitting," it is "and he was seated." And from Ibn ʿAṭiyya, instead of

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 71:**

﴿And his wife was standing﴾, meaning she was standing. Here there is a pronoun without a prior antecedent, and this is possible because the referent is understood from the context of the speech. The clause is either in the position of a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause, a clause describing the state of the subject) relating to the pronoun in (qālū, "they said"), or it is a new, independent statement. ﴿So she laughed﴾: this is the well-known laughter. According to most scholars, it is to be taken in its literal sense. For some, it was out of joy at the removal of fear from Ibrahim, peace be upon him, since women cannot control themselves as men do when joy overcomes them. It was also said that it was joy at the destruction of the people of corruption, and it was said that it was a combination of both. Ibn al-Anbari said: her laughter was out of joy at the truth of her assumption, because she used to say to Ibrahim: "Take Lut to yourself, for I see that the punishment will descend upon his people." Lut was the son of his brother. It was also said that he was the son of his maternal aunt, and it was said that he was the brother of Sarah. It has already been mentioned earlier that she was the daughter of the paternal uncle of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. And it is reported from Ibn Abbas that she laughed out of the intensity of Ibrahim's fear while he was among his family and servants, and those who came to him were three, while she knew that he was a match for forty, and it was said a hundred. Qatada said: that was due to the heedlessness of the people of Lut and the nearness of the punishment to them. Al-Suddi said: she laughed at the guests refraining from eating, and she said: "How strange! We serve our guests with our own hands, and they do not eat our food." Wahb ibn Munabbih said: It is also reported from Ibn Abbas that she laughed at the good news of Ishaq. In that case, there is an inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the sentence. It was also said: (laughed) refers to the miraculous sign that was mentioned earlier as transmitted from Jibril, peace be upon him.

Page 98

Perhaps the most apparent view is what we mentioned first from some scholars. Others held that the meaning of laughter is smiling, and that it is used for mere joy, as in the phrase *musfiratun ḍāḥikah* (a face radiant and laughing), and from it the saying: "a garden that laughs" (rawḍatun tadḥak). ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Abu al-Shaykh and others reported from Ibn Abbas that (ḍaḥikat) means "menstruated" (ḥāḍat). This was also reported from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and from Mujahid and ʿIkrima. And the saying "the hare laughed" is used in this sense too. Abu ʿUbayda, Abu ʿUbayd and al-Farra' denied that *ḍaḥika* can mean "menstruated" (ḥāḍa), while most of the lexicographers affirmed it and cited as evidence his saying:

*"And the hares laughed upon the rock, like the blood of the belly on the day of the encounter."*

And his saying:

*"My promise with Salma was (laughing) in the Lubaba, and her breast did not yet begin to swell."*

And his saying:

*"Indeed I come to the wedding at its purification, and I abandon her on the day she is (laughing)."*

The affirmative statement takes precedence over the negative, and the one who memorized is a proof against the one who did not. Yes, Ibn al-Munir said: the interpretation of this here is made unlikely by her saying: "Shall I bear a child when I am an old woman?" etc., for if menstruation had occurred before the good news, she would not have been amazed, since there is no wonder in a woman who menstruates, and menstruation is customarily the measure of the possibility of conception. It is answered that menstruation out of its time is also an emphasis on amazement, and because it is possible that she thought her blood was not menstruation but irregular bleeding (istiḥāḍa), and therefore she was amazed. Muhammad ibn Ziyad al-Aʿrabi, one of the readers of Makka, read (fa-ḍaḥikat) with a *fatḥa* on the ḥāʾ. Al-Mahdawi claimed that this reading is not well known, and that (ḍaḥika) with a *kasra* is the well-known form. Its verbal noun is *ḍaḥkan* and *ḍiḥkan* with the ḥāʾ silent and the ḍād either open or with a *kasra*, and *ḍaḥikan ḍiḥikan* with a *kasra* on the ḥāʾ and the ḍād either open or with a *kasra*. The apparent point is that these are verbal nouns of *ḍaḥika* whatever its meaning. It is understood from Majmaʿ al-Bayan that the verbal noun of *ḍaḥika* in the sense of "menstruated" is only *ḍaḥkan* with a *fatḥa* on the ḍād and silence on the ḥāʾ. We have not seen this restriction in any other source. It is also reported from some that opening the ḥāʾ in the past tense is specific to *ḍaḥika* in the sense of "menstruated". Accordingly, the mentioned reading supports interpreting (ḍaḥikat), in the reading of the majority, as "menstruated" (ḥāḍat).

﴿So We gave her the good news of Ishaq﴾. It was said: that is, We followed her joy with a joy more complete than it, through the tongues of Our messengers. ﴿And after Ishaq, Yaʿqub﴾: read with a *fatḥa* (naṣb). This is the reading of Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, Hafs and Zayd ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them, on the basis that it is in the accusative by an implied verb which is explained by what the sentence indicates, that is: "And We granted her, after Ishaq, Yaʿqub." Abu ʿAli preferred this. Some objected that in this case what is mentioned would not fall under the good news, and it is answered that mentioning this gift before the existence of the one given is a good news in meaning. It was also said that it is conjoined to the position (maḥall) of (bi-Ishaq), since that is in the position of the accusative. The objection is that conjunction to the position is only possible when the position may appear in eloquent speech, as in his saying: "We are not with the mountains, nor is the iron." And *bashshir* (give good news) does not drop its preposition *bāʾ* before the one given the good news in eloquent usage. Some claimed that the conjunction to (bi-Ishaq) is on the assumption of its accusative, because it has the meaning of "We granted her Ishaq", so it is like his saying:

*"Ill-omened ones, they are not reformers of a tribe, nor a crier except with the separation of its raven."*

But in this case he assumed the presence of the *bāʾ* in the conjoined word, the reverse of what is in the noble verse. This is called "conjunction by assumption" (ʿaṭf al-tawahhum), and there is no hiding the ugliness of this name here. Moreover, this conjunction is anomalous, and it is not fitting to resort to it when there is another option. On this basis al-Zamakhshari was criticized for his statement: "It was read with the accusative, as if it said: We granted her Ishaq and after Ishaq Yaʿqub, after the manner of his saying: 'Ill-omened ones...'" The statement is interpreted as such because that is its apparent meaning. In al-Kashf he said that he meant it to be a conjunction in meaning, and similar to it is common and widespread in conjunction and in the implied, under the condition of explanation and otherwise. He only compared it to his saying "nor a crier" to point out that, though that is far-fetched, it did occur, so this is more deserving. The purpose of the comparison is that what is not present in the wording is treated as if it were present and is made operative. It is not hidden that this differs from the obvious meaning of his expression. It was also said that it is conjoined to the wording of (Ishaq), and its vowel is the *kasra* of the genitive, because it is not declined due to being a proper name and being non-Arabic. On this basis, its inclusion in the good news is clear, except that it was objected: this requires separating the substitute of the preposition from its object, and that is further removed than separating the preposition from its object. In al-Bahr it is stated that whoever holds that it is conjoined to what was mentioned, his statement is weak, because it is not permitted to separate the conjunction particle from its conjoined genitive by an adverbial phrase or a genitive phrase. So one cannot say "I passed by Zayd today and [the] Amr of yesterday." If it occurs, it is in poetry. If the conjoined word is in the accusative or the nominative, there is disagreement about the permissibility of that, as in "Zayd stood, and today ʿAmr [stood]" and "I struck Zayd, and today ʿAmr [I struck]."

The two Harams, the two grammarians (al-Kisa'i and Hamza? in this context the two Nahwiyyun), Abu Bakr and Yaʿqub read it with the *ḍamma* (rafʿ) as a beginning (mubtada'), and (min warā'i) is the predicate, as if it said: "and after Ishaq there is Yaʿqub, existing, present or born." Al-Nahhas said: the clause is a circumstantial clause included in the good news, that is: "So We gave her the good news of Ishaq, joined to him Yaʿqub."

Abu ʿAli permitted that it be nominative by the prepositional phrase, as al-Akhfash permitted it. It was also said that it is permissible according to the view of the majority too, because it relies on the one it modifies (dhū al-ḥāl). This was objected to as a mistake, because when a prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause, it is not permitted to be prefixed with *wāw*, so let this be considered carefully.

Al-Nahhas also permitted that it be the subject (fā'il) with an implied verb whose estimate is: "and there will arise after Ishaq, Yaʿqub." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: according to this, it does not enter into the good news, and what would answer this has already passed.

Here (warā') means "behind" (khalf), and al-Raghib and others explained it so here, and it is a report from Ibn Abbas. In another report from him, it is explained as "son's son" (walad al-walad), which is one of its meanings as in al-Sihah and al-Qamus. Al-Shaʿbi said this, and Abu ʿUbayda preferred it. It was objected that Yaʿqub is the son of Ishaq, peace be upon him, by his loins, not the son of his son. To remove this, al-Zamakhshari said, as transmitted from him: the way of this interpretation is that Yaʿqub is meant to be his descendants, as one says "Hashim" and means his descendants, so it is as if it said: from the son of Ishaq's son, the descendants of Yaʿqub, and this includes the good news of Yaʿqub by way of priority. It was also said: the way of this is that the son of Ishaq was called "behind" (warā') in relation to her, that is, her posterity from Ishaq, as if they gave her the good news that she would live until she sees her son's son, or that a son would be born to her son. It was said: this is closer. What is transmitted from al-Zamakhshari is more apparent, and what is relied upon is his interpretation in the sense of "successor" (khalf), since both of these explanations contain evident strain. Both names may be included in the good news, as in his exalted saying: "We give you good news of a boy whose name is Yahya", and this is the more apparent.

It is reported from al-Suddi: it is also possible that she was given the good news of a son and a son's son without naming them, and then they were named after birth. The good news was directed to her, although the original recipient of such news is Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and it was directed to him in the two verses of al-Hijr and al-Dhariyat, to indicate that what was announced would come from both of them. And because she was barren and eager for a child, and she had wished for it when Isma'il, peace be upon him, was born to Hajar.

**"She said"**: a resumptive explanatory clause (*istinaf bayani*), as if a questioner had asked, "What did she do when she was given the good news?" So it was said: she said, **"Woe is me!"** *(ya waylata)*. *Al-wayl* originally means disgrace, and it is used for any dreadful matter. Here it expresses amazement. This word is very common on the lips of women when something happens to them that causes them to wonder. The apparent view is that the *alif* is a substitute for the first-person *ya'* (of possession), which is why Abu 'Amr and 'Asim (in one narration) pronounce it with *imalah* (a vowel inclination toward *i*). On this basis a riddle is posed: "What is an *alif* that is a first-person singular pronoun?"

Al-Hasan recited *ya wayleti* with the *ya'* in its original form. It was also said that the *alif* is the *alif* of lamentation (*nudbah*), which is why they add a *ha'* to it and say *ya waylatah*. **"Shall I bear a child when I am an old woman"**, aged ninety years according to what is narrated from Ibn Ishaq, or ninety-nine according to what is narrated from Mujahid.

[Page 100]

**"And this"**, whom you see, **"is my husband (*ba'li*)"**, i.e. my husband. The root meaning of *al-ba'l* is one who is in charge of a matter, and it was applied to the husband because he manages the affairs of the wife. Al-Raghib said: it is the male of the two spouses, and its plural is *bu'ulah*, like *fahl* and *fuhulah*. Because they perceived in the man a superiority over the woman, he was made her governor and the one in charge of her. The term was also applied to anything that resembles a dominant thing over another, and so it took its name. From this, the Arabs called the deity they worshipped, through which they drew near to God Most High, *ba'l*, because of their belief in that. **"An old man (*shaykhan*)"** of one hundred years, or one hundred and twenty, from *shakha yashi'u*. It may also be said of a female *shaykhah*, as the poet said:

*"And a Abshamite *shaykhah* laughs at me."*

Its plural is *ashyakh*, *shuyukh* and *shiykhan*. Its accusative (*nasb*) is as a circumstantial state (*hal*) according to the Basrans, and the governing element in it is the sense of indication or alerting contained in *hadha*.

Al-Zajjaj said: such a circumstantial clause is among the subtle and obscure points of grammar, since it is permissible only where the predicate is known. In your saying *hadha Zayd qa'iman* ("This is Zayd standing"), it is said only to someone who knows him, so that his standing adds information. If it were not so, it would follow that this is not Zayd when he is not standing, and that is not correct. Here, her husband's identity is known, and the purpose is to state his old age; otherwise it would follow that he was not her husband before old age. This was said by al-Tibi, and it was objected to: that objection applies only when the state is not a permanent, inseparable attribute. But in a case like *abuka 'atufan* ("your father, affectionate"), the stated problem does not arise. Here the circumstantial clause describes the condition of the agent or the object, since the governing element in it is what has been pointed to; and with that interpretation, the governor of the state and its subject are one.

The Kufans held that *hadha* functions as *kana*, with *shaykhan* as its predicate, and they called this "approximation" (*taqrib*).

Ibn Mas'ud, whose *mushaf* contained it, and al-A'mash recited *shaykhun* with *raf'* (nominative), taking it as the predicate of an omitted subject: *huwa shaykhun*, "he is an old man"; or as a predicate following a predicate. In *al-Bahr* it is said that on this reading the sentence is like the expression *hadha hulwun hamid* ("this is sweet, sour"); or *huwa* is the predicate. **"My husband"** is either an appositive (*badal*) of the demonstrative, or an explanatory apposition (*bayan*) of it. It is also permitted that *ba'li* be the predicate and *shaykhun* a following modifier of it.

Both sentences are in the circumstantial position relative to the pronoun in *a-alidu*, to establish the astonishment contained in it and to give its reason: "Shall I bear a child while both of us are in a state that contradicts that?" She mentioned her own state before his, peace be upon him, because the contrast between her condition and childbearing is greater: old men may father children from young women, but old women's wombs are barren. Also, the good news was addressed to her directly. And also, reversing the order in the explanation might initially suggest attributing the barrier to childbearing to Abraham, peace be upon him, and in that there is what is well known to be objectionable. Her limiting the astonishment to her own childbearing, without referring to the state of the grandchild, is because she is the one who is considered unlikely; as for the birth of her son, no astonishment attaches to it. This was said by Shaykh al-Islam.

**"Indeed this"**, i.e. what has been mentioned, the attainment of a child from two aged persons like us. It was said that it refers to the birth, or to the good news of it, and the masculine form is used because the verbal noun (*masdar*) with *inna* and the verb together is in the sense of the masculine. The outcome is: **"is truly a wondrous thing"**, i.e. from the custom of God Most High practised among His servants. The sentence is a justification in the form of a verified resumptive clause (*istinaf tahqiqi*). Its purpose, as has been said, is to magnify the blessing of God upon her within the framework of an ordinary expression of wonder, not to deem it unlikely in terms of divine power.

﴿Qāla ataʿjabīna min amri Allāh﴾ (They said: "Do you wonder at the command of Allah?"). That is, at His power and His wisdom, or at His creation and His affairs, glorified is He. They rebuked her for her amazement, because she had grown up in the house of prophethood, the place of descent of revelation, and the locus of extraordinary events. So it was her due to be dignified and not to be elated by what elates other women, namely such extraordinary things, which are among the subtle favours of Allah, glorified is He, and the gentle workings of His creation that overflow upon everyone whom His eternal will touches, especially the People of the House of prophethood, who are the very ones they are. And it was her due to glorify Allah, exalted is He, to magnify Him and to praise Him. To this they alluded with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Raḥmat Allāh﴾ (The mercy of Allah), which entails every good.

[صفحة 101]

Placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun serves to increase her honour and to hint at her greatness. ﴿Wa-barakātuhu﴾ (and His blessings), that is, His complete and abundant good, of which the bestowal of children is part. It has also been said: the mercy is prophethood, and the blessings are the tribes (asbāṭ) of the Children of Israel, because the prophets, peace be upon them, were among them, and all of them are from the offspring of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. It has also been said: His mercy is His greeting, and His blessings are the abundant favours of His goodness through the close friendship (khullah) and the imamate.

﴿ʿAlaykum ahla l-bayt﴾ (Upon you, O People of the House). It is in the accusative, either as a term of praise (madḥ) or of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ), as many grammarians have held. Abu Hayyan said: "There is a difference between them, and for this reason Sibawayh placed them in two separate chapters. The accusative of praise is a word which by its very form includes praise, just as the accusative of censure includes censure by its form, whereas the accusative of specification is intended to convey praise or censure, but its wording does not by its form include that, such as the line of Ru'bah: 'Through us Tamim uncovers the darkness.'"

End of quotation. In al-Hama' it is stated that the accusative in specification is governed by a verb that must be omitted, and Sibawayh estimated it as aʿnī (I mean). Specification is restricted to ayyu (the word "ayyu") occurring after a first-person pronoun, as in "We, O man, do such-and-such," and "O Allah, forgive us, O company." Its rule in this chapter, except according to al-Sirafi and al-Akhfash, is the same as its rule in the chapter of the vocative, and it is mostly replaced by it, as Sibawayh said, namely "Banū," as in his saying: "We are the sons of Dabba, the people of the camel." From this is also his saying:

"We are the daughters of Ṭāriq, walking upon the cushions."

And "Maʿshar," as in his saying:

"For us, O company of the Helpers, is an established glory, / through our pleasing the best of creation, Aḥmad."

And in the hadith: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited." "Āl" and "Ahl" and "Abu ʿAmr" govern only these, but this is not correct. It is rare for this to be a proper name, as in the line of Ru'bah cited earlier in the words of Abu Hayyan. It does not come as a demonstrative (ism al-ishārah) or otherwise, nor ever as an indefinite noun. The specifying noun may not precede the pronoun. It is rare for specification to occur after a second-person pronoun, as in "Subḥānaka Allāh al-ʿAẓīm" (Glory be to You, Allah, the Mighty). It also occurs after a third-person word that is interpreted as first or second person, as in ʿalā al-maḍārib al-waḍʿiyyah ayyuhā al-bāʾiʿ (upon the hardened hides, O seller). Here "al-maḍārib" is a third-person noun, but it has the meaning of "ʿalā" or "ʿalayka." Al-Saffar, however, absolutely prohibited this, because specification resembles the vocative, and just as the absent one is not addressed, so too specification does not occur with him. End of quotation, with slight addition and alteration. From this one learns some of what is in the words of Abu Hayyan, and that to understand the noble verse as specification involves an expression of what is rare in their speech. Al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf permitted its accusative to be the vocative, and he put it first, over the possibility of the accusative of specification. Perhaps he indicated by this a preference for it over the second possibility. However, some of the eminent scholars mentioned that in this there is the loss of the meaning of praise appropriate to the context.

The "bayt" intended here, as in al-Bahr, is the house of dwelling. Its origin is a person's shelter at night, though it may be said without considering the night in it. It applies to what is made of stone, of clay, of wool, or of hair. The place of a thing is also expressed as its "bayt." Its plurals are buyūt and abyāt, the plural of the plural is abāyīt, buyūtāt, and abayāwāt. Its diminutive is buyayt and buyīt with kasra, and it is said buwayt, as common people say. The shifting of the address from the singular form to the plural is so that their reply to her, peace be upon them, would be an answer to anyone who comes to mind like what came to her mind from the rest of the People of the House.

The sentence is a separate statement, given as the reason for denying her amazement. Therefore it is a declarative sentence (jumlah khabariyyah). A group of verifying scholars chose this. It has been said that it is supplicatory (duʿāʾiyyah), but that is not right. The verse is cited as evidence that the wife enters the People of the House, and this is what the Sunnis hold, and the surah of al-Aḥzāb supports it. The Shiʿa disagreed on this and said: she does not enter unless she is a close relative of the husband, and whoever related him to it, the intended "bayt" is the house of lineage, not the house of clay and wood. The entry of Sarah, may Allah be pleased with her, here is because she was his paternal cousin. It seems they took "bayt" to mean nobility, as it is one of its meanings, and it was explained in this sense in the words of al-Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, praising the Prophet (ﷺ):

[p. 102]

"Until your abased house encompassed the lofty Khindif, beneath which are the drops of seed."

Then they restricted nobility to lineage nobility. Otherwise "bayt" in the sense of lineage has not been widely used among the lexicographers. Perhaps what drove them to this is their hatred for ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, so they wished to exclude her from the ruling of ﴿Innamā yurīdu Allāh li-yudhhiba ʿankumu r-rijsa ahla l-bayti wa-yuṭahhirakum taṭhīrā﴾ (Allah only wants to remove uncleanness from you, O People of the House, and to purify you with complete purification). The detailed discussion of this matter will come, Allah willing. The verse is also cited as evidence for the disliking of adding to the greeting "al-salāmu ʿalaykum wa-raḥmatu Allāh wa-barakātuh" (Peace be upon you, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings). This was narrated from more than one of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that a man said to him: "Salāmun ʿalayka wa-raḥmatu Allāhi wa-barakātuhu wa-maghfiratuhu," and Ibn ʿUmar rebuked him and said: "Enough for you is what Allah the Exalted has said." And he narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that a questioner stood at the door while he was with Maymunah, and said: "Al-salāmu ʿalaykum ahla l-bayti wa-raḥmatu Allāhi wa-barakātuhu wa-ṣalawātuhu wa-maghfiratuh." He said: "Confine your greeting to what Allah, glorified is He, has said." In another narration from ʿAṭāʾ, he said: "I was sitting with Ibn ʿAbbas when a questioner came and said: 'Al-salāmu ʿalaykum wa-raḥmatu Allāhi wa-barakātuhu wa-maghfiratuhu wa-riḍwānuh.'" He said: "What is this greeting?!" and he became angry until his cheeks reddened, and said: "Allah has set a limit for the greeting, then He stopped and forbade what goes beyond it." Then he recited: ﴿Raḥmatu Allāhi wa-barakātuhu ʿalaykum ahla l-bayt﴾ (The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O People of the House). ﴿Innahu ḥamīd﴾ (Indeed He is Praiseworthy). Abu al-Haytham said: that is, His actions are praised. In al-Kashshaf: that is, He does what merits praise from His servants, so "faʿīl" is in the sense of "mafʿūl." Al-Raghib permitted that "ḥamīd" here means "ḥāmid" (one who praises), but the first is probably better. ﴿Majīd﴾ (Glorious): that is, abundant in goodness and beneficence. Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: it is the exalted. One says: majada, like naṣara and karuma, majdan and majādatan, that is, he was noble and distinguished. Its origin is from majjadati l-ibilu, when the camels fell into abundant and wide pasture, and the herdsman "amjadahā" when he caused them to fall into it. Al-Asmaʿi said: one says amjadtu d-dābbah when you increase its fodder. Al-Layth said: amjada fulānun ʿaṭāʾahu wa-majjadahu when he multiplied it. From this is the saying of Abu Ḥayyah al-Numayri:

"She surpasses her companions, yet she is not one of abundant food or drink."

That is, she is not one of much food or drink. Among their proverbs: "In every tree there is fire." And "istamjada al-markh wa-l-ʿiffār," that is, he gathered much of that. Al-Raghib said: that is, he sought abundance in giving the excess particular to himself. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "majada" the thing means when its attributes are beautiful. The sentence, according to al-Kashf, is a fine tadhyīl (concluding appended statement) to explain that the requirement of her situation is that she should praise the One who merits praise, the Benefactor to her, for what He has done well, and glorify Him, since He honoured her with what is honourable. It has also been said: it is a reason for what preceded in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Raḥmatu Allāhi wa-barakātuhu ʿalaykum﴾,

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 74:**

﴿When the fear had left Abraham﴾, i.e., the dread and alarm. The poet says:

When the trembling of *al-raw'* (fear) seizes her, she grips the shoulder of a bold man, courageous in the face of terror.

The verb is *raʿa*, which takes a direct object, as in his saying:

*"Mā raʿanī"* (It did not frighten me) except the camels of its people, in the midst of the abodes, sweeping up the seeds of the *khamkham* plant.

*Al-rawʿ*, with a *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ*, means the self (*nafs*), and it is the seat of fear. The *fāʾ* (in *fa-lammā*) links one of Abraham's states, peace be upon him, to something that followed after their departure, and this is not foreign in every respect, but has a connection to the context and what precedes it. The subject is placed after the adverbial phrase (*al-ẓarf*) because it is the point where the benefit lands. The meaning is: when the fear he had sensed from them ceased to be with him, and his soul was reassured by coming to know the clear truth of their matter. ﴿And the good news came to him, and he began to argue with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾, i.e., he argued with Our messengers about their condition and affair, so there is a metaphor (*majāz*) in the attribution. His arguing with them, peace be upon him, is what Allah, glorified is He, related in His saying in surah al-ʿAnkabut:

[p. 103]

﴿And when Our messengers came to Abraham with good news, they said: "We are going to destroy the people of this town, for its people have been wrongdoers." He said: "Indeed, Lot is in it."﴾ His saying, peace be upon him, *"Indeed, Lot is in it"*, is an argument, and this is counted as arguing, because its outcome, as it has been said, is: how can a town be destroyed when there is in it one who is a believer and does not deserve the punishment? This is why they answered him with their words: ﴿"We know best who is in it. We will surely save him and his family, except his wife"﴾. This much of the speech is the certain part.

It is related from Hudhayfah that when they said to him, peace be upon him, what they said, he said: "What do you think? If there are fifty Muslims in it, will you destroy it?" They said: "No." He said: "Then thirty?" They said: "No." He said: "Then twenty." They said: "No." He said: "Then if there are ten or five in it" (the narrator is in doubt) "?" They said: "No." He said: "What do you think? If there is one man among the Muslims in it, will you destroy it?" They said: "No." At that point he said: *"Indeed, Lot is in it."* Then they answered him with what they answered. Something similar has been transmitted in several narrations, and Allah the Exalted knows best their soundness. Some have interpreted the argument as a request for intercession. It has also been said that it was his asking whether the punishment would certainly befall them, or whether it was meant as a warning so that they would return to obedience. Whichever it is, *fa-yujādiluna* (he began to argue) is the answer (*jawāb*) of *lammā*. The apparent form would be *jādalanā*, but he used the present tense to narrate a past state and to bring its image to mind. It has been said that *lammā*, like *law*, turns the present into the past, just as *an* turns the past into the future. It has also been said that the answer is omitted. This clause is in the position of a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of its subject, meaning: he took up or came forward arguing with us. Al-Zajjaj preferred this view, but he treated it together with the narration of a state as a single view, because he said: "*Akhadha* (began) is not mentioned in the speech, because when speech is meant to narrate a past state, *akhadha* and *aqbala* (came forward) are supplied in it, since when you say *qāma Zayd* (Zayd stood), it indicates a past act, but when you say *akhadha Zayd yaqūm* (Zayd began to stand), it indicates an extended state for which *akhadha* and *aqbala* were mentioned." The practice of al-Zamakhshari indicates that they are two views. Its verification, according to *al-Kashf*, is that if the continuation of the past is meant, then it is as al-Zajjaj mentioned, but if mere depiction is meant, then it is not. It has also been said that the answer is omitted.

The clause is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf*), either grammatical or explanatory (*bayānī*), and it indicates the omitted element. The estimated sense is: he dared to address Us, or he was perceptive in his argument with Us and said such-and-such. Al-Zamakhshari chose this in *al-Kashshaf*. It has also been said that this clause, and likewise the clause before it, is in the position of a circumstantial state from Abraham, by way of *tarādif* (parallelism) or *tadākhul* (interpenetration). The answer of *lammā*, we say, is to be estimated before ﴿O Abraham, turn away from this﴾. The most likely of the views is the first. As for *al-bushrā* (the good news): if it is interpreted as their saying "Do not fear," then the causal link between the departure of fear and the coming of joy through the argument is clear. But if it is interpreted as the good news of a son, as Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Qatadah, and as a group chose, or as something that encompasses both, then its causal link to the argument may lie in the fact that it increases the tranquility of his heart, peace be upon him, in his own safety and the safety of his whole family. This is what our master Shaykh al-Islam said. Then he said: If it is said that what is understood from this speech is that Abraham, peace be upon him, had known that they were sent to destroy the people of Lot before the fear left him, but he was unable to argue with them about their affair because he was occupied with his own concern, then (*fa-lammā dhahaba ʿanhu al-rawʿ*) he was free for it. However, the departure of fear was before he knew this, as shown by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿They said: "Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lot"﴾. We say: Lot, peace be upon him, was upon the law (*sharīʿa*) of Abraham, peace be upon him, and his people were obligated by it. When he saw from the angels, peace be upon them, what he saw, he feared for himself and for the whole of his community, of which the people of Lot were a part. There is no doubt that this fear preceded their saying "Do not fear." As for what he knew, peace be upon him, after the prohibition, it was that the people of Lot were singled out for destruction, and they were not included in the general sense. So consider this. End of quotation.

In it there is this: that the whole of them being his community is open to objection. And what he pointed to, namely the unity of the two laws, if by it he means unity in the fundamentals, as the law of our Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, is one with the law of Abraham, peace be upon him, then it is granted, but this does not necessarily follow from it. If he means unity in both fundamentals and details, then it is not granted, and even if granted, there is doubt about whether it follows that the whole of them are his community. Moreover, even if we grant all of that, [p. 104] someone could say: we grant that when he saw from the angels, peace be upon them, what he saw, fear arose in him for himself and for his whole community, of which the people of Lot, peace be upon him, were a part. But we do not grant that this fear was from knowledge that those angels had been sent to destroy the whole group in which the people of Lot were included, but rather it was from hesitation and bewilderment about their affair. In that case the question is not resolved by this answer, as is not hidden from one who reflects. Perhaps this is why he ordered reflection. It may be said: what is understood from the speech is that the argument occurred after the realization of both matters together, the departure of fear and the coming of the good news. This does not require anything but prior knowledge that they were sent to destroy the people of Lot, at the time when the whole was realized. And it suffices for that that this knowledge preceded the realization of the good news. This knowledge is derived from their saying to him: ﴿Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lot﴾. It seems that he, peace be upon him, did not argue after this knowledge, and postponed the argument until the coming of the good news, so that he might see where the speech of the angels, peace be upon them, would lead. Or because no pause of silence occurred between them in which he could have argued. But this does not hold unless the announcement of being sent to the people of Lot preceded the good news of the son, and there is doubt about this.

Some verses clearly indicate that the good news preceded the announcement of that. Yet it is possible to maintain that the announcement preceded the good news, and to say: they informed him first and then gave him good news second. Then, after both matters were realized together, he said: ﴿"What is your business, O messengers?"﴾. It may also be said that what is meant by it is asking about the condition of the punishment, whether it would certainly befall them, or whether it was meant as a warning so that they would return to faith. And the interpretation of the argument as this is as mentioned earlier from some. So reflect on that. And Allah, glorified is He, will guide you.

Indeed, Ibrahim was forbearing (ḥalīm), not hasty to take revenge on the one who wronged him (ghayr ʿajūl ʿalā al-intiqām ilā al-musī' ilayhi), (awwāh) one who often sighs over sins and grieves over people, (munīb) one who turns back to Allah the Exalted.

The purpose of describing him, peace be upon him, with these attributes, which indicate compassion and tenderness of heart, is to explain what moved him to the argument he made (al-mujādalah) that proceeded from him. The forbearance (al-ḥilm) is understood here as not being hasty and being patient and deliberate in any matter whatsoever. The purpose of describing him with those attributes has been taken to be the explanation of what moved him to argue and to carry on with the argument after the fear had departed and the good news had come; his condition is not hidden.

﴿O Ibrahim﴾, supplied as the object of an understood verb of saying (taqdir al-qawl), so that it connects with what precedes it. That is, [the angels said] or [We said]: "O Ibrahim."

﴿Turn away from this﴾, meaning the disputing, ﴿for indeed it﴾, meaning the matter, ﴿has come, the command of your Lord﴾, meaning His decree, exalted is He, that their punishment has been determined. It may also be explained as the punishment itself. "Coming" here may mean "approaching," so that it does not repeat His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and indeed there will come upon them a punishment that cannot be averted﴾, meaning neither by disputing, nor by supplication, nor by anything else. For the result of that approach is that the punishment has come close to them and then befell them. It was also said: there is no need to take "approaching" into account, and the repetition is resolved by saying that the first statement is a preparation for mentioning that it cannot be averted.

Amr ibn Haram recited "wa-innahum atahum" with the verb in the past tense (al-madi), with ʿadhabun (ʿadhābun) as its subject. He used the past tense to affirm that the event has definitely occurred.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 77:

﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut,﴾ On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, he said: They set out from the presence of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and between the two towns there were four farsakh (a measure of distance). They entered upon him in the form of beardless young men of fair countenance. Therefore ﴿he was distressed on their account﴾, meaning that their coming caused him, peace be upon him, distress, because he thought they were people, and he feared that his people would target them and that he would be unable to defend them. It was also said: the distance between the two towns was eight miles, and they reached it at nightfall; and it was said at midday, and they found Lut in his field.

It was also said: they found his daughter drawing water from the river of Sodom, which was the largest settlement of the people. They asked her to direct them to someone who would host them, and she saw their appearance and feared for them from her father's people. She said to them: "Wait here," and she went to her father and informed him. He came out to them, and they said: "We wish that you host us tonight." He said: "Have you not heard of the deeds of these people?" They said: "And what is their deed?" He said: "I bear witness before Allah, the Exalted, that they are the worst of people on earth." Allah, the Exalted, had said to the angels: "Do not punish them until Lut bears witness against them four times." When he said this, Jibril, peace be upon him, said: "This is one." The statement was repeated by him until Lut had repeated the testimony, and the four were completed. Then he entered the city, and they entered with him into his house. ﴿And he was distressed by them, and his capacity was straitened﴾, meaning he had no power or strength. Originally, it is the verbal noun of "dhara'a al-ba'ir biyadayhi yadhra'u fi masirihi" (the camel stretched out its forelegs in its stride) when it walks extending its step, derived from "al-dhira'" (the forearm), the well-known limb. Then it was used broadly and placed in the position of capacity and effort, because just as the hand is made a metaphor for power, so is the well-known forearm. In al-Sihah it is said: "Dagt bi-al-amr dhar'an" (I was straitened by the matter) when you could not bear it and were not able to deal with it; the origin of "dhar'" is the spreading of the hand, as if you mean "I stretched my hand toward it and did not reach it." They sometimes say: "Dagt bihi dhira'an." Humayd ibn Thawr said, describing a wolf:

And if it spends a night wild, it is not straitened thereby (dhira'an), nor does it rise therefrom while humbled.

In al-Kashshaf: the Arabs made the narrowness of the forearm and the "dhar'" an expression for the loss of capacity, as they said: "rahuba al-dhira' bi-kadha" (the forearm was spacious for such a thing) when one was able to bear it. The origin of this is that when a man's forearm is long, he reaches what the short-armed cannot reach, so this was made a proverb for inability and ability. Its accusative is as a tamyiz transferred from the agent, meaning: his capacity regarding their matter and condition was straitened. It is also permitted that "dhar'" be a metonymy for the breast and heart, and its narrowness a metonymy for intense constriction due to inability to repel the disliked matter and to devise a remedy for it. This, as it is said, is a metonymy branching from another well-known metonymy. It is also said that it is a metaphor, since the literal meaning is not intended here. Some have strayed far in explaining this statement, interpreting it to mean that his body was too small in capacity to bear what befell him. ﴿And he said: This﴾ day ﴿is a distressing day﴾, meaning severe. Its origin is from "al-'asab," meaning binding, as if because of its great evil some of it is bound to another. Abu 'Ubayda said: it was named so because it binds people with evil. The reciter said:

A distressing day that binds the brave ∗∗∗ as it binds the strong the long ropes.

And in its meaning are "al-'asabsab" and "al-'asawsab."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 78:

﴿And they came to him﴾, that is, Lut, while he was in his house with his guests, ﴿his people, rushing towards him﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: that is, they were urging one another on towards him, as if one of them were spurring the others; or their elder was urging them on and driving them; or it was the desire for the abomination. The common reading is with the verb in the passive form (yuhra'una). A group of readers read (yahra'una) with a fatha on the ya', in the active form, from hari'a. Its root is from al-hara', which is intense, rapid flowing blood, as if some of it pushes the rest. It is also said: ahra'a al-qawm ("the people hastened") when they hurried. Some commentators explained ihra' as walking between running (harwala) and a sprint (jamz). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked about what is in the verse, and he said: the meaning is that they came to him in anger. Then he recited the verse of Muhalhil:

"They came rushing, while they were captives, whom we lead against the will of their noses."

In another report from him, he explained it as yusri'una (they hasten), which is a clarification of the intended meaning, and it is consistent with both readings. The clause ﴿yuhra'una﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿his people﴾, meaning they came hastening towards him. It is narrated that when Lut brought his guest, no one knew of it except the people of his household. His wife went out until she reached the gatherings of her people and said: "Lut has hosted tonight a group the like of whom has not been seen for beauty." Then they came rushing to him. ﴿And before this﴾, that is, before the time of their coming. It is also said: "before this" refers to Lut being sent as a messenger to them. ﴿They used to do evil deeds﴾. It is said: the intended meaning is the evil of mounting males, but it was expressed in the plural in view of its repetition, or in view of its doers.

It is also said: the intended meaning is what encompasses that and also intercourse with women in their posteriors, the whistling and clapping, playing with pigeons, gambling, mocking people, and other things. The purpose of mentioning their evil deeds before this is to show that they had become accustomed to wrongdoing and were not ashamed, and therefore they hastened to seek the abomination from his guests, openly and without concern. So the sentence is a parenthetical insertion to emphasize what precedes it.

It is also said: it explains the reason for his distress, since he knew their custom. Shaykh al-Islam took it as a circumstantial clause like the one before it, meaning they came hastening, while they were engrossed in committing evil deeds.

﴿He said: O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you﴾, so marry them. They had been seeking them before this, but he did not give them to them because of their wickedness and their unsuitability, not because it was impermissible to marry believing women to disbelievers, for that was permissible. The Prophet (ﷺ) married his daughter Zaynab to Abu al-'As ibn al-Rabi', and his daughter Ruqayya to 'Utba ibn Abi Lahab, before revelation, and both were disbelievers. However, 'Utba did not consummate the marriage, and he divorced her at his father's demand when the verse ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ was revealed. Then 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) married her. Abu al-'As had consummated the marriage, but when he was taken captive at the Battle of Badr and ransomed himself, the Prophet (ﷺ) took a pledge from him that he would return her if he came back. The Prophet (ﷺ) then sent Zayd ibn Haritha and a man from the Ansar to seek her, and they brought her back. Then he embraced Islam and came to Medina, and the Prophet (ﷺ) returned her to him, by a new marriage contract or without one, according to the differing opinions.

Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: he (peace be upon him) offered his daughters to them on condition of Islam, and al-Zajjaj adopted this view. This is based on the premise that marrying Muslim women to disbelievers was not permissible at that time. It is also said: he had two respected leaders among them, and he wished to marry his two daughters to them, and he (peace be upon him) had no others besides them. The name of one of them, according to some reports, was Za'ura and the other Zi'taʾ. It is also said: he (peace be upon him) had three daughters, and al-Hakim recorded and authenticated it from Ibn 'Abbas, and the apparent plural supports it, although the term is also used of two. In any case, he (peace be upon him) intended by this to protect his guests, and this is the utmost generosity. So it cannot be said: how is it fitting for him (peace be upon him) to offer his daughters to his enemies to marry them to them? Yes, the offering of his daughters has been questioned, whether they were two, as is well known, or three, as has been said, to those who were rushing, for them to marry them, given that they were more in number than the daughters, since it is not permissible to permit a group to marry fewer than their number at the same time. For this reason some eminent exegetes said: that statement from him (peace be upon him) was not meant literally as a proposal of marriage; rather it was an exaggeration of humility towards them and a display of his extreme distress at what they had brought upon him, hoping they would feel shame before him and be softened towards him when they heard it, and leave his guests, while the matter was clear and it was known to them that there was no marital union between him and them. This is most fitting with their answer that follows. Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Abi Hatim from Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn 'Asakir from al-Suddi, that the intended meaning of "his daughters" was the women of his nation. The demonstrative "these" is used to place them in the position of those present before him, and their attribution to him is because every prophet is a father to his community. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him): "The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves, and he is their father, and his wives are their mothers."

Ubayy (may Allah be pleased with him) read similarly, but he placed ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾ before ﴿and he is their father﴾.

By his words ﴿they are purer for you﴾ he (peace be upon him) meant: cleaner in action, or less indecent, as when you say: carrion is better than usurped property and more lawful than it. The purity meant in the first sense is physical purity, namely being free of the filth and impurity present in sodomy, and in the second sense it is moral purity, namely abstention from indecency and sin. The form "afʿal" in this sense is metaphorical. The apparent reading is: "these are my daughters" as subject and predicate, and likewise "they are purer for you." Abu al-Baqa' permitted "daughters" to be an apposition or a substitution, "they" to be a pronoun of separation, with "purer" as the predicate; or "they" to be a second subject, with "purer" as its predicate, and the whole clause the predicate of "these."

Al-Hasan, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Isa al-Thaqafi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-Suddi read "purer" (atharra) in the accusative. Its meaning has been obscure, to the point that 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: whoever reads "atharra" in the accusative has indeed erred grossly in his grammar. This is because its accusative status is either that it is made a circumstantial clause, the element of demonstration or attention contained in "these" governing it, or "these" is accusative by a hidden verb, as if it were said: "take these," with "daughters" as a substitution, and this hidden verb governs the circumstantial clause, and "they" in both cases is a separating pronoun. This is not permitted, because separation occurs only between the predicate and its subject, and does not occur between a circumstantial clause and its owner, so it is said. This prohibition is what is reported from Sibawayh, but al-Akhfash differed, permitting the separating pronoun to come between a circumstantial clause and its referent, so he says: "Zayd came, he laughing," and he took this verse with this reading as an example. It is also said that it occurs as an anomaly, as in their saying: "Most of my eating is the apple, it being ripe." Whoever forbids this takes it as an implied "was" (kāna). The noble verse, on the view that "they" is the subject and "for you" the predicate, has "purer" as a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in the predicate. It was objected that this involves placing a circumstantial clause before its adverbial governor, and most grammarians prohibit this, or else "these" is the subject and the clause "my daughters, they" is in the position of the predicate of the subject, as in your saying: "This is my brother, he," and "purer" is a circumstantial clause. This is reported from al-Mubarrad and Ibn Jinni. Or else "these" is the subject, "my daughters" a substitution or apposition, "they" the predicate, and "purer" remains as it is.

It was objected that there is no great meaning in this, and it was answered that the intended benefit is the circumstantial clause, as in your saying: "This is your father, gentle." In al-Kashf it is claimed that the more likely view is that they should assume "take these, purer for you," and his words "my daughters, they" are a parenthetical clause giving the reason for the command, and that their being more appropriate was placed first for emphasis, as if it were said: "Take these chaste ones, purer for you, since my daughters are they, and you know my purity and the purity of my daughters." It is also permissible to say that "they" is an emphasis for the hidden pronoun in "my daughters," since it is a derived descriptive term, especially according to the Kufan school, so understand this and do not be negligent.

﴿So fear Allah﴾ by abandoning the abominations, or by preferring them over them. ﴿And do not disgrace me regarding my guests﴾, that is, do not shame me in their matter, for disgracing a man's guest is disgracing him. Or: do not embarrass me concerning them. The verbal noun in the first sense is "khizy" and in the second sense "khiza'a." The original meaning of "khizy" is that the person is overcome by humiliation, either from himself, which is excessive shame, or from others, which is belittlement and exposure. The word "dayf" is a verbal noun, and therefore when it is applied to a dual or plural it does not agree in number, according to the well-known view; it is also heard as "duyūf," "aḍyāf," and "ḍayfān." "Wa-la" is a prohibitive particle, the verb is jussive by the deletion of the nūn, the remaining nūn is the nūn of protection, and the ya' is deleted, sufficed by the kasra; it is also read with the ya' retained, according to the original form. ﴿Is there not among you a man of right mind﴾, who is guided to the clear truth and refrains from the ugly falsehood. Ibn Abi al-Dunya recorded from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: one who enjoins good or forbids evil. It means either "one possessing right guidance," or "one who guides," like "ḥakīm" meaning "muḥkim." The interrogation is for wonder, and taking it literally is not fitting to the context.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 79:

﴿They said﴾, turning away from the advice he gave them concerning fearing God and refraining from disgracing (his guests), from the very beginning of his speech: ﴿Indeed you know that we have no right concerning your daughters﴾. That is, no ḥaqq (right), and it is one of the plural ḥuqūq (rights). By this they meant the fulfilment of desire, that is, "we have no need of your daughters." It may also be explained as the opposite of falsehood (bāṭil), that is, "we have no lawful marriage (nikāḥ ḥaqq) concerning your daughters, because you do not hold it permissible for us to marry Muslim women." And this is merely an ʿarḍ sābirī (a passing, insubstantial pretext), so it is said. This clearly shows that it was part of his sharia, peace be upon him, that a disbeliever may not lawfully marry a Muslim woman.

It is also said: they only denied that they had any right concerning his daughters because they had proposed to them and he had rejected them, and it was their custom that whoever was rejected in a proposal for a woman, she would never be lawful to him ever again. It is also said: when they adopted intercourse with males as a doctrine, they regarded it as the truth, and marrying females as falsehood, so they said what they said. It is also said: they said that because their custom was that a man among them would not marry more than one wife, and they were all married ﴿And indeed you know what we desire﴾, that is, of having intercourse with males. The apparent reading is that (mā) is the object of taʿlam (you know), and it carries the meaning of taʿrif (you recognise). It is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla) and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning "that which we desire." It is also said that it is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), so no omission is needed, meaning "our desire."

He also permitted that it be an interrogative (istifhāmiyya) that stands as the object of nurīd (we desire), and in that case it is suspended (muʿallaqa) with respect to taʿlam (you know). This is because he, peace be upon him, had despaired of their turning back from the error they were in.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 80:**

﴿He said: "If only I had power against you"﴾. That is, if it were established that I had power joined with you in resisting you by myself, I would have done it. ***Law*** (if) here is a conditional particle (*shartiyyah*), and its answer is omitted, as it is omitted in His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which the mountains could be moved﴾. It is also permissible for it to be for wishing (*tamanni*). The phrase ***bikum*** (with you) is a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of ***quwwah*** (power), as is well known in the case of an indefinite noun when its qualifier is placed before it. Its connection to it is weak, because the complement of a verbal noun (*masdar*) does not, according to the well-known view, precede it. His saying ﴿or that I could take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾ is coordinated (*'utifa*) to what precedes it, based on what you have learned of its meaning, which is required by the position of al-Mubarrad. The imperfect verb here stands in the place of the perfect, and Abu Hayyan favored this view. Al-Hawfi said that it is coordinated to what came before on the basis that the intended meaning is "or that I [could] take refuge," and Abu al-Baqa' also permitted this. Likewise, he permitted that the sentence be a resumptive sentence (*mustaʾnafah*), meaning one that begins a new statement. The word ***al-rukn*** (pillar), originally, is the side of a house or of a mountain. It is said *rakun* with a *damma* on the *kaf*, and it has been read that way. Its plural is *arkan*. By it, peace be upon him, meant the strong one, likening him to the pillar of a mountain in its firmness and its protection. That is: "or I could join a strong one by whom I may keep myself safe from you and by whom I may prevail over you."

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) counted this saying of his, peace be upon him, as a hasty utterance and regarded it as strange. Al-Bukhari and Muslim related from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May God have mercy on my brother Lot; he used to take refuge in a mighty pillar." He meant, peace be upon him, God, for there is no pillar mightier than Him, exalted and majestic is He.

*If anything other than God is a man's resource,*
*calamities will come upon him from all the directions of benefit.*

It has come that He, glorified be He, did not send any prophet after Lot, upon this word, except in the protection of his clan. In al-Bahr (the book *al-Bahr al-Muhit*) it is said that it is permissible, according to the opinion of the Kufans, for ***aw*** (or) to mean ***bal*** (rather), and that he, peace be upon him, then turned away from the preceding sentence and said: "Rather, I take refuge, in my state with you, in a mighty pillar," and by it he referred to the presence of God, exalted is He. It is not hidden that this interpretation as a figure of speech is rejected by the clear sound reports that contradict it.

Shaybah and Abu Ja'far read ***aviya*** with the accusative, by implying *an* (that) after *aw* (or). It is thus interpreted as a verbal noun, coordinated to ***quwwah*** (power). A parallel to this is the saying of the poet:

*Had it not been for men of Rizam, honorable,*
*and the family of Sabi', or I would have made you bitter as colocynth.*

That is: "If only I had power with you, or refuge." It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, closed his door against his guests and began to argue with his people on their behalf from behind the door, so they climbed over the wall. When the angels, peace be upon them, saw what distress Lot was in—

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 81 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They said: "O Lut, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So set out with your family in a part of the night, and let none of you look back, except your wife. Indeed, she will be struck by what strikes them. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?"﴾

Note: the verse as cited in this passage reads ﴿قالُوا يا لُوطُ إنّا رُسُلُ رَبِّكَ لَنْ يَصِلُوا إلَيْكَ﴾, so the rendering above follows the verse text given here, and the wording beyond that point is not part of this excerpt.

Correction to the above: the excerpt contains only the opening portion of verse 81 as cited here, which reads:

﴿They said: "O Lut, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you."﴾

The remainder of the commentary follows:

They said, "O Lut, we are the messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you with harm or any displeasure. So open the door and leave us and them." He opened the door, and they entered. Jibril, peace be upon him, asked the Lord of Might for permission to punish them, and He permitted him. When they drew near, he obliterated their eyes, and they departed blind, stumbling over one another, saying: "Escape! Escape! For in the house of Lut there are sorcerers." In another narration, he, peace be upon him, had locked the door on his guest, and they came and broke the door, so Jibril obliterated their eyes. They said: "O Lut, you have brought us sorcerers," and they threatened him. He felt fear within himself. He said: "Will these leave and abandon me?"
