When Jibril, peace be upon him, said: "Do not fear; indeed we are messengers of your Lord," ﴿So set out with your family﴾ by cutting off from the travel (al-qat' min al-isra', i.e., the verb in the form with hamza, "asri" as a command in the cut form). Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read it with the wasl form wherever it occurs in the Qur'an from al-sara; and it has come as "sari." 

Page 109

Both mean the same according to Abu 'Ubayda and al-Azhari. According to al-Layth, asra means he traveled at the beginning of the night, and sara means he traveled at its end; and it is not said of daytime except "sara," and it is not an inversion of "sara." The fa' indicates the ordering of the command to travel upon the report of their messengerhood, which signals the arrival of command and prohibition from Him, glorified and exalted, to him, peace be upon him. The ba' is for transitivity or for accompaniment, i.e., travel accompanied by your family. ﴿In a part of the night﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "in a portion of it." Qatadah said: "after a portion of it has passed." It was said: "its half." In another narration from the Scholar (al-Hibr), its last part. He recited the verse of Malik ibn Kinana:

And a wailing woman rising in a part of the night, upon a saddle that the tribes have humiliated.

It is not from the category of evidence. This is also the view of Muhammad ibn Ziyad, based on His saying, glorified is He: ﴿We saved them at dawn﴾. Ibn 'Atiyya objected that it is possible that he traveled with his family from the beginning of the night until they passed the uprooted town, and their rescue occurred at dawn. The root of "qat'" is a piece of something; but Ibn al-Anbari said that this is specific to the night, so one does not say "indi qat' min al-thawb" (I have a piece of the garment).

Some scholars interpreted "qat' min al-layl" as a portion of its darkness, and from the Scholar also its interpretation as the very blackness; perhaps this is a matter of leniency. ﴿And let none of you look back﴾: that is, let none lag behind, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas; or let none look behind him, as narrated from Qatadah. It was said: this is the well-known meaning and the literal sense of "iltifat." As for the first, it is because one says: "laftuhu 'an al-amr" when you turn him away from it, so "iltafata" means he turned away; and lagging behind is a turning away from the journey. The Exalted said: ﴿Have you come to us to turn us away from what we found our fathers upon?﴾, i.e., to turn us away. Thus al-Raghib said.

In al-Asas, it is a figurative meaning. The prohibition is in form addressed to someone, but in meaning it is addressed to Lut, peace be upon him, according to what is reported from al-Mubarrad. This is like when you say to your servant: "Let no one stand up," while the prohibition is apparently addressed to someone, but in reality it is to the servant that he should not allow anyone to stand up. The meaning here is: "So set out with your family and do not let any of them look back." It is not hidden that on this view the correspondence between the conjoined and the conjoining is complete, since the first is his command and the second his prohibition. From this it is known that the pronoun in ﴿minkum﴾ refers to the family.

Shihab Fakhr al-Fadl al-Khafaji has stated this explicitly, saying: "Here is a subtle point: the later scholars of rhetoric (badi') invented a type of badi' they named 'tasmiyat al-nawc' (naming the type), which is that an example of badi' is given and its name is mentioned by way of tawriya, as in his saying in the Badi'iyya on istikhdam:

They employed the eye from me, so it runs, and how often I have granted it on a day among them.

They boasted of inventing it. As for me, by the grace of God Most High, I say: it occurs in the Qur'an in this verse, because His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So set out with your family﴾ etc., contains the pronoun 'minkum' referring to the family; so His saying, exalted is He, '(let none) look back' is from 'tasmiyat al-nawc,' and this is from the marvels of subtle points." End of quotation. The secret of the prohibition against iltifat in the sense of lagging behind is evident. As for its secret when it means looking back, it is that they should hasten in their travel, for whoever looks behind him does not avoid some pause; or that they should not see what descends upon their people of punishment and be softened toward them.

Some scholars mentioned that the prohibition, and likewise the pronoun, refer to Lut, peace be upon him, and his family, i.e., let none of you, you and your family, look back. ﴿Except your wife﴾ in the accusative, which is the reading of most of the Seven.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it in the nominative. Much has been said on this. Al-Zamakhshari said: He, glorified is He, excepted her from His saying "So set out with your family," and the reading of 'Abd Allah supports this: "So set out with your family in a part of the night, except your wife." It is also permissible that it be in the accusative from "let none look back" on the original basis of exception, though the eloquent form is the substitution, namely the reading of whoever reads it in the nominative, substituting her for "one of you." Regarding her departure with his family there are two reports: it is narrated that he took her out with them and commanded that none of them look back except her; when she heard the crash of the punishment she looked back and said: "O my people!" and a stone struck her and killed her. It is also narrated that when he was commanded to leave her behind with her people, her desire was toward them, so he did not travel with her; and the difference of the two readings corresponds to the difference of the two reports. End of quotation.

Ibn al-Hajib objected to this with a summary: either he traveled with her, so the exception from "one of you" is necessary, or he did not, so it is necessary from "So set out with your family," and the story is one; so one of the two interpretations is certainly false, and the two readings that are certainly established cannot be taken to imply the invalidity of one of them. So it is better that "except your wife" be both nominative and accusative, like ﴿they did not do it except a few of them﴾. It is not far-fetched that some readers follow the stronger reading and most follow what is less strong; indeed some allowed that the readers may agree on a reading other than the stronger.

Some Maghribis answered him with what the author of al-Kashf indicated, namely the denial of contradiction: the exception from "family" requires that Lut, peace be upon him, was not commanded to travel with her, and this does not prevent her from setting out on her own; and this measure suffices for the validity of both exceptions. How, when he did not forbid her departure, but he commanded the departure of others! Yes, what is objectionable is his saying: "the difference of the two readings corresponds to the difference of the two reports," for this implies doubt in a speech in which there is no doubt from the Lord of the Worlds. It may be answered that its meaning is that the difference of the two readings is a cause and occasion of the difference of the two reports, as you say: "the weapon is for the raid," i.e., it is a tool and suitable for it; it does not mean that the difference of the two readings arose because of the difference of the two reports; and there is no doubt that each report suits one reading, even if reconciliation is possible. As for his saying: "He was commanded that none of them look back except her," this is cited as a report, not an explanation of the Qur'anic wording; what is in the text is only the exception of her from the ruling that is for welfare, since she was not intended by it. To the meaning indicated by the author of al-Kashf regarding the denial of contradiction, Abu Shama pointed when he said: "There occurred in correcting what the grammarians parsed a good meaning: that there is an ellipsis in the speech, which the difference of the two readings points to, as if it were said: 'So set out with your family except your wife, as 'Abd Allah read it,' and Abu 'Ubayda narrated it from his codex. This is evidence that her exception is from the travel with them. Then it is as if He, glorified is He, said: 'If she goes out with you and follows you without you having traveled with her, then she will be destroyed and what befalls her people will befall her.' So the reading of the accusative indicates the earlier meaning, and the reading of the nominative indicates this later meaning, and both together indicate the whole of the explained meaning." And there is no hiding what there is in this of artificiality, as Ibn Malik said. For this reason he preferred that the nominative is on the basis that the exception is disconnected (munqati'), "imra'atuka" is the subject (mubtada'), the sentence after it is its predicate, and "illa" means "but" (lakin).

Ibn Hisham said in al-Mughni, in the eighth aspect of the fifth chapter: what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, which others had preceded him to in the verse, is contrary to the apparent meaning; and what led those who said it is that the accusative is the reading of most, so if the exception is made from "one of you," their reading would be in the less preferred form. Some committed to permitting both to come, citing the verse: ﴿Indeed We created everything with measure﴾, for the accusative there, according to Sibawayh, is like the saying "Zaydan darabtuhu" (Zayd, I struck him); and he did not see the fear of confusing the explanatory word with an adjective as making a preference, as some later scholars did. Then he said: What I am certain of is that the reading of most is not thereby preferred, and that the exception on both readings is from the whole of the command, by the evidence of the dropping of "wa la yaltafit" etc. in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, and the exception is disconnected (munqati'), by the evidence of its dropping in the verse of al-Hijr; and because the intended meaning of "family" is the believers, even if they are not of his household, not the household of his house even if they are not believers, as in His saying, exalted is He, to Nuh, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed he is not of your family﴾. The reason for the nominative is that it is the subject, and what follows is the predicate, and the exception is the sentence, and its parallel is: ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾ ﴿except one who turns away and disbelieves﴾ ﴿then God will punish him﴾.

Abu Shama chose what I have chosen, that the exception is disconnected, but he said: "The accusative came in the Hijazi dialect and the nominative in the Tamimi dialect." This indicates that he made the exception from the whole of the prohibition. What I have advanced is preferable, because of the weakness of the Tamimi dialect, and because of what I have mentioned regarding the dropping of the sentence of the prohibition in the reading of 'Abd Allah. End of quotation.

and the commentator Al-Himsi also upheld this in his glosses on al-Tasrih, and many found it commendable. Abu Hayyan transmitted the view that the exception is disjunctive (munqati') under both readings, with the accusative explained by the Hijazi dialect and the nominative by the other. Then he said: "It is a statement without verification, for if it is not intended to exclude her from those commanded to travel by night with them, nor from those forbidden to look back, and the meaning is 'but your wife, such-and-such befalls her,' then it is an exception to which the governing verb does not extend. This type of disjunctive exception requires the accusative by the consensus of the Arabs. The disagreement is only concerning the disjunctive exception where the governing verb can extend to it, and this is open to question." In al-Tawdih of Ibn Malik: "The stated exception with illa, from a complete affirmative sentence, whether singular or complementing in meaning what follows it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We will save them all﴾ ﴿except his wife; We have decreed that she will be among those who remain behind﴾, takes the accusative. Most later Basran grammarians know only the accusative, and they have overlooked its occurrence in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence with an established predicate, as in the saying of Abu Qatadah: 'They all entered the state of ihram except Abu Qatadah, who did not enter ihram.' Its omitted form is like ﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾ except Allah. Here 'illa' carries the meaning of 'lakin' (but), i.e., 'but Abu Qatadah did not enter ihram, and but Allah knows.'" The end of the quotation. What we are discussing belongs to this category. In the glosses of al-Badr al-Damamini and Taqi al-Din al-Shamni, it is noted that al-Radi answered in a way that implies the exception is connected (muttasil) and there is no contradiction. He said: "Since it has been established that following (the nominative/ itba') is the preferred form, subject to the stated conditions, and most readers read the verb ﴿wa la yaltafit﴾ with the accusative, al-Zamakhshari went to great lengths, lest the reading of the majority be interpreted as an unpreferred form, by taking the pains that he took." Ibn al-Hajib objected to him, citing the resulting contradiction: the exception from "travel" (asri bi-ahlika) implies she is not to travel with them, while the exception from "let none of you look back" implies she is to travel with them, since looking back is part of the travel. The response: although travel is absolute in outward appearance, in meaning it is restricted by not looking back. Its outcome is: "Travel with your family in a journey without looking back, except your wife, for you will travel with her in a journey with looking back." So you may make the exception, if you wish, from "asri" or from "la yaltafit," and there is no contradiction. This is like saying: "Walk, and do not strut," meaning: walk in a walk in which you do not strut. It is as if it were said: "None of you shall look back during the travel," and likewise "Walk, and do not strut in walking," so the prepositional phrase is omitted because it is known. The end of the quotation.

Al-Sayyid al-Sanad objected to this in his glosses: if the exception returns to the qualifier, the meaning becomes "Travel with all your family in a journey without looking back, except your wife," so her travel with them is included in what is commanded. If it returns to the qualified element, her travel is not included in what is commanded, and the difficulty remains unresolved. The only escape is to say that the general term's inclusion of her is not certain, since it may be specific to her, so it does not follow from the exception's reference to His saying "wa la yaltafit" that he, peace be upon him, was commanded to travel with her. In that case the exception may be explained as stated: that she followed them, or that he traveled with her while not being commanded to do so, since the absence of a command does not entail a prohibition. Consider this. The end of the quotation.

Al-Shihab examined this and did not accept the possibility of specification, since there is no evidence for it, and his treatment implies approval of al-Radi's statement. He then said: "His intent by the restriction is that he mentioned two items joined by a conjunction, so the apparent meaning is that the intent is to combine both, not that the clause is circumstantial (hali), and so it is not objected that restriction is unlikely when the waw is for coordination, nor that making it circumstantial with the prohibitive la is impermissible. Moreover, the reading without it indicates that this restriction is not considered, and this is not free of difficulty." Several treatises have been composed on verifying this exception, among them one by al-Himsi, and another by the scholar al-Kafiyaji, whom he composed for one of the sultans of the House of Uthman, may God envelop them in kinds of grace and beneficence, when he was asked for a discussion that arose in his assembly. In sum, the view of disjunction appears less strained, and the claim that there then remains no connection between His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, what befalls them will befall her﴾ and the non-looking-back is a view that should not be entertained, as is clear to anyone who has full knowledge of what was previously quoted. So consider this.

The pronoun in "innahu" is for the matter/situation (li-al-sha'n), "ma asabahum" is the subject, "musibuha" is its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of "inna" whose subject is the pronoun of the matter. In al-Bahr: "inna musibuha" is the subject, "ma asabahum" its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of inna. It is permissible, according to the Kufan view, that "musibuha" be the predicate of inna and "ma" be the agent of it, since they allow "qa'im akhawaka" (your two brothers are standing). The Basran view is that the pronoun of the matter cannot have as its predicate anything except a fully expressed clause with both its parts stated, so this parsing is not permitted by them. The first parsing mentioned is preferable. The clause is either an explanation in the manner of a resumptive statement, or the predicate of "li-imra'atika" (for your wife) on the nominative reading. By "ma" is meant the punishment, and by "asabahum" is meant "yusibuhum," and the use of the past form instead of the present is to indicate the certainty of its occurrence. In the indefiniteness, the nominal form of the clause, and the emphasis, there is what is not hidden.

﴿Indeed, their appointed time is the morning﴾, i.e., the appointed time for their punishment and destruction is that. This seems, as has been said, to be a reason given for the command to travel by night and the prohibition against looking back, which suggests urging haste. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾ is an emphasis of the reason, for the nearness of morning calls for haste to distance oneself from the places of punishment. It is reported that he, peace be upon him, asked the angels, peace be upon them, about the time of their destruction, and they said: "Their appointed time is the morning." He said: "I wish it were sooner than that." They said to him: ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾

Perhaps he made the morning the time of their destruction because it is the time of ease and rest, so the descent of punishment then is more dreadful, and because it is more fitting for that to be a lesson for onlookers.

ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "al-ṣubuḥa" with a ḍamma on the bāʾ. It was said: this is a dialect form, so it is not an imitation (of the following vowel).

﴿When Our command came﴾, that is, Our punishment, or the command to carry it out. If it means the punishment, then "command" is the singular of "affairs" (*umur*). If it means the command to punish, then it is the singular of "commands" (*awamir*). It has been said that attributing "coming" to it in either sense is metaphorical, and that what is meant is "when its occurrence drew near." There is no need to posit an implied word for "time," since *lamma* ("when") already indicates it.

It has also been said that on the second reading one should posit "the time of Our command came," because the command itself had already been issued earlier, and we have no need to claim that it is repeated. The interpretation of "command" as the singular of commands, meaning the opposite of prohibition, is preferred, because it is the original sense of the word, being the verbal noun of *amara* (he commanded). As for its meaning punishment, that takes the word out of its original verbal-noun sense and out of its well-known, common meaning. Making the overturning a consequence of the command is also supported by the words of the Exalted: ﴿We made its highest part its lowest﴾, since this is the answer to *lamma*, while the punishment itself is the very act of inflicting the punishment. So it is not appropriate to make the command a cause of the punishment; rather, the reverse is more fitting, unless "coming" is interpreted as His will to bring it about. The pronouns in *ʿaliyaha* ("its highest") and *safilaha* ("its lowest") refer to the cities of the people of Lot, which are known from the context. They are the *Mu'tafikat* (the overturned cities), and they are five cities: Mayʿa, Ṣaʿra, ʿAṣra, Dūma and Sadūm.

It has also been said that there were seven, the greatest of which was Sadūm, the town in which Lot, peace be upon him, lived. According to what was transmitted from Qatada, there were in it four thousand thousand people, or as many as God Most High willed. It has been said that this number was across all the cities together, and it has been said that the population of the cities was far greater than this. And God Most High knows best.

*ʿAliyaha* and *safilaha* are in the accusative because they are the two objects of *jaʿala* (made). The meaning is that We turned it over in that form, making the highest part the lowest. It was overturned in this way and not reversed in order to magnify the matter and to make the calamity appalling, because making its highest part, which was their place of dwelling and residence, its lowest is harder than making its lowest its highest, even though the former entails the latter.

It is narrated that Lot, peace be upon him, set out with those who were with him before dawn, and God Most High folded the earth for him until he reached Abraham, peace be upon him. Then Jibril, peace be upon him, uprooted the cities with his hand. In another narration, he put his wing beneath the cities and lifted them until the people of the heavens heard the crowing of roosters and the barking of dogs, and then he overturned them. How great is God Most High's wisdom in this overturning, which is most like what they had been doing, namely committing abominations and turning away from what sound natures require!

One should not take this speech as a metaphor for the sending down of a great affair upon them, as someone says, "Today the world has been turned upside down for so-and-so," because this involves deviating from the apparent meaning and departing from what the reports have stated, without any reason other than finding such a thing unlikely. Yet such a thing is not far-fetched. The attribution of the making to His pronoun, Exalted is He, is on the basis that He is the one who causes it; so it is a metaphorical attribution in terms of language, although He, Glorified is He, is the true agent. The purpose of this is to magnify and to make the matter appalling, for whatever the Mighty undertakes is itself mighty. The pronoun of greatness (the royal "We") also reinforces this. In the same manner is the saying of the Glorified: ﴿And We rained upon it﴾, meaning upon the cities or upon the outcasts of their people, ﴿stones of baked clay﴾. This was an addition to the appalling nature of their condition, or a cutting off of their root and a total uprooting of them.

It is narrated that one of them was in the Sacred Precinct (*al-Haram*), and a stone remained suspended in the air until it came out from him, then fell upon him and destroyed him. *Sijjil* means clay that has become hardened into stone, based on the words of the Exalted in another verse: ﴿stones of clay﴾. The Qur'an explains one part of it by another, and it is necessary to refer one part to another within a single story. This is as ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid: it is an Arabized word (*muʿarrab*) from the Persian *sang-i gil* (*سِنِّكَ كَلَّ*), meaning "stone and clay."

Abu ʿUbayda said: *sijjil* is like *sijjin* (a severe stone). It has also been said that it comes from *asjalahu*, meaning "he sent it" or "he lavished his gift," and the meaning is stones that come from something like what is sent, or like a gift in its abundance. On this understanding it is used in a mocking sense. It has also been said that it comes from *sijill* with the *lam* doubled, meaning a certificate. The meaning of its being from that is that it is among what God Most High has written against them, that He would punish them with it. It has also been said that its origin is *sijjin*, which is a name for Hell or for a valley within it, and its *nun* was changed to a *lam*.

Abu al-ʿAliya and Ibn Zayd said: *sijjil* is a name for the lowest heaven. Abu Hayyan said: this is weak, because it is described by the words of the Glorified, ﴿*manḍūd*﴾, meaning arranged, placed one part upon another, prepared for their punishment, or arranged in their sending, sent one after another, like the streams of rain. It is not hidden that these meanings, just as they contradict what Abu al-ʿAliya and Ibn Zayd said, also contradict, on the apparent reading, what has been said: that the intended meaning is Hell. Some have strained and said: it is possible to describe Hell with this on the basis of the first meaning, given that it has levels, one above another; or that the original sense is "arranged within it," and then it was broadened in usage. One may strain in a similar way to support what Abu al-ʿAliya and Ibn Zayd said. It is also permitted that *manḍūd* be an attribute of *ḥijāra* (stones), treating *ḥajar* (stone) as feminine, with the word in the genitive by proximity (*jarr li-l-jiwār*). On this reading the matter is clear, except that it is a considerable strain.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 83:**

﴿Marked﴾, meaning: it bore a mark by which it was known that it was not from the stones of the earth. This was said by Ibn Jurayj. It was also said: it was marked with white and red. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas it is reported that some of them were black with a white spot, and some were white with a black spot.

It is narrated from al-Rabi' that they were marked with the name of the one who would be struck by them. He also said that some of them, as it was said, were like the heads of camels, some were like their resting places (their droppings), and some were like a man's fistful. ﴿With your Lord﴾, meaning: in His treasuries, which none owns but Him, glorified is He, and none disposes of them other than Him, Mighty and Majestic is He. The adverbial phrase (ẓarf, ظرف, adverbial complement) is said to be in the accusative, governed by ﴿مُسَوَّمَةً﴾ (marked), or to be attached to an omitted word that serves as a descriptor for it. What is related from Muqatil is that the meaning is that they came from your Lord. And from Abu Bakr al-Hudhali: they were prepared with Him, glorified is He.

Ibn al-Anbari said: what is meant is that He required this marking for the stones in His presence, exHigh is He, as a notice of His power and the severity of His punishment, so let this be understood.

﴿And it is not﴾, meaning: the stones described as mentioned, ﴿far from the wrongdoers﴾: from every wrongdoer it is not far.

- That is, because of their wrongdoing they deserve it. In this there is a warning to all people of wrongdoing. This was narrated from al-Rabi'.

Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Qatada that what is meant by the wrongdoers is the wrongdoers of this community. There is a report mentioned by al-Tha'labi, about which al-Iraqi said: "I have not found a chain of transmission for it," that the Prophet (ﷺ) asked Jibril, peace be upon him, about this, and he said: "It means the wrongdoers of your community. There is not a wrongdoer among them but he is at the edge of a stone that falls upon him from one hour to the next." It was also said: what is meant by the wrongdoers is the people of Lot, peace be upon him, and the meaning is that the stones would not miss them.

And from Ibn 'Abbas: the meaning is that their punishment, for those who do their deeds, is not far. Its apparent sense is that the pronoun refers to the punishment understood from the context, and ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ are those among people who resemble them. It is possible to say that his intention was to state the resulting meaning, not to determine the referent of the pronoun.

Abu Hayyan held that the apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿it﴾ refers to the towns whose highest part was made the lowest, and that what is meant by the wrongdoers is the wrongdoers of Makkah, which was near to them, as they passed by it on their journeys to Syria. The masculine form of ﴿far﴾ may be explained either by taking the stones as a collective noun (ḥajar, حجر, with the sense of a kind), or by treating it as agreeing with an implied masculine noun, meaning: "a thing far off" or "a place far off." For although the stones were in the sky, which is at the utmost distance, yet they fell from it, so they are the swiftest thing in reaching them, and it is as if they were in a place near to them. Or it may be because the word is in the pattern of a verbal noun (maṣdar, مصدر), like *zafīr* (roaring) and *ṣahīl* (neighing), and verbal nouns are the same for masculine and feminine in describing.

[Page 115]

﴿And to Madyan﴾: that is, to the descendants of Madyan ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon him. The noun modified has been omitted, or Madyan has become a name for the tribe by predominance. Tribes are often named after their father, as with Mudar and Tamim. This is probably the better reading. It is also permitted that Madyan refers to the city founded by Madyan, which took his name. In that case a modified noun must be supplied: "and to the people of Madyan." ﴿their brother﴾, meaning their kinsman, ﴿Shu'ayb﴾. What has been said about his lineage, peace be upon him, has already been mentioned. The clause is conjoined to the words of Him, glorified is He: ﴿And to Thamud, their brother Salih﴾. The meaning is: "And We sent Shu'ayb to Madyan."

﴿He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him.﴾ This is a command to monotheism in an emphatic form. Since this is the foundation of the matter, he placed it before the prohibition of what they had become accustomed to, namely defrauding (bakhs), which contradicts justice and disrupts the wisdom of exchange (al-ta'arud, mutual exchange) and the delivery of rights to their owners, in His words: ﴿And do not diminish the measure and the scale.﴾ It has been said: that is, do not diminish people's measures and scales, meaning what is measured and weighed, by mentioning the place and intending what is in it. It has been inferred that what is meant is: do not reduce the volume of the measure below the customary standard, and likewise the weights. Al-Kayl (measure) has been mentioned in place of al-mikyal (measuring vessel) in al-A'raf, so reflect on this and consider it carefully. ﴿Indeed I see you in prosperity﴾, that is, enjoying wide wealth which makes you independent of that, or in a blessing from Allah, the Exalted, whose due is to be met with something other than what you are doing, by being generous to people in gratitude for it, for the most noble thanks for blessings is beneficence and generosity toward the servants of Allah, the Exalted. Or: "I see you in good and wealth, so do not remove it by the evil you commit." In every case, the clause is in the position of a reason for the prohibition. He followed it with another reason, namely His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed I fear for you﴾, if you do not desist from that, ﴿the punishment of an encompassing day﴾.

It is also permitted that this is a reason for both the command and the prohibition together. "Encompassing" has been explained as "one from which none of them will escape." Al-Zamakhshari explained it as "destroying," drawing on His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And its fruit was encompassed﴾, and its origin is from the encompassing of an enemy. He claimed that describing the day as encompassing is more eloquent than describing the punishment, because the day is a time that includes events. When it encompasses its punishment, the one punished has gathered what it contains of that, just as when it encompasses his bliss. That is, since the day is a time containing the events that occur in it, whether punishment or otherwise, when it encompasses the one punished while he is involved in its punishment, because it is an event, then the punished one has gathered what the day contains, which is the punishment, just as when it encompasses him, involved in his bliss.

The summary is that the encompassing of the day indicates the encompassing of everything in it of punishment. As for the encompassing of punishment over a people, it may occur by each individual being struck by one instance of punishment. In our case, however, it indicates the encompassing of the kinds of punishment that the day includes, upon every individual. There is no doubt about the greater eloquence of this, as in al-Kashf, and the full discussion of it is there. Some of the verifiers said in explaining the greater eloquence: the day is a time for all events, so the day of punishment is the time of all the kinds of punishment that occur in it. When it encompasses the one punished, the kinds of punishment have gathered for him. This is like his words:

"Indeed, manliness, generosity, and liberality
are in a dome raised over the son of al-Hashraj."

For the occurrence of punishment in the day is like the existence of the qualities in the dome, and making the day encompass the one punished is like raising the dome over the one praised. Just as this is a metonymy for the establishment of those qualities for him, so that is a metonymy for the establishment of the kinds of punishment for the one punished. As for describing the punishment with encompassing, there is a metaphor of its encompassing him, because it includes the one punished. Just as nothing of the parts of the encompassed escapes the encompassing one, nothing of the parts of the punished escapes the punishment. This metaphor indicates that the punishment is for the whole of the one punished, and that metonymy indicates that all of the punishment is for him. The difference between them in eloquence is not hidden.

It is also permitted that "encompassing" (muhit) be an adjective of "punishment" and be put in the genitive by proximity (li'l-jiwar). It has been said that it is an adjective of "day," agreeing with the noun in a way other than with the one it belongs to, the sense being "the punishment of a day whose punishment is encompassing." This is not something of substance, as is not hidden. In any case, what is meant is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, or the punishment of annihilation in this world. Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he explained "good" as cheapness of prices and "punishment" as their expensiveness.

And O my people, give full measure and weight (﴿Awfu al-mikyal wal-mizan﴾), that is, complete them both.

The purpose of stating this explicitly, although the required abstention from the earlier prohibition cannot be realized without completing the measure, is that completion becomes required secondarily (tab'an). This is agreed upon by those schools that hold that a prohibition of something is identical with a command to its opposite, or that it entails that command either by inclusion (tadammun) or by necessary implication (iltizam). The dispute concerns what the wording demands, not whether prohibition or obligation can be separated from the corresponding opposite. The verse does not limit itself to the one thing they were doing wrong, which is cutting short, in order to intensify the restraint. Then the command to the opposite intensifies the encouragement and signals that completion is required both in itself and secondarily, along with a signal that restraint is secondary, in reverse. Its restriction by His words, glorified is He, ﴿bil-qist﴾ (with justice), means with fairness, without excess or deficiency. Then there is the incorporation (idmaj) that the required thing in completion is justice. For this reason, excess may be forbidden, as in the case of ribawi goods (goods subject to the rules of usury). The words of al-Zamakhshari point to this, and their apparent meaning is to take the measure and the scale as referring to what is measured and weighed. Some scholars took both in the two places to refer to the two well-known verses, and they explained qist with what we mentioned. Then he said: excess in measuring and weighing, even though it is a recommended favor, is nevertheless forbidden in the instrument, like deficiency. So perhaps the one that is excessive is for use when taking, and the one that is deficient is for use when giving.

The purpose of the command to equalize and calibrate the two instruments after the prohibition of their shortfall is to intensify the urging toward fulfilling, preventing, and avoiding diminishing (al-bakhs), and to alert that mere restraint from shortfall and diminishment is not sufficient for them. Rather, they are obligated to repair what they have corrupted and made a standard for their injustice and a law for their aggression. This carries the wording to its immediate sense, for carrying it to the other meaning is a metaphor, as we indicated. The scholar al-Fadil al-Jalabi claimed that this command after the earlier prohibition is not a matter of repetition at all. He said: the prohibition was about the shortfall in the size of the measure and the weights of the scale, and the command to fulfill the measure and the scale its due is that there be no shortfall in measuring and weighing. This command comes after the measure and scale are made equal to what is known, so there is no repetition. How could it be repetition for emphasis and intensification? If it were, the conjunction "wa" would not have been placed there, since the two sentences would have full connection. End of quote.

It was objected that carrying these two expressions, which have repeated in one of the two places, to one of two distinct meanings is contrary to the apparent sense, and that repetition has benefits that make it stronger than establishing a new meaning (ta'sis), so one should not flee from it. As for the conjunction, the difference of purposes in those two conjoined clauses made them like two distinct things, so it is fitting for that reason. The rhetoricians (ahl al-ma'ani) have stated this regarding His words, glorified is He: ﴿yasumunakum su'a al-'adhab wa-yudhabbihuna abna'akum﴾ (they afflicted you with the worst torment, slaughtering your sons). End of quote.

There is room for reflection on the validity of the first objection, so reflect. His words, exalted is He: ﴿wa-la tabkhasu al-nasa ashya'ahum﴾ (and do not diminish people's things), may be a generalization after a specification, for it includes quality and inferiority, and also things that are not measured or weighed. So it is a conclusion and completion of what came before. Likewise His words, glorified is He: ﴿wa-la ta'thaw fi al-ardi mufsidin﴾ (and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief).

For al-'uthiy (corruption) encompasses the violation of rights and other things, because it is an expression for absolute corruption. Its verb follows the patterns of ramā, sa'ā, and radiya, and comes both as a weak-waw and weak-ya root. It may be that this is a prohibition of diminishing measured and weighed things after the prohibition of shortfall in the standard, and the command to fulfill it, that is: do not shortchange people through the shortfall of the measure and scale and their lack of balance, of the things they buy with them. The explicit statement of this prohibition after the two earlier commands were already understood in the prohibition itself is for the sake of its importance and to encourage fulfilling rights after warning and deterrence against diminishing them. Each of the two possibilities was held by some scholars, and this is based on the earlier disagreement about explaining what came before, as you know. It was also said: by al-bakhs is meant the unlawful levy (maks), like collecting tithes in the manner done today. Al-'uthiy is theft, highway robbery, and raiding. The phrase ﴿mufsidin﴾ (causing mischief) is a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿ta'thaw﴾. The benefit of this is to exclude what is intended for reform, as al-Khidr, peace be upon him, did in killing the boy and piercing the ship. So it is an establishing (ta'sis) circumstantial phrase. It was also said: the benefit is not the exclusion mentioned. The meaning is: do not commit corruption on the earth by diminishing rights, for example, corrupting the interests of your religion and the matter of your hereafter. The result of this, as it was said, is a reason for the prohibition, as if it were said: do not corrupt on the earth, for it corrupts your religion and your hereafter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 86:

﴿Baqiyyat Allah (what Allah leaves for you)﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: That is, what Allah, glorified is He, leaves for you of the lawful (ḥalal) after giving full measure is better for you than what you gather through defrauding, for that is "scattered dust" (habaʾ manthur). Rather, it is pure (maḥḍ), even if you suppose that it is good. ﴿If you are believers﴾, that is, on the condition that you believe, for with disbelief there is no good in anything at all. Or it means: if you are those who give credence to me in what I say to you. In another narration from the rabbi (al-Ḥabr, i.e. Ibn ʿAbbas), he interpreted the remainder (al-baqiyya) as provision (al-rizq).

Al-Rabiʿ said it is His command (wasiyyatuhu, ta'ala). Muqatil said: its reward in the Hereafter. Al-Farra' said: His watchfulness (muraqabatuhu, ʿazza wa-jall). Qatada said: His treasure (dhakhiratuhu). Al-Hasan said: His obligations (fara'iḍuhu, subhanahu).

Ibn ʿAṭiyya claimed that none of all this is conveyed by the wording of the verse, and that its meaning is only "preservation" (al-ibqa'), which is derived from what is narrated from Ibn Jurayj, who said: The meaning is that Allah's preservation of blessing for you is better for you than what results from loss through short-measuring (al-taṭfif).

In any case, the response of the conditional is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, according to the view of the majority of the Basran grammarians, and this is the sound position. Ismaʿil ibn Jaʿfar, from the people of Madina, read (baqiyyatu) with the yāʾ lightened (tashdid removed). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is a dialectal form. Abu Hayyan said: the rule for the adjectival form of an intransitive verb is that it be on the pattern fāʿil, as in shajiyat al-mar'a, fa-hiya shajiyya; when the yāʾ is doubled it takes the pattern faʿīl for emphasis. Al-Hasan read (taqiyyatu Allah) with a tāʾ, and the intended meaning is His piety and His watchfulness, which restrains from sins. ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾: I do not protect you from abominations, or I do not keep watch over your deeds and recompense you for them. I am only a counselor and a conveyor (of the message), and I have been excused, since I have warned and have spared no effort. Or it means: I am not a keeper over you of the blessings of Allah, ta'ala, if you do not abandon your evil conduct.

[Page 118]

The verse ﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped?"﴾ refers to the idols. They answered with this because of his peace be upon him command to them to worship God Almighty alone, which implied prohibiting them from worshipping idols. Their aim in this was to deny the revelation that commands him. But they went to such lengths in this that they denied that there could be any command from the intellect, and they claimed that this was a product of whispering and madness. God Almighty curse them: ﴿How are they turned away?﴾. On this basis they framed their question and phrased their words, and they said, by way of mockery: ﴿Does your prayer﴾, which is among the results of whispering and the acts of madmen, command you to abandon what our fathers continued to worship, generation after generation, of idols and images? They made him peace be upon him the one commanded, although what issued from him was in fact the command to worship God Almighty and other laws, because he peace be upon him did not command them of his own accord but by way of revelation. He would inform them that he was commanded to convey it to them. Their specifying the attribution of the command to prayer, out of all the other rulings of prophethood, was because he peace be upon him was much given to prayer and was known for it. Indeed, Ibn 'Asakir transmitted from al-Ahnaf that he peace be upon him was the most prayerful of the prophets, and when they saw him praying they would wink at one another and laugh, so that it became, among the rites of the religion, a source of laughter for them. It was also said that this was because he peace be upon him would pray and say to them: "Prayer commands what is right and forbids indecency and wrongdoing." This was related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father. Many scholars held the first view. This attribution is literal, not metaphorical. The most that can be said is that they intended the literal meaning in mockery. The choice of the imperfect verb (mudari', the present/future tense) is to indicate generality with respect to time. As for His, glorified be He, saying ﴿that we abandon﴾, it is on the assumption of a hidden phrase: "by the imposition that we abandon," so the noun "imposition" (taklif) was omitted, and the preposition entered upon (an) (that), and then it was omitted. Omitting it before (an) is regular, and the usage of discourse in such a case requires this. It was also said that the motive for this is that a person is not charged with the act of another, since it is not within his power at all. It was also said: there is no hidden phrase, and the meaning is: "Does your prayer command you with what is not within your capacity and responsibility, namely the actions of others?" Their aim in this was to disparage his judgement, far be it from him peace be upon him, and to mock him from that angle. It has been objected that this is precluded by the entry of the interrogative hamzah (the question particle) upon something other than the command, and that it requires that something should have issued from him peace be upon him during the course of the call which indicates this or gives this impression. But how is that possible? So reflect.

The majority of the Seven (al-sab'ah, the seven canonical readers) read ﴿أصَلَواتُكَ﴾ ("your prayers") in the plural. Reconciling the two readings is easy. As for His, exalted be He, saying ﴿or that we do with our wealth what we please﴾: they answered with this his command, peace be upon him, to give full measure and his prohibition of fraud and shortchanging. It is coordinated upon (ma) ("what"), and (aw) (or) has the sense of (wa) (and). That is: "and that we abandon our acting, what we please, with our wealth, through cheating and other things." Its coordination upon "that we abandon" is not valid, because the meaning becomes impossible: it would then be "your prayer commands you [to do] our acts with our wealth, what we please, of cheating and other things," and they are forbidden from that, not commanded to it. Taking (ma) as referring to what we have indicated is the apparent meaning. It was also said that they used to clip dirhams and dinars and pass them along with the sound coins by way of deception, so they were forbidden from that and said what they said. This was related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b. Some also included that act in the corruption on earth, so the prohibition of it would be a prohibition of it. There is no barrier to its inclusion under the generality of (ma). Al-Dahhak ibn Qays, Ibn Abi 'Ablah and Zayd ibn 'Ali read both verbs with the ta' (second person), as address. The coordination is then upon the object of ﴿commands you﴾, that is: "does your prayer command you to do with our wealth what you please," i.e. of giving full measure of the measure and the balance, as is apparent. It was also said that it is of the zakat (obligatory alms), for he peace be upon him would command them with it, as related from Sufyan al-Thawri. It was said: according to this, together with taking "prayer" in its common sense, the verse is evidence that his law, peace be upon him, included prayer and zakat. This is supported by what was related from al-Hasan that he said: "God Almighty did not send any prophet without imposing on him prayer and zakat." But you know that taking "what you please" to mean zakat is not definite; rather it goes against the apparent flow of the context. And taking "prayer" in that sense, although it is apparent, Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from al-A'mash its interpretation as recitation (of the Qur'an). It is also reported from others its interpretation as supplication, which is its linguistic meaning.

And it is related from Abu Muslim that its interpretation is religion, because it is among the most important of its matters. And on the assumption that the prayer in the other sense is meant, the verse does not indicate more than that he peace be upon him had a prayer, nor does it indicate that it is among the matters enjoined upon any of his community, so it is possible that this was one of his particular distinctions peace be upon him. What was related from al-Hasan is not explicit regarding the point, as is not hidden. It was also permitted that the coordination be upon the reading (ma) ("what"). It was objected that this requires that abandoning be taken in two different senses, and abandoning is not taken in a sense other than what is immediately understood from it.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and Talhah read with the nun (we) in the first and the ta' (you) in the second, with the coordination upon the object of ﴿commands you﴾. The meaning is clear from what has preceded. ﴿Indeed you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾: they described him peace be upon him with these two noble attributes by way of sarcastic metaphor (isti'arah tahakkumiyyah), so what is meant by them is the opposite of their meaning. This is what was related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, and Qatadah and al-Mubarrad held it.

It was also permitted that they described him with this on the basis of their claim, and the sentence is a reason for what preceded, namely the remoteness of what they mentioned, as if they said: "How can you impose on us what you impose, when you are, by your own claim, the forbearing, the rightly guided?" It was also said that it may be a reason still on its apparent sense, on the basis that he peace be upon him was described by them as forbearing and rightly guided, and that this, in their view, prevented what he peace be upon him had done from issuing from him. The first was preferred because it is most suited to what precedes it, since it is also sarcasm. The last was preferred because the statement would then be like what occurred in the story of Salih peace be upon him, from their saying to him: ﴿You were among us a hope before this﴾, and its being followed by something like that with which that was followed, according to what it contains.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 88 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He said, "O my people, tell me, if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord and He has given me from Himself a good provision"﴾, meaning a manifest proof, and my Lord, the Owner of my affairs, has given me from Him, from before Him, glorified is He, a good provision, which is prophethood and wisdom. What points to this is the context. The answer to this is in the manner of letting the reins loose (ird' al-'inan), and the phrased speech is as if he, peace be upon him, said: "You have spoken truly in what you said, that I have never ceased to be a guide to you and forbearing among you. But what I have brought is nothing other than guidance and counsel for you. Look with an eye of fairness, and you are sensible people. If I am upon a clear proof and certainty from my Lord, and I am truly a prophet, is it proper for me, while I am your guide and your adviser, that I should not command you to abandon the idols and to refrain from sins? Prophets are sent only for this." Then he, peace be upon him, emphasised the meaning of guidance and included forbearance (al-hilm) with it in what follows of his speech, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. This is how al-'Allama al-Tibi (al-Ṭībī) established it.

Shaykh al-Islam (Abu al-Su'ud) chose that it is not to be kept on its apparent meaning, because the context of mockery rejects it. He, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned that what is meant by "proof" and "good provision" is prophethood and wisdom, and that expressing them in this way is to draw attention to the fact that they, together with being a proof and a good provision, are how could they not be, since that is the basis of eternal life for him, peace be upon him, and for his community. He also said that this statement from him, peace be upon him, is a refutation of
[Page 119]
their shameful claim, which implies the assertion that his commands and prohibitions had no basis in any authority. Then he said: The answer to the conditional clause is omitted, and it is indicated by the sense of the speech, meaning: "Do you say...?" The meaning is that you have counted what came from me of commands and prohibitions as being of the kind that no sane person could utter, and you have made it one of the rulings of whisperings and madness, and you have mocked me and my actions, and you have said what you have said. So tell me: if I am from the side of my Lord, the Owner of my affairs, established in prophethood and wisdom, beyond which there is no further stage of perfection and no aim for an aspirer, and He has given me for that a good provision, do you say about my affair and the affair of my actions what you say, which has no good in it and no evil behind it?" He claimed that this is the answer which the context calls for and which the noble arrangement of the words supports.

Al-Qadi (al-Baydawi) interpreted "good provision" as the lawful wealth which God Most High gave him. The meaning of this being from Him, the Most High, is that it is from Him, glorified is He, and by His help, without toil in acquiring it. He estimated the answer to the conditional as: "Then can it be fitting, with this bounty which combines the spiritual and bodily happiness, that I should betray His revelation and oppose His command and prohibition?" He mentioned that this statement from him, peace be upon him, is an excuse for what they denied against him of changing the familiar and forbidding the religion of the fathers. Some others estimated what al-'Allama al-Tibi estimated.

Shaykh al-Islam claimed that those two estimations are far from what the context calls for, and that they fit only if their words are taken literally and "prayer" is taken to mean religion, as reported from Abu Muslim and 'Ata', and in that case the meaning of "good provision" would be what God Most High gave him of lawful things only, as reported from al-Dahhak. The meaning then would be: "Tell me, if I am a prophet from God Most High and He has given me lawful wealth by which I am sufficient from the worlds, is it proper that I should oppose His command or agree with you in what you do and what you leave undone?" End of quotation.

I say: It is not hidden that what suits the situation is to take "good provision" as what God Most High has given of lawful things free from fraud and diminishing (of measure and weight). The estimation of the answer to the conditional, like what al-Qadi estimated, has nothing in the speech that rejects it, and it does not depend on taking the speech literally and "prayer" as religion. Rather, that estimation is possible even if the speech is in the manner of derision and "prayer" is in its obvious meaning, namely that they, may God fight them, when they said, in the shades of error, and said what they said about their prophet and what proceeded from him of actions, had no aim except to abandon the call and to leave him and what they do. He, peace be upon him, did not explicitly address their saying, which implied that he was accused, and God forbid, of whisperings, madness, foolishness and misguidance, as a notice that this is not deserving of an answer because its falsehood is manifest. He addressed their aim in what they meant by that speech, in a way that cuts off their hopes from the beginning, with an indication toward refuting what their shameful claim contained. So it is as if he, peace be upon him, said to them: "O my people, you have dared to this shameful statement and included in it what is manifestly false, for the aim that I would leave you to yourselves in worshipping idols and in diminishing the measure and the balance. So tell me: if I am a prophet from God Most High, and I am exempt, by the lawful wealth He gave me, from you and from others, is it proper that I should oppose His revelation and agree with your desires? That will not be from me at all. Therefore there is no benefit for you in this shameful speech." It may also be said that in this answer there is an indication toward describing them with something like what they described him with. It is as if he said: "Your demand of me that I abandon the call and agree with your whims, while I am commanded to call you and am free of you, is something that does not proceed from a sane person and is not committed except by a foolish, misguided one." It seems that mentioning the provision together with being upon a clear proof is to indicate the existence of the cause and the removal of what might be thought to be an obstacle. The beauty of bringing the answer in this way is not hidden, so reflect.

What remains is that the grammarians, as Abu Hayyan said about a speech like this, namely "Tell me if I am..." etc., have mentioned that the interrogative clause is estimated to be in the place of the second object of "ara'aytum" (tell me), which includes the meaning of "akhbirūnī" (inform me), which takes two objects. The more common case for the second is that it is an interrogative clause, and the answer to the conditional is what the preceding clause together with its complement indicates. The estimate is: "If I am upon a clear proof from my Lord, then tell me: is it proper for me that..." etc. So understand this and do not be heedless.

As for His words, what I intend by forbidding you from what I forbid you of defrauding and diminishing: ﴿I do not wish to oppose you to what I forbid you from﴾, meaning I intend it after you have turned away from it, and so I would be independent in it without you. This is like the situation of some people in forbidding some matters. It is said: "Fulan opposed me to such-and-such" when he intends it while you are turning away from it, and "he opposed me from it" when he turns away from it while you are intending it.

Al-Zamakhshari (this is quoted) said in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit): The apparent reading, as they mentioned, is that ﴿an ukhalifakum﴾ (that I oppose you) is in the place of the object of "urid" (I wish), meaning: "I do not wish to oppose you," and "khalafa" takes the meaning of "khalafa" (to succeed, to be left behind) like "jawaza" and "jaza" (to pass beyond), and the meaning would be: "I do not wish to be a successor from among you." And "ila" (to) is connected to "ukhalifa" or to something omitted, meaning "inclining toward what I forbid you from." It was said: in the speech there is an omitted verb coordinated with the mentioned one, meaning "and I incline toward..." etc. It is also permissible to keep "ukhalifu" on its apparent meaning of opposing, and "an" with what follows is in the place of the object of "urid," and one estimates "mā'ilan ilā" (inclining to) as previously mentioned. Or "an" with what follows is in the place of the object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and "ila ma" is connected to "urid," meaning: "I do not intend, for the sake of opposing you, toward what I forbid you from." Al-Zajjaj said regarding this meaning: "I do not intend, by opposing you, to commit what I forbid you from." ﴿In I do not wish﴾, meaning I do not wish by what I say to you ﴿except reform﴾, meaning except that I reform you by advice and admonition as much as I am able, meaning for the duration of my ability to do so and my capacity for it, I spare no effort in it. So "ma" is a temporal verbal particle (masdariyyah zarfiyyah).

It was also permitted that "ma" be a relative pronoun (mawsulah) in apposition to "al-islah," meaning the measure which I am able to do, or "except the reform of what I am able to reform." It is either a partial apposition (badal ba'd) or a whole apposition (badal kull), because what is understood from "reform" is what one is capable of. It was said it is an apposition of inclusion (badal ishtimal), and according to this and the first, a pronoun is estimated, meaning "from it," because in such a case it is necessary. It was also permitted that it be the object of the mentioned verbal noun, like the poet's saying:

Weak in striking his enemies, he appears to flee, and delays the appointed time.

Meaning: "I do not wish except that I reform what I am able to reform of your corruption." The more eloquent and manifest is what we have mentioned before, because in the possibility of apposition there is an implied element and the loss of emphasis, and in the last possibility there is the operation of a definite verbal noun on its object, which is not permitted according to the Kufans and is rare according to the Basrans, along with the loss of that emphasis and the addition of an implied object of "istata'tu" (I was able). ﴿And my success is not except through God﴾, meaning my being granted success in achieving what I aim for of reforming you is not except through God, meaning by His support, glorified is He, and His help.

Some have chosen that what is meant is: "And my success is only for hitting the truth and the right in everything I do and leave undone, except by His guidance and help, Most High." The apparent meaning is that what is meant is "and every single instance of my success" (the individual cases of my success), for what they stated, that a verbal noun in the genitive form (mudaf) is among the forms of generality, and to this is traced what was said: "the meaning is: what is the kind of my success?" because the restriction of a kind requires the restriction of its instances. But on the first, it is by way of the implicit meaning (mafhum), and on the second, by way of the explicit meaning (manṭūq). The estimation of the genitive noun after the preposition "bi" (by) is among what many have committed to, and in it, according to what has been said, is the removal of the problem that the doer of success is God Most High, and the Arabic scholars dislike attributing an action to its doer with "bi," because it enters upon an instrument. So "darabtu bi-Zaydin" (I struck with Zayd) is not good, but one says "min Zayd" (from Zayd). So the eloquent usage according to this is: "And my success is only from God."

The way of removing it by that estimation is clear, because the entering of the preposition is then not upon the doer.

It was also permitted that this estimation be for the reason that success, which is the agent's action conforming to what God Most High loves and is pleased with, can only occur by God Most High's guidance, and mere guidance is of no use without help from Him, glorified is His majesty. ﴿Upon Him I rely﴾, meaning in that or in all my affairs, not upon anyone else, for He, glorified is He, is the Capable, who has full power over everything, and other than Him, glorified is He, is powerless in itself, indeed nonexistent and fallen from the rank of consideration, as the Book indicated and as the people of insight and intellects witnessed. ﴿And to Him I turn﴾, meaning I return to Him in what I am engaged in, or I turn to Him in an evil that has spread through the gatherings of my affairs, and not to other than Him. The clause is coordinated with what precedes it. The choice of the present tense form in it over the past is most suitable for establishment and certainty, as in reliance (tawakkul), to bring the image to mind and to indicate continuity. The beauty of his answer, peace be upon him, is not hidden, for something like it hardly exists in the speech of any orator, unless he were a prophet.

In Anwar al-Tanzil (*Lights of Revelation*, al-Baydawi's commentary), regarding his three replies, peace be upon him: "O my people, tell me..." etc. "And I do not wish to oppose you..." etc. "And I only desire..." etc. In this sequence there is an indication that the rational person must observe, in everything he does and abstains from, three rights, the most important and highest of which is the right of God Most High. The first reply includes a statement of God's right, namely giving thanks for His blessings and striving in His service. The second is the right of the self, since the second reply includes a statement of the self's right to be restrained from what others ought to refrain from. The third is the right of people, since the third reply includes an indication that the right of others is to be reformed and guided. He did not join his saying "If I only desire..." etc. to what precedes it because it is emphatic and confirmatory of it, for if he had desired to monopolize what he was forbidden from, he would not have been desiring reform. This does not preclude its including another reply. It seems that his saying "﴿And my success is only through God﴾" etc. is a removal of what might give the impression that attributing the capacity to himself, through his will, implies his independent control over that. A parallel to this is "﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾," and with what follows it there is an indication of pure monotheism (tawhid).

Others have said that his speech, peace be upon him, included observing gentleness in returning to the matter, gentleness in drawing them down, preserving good conduct in discourse and dialogue, paving the way for the foundations of truth by seeking success from God's side, seeking help from Him, may He be exalted, in their affairs, cutting off the greed of the disbelievers, showing indifference to them, and not caring about their hostility. It has been said: there is also in it a threat to them by returning to God Most High for recompense, from His saying "﴿And to Him I turn in repentance﴾," because returning to Him, glorified is He, is used as an allusion to recompense. Although this is specific to Him here, due to the requirement of the context, there is no difference in this between Him and others. But in it, along with the obscurity of the aspect of the indication, is that repentance (inabah) is only the voluntary return to Him, glorified is He, in action, not the compelled return for recompense and what encompasses it. And it may be said: in his saying "(In Him I have put my trust)" there is also an indication of threatening them, because He, mighty and majestic, is the Sufficient and the Helper for whoever relies on Him. But it is not necessary that this be a threat of recompense on the Day of Resurrection. And he says

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 89:

﴿Let not my dissension (shiqaq) bring upon you﴾ — that is, let not my opposition (mu'adah) to you earn for you. Its origin is that one of two opponents is on one side and edge (fi 'udwatin wa shiqq), and the other is on another. This has been related from al-Suddi and from al-Hasan, who read "dirari" (my harm to you), and from some who read "firaqi" (my separation from you); all of these are close in meaning. The verb is "yajrimannakum" (bring upon you), its subject is the phrase, and the kaf is its first object. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿that it befall you﴾ is its second object. The verb jaruma (to earn, to bring about) has come with two objects just as it has come with one, and it is like kasaba (to earn) in this. From the first usage is his saying:

"Indeed I struck Abu 'Uyayna with a blow, which Fazara after it brought upon itself, that they should be angry."

The annexation of shiqaq to the first-person pronoun (ya' al-mutakallim) is an annexation of the verbal noun to its object, meaning: let not your opposition to me bring upon you that it befall you

[page 122]

like what befell the people of Noah from the drowning, or the people of Hud from the wind, or the people of Salih from the quake and the cry. The prohibition directed at the dissension is a metaphor or a metonymy for the prohibition of them, and it is more eloquent than directing the prohibition at them, because when a thing that does not understand is forbidden, the prohibition of those who oppose is understood by way of priority. Ibn Wththab and al-A'mash read "yujrimannakum" with a damma on the ya', and it is also related from Ibn Kathir; in that case it is from ajramtuhu dhanban, when you make him one who earns it, that is, a doer of it. The hamza is for transitivity, from jarama, which is transitive to one object. Its counterpart in this transitivity is kasaba al-mal, which is said as aksabahu al-mal. The two readings are the same in meaning, except that the well-known reading follows what is most common in the speech of the eloquent Arabs whose Arabic is trusted. Mujahid, al-Jahdari and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "mithla" with a fatha, and this is related from Nafi'; a group construed it as also the subject, but built on fatha because it is annexed to a non-declinable word. It has been permitted for it, and likewise for ghayra, with ma, and with the light and heavy an, that this is like the annexed adverbs to an indeclinable word. On this basis is his saying:

"Nothing prevented them from drinking from it except that a dove spoke in the branches of the thorny trees."

Some held that it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, and the fatha is the i'rab (grammatical case marking), meaning: a befalling like the befalling of the people of Noah. The subject of yusibukum is a hidden pronoun referring to the punishment understood from the context, and there is strain in this. ﴿And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾ in time, as related from Qatada, or in place, as related from others. His meaning, upon him be peace, is that if you do not take warning from those before you because of the long time or the distance of place, then take warning from these, for they are within sight and hearing of you. It seems he changed the manner of warning with them and suffice with mention of their nearness, indicating that this is sufficient without mention of what befell them, because of the fame of it being strung in the string of what has been mentioned of the causes of the recorded nations. It is also permitted that by distance be meant distance in meaning, that is, they are not far from you in disbelief and wrongdoing, so beware lest there descend upon you what descended upon them of punishment. Some later scholars took this meaning and said: "If you are the people of Lot themselves, then the people of Lot are not far from you." The singular "ba'id" and its masculine form with the subject being "qawm," which is a collective noun and grammatically feminine, as al-Zamakhshari stated explicitly and supported by its diminutive "qawaymah," would require that one say "ba'idah" to agree with the wording, and "ba'da'" to agree with the meaning, because the intended sense is: "and their destruction is not something far," or "they are not in a far time or a far place." It is also permitted that this is because "ba'id," being on the pattern of verbal nouns like "nahiq" and "sahil," is used equally for masculine and feminine.

In al-Kashf, from al-Jawhari, that "qawm" may be masculine or feminine, because collective nouns that have no singular of their own in form, when they refer to human beings, may be masculine or feminine, like raht, nafar and qawm. When diminutized, the ta' is not added to them, and one says quwaym, ruhayt and nufayr. The ta' enters what refers to non-human beings, like al-ibil (camels) and al-ghanam (sheep), because the feminine is obligatory. The distance between this and what was transmitted from al-Zamakhshari is far, and according to this there is no need for interpretation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 90:

Furthermore, when he (peace be upon him) had warned them of the evil consequence of their deeds, he followed this up, hoping to turn them away from the misguidance they were in, by urging them to seek forgiveness and repent. So he said: ﴿And seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance﴾. The explanation of the like of this has already passed. ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Merciful﴾, of great mercy, so He shows mercy to whoever asks Him for forgiveness. ﴿Loving﴾ (wadud), i.e., abundant in affection and love, so He loves whoever turns back to Him in repentance and returns to Him. The well-known view is to take wadud as a metaphor (majaz) based on its end result (ghayah), i.e., one who is exceedingly active in doing what a loving person does for the one he loves, namely kindness and benevolence.
Page 123
It is also permissible for it to be a metonymy (kinayah) according to those who do not require that the literal meaning be possible. The reason for resorting to metaphor or metonymy, as has been said, is that love (mawaddah) in the sense of an inclination of the heart is something that cannot rightly be attributed to Him, the Exalted. The Salafi scholar says: "Mawaddah in us is the inclination mentioned, and in Him, glory be to Him, there is beyond that something befitting the majesty of His essence, exalted is His majesty." It has also been said: the meaning of wadud is one who makes Himself beloved to His servants by bestowing favour upon them, and it has been said: the one beloved by the believers. Interpreting it here in the sense already mentioned is preferable. The clause is in the position of giving the reason for the preceding command. Most scholars did not take into account what we have pointed to, such as the distribution (of meanings), but said: "great in mercy towards those who repent," intensive in gentleness and kindness towards them, and this is acceptable.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 91:

﴿They said: "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say."﴾ That is, we do not comprehend it. It is as if they regarded his speech, which contains various kinds of wisdom and admonitions and types of knowledge and insights, as nonsense and babbling whose meaning cannot be understood and whose purport cannot be grasped, since their stratagems had run out and their excuses had failed them, and they found no way to engage him in discussion (peace be upon him). It was said: they said this to belittle him (peace be upon him), as a man says to one he does not care about: "I do not know what you are saying." This does not differ much from the first explanation. It is also possible that this was because they did not pay attention to listening to his speech (peace be upon him), due to their extreme aversion to him, or due to their dullness and the deficiency of their intellects. It was said: their saying "much" was a way of escaping by obstinacy. It cannot be meant as "all," even though it is used that way in the language, because "of what you say" rules that out. Likewise, many of them refuse to take their statement here as a metonymy (kinaya) for non-acceptance. Some claimed that they did not understand much of what he said because he (peace be upon him) had a lisp (alsa'). I do not think there is a sound report that makes this explicit, and the apparent meaning of what has come describing him (peace be upon him) as "the orator of the prophets" rejects this. Perhaps the use of the present tense indicates continuity. ﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾, that is, among us, ﴿weak﴾, having no strength, and no power to harm, benefit, inflict or repel anything.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Sufyan al-Thawri and Abu Salih that "weak" was interpreted as "blind," which is the dialect of the people of Yemen. They say of a blind man "darir," and this is a metonymy (kinaya), as some have stated. Calling him "sighted" (basir), as is common, is a metaphor (isti'ara) with an allusion (talmih). This interpretation has been weakened on the grounds that the restriction by their saying "among us" would be pointless, because whoever is blind is blind among them and among others, and it would also require an implied meaning, namely weakness among those who support him and those who oppose him. Its strain is not hidden. For this reason al-Imam (al-Razi) said: some of our companions permitted blindness for the prophets (peace be upon them), but it is not fitting to read it that way here. You know that the view approved by the people of the Sunna is that there is no blind man among the prophets (peace be upon them). What Allah the Exalted related about Ya'qub (peace be upon him) was a temporary condition that passed.

As for the reports transmitted from those we mentioned concerning Shu'ayb (peace be upon him), we have not found any of them authenticated, except what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). al-Hakim authenticated some of its chains, but al-Hakim's authentication is, like Ibn al-Jawzi's weakening, not relied upon. Perhaps something similar may be said of it as was said about Ya'qub (peace be upon him). al-Wahidi and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Shaddad ibn Aws, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) wept out of love for Allah, the Exalted, until he went blind. Then Allah, the Exalted, returned his sight to him and revealed to him: 'O Shu'ayb, what is this weeping? Is it longing for Paradise or fear of the Fire?' He said: 'No, but I have believed in Your love in my heart, so when I look at You I do not mind what You do with me.' Allah, the Exalted, revealed to him: 'O Shu'ayb, if that is true, then congratulations on meeting Me. O Shu'ayb, for this I made Musa ibn 'Imran, My interlocutor, your servant.'"

Some of the Mu'tazila held that it is not permissible for a blind man to be a prophet, because blindness is a singular attribute, since one is not protected from impurities with it, and because it impairs judgeship and testimony, so that impairing his station of prophethood is more fitting. It is answered that we do not accept that one is not protected from impurities with it, for many of the blind whom we see are more careful about them than others. And that a judge and a witness need to distinguish between the claimant and the defendant, whereas a prophet does not need to distinguish those whom he calls, and moreover he is infallible, so he does not err as others do. Thus it has been said, so let it be considered.

﴿And were it not for your clan﴾, that is, your group. al-Raghib said: they are fewer than ten. al-Zamakhshari said: from three to ten. It was said: up to seven. It was said: rather, up to forty. What is said of them, like "'usba" and "nafar," applies only to men. Similarly "rahit," whose plural is "arhut," and the plural of the plural is "arahit." Its root, as reported from al-Rummani, is tightening. From it comes "rahid," for the strength of eating, and "rahita'," for the burrow of the jerboa, because it secures itself with it and hides its young in it.
