The apparent meaning is that they meant: were it not for consideration of the side of your clan, ﴿we would have stoned you﴾, that is, we would have killed you by pelting stones. This is what is reported from Ibn Zayd. It was said that this is a metonymy for the harm of killing, as if they said: we would kill you in the most painful way. al-Tabari said: they meant "we would have cursed you," as in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿I will surely stone you, so leave me alone for a long time﴾. It was also said: "we would have expelled you and driven you from our land." They did not allow that the meaning be: were it not for the resistance and defence of your clan, because the resistance of a clan, which is a small number, against thousands in formation is hardly conceivable. The meaning of ﴿and you are not dear to us﴾ is: you are not honoured and respected among us so that we would refrain from stoning you. We refrain from you only out of regard for the sanctity of your clan, who remained upon our religion and did not choose you over us. The first preposition phrase is connected to "dear" (ʿazīz), and it is permissible because the governed element is an adverbial phrase (zarf), and the "ba'" is superfluous. You may also make it connected to an omitted element that the apparent word explains, and that is the predicate of "you" (anta). al-Sakkaki stated in al-Miftah that by placing this pronoun, which is a semantic subject, first, even though the predicate is not a verb but a descriptive adjective (sifa mushabbaha), and by following it with the negation, he intended restriction and exclusivity, meaning that the lack of dearness is confined to you and does not extend beyond you to your clan. He did not mean negating exclusivity in the sense of "you are not alone in dearness." This is clear, as stated by the second 'Allama. al-Sayyid al-Sanad said: he intended by it the negation of dearness from Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) and its affirmation for his clan, so it would be a restriction of dearness to them, and this would entail restricting its absence to him. However, what is more immediate, as sound taste witnesses, is the intention of the first. Al-Sakkaki based the restriction on the words of the one who replied to this speech, as related by His saying, glorified be His majesty:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 92:

﴿He said: "O my people, is my clan more honored by you than God?"﴾ That is, than the Prophet of God, as he (may God have mercy on him) said. The basis of the inference, as the Allamah (al-Allamah) and others have stated, is this: had their intention not been to restrict the negation of honor to him, but merely to inform him that he was not honored among them, this reply would not have been appropriate or in accord with their statement, since negating honor from him does not indicate that honor is affirmed for others. Rather, what indicates that is the restriction (ikhtisas) of the negation of honor to him.

The author of al-Idah (Sahib al-Idah) objected that this is of the type "I am a knower" (ana 'arif), which, by agreement, does not convey restriction. Rather, restriction is conveyed by placing the subject before the verb, as in "I knew" (ana 'arafت) [in the sense of "it was I who knew"]. That derivative nouns (mushtaqqat) are close to verbs in conveying affirmation does not require that they be like verbs in conveying restriction. Moreover, relying on the reply is weak, because it may be a response to their statement: "Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you" (﴿ولَوْلا رَهْطُكَ لَرَجَمْناكَ﴾). That statement indicates that his clan are the honored ones, since the refraining from stoning him was due to them and not to him. And it is known from the circumstances and context that this was due to their honor, not their fear.

Al-Sayyid al-Sanad (al-Sayyid al-Sanad) responded that the author of al-Kashshaf (Sahib al-Kashshaf) explicitly stated restriction in His saying, ﴿No! It is merely a word he speaks﴾. So how can it be said that the pattern "ana 'arif" does not convey restriction by agreement? And making it a reply to "…you are not mighty over us" is the clearest reading, provided that the tanwin (nunation) in "'azīz" is taken as the tanwin of magnification (li'l-ta'zim), which indicates that the basic honor belongs to him, peace be upon him. This is consistent with their statement, "Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you," which indicates that honor is shared, so it does not fit with "Is my clan more honored by you…?"

He then said: If it is objected that the condition of restriction according to al-Sakkaki (al-Sakkaki) is that the fronted element, if postponed, would be a semantic agent (fa'il ma'nawi), and this cannot be imagined in our case, we reply: after the negation, the attribute together with its agent forms an independent sentence. Thus it is permissible to say, "You are not mighty" (ma 'azīzun anta), with "anta" being an emphasis for the concealed pronoun; then it is fronted, and the bā' is added to "'azīz" after "anta" has been fronted and made a subject. Likewise is His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿I am not one to drive away those who believe﴾ and ﴿you are not a guardian over them﴾, where the negative particle precedes and the predicate is an attribute. The author of al-Kashshaf and others have explicitly stated that fronting in all of these conveys restriction. As for the affirmative form, such as "ana 'arif," this does not apply to it, so according to him it does not convey restriction, although according to those who do not require this condition, it does.

The author of al-Kashf (Sahib al-Kashf) responded to what the author of al-Idah said, after quoting its summary: that what has a predicate that is a descriptive attribute (wasfan) resembles, in conveying affirmation, what has a predicate that is a verb, as the objector granted; and it resembles it in conveying restriction by that very same proof. He also said that their statement, ﴿Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you﴾, is sufficient evidence that the proper meaning of the speech is that restriction is conveyed, not the basic honor. So his understanding of it from that does not contradict its being a reply to this statement; rather, it confirms it. Al-Zamakhshari (al-Zamakhshari) explicitly stated that this kind of structure conveys both possibilities in ﴿It is merely a word he speaks﴾. Al-Allamah al-Tibi (al-Tibi) said: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you﴾, and His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿you are not mighty over us﴾, are of the type of "reversal and inversion" (al-tard wa'l-'aks), out of their obstinacy. Therefore, each of the two expressions must convey both the explicit (manṭūq) and implicit (mafhūm) meanings. End of quote.

From all that has been mentioned, the weakness of the objection of the author of al-Idah becomes clear. It is strange that the Allamah said it is a strong objection. Al-Sakkaki, by supplying an omitted noun (taqdir al-mudaf), pointed to resolving the difficulty: their statement was made concerning Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, and his clan, and that they were the honored ones, not him, without any indication that they were more honored than God, Exalted is He.

It was also answered that their contempt for the Prophet of God, Exalted is He, is contempt for Him, Glorified is He. So when their clan was more honored to them than He, their clan was more honored to them than God, Exalted is He. Or it means: "Is my clan more honored by you than God, Exalted is He, to the extent that your refraining from stoning me was due to my affiliation with them and that they are my clan, not due to my affiliation with God, Exalted is He, and that I am His messenger?"

As for what al-Sayyid, may God sanctify his secret, mentioned regarding making the tanwin in "'azīz" a tanwin of magnification, and that in that case the speech indicates the affirmation of basic honor for him, peace be upon him, so that "Is my clan more honored…" fits it: this is correct in itself. However, that is very far from the condition of the people. For the apparent meaning is that they only intended to negate honor from him, peace be upon him, absolutely, and to affirm it for his clan, not to negate great honor from him and affirm it for them, so that the speech would indicate that both share basic honor, with an increase in it for them. This is because honor, even if it is not great, prevents being stoned, which is among the worst kinds of killing. I do not think denying this is anything but obstinacy. Perhaps for this reason our master Abu al-Su'ud (may God have mercy on him) did not consider making the tanwin one of magnification, so that sharing could be realized and the point of denying superior honor would become clear. He therefore needed to uncover this with the absence of sharing, and said:

"He, peace be upon him, denied them the superior honor of his clan over Him, Exalted is He, even though what they affirmed was only the absolute honor of his clan, not their being more honored than Him, Mighty and Majestic, together with sharing in basic honor. This was to double the rebuke and repeat the reproach: first, he denied them their preference of the clan's side over the side of God, Exalted is He; and second, he denied honor altogether. The meaning is: 'Is my clan more honored by you than God?' For this is something that hardly holds true, while you have not assigned to Him, Exalted is He, any share of honor at all, and you have taken Him [﴿وراءَكم ظِهْرِيًّا﴾ — cast behind your backs] as something neglected, because you do not regard One who neither responds nor acts except by His command…" [﴿cast behind your backs﴾: something thrown away, forgotten]. End of quote.

I say: al-Radi (al-Radi) mentioned that the noun governed by min of comparison (min al-tafdiliyyah) is never free of sharing, the one preferred sharing in meaning, either in reality, as in "Zayd is better than 'Amr," or by supposition, as in the saying of Ali, may God honor his face: "To fast one day of Sha'ban is dearer to me than to break one day of Ramadan." That is because breaking the fast on the doubtful day, which might be from Ramadan, is beloved to the opponent. So Ali, may God honor his face, supposed it to be beloved to himself also, and then preferred the day of Sha'ban over it. It is as if he said: "Grant that it is beloved to me too; fasting one day of Sha'ban is not more beloved than it." End of quote. What is in the verse can be interpreted in the manner of the latter, so that his denial of their superior honor of his clan over Him, Exalted is He, would be on the supposition that He, Mighty and Majestic, is also honored among them. From this, his denial of what they hold is understood a fortiori. This is probably the reason for choosing this style of denial. Its occurrence in the reply does not fit this, even if it is said that a noun governed by min can be free of sharing with the preferred and that it intends mere emphasis from the comparative form with it, based on this being rare, as al-Jalal al-Suyuti said in Hama'i' al-Hawami', with examples such as: "Honey is sweeter than vinegar" and "Summer is hotter than winter." Here he relied on the evidence of the preceding and following context, so the matter is clear.

He considered it good that His saying, ﴿and you have taken Him…﴾ and so on, be an interjected clause (i'tiraḍ), and its benefit is to emphasize their contempt for God, Exalted is He, by showing that they are a people whose custom is not to heed God, Exalted is He, and to treat Him as something cast aside. Some permitted that it be a conjunction with what precedes, in the sense: "Have you preferred my clan over God, Glorified is He, and held Him in contempt, and forgotten Him, and not feared His recompense, Mighty and Majestic?" Many said: it may be that the purpose of his, peace be upon him, saying "Is my clan…" etc. is to refute and reject his people. When they claimed that they did not refrain from stoning him, peace be upon him, because of his honor but out of regard for his clan's side, he answered them: "You have not estimated God, Exalted is He, with His due measure, and you have not respected His mighty side; so how will you respect my weak clan?" In any case, the pronoun in "you have taken Him" refers to God, Exalted is He, and this is what the majority of commentators held. It was narrated from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and others.

The word "ẓihrīyan" is derived from "ẓahr" (back), and its original sense is "that which is thrown behind the back." The kasra is one of the changes in forming the relative adjective, as they said regarding the relative of "amsi" (yesterday): "amsī" with a kasra, and of "al-dahr" (time): "duhrī" with a damma. Then they extended its use to mean "the forgotten and abandoned." They mentioned that the speech may contain an explicit metaphor (isti'arah taṣrīḥiyyah) or an allegorical metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah).

Some claimed that the pronoun refers to God, Exalted is He, and "ẓihrīyy" means "helper" and "that by which one is strengthened," and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl). The meaning is: "Have you preferred the clan over God, Exalted is He, not regarding His right, Glorified is He, while you take Him as the support of your backs and the pillar of your hopes?" Ibn 'Atiyyah (Ibn 'Atiyya) reported this meaning from a group. It was also said: "ẓihrīyy" means "forgotten," and the pronoun refers to the Sharia that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, brought, even though it was not explicitly mentioned. It was narrated from Mujahid. Or it refers to the command of God. It was reported from al-Zajjaj. It was also said: "ẓihrīyy" means "helper," and the pronoun refers to God, Exalted is He, and there is an omitted noun in the speech, that is, "disobedience to Him," and the meaning, as established by Abu Hayyan, is: "you have taken His disobedience as a helper and a means for repelling me." It was also said: there is no omission, and the pronoun refers to disobedience, which is what al-Mubarrad's statement implies. There is no concealing the departure from the apparent meaning without benefit in these opinions. Among those that fall into this category is interpreting "'azīz" as "king," on the claim that they used to call the king "'azīz." But whoever has even a little taste would hardly accept the correctness of that, so be discerning. The accusative "ẓihrīyyan" is the second object of "ittakhadhtumūhu" (you have taken Him), with the hā' as its first object, and "warā'akum" (behind you) is an adverbial complement to it, or a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) of "ẓihrīyyan."

﴿Indeed my Lord encompasses what you do.﴾

This is a severe threat to those disbelieving, sinful wrongdoers. That is, He, Glorified is He, has encompassed in knowledge your evil deeds, among which is your regard for the clan's side without regard for His side, Majestic is His majesty, so that He will recompense you for that. And likewise His saying:

Page 127

*[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 11, verse 93]*

﴿And O my people, act according to your position﴾: that is, to the utmost of your capacity in your affairs, your highest effort and your ability. It is a verbal noun (masdar) of *makkana*. It is said, "*makkana makanatan*" when one becomes firmly established, and it is more emphatic. On this reading the *mim* is original (*asliyyah*). In *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*, Abu Hayyan's Qur'an commentary) it is said that *al-makan* and *al-makanah* are of the form *maf'al* and *maf'alah*, from *al-kawn* (being), and the *mim* is then augmenting (*za'idah*). Ibn Zayd explained *al-makanah* as *al-hal* (condition, state). It is said, "*ala makanatika ya fulan*" (stay in your position, O so-and-so) when you order someone to remain firmly in his state, as if you said: "Remain in your state in which you are, do not deviate." This is a metaphor (*isti'arah*) of the essence for the meaning (*isti'arat al-'ayn lil-ma'na*), as several scholars have stated. The essential meaning here is: remain in what you are upon of disbelief, opposition to me, and all else that contains no good.

Abu Bakr read *makanatikum* in the plural (*makanatikum*). This is in view of the plurality of the addressees, just as the singular is in view of the category (*jins*). As for the prepositional phrase (*al-jar wal-majrur*), as some have said: it may be connected to what is "*indahu*" (with him) through implicit meaning of the verb (*tadmin*), in the sense of building or similar, as you say: "*'amila 'ala al-jiddi*" (he worked at seriousness) and "*'ala al-quwwah*" (at strength) and the like. It may also be in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: act while remaining firm and fixed upon your position.

﴿Indeed I am acting﴾ upon my position, according to what Allah the Exalted supports me with and grants me success in, with various kinds of support and success. It seems that "*'ala makanati*" (upon my position) was omitted for brevity and because of the greater intimidation it carries. His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿You will come to know﴾ is a resumed sentence (*isti'naf*) which came as an answer to an implied question arising from his peace be upon him threat to them with the words "act," etc. It is as if one of them asked: "What will happen after that?" and it was said: "You will come to know." For this reason the *fa'* (the particle of consequence) was dropped. It was mentioned in the verse of al-An'am for the explicit statement that the threat arises from and branches off from their persistence in what they are upon and their firm establishment in it. What is here is more forceful in intimidation, to signal that this is something to be asked about and to be attended to. The implied question indicates what the *fa'* indicated, together with the increase of meaning through the reduction of wording. It seems that the motive for using the more forceful expression here, rather than what preceded, is that the people, may Allah fight them, went to extremes in belittling him peace be upon him and reached the limit in that. So it was fitting that he exaggerate for them in threat and reach the limit in it, even though they were, in their lack of benefit, like cattle and what is similar to them.

Some eminent scholars said: The choice of one of the two ways there and the other here, although such a thing is not asked about, because it is circular (*dawri*), since the first mention requires explicitness, so the second suits the opposite of that. End of quote. This is inferior to what we have said.

The *man* (who) in His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿who will be given a punishment that will disgrace him﴾ is said to be a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*), the object of the knowing, and it has the meaning of recognizing. The clause "*ya'tihi al-'adhab*" (the punishment comes to him) is the relative clause (*silah*), and the clause "*yukhzihi*" (disgraces him) is an attribute of "*'adhab*" (punishment). He described it with disgrace as an allusion to what they threatened him with, namely stoning, for it, while being a punishment, has clear disgrace in it. His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿and who is a liar﴾ is a conjunction upon "*man ya'tihi*" (who comes to him), and "*man*" is also a relative pronoun. He allowed that "*man*" in both places be interrogative, and the knowing be in its proper sense, and the interrogative would then suspend it from operating.

Abu Hayyan preferred the relative reading. This conjunction is not the conjunction of a counterpart upon its counterpart, as in "*sa-ya'lamu al-sadiqu wal-kadhib*" (the truthful and the liar will come to know), since the intent is not to mention the two groups. Rather, the intent is to respond to the people concerning their determination to punish him by their saying: "We will surely stone you," and their insistence on denying him by their saying: "Does your prayer command you ...?" (Hud 87), and so on. It is as if it was said: "It will become clear to you who is punished, you or we, and who is the liar in his claim, I or you." This also includes the state of both groups.

In *al-Irshad* (*Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*, Abu al-Su'ud's commentary) it is stated that in it there is an allusion to their lying in their claim of strength and power to stone him peace be upon him, and in ascribing to him weakness and humiliation, and in their claim of sparing him out of consideration for the clan. Al-Zamakhshari said: The analogy would have been "*wa-man huwa sadiq*" (and who is truthful) in place of this conjoined clause, since he had mentioned their action upon their position and his action upon his position, then followed it with mention of the outcome of those who act from him and from them. Then "*man ya'tihi*" etc. refers to the deniers, and "*man huwa sadiq*" refers to the Prophet sent. But since they used to call him peace be upon him a liar, he said "*wa-man huwa kadhib*" (and who is a liar) with the meaning of "in your assumption and your claim," as a way of showing their ignorance. That is, he peace be upon him proceeded in the mention upon what they had become accustomed to in naming him a liar, to show their ignorance. The meaning is: you will come to know your state and the state of the truthful one whom you named a liar out of your ignorance. The intent is not that you will come to know that he is a liar in your assumption, so there is no objection to what may be imagined, that his lying in their assumption is a known fact for them now, so there is no sense in tying their knowledge to the future.

Ibn al-Munir said: It is apparent that both statements are addressed to them. "*Fa-man ya'tihi*" etc. includes mention of their recompense. "*Wa-man huwa kadhib*" includes mention of their crime for which they are repaid, which is lying. This is the conjunction of attribute upon attribute while the described is one, as you say to one whom you threaten: "You will come to know who is humiliated and who is punished," while meaning the addressee in both statements. So in the mention of their lying there is an allusion to his truthfulness, and this is more eloquent and more effective than explicit statement. For this reason he did not mention the outcome of Shu'ayb peace be upon him, being content with mention of their outcome. A similar thing passed at the beginning of the surah, in His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿So you will come to know who will be given a punishment that will disgrace him and upon whom will descend a lasting punishment﴾ (Hud 39), where he was content with that instead of saying: "and who is on the contrary of that." Its counterpart is: ﴿So you will come to know to whom the final home will belong﴾ (al-An'am 135), where he mentioned one of the two outcomes, because the intended "outcome" here is the outcome of the report, since whenever it is used absolutely it means nothing other than that, as in ﴿and the outcome is for the righteous﴾ (al-A'raf 128). And because the *lam* in "*lahu*" (for him) indicates that it is not upon him, and he dispensed with mentioning its counterpart. End of quote.

Al-Tibi criticized him with what al-Fadil al-Jalabi refuted.

﴿And wait﴾: that is, await what I tell you of the arrival of what I promise you, and the manifestation of its truth. ﴿Indeed I am with you a watcher﴾: that is, awaiting that. It was said: The meaning is: await the punishment; indeed I am awaiting victory and mercy. This was related from Ibn 'Abbas. "*Raqib*" (watcher) is either in the sense of *murtaqib* (one who waits), like *al-rafi'* (the elevated) in the sense of *al-murtafi'*, or *raqib* (one who watches) like *al-sarim* in the sense of *al-sarim* (the sharp), or *muraqib* (one who observes), like *'ashir* in the sense of *mu'ashir* (companion). It is said that the more suitable reading is that it goes with the first "*irtaqibu*" (wait), although the coming of *fa'il* in the sense of the active participle of the derived form is not common. In the addition of "*ma'akum*" (with you) there is a showing by him peace be upon him of complete reliance upon his command.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 94:**

﴿When Our command came﴾, i.e., Our punishment, as indicated by His saying, ﴿You will know﴾, etc. Or [it means] its time, for the expectation (*irtiqab*) indicates that. ﴿We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us﴾. This mercy is the faith to which We guided them, or a mercy that was theirs. The particle *fa* (then) was used in the stories of Thamud and Lut, where it is said: ( ﴿So when Our command came﴾ ), while *wa* (and) is used here and in the story of 'Ad, where it is said: ( ﴿And when Our command came﴾ ), etc. This is because a prior promise had already been mentioned there, through His saying: ﴿That is a promise not to be denied﴾ and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, their appointed time is the morning﴾. This functions as the cause that requires the *fa* to enter its effect. Here and in the story of 'Ad, however, no such thing preceded. Rather, the coming of the punishment is mentioned as a story in itself, and what precedes it is another story. But both are related to one people, so they share some aspects and differ in others, and this is the position of *wa*. So it is said.

Here the mention of the promise is also followed, namely His saying, exalted is He: ( ﴿O my people, act according to your position﴾ ) up to His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Watchful﴾. The most that can be said is that it was not mentioned in the wording of a promise, and such a thing is not sufficient to make the distinction. It has also been said that the use of *fa* in the two places is because of the nearness of the punishment of the people of Salih and Lut to the mentioned promise, for between the first two and the punishment there were three days, and between the other two and it there is only what lies between the angels' words, ﴿Indeed, their appointed time is the morning﴾, and "the morning," which are brief moments. This is not the case with the punishment of the peoples of Shu'ayb and Hud, peace be upon them both. Rather, in the story of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, there is an indication that the time of the coming of the punishment was not narrowed, based on the common usage of *sawfa* (will). Whoever is fair to himself will not doubt the distinction between the promise in the stories of Salih and Lut, peace be upon them both, and the promise in the others, for the indication of the coming is clear in them, so it was appropriate to connect it with *fa*, and this is not the case in the others. So it is said, but there is in it what is not hidden. Perhaps limiting the distinction to nearness and its absence is less problematic than what has been said. Likewise [less problematic] than what is said: that the use of *fa*, despite there being a promise there, and the omission of it [in the case of Shu'ayb and Hud], is to indicate the evil state of those two peoples and the greatness of its atrocity, to the extent that the punishment befell them not because of a prior promise, but merely because of their wrongdoing. The reason for considering this regarding them, and not the peoples of Lut and Salih, peace be upon them both, is probably that they were distinguished from them by hurling the accusation of madness at those two prophets, and by addressing them directly with what the people of Salih and Lut did not say to their prophets, as recounted about them in this noble surah. There is in this what is hardly hidden from you, so reflect.

﴿And the cry seized those who did wrong﴾. He shifted from the pronoun to record their wrongdoing against them and to indicate causation, i.e., the cry seized those wrongdoers because of their wrongdoing that was detailed. ﴿The Cry﴾. It was said: Jibril, peace be upon him, cried out at them, and they perished, and it was a cry in the literal sense. Al-Balkhi permitted that what is meant by it is a kind of punishment. The Arabs say, "Time cried out at them," when they perished. Imru' al-Qays said:

*So leave aside plunder that was cried out upon in its chambers,*
*But rather the account of the riding camels' story.*

The reliance is on the first. It has been mentioned in al-A'raf that ﴿the earthquake﴾, i.e., the tremor, replaces it. Perhaps it was among its beginnings, so there is no contradiction. It has also been said that it is other than that, so reflect. ﴿So they became in their homes, prostrate﴾, i.e., dead, from *jatham* when a bird presses its belly to the ground. For this reason *juthman* was specifically applied to a person sitting. Then they extended the usage and applied *juthum* to the meaning of residing. Then *jathim* was borrowed for the dead, because he does not leave his place.

Since in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You will know who will receive a punishment﴾, etc., the object of knowledge was not the coming of the punishment itself, but rather who will be struck by it, He made its coming afterwards a matter of certain occurrence, not needing to be reported, since He made it a condition. He made the saving of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, and the believers, and the destruction of the disbelieving wrongdoers, its answer, and the purpose is the benefit. He mentioned the saving first, out of concern for its matter and as a notice that mercy precedes wrath. So said Shaykh al-Islam. And *asbaha* is either defective (*naqisa*) or complete (*tamma*): i.e., they became prostrate, or they entered upon the morning in a state of being prostrate.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 95:**

﴿As though they had never dwelt therein﴾, that is, had never lived in it, moving about its lands and roaming its territories. The clause is either a predicate following another predicate, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) following another.

﴿Away with Madyan, just as Thamud was taken away﴾. The shift from the pronoun to the explicit noun serves to intensify the description of their condition, and so that the phrase suits those who likened their destruction to the destruction of the others. Their destruction was likened to that of Thamud because the punishment of each was by a Shout (ṣayḥa). However, al-Kalbi related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Shout of Thamud came from beneath them, while the Shout of Madyan came from above them.

al-Sulami and Abu Ḥaywa read (baʿudat) with a ḍamma on the ʿayn, whereas the majority read it with a kasra, as being from baʿida, yabʿadu (with a kasra on the ʿayn in the past tense and a fatḥa in the present), meaning "perished." From this is the line of poetry:

"They say: 'Let him not perish,' while they bury me, and where is the place of perishing except my place?"

As for baʿuda, yabʿudu with a ḍamma, it means distance, the opposite of nearness, as said by Ibn Qutayba. It has been said that the Arabs intended by this change to distinguish between the two meanings. Ibn al-Anbari said: Among the Arabs are those who equate perishing with distance, which is the opposite of nearness. In the Qamus: al-buʿd means distance and also death, and their verb is like karuma and fariḥa: buʿdan and baʿadan, with two fatḥas. al-Mahdawi said: baʿuda with a ḍamma is used for both good and evil, while baʿida with a kasra is used for evil specifically. Whatever the case, the meaning of "baʿidat" according to that reading as well is "perished." In any event, whether this is literal or figurative, whoever perishes has become distant and remote, as the poet said:

"Whoever is between you and him in the dust, two months' distance away, is in the furthest reach of distance."

In the verse there is what is called **istiṭrād** (digression, a transition from one subject to a related one within the same passage). It has been said that no example of this kind occurs in the Qur'an except this one, but the Arabs used it in their poetry. Among examples is the saying of Ḥassan, may Allah be pleased with him:

"If what you have told me is false, then I escaped as al-Ḥarith ibn Hisham escaped,
He left his beloved to fight in his stead, and fled with the head of a swift horse and its bridle."

* * *

Here (and from the category of **ishāra**, allusory indication, in the verses) is His word, glorified is He, in the story of Hud, peace be upon him: ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Surely my Lord is upon a straight path﴾. In it is an indication that every living soul is under His dominion and authority, a captive in the grasp of His disposal and possession, powerless to act except by His permission; and that He, mighty and majestic, does not give power to anyone over anyone except on account of deserving a sin, or raising a rank and elevating a station, since He, blessed and exalted, is upon the path of justice in which there is no crookedness.

The Greatest Shaykh (al-Shaykh al-Akbar, Ibn ʿArabi), may his secret be sanctified, mentioned in his **Fuṣūṣ**: Everything other than the Real is a "beast" (dābba), for it has a spirit, and there is none that moves by itself; it moves only by another, by way of subordination to the One who is upon the straight path. Thus every walker is upon the straight path. In that case, there is neither one who has earned anger nor one who is astray from this perspective. Yes, people are of two kinds: the people of unveiling (ahl al-kashf) and the people of veiling (ahl al-ḥijāb). The former walk on a path whose nature they know and whose end they know; so it is for them a straight path, just as it is so in reality. The others walk on a path whose nature they do not know and whose end they do not know, which ends in the Real; so for them it is not a straight path, even though for the one who knows, and in reality, it is a straight path.

He, may his secret be sanctified, also deduced from the verse that the final destiny of all creation is the Mercy which encompasses all things, which is the Mercy that precedes wrath, and he claimed that in it is good news for creation, what excellent news!

al-Qayṣari said in its interpretation: That is, there is no existing thing except that He, glorified is He, holds its forelock. It was made a "beast" because all, in the view of the people of witnessing and the people of existence, are living. So the meaning is: there is no living thing except that the Real holds its forelock and disposes of it according to His Names, guiding it by whatever path He wills of His paths, and He is upon a straight path. By His saying, glorified is He, "holds" (ākhidh), He indicates the Identity of the Real which is with each of the Names and their manifestations. He said: ﴿Surely my Lord is upon a straight path﴾ with the addition of "Lord" to His own self and the indefiniteness of "path," to alert that every lord is upon his own straight path which was determined for him from the Divine Presence. The straight path which comprises all paths is the one specific to the Divine Name and its manifestation. For this reason, in the Opening (al-Fātiḥa), which is specific to our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, He said: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, with the definite article of previous mention or of the essence from which its particulars branch out. Therefore it may not be said: If every person is upon the straight path, what is the benefit of the call (to faith)? For we say: the call is to the guide from the misguider, and to justice from the tyrant, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿On the day when We gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾. End of quotation, word for word.

Even more serious as a problem is the question of obligation (taklīf) together with the doctrine of Unity, and likewise reward and punishment. For the apparent meaning of the formulation of the verified Sufis is that the one obligated is a being who is a portion of Absolute Existence, which overflows upon the realities of the possible things, and is specified by various specifications required by the essential predispositions of the realities, which are the non-existent things distinct in reality, disposed by essential predispositions that are not created. So the obligated one is a restricted (muqayyad) of the restrictions of Absolute Existence which overflows, and the restricted cannot exist without the Absolute, because it is its sustainer (qayyūm). And the Absolute, in terms of its absoluteness, is the very essence of the Real. There is no doubt that the rule of obligation requires that there be between them a real, essential difference and separation, so that obligation may be valid, and what follows from it of punishment and reward.

It has been answered that the reality of the possible is a non-existent matter distinct in itself with an essential distinction that is not created, and its existence is particular, restricted by a certain specificity required by its essential predisposition toward its non-existent quiddity. So it is composed of existence and non-existence, and its reality is different from its existence in the intellect, because their distinction is mental. This does not contradict the saying of al-Ashʿari: "The existence of every thing is the very essence of its reality," as explained in its place. The reality of the Real, exalted is He, is not different from His existence, and His existence, glorified is He, is the Absolute Existence with true absoluteness, as the verified Sufis have established. So the essential difference between the obligated and the Obligator is most manifest, because the obligated is the non-existent who wears a portion of existence specified according to his reality, and the Obligator, glorified is He, is the Real, mighty and majestic, who is the very essence of Absolute Existence, not conjoined with a non-existent quiddity. In other words: the reality of the possible is a non-existent matter, and the reality of the Necessary Existent, glorified is He, is Absolute Existence, even beyond the restriction of absoluteness. And there has occurred in between the manifestation of the Identity (tajallī al-Huwiyya) in the servant, and that manifestation is what unites power and the other perfections upon which obligation depends according to the requirement of wisdom, and it establishes the difference.

The summary of this is that the true nature of the blending between the manifestation of the Identity and the created form specified by the requirement of the non-existent reality is what produced that by which obligation and what follows from it are valid. And the fact that the Real, glorified is He, is the sustainer (qayyūm) of restricted existence does not detract from this; rather, sustainment is what validates it, because it has been clarified from the texts that there is no obligation except according to capacity, and there is no capacity for the possible except through His sustainment, mighty and majestic, by the text: ﴿Whatever Allah wills; there is no power except through Allah﴾. And what is through Allah belongs to Allah, mighty and majestic. The discussion of this is lengthy. Some of their expressions appear to indicate the absence of difference between the obligated and the Obligator, among which is what has been said:

"You were for an age before the veil was lifted; I think that I am remembering you and thanking you.
Then when the night shone, I became a witness that you are the one remembered, and the remembrance, and the one remembering."

However, one should not let the listener of these verses rush to deny them, and should refer regarding their intended meaning to those who know the subtleties of the secrets.

This is what has been said. The discussion of the she-camel of Ṣāliḥ, peace be upon him, has already preceded. And in what Allah, mighty and majestic, related here about Ibrahim, peace be upon him, there is an allusion to some of the etiquettes of **futuwwa** (chivalry). They have said: among its etiquettes, when a guest arrives, one should begin with honor in receiving him, then follow with honor in serving him food. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, only felt fear within himself because he thought it was anger, and the intimate friend (khalīl) fears the anger of his intimate friend, while his aspiration is his pleasure. How excellent is the one who said:

"Perhaps you are angry, and you do not know the greeting of peace in both abodes, if you are content."

In this story there is evidence that the door of **firāsa** (physiognomic insight) may be closed to the perfected ones for wisdoms that Allah, mighty and majestic, intends. For this reason, Ibrahim, and likewise Lut, peace be upon them both, did not recognize the angels, peace be upon them, at first. And his, peace be upon him, argumentation was, it has been said, from the effects of the station of reliance (al-idlāl). And the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic, about Lut, peace be upon him: ﴿If only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾. It has been said: by "strength" he indicates resolve (himma), which for them is the influential force upon souls, because strength is of two kinds: bodily and spiritual. This spiritual kind, called resolve, is more powerful in its influence, for it may affect most of the world or all of it, unlike the bodily kind. And by the "mighty pillar" he intended the tribe, because he knew that the acts of Allah, mighty and majestic, do not manifest externally except through the hands of manifestations. So he turned to Allah, glorified is He, and asked Him to make for him helpers who would support him against the enemies of Allah, mighty and majestic. He weighed the matter between this and that He might give him an influential resolve from Himself with which to confront the enemies. You have already known what was related from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, of his saying: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Lut..." and the rest of the report.

The Greatest Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned that, peace and blessings be upon him, by that report he alerted that Lut was with Allah, mighty and majestic, in the sense that ﴿a mighty pillar﴾ [refers to Allah Himself]. And the allusion in the story of Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, is that one who is in a position of authority should not disobey Allah, mighty and majestic, and the preacher should not contradict his deed with his speech:

"Do not forbid a trait and then commit its like; it is a shame upon you, a great one, if you do it."

And that nothing should be dearer to the servant than Allah, mighty and majestic, and so on. And Allah, mighty and majestic, is the Guide to the path of right direction.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 96:**

﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾. These are the nine signs: the staff, the white hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, and the loss of fruits and lives. The preposition *bi* (بِ) is connected to an omitted element that functions as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative) of the object of *arsalnā* (أرْسَلْنا, "We sent"), or as a *naʿt* (qualifying adjective) of its emphatic verbal noun (*maṣdar mu'akkad*). The meaning is: We sent him while he was accompanied by Our signs. Or: We sent him with a sending accompanied by them.

﴿and clear authority﴾. This refers to the dazzling miracles among them, namely the staff. It is singled out by mention to show its nobility, since it was the most dazzling of them. The "signs" are taken to mean what is other than it. It is permissible for both to refer to one thing, and the conjunction (*ʿaṭf*) is based on a difference in attributes. That is, We sent him combining the fact that it is a sign of Ours with the fact that it is an authority for him in proof of his prophethood, clear in itself, or making it clear. *Abāna* (أبانَ) is intransitive in the sense of "became evident" (*tabayyana*) and transitive in the sense of "made evident" (*bayyana*). Some scholars held that the signs and the authority are one thing in reality, but that this involves *tajrīd* (abstraction), as in the phrase "I passed by the noble man," and "the blessed soul." It is as if the proof was abstracted from the signs, made something other than them, and conjoined to them for this reason. It is also permissible that the "signs" refers to what you have heard, and the "authority" refers to what he, peace be upon him, explained within his call when Pharaoh said to him: ﴿Who then is the Lord of you both?﴾, and ﴿What then of the earlier generations?﴾, from the luminous realities and the fitting subtleties. Or the "authority" is domination and dominance, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and We will give you both an authority﴾. Some understood it as an expression for the Torah. Or its inclusion in the category of the signs is refuted by what Abu Hayyan said, namely His saying, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿To Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾. Its revelation came only after Pharaoh and his people were all destroyed, so that the Children of Israel might act upon it in what they do and abstain from. As for Pharaoh and his people, they were commanded to worship the Lord of the worlds and to abandon the monstrous, abominable claim that the tyrant made, which the rebellious faction accepted from him, and to release the Children of Israel from captivity and coercion. From this it becomes clear what is wrong with counting the loss of fruits and of lives as one of the nine signs, and with counting the shading of the mountain among them, because that was for receiving the Torah when the Children of Israel refused it, so it is likewise necessarily later. In the same way, the splitting of the sea is counted, and the shading of the cloud in its place, because this shading also came after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people.

Some eminent scholars answered the objection to counting the Torah among the signs by saying that the correction is possible. First, by what they have stated about the permissibility of returning a pronoun (al-damir, الضمير, the pronoun) and of attaching a prepositional phrase and the like to the unrestricted (al-mutlaq, المطلق) that is contained within the restricted (al-muqayyad, المقيد). Thus His saying, glorified is He, ﴿to Pharaoh﴾ may be attached to the unrestricted sending, not to the sending restricted to being by means of the Torah. Second, it may be said that Moses, peace be upon him, was sent to the Pharaohs and was also sent to the Children of Israel. Therefore the phrase "Pharaoh's chiefs" must be understood as including them, so that the statement becomes distributive, in the sense of: We sent him to Pharaoh with a clear authority, and to his chiefs with the Torah. This is then a laff wa nashr (لفّ ونشر, a figure in which items are listed and then matched to their referents) without order. The same may be said on the assumption that the shading of the mountain or of the cloud is counted among the signs.

In the collection of Sarri al-Din al-Misri it is stated that this question was raised by the memorizer al-Tashkandi (al-Hafiz al-Tashkandi) against Makhdum al-Malik, and he answered that His saying, glorified is He, ﴿with Our signs﴾ is a haal muqaddara (حال مقدرة, a circumstantial clause that is anticipated) meaning: those who anticipate his being clothed with or supported by the signs and the authority, sent to Pharaoh and his chiefs. Therefore the appearance of some of them after Pharaoh's death, such as the Torah and the bursting of water and other things, does not harm this. Also it was said that the giving of the Torah as a complete, ordered whole written upon the tablets came after Pharaoh's drowning, and it was revealed to Moses, peace be upon him, during Pharaoh's lifetime, and he used to command his people with it and convey it to Pharaoh and his chiefs. This is supported by what was said: some of the tablets were sent down before the complete Torah was sent down, and those tablets were of wood, while the tablets in which the whole Torah was contained were of emerald, or of red ruby, or of solid rock. End of quotation. It is not hidden that going to the view that the circumstance is anticipated is something the sound disposition can hardly accept. What is related, that the giving of the Torah as a whole came afterwards while its revelation came before, and so on, has no basis in sound reports. What was mentioned first, concerning attaching to the unrestricted, and second, concerning understanding "the chiefs" as including the Children of Israel, and so on, is something that the sanctity of the revelation should be held free from. How can "the chiefs" be understood as including the Children of Israel when it is additionally attributed to Pharaoh and they are counted among the people of the Fire? I do not think you have any doubt about the invalidity of this view. It was also said: if ﴿to Pharaoh﴾ is taken as dependent on ﴿with a clear authority﴾, either verbally or in meaning, with the assumption of "and an authority sent with him to Pharaoh", it would not be far-fetched, given the suitability of the connection between it and the authority. But in it there is what is not hidden, so reflect.

The singling out of "the chiefs" for mention, despite the generality of Moses' mission to the whole people, is because they are the foundation of opinion and the management of affairs, and others follow them in what they bring and in what they take. He did not explicitly mention Pharaoh's disbelief in the signs or his immersion in the error and misguidance he was upon, but restricted himself to mentioning the state of his chiefs. Thus He said: ﴿but they followed the command of Pharaoh﴾, that is, his command to disbelieve in what Moses, peace be upon him, brought of the truth, to indicate the clarity of his condition. So it is as if his disbelief and the command of his chiefs to it were of certain existence and did not need to be stated explicitly. What needs to be mentioned is the state of his chiefs, who were torn between one guiding to the truth, namely Moses, peace be upon him, and one calling to error, namely Pharaoh. So He rebuked them for their poor choice. The use of the fa' (الفاء, the particle of immediate sequence) indicates their sudden following and Pharaoh's swift move to disbelief and to commanding it, as if this did not delay after the sending and the conveying.

It was also permitted that "command" means the way and the matter. It was said: the meaning of ﴿they followed﴾ is that they continued to follow, and the fa' is like what is in your saying: "I admonished him but he did not heed, and I rebuked him but he did not desist". For the bringing of a thing after what requires abandoning it, even if it is a continuation of it, is in terms of its description a new act and a fresh deed. It is also possible that what is meant is that they were characterized by what Pharaoh was characterized by, namely disbelief in what Moses, peace be upon him, brought and the denial of him, and they agreed with him in that. The use of the fa' indicates their sudden agreement with Pharaoh in disbelief and his swiftness toward it, as if when the sending and conveying occurred, Pharaoh's disbelief in what Moses, peace be upon him, brought occurred, and their agreement followed immediately upon it. Do not imagine that this agreement was already present for them before, because it depends on Pharaoh's characterization by disbelief in what Moses, peace be upon him, brought, and that only renewed for him after the sending and conveying. So there is no necessity to read it as continuation. And making the fa' like what is in your saying "I rebuked him so he desisted" is possible, so reflect.

He turned from "his command" to "the command of Pharaoh" to remove the suspicion that the pronoun returns to Moses, peace be upon him, from the beginning, and to increase the ugliness of the state of those who followed. For Pharaoh is a byword for corruption, causing corruption, misguidance and leading astray. So their following him was from excessive ignorance and lack of insight. The same applies to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾, that is, not guided or possessing guidance. Rushd (الرشد, rectitude) is the opposite of ghayy (الغي, error), and attributing it to the command is metaphorical (majaz, مجاز, figurative use). It seems that in the shift from "and the command of Pharaoh is error and misguidance" to the noble wording there is added emphasis on the ugliness of their act and a lament over their missing what holds the good of both abodes, namely rectitude.

It is also possible that rushd be taken as a kinaya (كناية, an allusive expression) for being praiseworthy, and the attribution then is literal, meaning: "and the command of Pharaoh is not good, with praiseworthy outcome."

[Page 134]

The Almighty's saying: ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them down into the Fire﴾. According to the first view, this is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) that answers someone who asked about the outcome of the leader and the followers. According to the second view, it is an explanation and clarification of the badness of his end, meaning: how can one who has such an end guide anyone's affair? The clause ﴿and the affair of Pharaoh is not rightly guided﴾ (wa-ma amru ...) etc. may be a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the subject of "ittaba'u" (they followed) or from its object. It is said: this is the preference of al-Zamakhshari. By "the people" is meant what includes the chiefs and others. ﴿Yaqdumu﴾ is like yanṣuru from qadama (kanaṣara), meaning "to go ahead," and from it comes qadimat al-rahl (the front of the saddle). This is like saying qaddamahu, meaning "to go ahead of him," from which comes muqaddimat al-jaysh (the vanguard of the army). And aqdama, meaning "to go ahead," from which comes muqaddim al-'ayn (the front part of the eye), which is only with a kasra, as al-Marzuqi said. Similar is mu'akhkhir al-'ayn (the back part of the eye), as in al-Muzhir. The meaning of ﴿awradahum﴾ is yūriduhum (he brings them down). The use of this form rather than the present tense is to indicate that its occurrence is certain without doubt. The view that it remains in its literal sense, with the meaning "he brought them down into the Fire in this world," meaning that which causes it, namely disbelief, is nothing (laysa bi-shay'). The word "the Fire" is in the accusative as a second object of ﴿awradahum﴾. It is an implicit sarcastic metaphor (isti'ara makniyya tahakkumiyya) for its opposite, which is water. Its indicator (qarina) has several possibilities, as is well known in the case of ﴿they break the covenant of God﴾. On the assumption of metaphor, the bringing down is a sequential metaphor (isti'ara tab'iyya) for driving them to the Fire.

It is also permitted to say: he likened Pharaoh to the fariṭ, who is the one who goes ahead of the people to the water. Thus there is an implicit metaphor, and he made their following a bringing down (waridah). Attributing bringing down to them is an imaginative depiction (takhyil). He also permitted making the whole a figurative illustration (tamthil).

Some have permitted that ﴿yaqdumu﴾ and ﴿awradahum﴾ be two verbs that compete for "the Fire" (mutanaziʻan fi al-nar), but he gave priority to the second and deleted the object of the first. This is not correct.

﴿And wretched is the watering-place to which they are brought﴾: meaning, wretched is the watering-place they come to, which is the Fire, because the watering-place is only brought to in order to quench thirst and cool the hearts. In the Fire there is the cutting of hearts and their burning, so it is said. Thus al-wird here means the portion of water, and al-mawrud is its adjective. The item of blame (al-makhsus bi-al-dhamm) is omitted, and it is the Fire. It has been objected that there must be agreement (tasadduq) between the subject of "bi'sa" and its specified item, and there is no agreement on this view. Also, regarding the permissibility of describing the subject of ni'ma and bi'sa, there is disagreement, and Ibn al-Sarraj and al-Farisi hold that it is not permitted.

Ibn 'Atiyya permitted al-mawrud to be an adjective and the specified item to be the Fire, but he made the speech contain the omission of a modifier (mudaf) and the placing of the modified-to (mudaf ilayhi) in its place. Thus the agreement is achieved in reality, meaning: wretched is the place of the bringing-down and of the brought-down, which is the Fire. Some make al-mawrud the specified item of blame, and by it is meant the Fire, and a modifier is supposed so that agreement is achieved as well, meaning: wretched is the place of the watering-place, the Fire. And some make al-wird the subject of "bi'sa" and interpret it as the group that comes down (al-jam' al-warid), and al-mawrud is an adjective for them, and the specified item of blame is their pronoun, which is omitted, meaning: wretched are the people who are brought down to it. Thus it is blame for those who come down, not for the place of the bringing-down.

**Page 135**

﴿And they were followed﴾, i.e., the chiefs (al-mala') who followed the command of Pharaoh. It is also said that "the people" is meant in general. ﴿in this [world]﴾, i.e., in this worldly life, ﴿a curse﴾, a great one, since those who came after them among the nations curse them. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection﴾ as well, since all the people of the place of standing (al-mawqif) curse them. So it follows them wherever they go and encircles them wherever they turn. Just as they followed Pharaoh's command, the curse followed them in both abodes, as a recompense in kind (jaza'an wifaqan).

Al-Kalbi said: the curse in this world is from the believers, or by drowning; and on the Day of Resurrection it is from the angels, or by the Fire.

﴿Wretched is the gift that is given﴾, i.e., wretched is the aid that is aided, as transmitted from Abu 'Ubayda. The one specified by the dispraise is omitted, i.e., "their gift." The word rifd may mean a gift, just as it may mean aid.

Abu Hayyan said: It is said, "rafada al-rajul yarfiduhu rafdan wa rifdan," meaning he gave to him and helped him, from "rafada al-ha'it," meaning he propped up the wall. From al-Asma'i: al-rafd with a fatha is the cup, and al-rifd with a kasra is what is in it of drink. Al-Layth said: The root of al-rifd is gift and assistance, and from it comes the rifadat Quraysh, which is their assisting the pilgrims with something they bring out for the poor. It is said, "rafadahu rifdan and rafdan," with the kasra and the fatha of the letter ra'. It is said that with the kasra it is the noun, and with the fatha it is the verbal noun. Several have interpreted it here as "gift."

As for one who claims that the context does not suit it, this is nothing. Yes, its interpretation as "aid" is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari. The intended meaning, on both interpretations, is the curse. Calling it "aid" according to the first interpretation is a sarcastic metaphor (isti'ara tahakkumiyya). As for it being "aided," this is because it was given further support in the Hereafter by another curse, so that the two would guide them to the path of Hellfire. The analogical expectation would have been that the aided thing be attributed to them, since the curse in this world follows them, and likewise in the Hereafter, according to His saying, ﴿and they were followed﴾, etc. But it was attributed to the gift, which is the curse, by way of metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), like "jadda jadduhu" (his grandfather was majestic) and "junununuka majnun" (your madness is mad). Likewise, the metaphor and figurative usage mentioned are considered on the second interpretation, so it is said.

Some of the scrutinizers said: In al-Zamakhshari's statement on explaining the verse according to the first meaning transmitted from Abu 'Ubayda, [it is said] that the curse in this world is a support for the punishment and an increase of it. It has been given support by the curse in the Hereafter, which indicates that it is not at all of the sarcastic metaphor type, since if it were a support for the punished, it would be of that kind. Then he said: Making it of the type of "jadda jadduhu" is further and further removed, since he mentioned that A'yan was given support with a gift. But if it is interpreted according to the second interpretation, then the first applies and not the second, since it is not a verbal noun; rather, al-'ata' means "what is given," so it is often applied to it. End of quotation. There is in this a consideration that is not hidden. Then, the claim that there are two curses, one of which is supported by the other, is what is transmitted from Mujahid and others. So "yawm" is conjoined to the position of "fi al-dunya."

Some people went to the view that the division is that they have a curse in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection, "wretched is what they are given," so it is one curse at first and an ugly giving at the end. End of quotation. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr criticized this, saying that this is not valid, because it implies that "yawm" is an object of "bi'sa," and it does not inflect, so its object cannot precede it. If "yawm" were after it, that would be valid, as the poet said:

"And how excellent you are as the padding of the coat of mail, when you are called to a duel, you enter into the terror."

This is a sound statement. The verse clearly shows the bad state of Pharaoh on the Day of Resurrection, since if the state of the followers is what God the Glorious has recounted, then what do you think of the state of one who misled them and cast them into this far-off error? This complicates the view of one who holds that he died pure and purified. Indeed, some said: it is a text refuting that view, since He, exalted is He, removed from him right guidance after his death in it, and the pure and purified believer is not deprived of right guidance after death. Perhaps one who holds that view would say: the door of interpretation is wide, and the door of mercy is wider than it.

﴿That﴾ refers to what was recounted of the reports of the nations, and it is distant [in reference] either by considering its having passed, or by considering what has been said in other places. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is the subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿of the reports of the towns﴾, those that were destroyed for what the hands of their people had committed. The alif-lam in "al-qura" (the towns) is for a previously mentioned referent (al-'ahd al-sabiq), estimated by mentioning their inhabitants. ﴿We recount it to you﴾ is a second predicate after the first, meaning: that news is part of the reports of the towns that are recounted to you. It was also permitted that ﴿of the reports﴾ be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and that this be the predicate. It was also permitted to reverse this.

﴿Of them﴾, i.e., of those towns, ﴿is standing and some is harvested﴾, i.e., and of them is some harvested. The conjunction is thus the conjunction of one clause to another, and this is what the meaning requires, as is not hidden. The part of them that remains has been likened to a crop standing on its stalk, and what has been effaced and perished has been likened to the harvested crop. The meaning, then, is: of them some remains, and of them some has been effaced. This is what is related from Qatadah, and similar to it is what is related from al-Dahhak: ﴿standing﴾ means it was not swallowed by the earth, and ﴿harvested﴾ means it was swallowed. It has been said: ﴿harvested﴾ (hasid) with respect to crops has come in their speech with the meaning of annihilation, as in his saying:

"Among people, in the allotment of death, is their share,
Like crops, of it some standing and some harvested."

Page 136

The form fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, i.e., mahsud (reaped), as al-Akhfash said. Its plural is hasda, and hisad, like marda and mirad. The clause ﴿of them is standing﴾ etc. is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) of grammatical resumption (isti'naf nahwi), to encourage reflection upon that and taking lessons from it; or of explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), as if it was asked, once their condition had been mentioned: "What is their state?" and it was answered with that. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "naqussuhu" (We recount it). Al-Tibi permitted it to be a circumstantial clause from "al-qura" (the towns). The author of al-Kashshaf claimed that making it a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "naqassahu" is corrupt both in wording and meaning, and likewise from "al-qura." In the Hawashi al-Shihabiyya, he intended by the verbal corruption in the first case the clause's lacking a waw and a pronoun, and in the second the coming of a circumstantial clause from the genitive noun (mudaf ilayhi) outside the familiar forms; and by the semantic corruption, that it implies that it is not among the things recounted but rather is an external circumstance, which is not intended. And it is not permissible to make what follows it the beginning of what is recounted. There is also a verbal corruption in this as well.

Some have claimed that he intended by the first corruption in the first case what was mentioned, and in the second the occurrence of a nominal clause as a circumstantial clause with the pronoun alone, and that with the pronoun there is a restriction of its being recounted in that particular state, since being recounted is established for it and for the report also at the time of some of it standing; and he was right in some and wrong in some. Al-Jalabi justified the absence of waw and pronoun by saying that the purpose of the pronoun is linkage, and that is achieved by the linkage of that to the related element of the possessor of the circumstance, which is the towns. So the meaning is: We recount to you some of the reports of the towns, and they are in this state, you witness Allah's action upon them. This was criticized: relying on what he mentioned for linkage, despite its obscurity, is a view unique to al-Akhfash, who did not mention it for the circumstantial clause but only for the predicate of the subject. Abu Hayyan's saying, that the circumstantial clause is more forceful in warning and in striking an example for those present, along with what you have heard of benefit, is not the truth; and there is no basis for what Abu al-Baqa' stated that one could rely upon, except inattentiveness.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 101:**

﴿And We did not wrong them.﴾ It has been said: the pronoun refers to the towns (al-qura), with their people (ahluha) intended by them. The literal sense of the word was intended first, so there is *istikhdam* (a figure of speech in which one word is used with two different meanings) in the sentence. It has also been said: the pronoun refers to the people of the towns, because there is an elided genitive construction, meaning "that is from the news of the people of the towns." Some pronouns refer to the first term of the construction (al-mudaf) and others to the second (al-mudaf ilayhi). When the matter is clear, such a usage is permitted.

It has also been said: "the towns" is to be taken in its literal sense, and attributing the "news" to them is *majaz* (figurative usage). The pronoun in "minha" (of them/from it) refers to the towns, and the pronoun in "zalamnahum" (We wronged them) refers to the people understood from them. It has further been said: "the towns" is figurative for their people, and both pronouns refer back to it on that understanding. Alternatively, the genitive construction may be elided, and both pronouns refer to it as well. On this reading is explained what is reported from some of them, that the meaning of ﴿Of them some are standing and some are reaped﴾ is: of them, some have surviving offspring, and of them, some have cut-off offspring. In any case, the sentence indicates the destruction of the people. So the meaning here is: "And We did not wrong them by Our destroying them," ﴿but they wronged themselves﴾, in that they committed, through the evil of their predisposition, that which entails such destruction according to the requirements of wisdom. ﴿So their gods which they called upon besides Allah did not avail them﴾, that is, they did not benefit them, nor did they repel the might of Allah Most High from them. ﴿Their gods which they called upon﴾, that is, which they worshipped. The imperfect form (yad'una) is used either to depict a past situation or to indicate the continuity of their worship of them. ﴿Anything﴾, that is, any benefit at all, or anything whatsoever. Here *ma* is a negation particle, not an interrogative, although al-Samin (al-Samin al-Halabi) permitted the interrogative reading. The phrase "'an" (from) is connected to "ma" (not), because it carries the meaning of repelling. The second *min* is extra (ṣila), and its genitive object is either an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) or a direct object (maf'ul bihi) of "repelling." As for His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿when the command of your Lord came﴾, meaning at the time of the coming of His punishment, it is in the accusative case, governed by "aghnat" (did avail). This, according to what is in al-Bahr (Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan), is based on a view contrary to the doctrine of Sibawayh (Sibawayhi), since his doctrine is that *lamma* is a particle of necessity governing necessity.

It has been read as "ālihatuhumu al-lati" (their gods, the feminine form), and "yad'una" in the passive voice. The relative pronoun is then a description of the gods, as in the well-known reading "allati," and there is agreement with the described noun in this reading, which is absent in "allati." However, it has been said, as in Jam' al-Jawami' by al-Jalal al-Suyuti, that *allati* used for a plural that is not of rational beings is more common than *allati* with the plural form. Indeed, the gods in the verse have been treated as rational beings, because their worshippers placed them in the position of rational beings, believing that they benefit and harm. Thus it is said: ﴿but they only increased them in ruin﴾. From here it has been said that *allati*, in that reading, stands in the position of *ulā* or *alladhina* (those, the masculine plural relative pronouns). *Tatbib*, according to al-Bahr, is ruin and loss, from *tabba* (he lost) and *tabbabahu* (he caused him to lose).

Al-Jawhari mentioned that *tabb* is loss and perdition, and *tatbib* is destruction. In al-Qamus, *tabb*, *tabab*, *tibab* and *tatbib* are deficiency and loss.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Umar and Mujahid the explanation of this as causing loss. Likewise al-Tustari reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, except that he cited as evidence for it the verse of Bishr ibn Abi Khazim:

*They slit the noses and then removed them, and they left the Banu Sa'd in ruin (tibaban).*

In that case the meaning is: "they only increased them in loss, or in ruin for their own souls, since they deserved the painful and everlasting punishment for their worship of them." We ask Allah Most High for pardon and well-being.

[p. 137]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 102:

﴿And thus﴾ i.e., like that seizing and destruction that was explained earlier. According to what al-Samin said, it is a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and the saying of the Exalted, ﴿the seizing of your Lord﴾, is a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). It has also been said that it is the reverse. The kaf may be a noun or a particle. It is also possible that the thing indicated is the seizing mentioned after it, as was established before. In the reading of Abdullah it is "kadhalika" without the waw.

﴿When He seizes the towns﴾, i.e., their people. He attributed it to the towns only to indicate that its effect spreads. Al-Jahdari and Abu Raja' read (wa-kadhalika akhadha rabbuka idha akhadha), taking akhadha rabbuka as a verb and subject, with the adverbial clause (al-zarf) referring to what has passed. This is a report about what has been the custom of God Most High in destroying the nations that came before. On this reading, "kadhalika" serves as a substitute for the generic verbal noun (al-masdar al-nau'i), and there is no objection to its preceding the verb. ﴿The towns﴾ is an object of contention between the verbal noun and the verb.

The saying of the Exalted, ﴿while they are wrongdoing﴾, is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from ﴿the towns﴾, and therefore the pronoun and ﴿wrongdoing﴾ are feminine. However, describing the towns as wrongdoing is metaphorical; in reality it is a description of their people. Making it a hal from the implied annexed noun (al-mudaf al-muqaddar) first, and making it feminine by borrowing from the annexed noun, is far-fetched (takallluf). The benefit of this circumstantial clause is to indicate that their seizing was because of their wrongdoing, and in this there is a warning to the wrongdoer that is not hidden. By "wrongdoing" is meant either disbelief (kufr) or what is more general than that. The apparent practice of some, taking it from its unrestricted sense, is that it includes wronging oneself and others.

﴿Indeed His seizing is painful﴾, meaning grievous, ﴿severe﴾, from which there is no hoped-for escape. This is an intensification in threatening and warning.

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) in their Sahihs, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and others related from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah Most High gives respite to the wrongdoer, until when He seizes him, He does not let him go." Then he recited: ﴿And thus is the seizing of your Lord﴾ to His saying, Most High: ﴿Indeed His seizing is painful and severe﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 103:

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, that is, in His, glory be to Him, seizing the destroyed nations, or in what has been recounted of their accounts, ﴿is a sign﴾, that is, a clear indication. Some have explained it as ʿibrah (a lesson drawn from events), because a sign implies it, and this is a good reading. The tanwin (nunation) of ﴿āyah﴾ is for magnification, meaning a great lesson, ﴿for those who fear the punishment of the Hereafter﴾. For when such a person sees what befell the criminals in this world of painful punishment, he takes a lesson from it regarding the state of the promised punishment, since he has sinned in some of its kinds and in a small part of much. He is restrained by that from the sins that entail punishment, and he devotes himself to piety and fear of God, exalted is He. The phrase ﴿for those who fear﴾ has been put in the place of ﴿for those who affirm this﴾, because of the necessary connection between them, and because consideration (iʿtibar) arises only from fear. He mentioned this restriction because whoever denies the Hereafter and holds that this world cannot perish attributes events to astral causes and particular conditions, so he takes no lesson from them at all and is certainly not restrained from misguidance. He says that what occurred happened only because of those causes and conditions, not because of the sins the destroyed nations committed.

It has also been said: the intended meaning is that in what has been mentioned there is proof of the punishment of the criminals in the Hereafter, because if they are punished in this world for their crimes, which is the abode of action, then they are more deserving of punishment in the Hereafter for them, which is the abode of recompense. It has also been said: the intended meaning is that in it there is proof of the resurrection and recompense. This is because the prophets, peace be upon them, had foretold the annihilation of those who denied them and associated others with God, and what they foretold occurred in accordance with their prediction. That is one of the evidences of their truthfulness, and so they are truthful in what they report about the resurrection and recompense, and it must therefore inevitably occur. The restriction to what is mentioned here is like the restriction in His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾, and this is, as you see, [a weak reading].

﴿That﴾ refers to the Day of Resurrection, indicated by the mention of the Hereafter. ﴿It is a Day on which mankind will be gathered﴾, that is, mankind will be gathered for it for reckoning and recompense, so ﴿mankind﴾ is the deputy subject of ﴿gathered﴾.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah permitted that it be a subject (mubtada') with ﴿gathered﴾ as its predicate, but this is remote, since the apparent form would then be "it is gathered." He departed from the verb, though the apparent form would have been the verb, so that the sentence would indicate the establishment of the meaning of gathering, the certainty of its occurrence without doubt, and that people cannot be detached from it. Thus it is more eloquent than His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the Day He gathers you for the Day of Gathering﴾. Its clarification is that this indicates the permanence of the attribute and the permanence of the predication, while the other indicates the occurrence of the connection of gathering to those addressed and its specificity to the Day. For this reason he corrected it with his saying "the gathering," thus attributing the Day to it so as to indicate its permanence for it, while what is newly occurring is the gathering of the first and the last at once. ﴿And that﴾, that is, the Day of Resurrection, together with the aspect of mankind being gathered for it, ﴿is a Day witnessed﴾, that is, a Day in which [something] is witnessed. The prepositional phrase was expanded, and the verb was made to reach the pronoun, treating it as the direct object, as in the saying:

"And a day we witnessed, safe and populated, few [of its] supplements other than the thrusting of the Dirak."

That is, in it all creatures witness the standing place, and none of them is absent from it. He did not make the day itself the thing witnessed, but made it witnessed in, and the witnessed thing was not mentioned, for the sake of awe and magnification, so that it would not run upon the tongue, and to indicate that the mind has no room to turn to anything else. It has also been said: the witnessed is that whose witnesses are many, and from this is their saying: "For so-and-so is a witnessed gathering and an attended feast." And Umm Qays al-Dabbiyyah said:

"A scene whose telling I have spared the speakers, in an assembly of the forelocks of people, witnessed."

They considered the multitude of its witnesses, reasoning that it is the one deserving that the name "witnessed" be applied to it absolutely. Had the day itself been made witnessed without this consideration, the purpose of magnifying and distinguishing the day would not have been achieved, for all other days are likewise. Rather, the distinction comes from what is attributed to it of the awe-inspiring and distinguishing multitude. By what has been mentioned, it is known that the objection is void which says: "Shuhud means presence, and the gathering of people is their presence, so 'witnessed' after 'gathered' is repetitive."

[p. 138]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 104:
