﴿And We do not delay it﴾, i.e., that day, which is regarded under the title of gathering and witnessing. Al-Hawfi reported that the pronoun refers to the recompense (al-jaza'). Al-A'mash and Ya'qub read "yu'akhkhiruhu" with the ya' (third person masculine).

﴿except for a limited term﴾, i.e., until the end of a short period. Thus, counting (al-add) is a metaphor (kinaya) for fewness, though it may also be taken as a metaphor for finiteness. Al-ajal (term) refers to the entire specified duration for a thing, and it may also be applied to its end. Preventing the intended meaning of the end here is because it is never described as "counted" (ma'dud) in their speech in any way. Some scholars permitted it, on the basis that a metaphor (kinaya) does not require that the original meaning be possible. This was objected to as a deviation from the apparent meaning, and supposing an omitted noun (taqdir al-mudaf) is easier than that. The lam here is for limitation (al-tawqif). In al-Majma', it is said that it indicates the purpose, and that wisdom required the delay; for this reason the wording deviated from "ila" to "ilayha". In the verse there is a refutation of the Dahriyya (materialists who deny a creator) and the philosophers who claim that the duration of the world has no end; this is a settled matter.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 11, verse 105:**

﴿On the day it comes﴾: i.e., that day, the one postponed until its appointed term (*ajal*) has run out, as wisdom requires. This is what is related from Ibn Jurayj. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the Requital (*al-jaza'*), and it was said that it refers to God, the Exalted. In this there is an exaltation of the day's status that is not hidden. It is supported by the reading *wa-ma yu'akhkhiruhu* (﴿and what He postpones﴾) with a *ya'* (third-person masculine form). Attributing "coming" and similar actions to Him, glory be to Him, occurs in more than one verse. The first view has been objected to on the grounds that the implied construction would be "the day of the coming of that day," which is not valid, because the definiteness of "the day" when it is defined by "coming" rules out the definiteness of "coming" when it is defined by "the day." Also, the coming of a day cannot be separated from the day of coming, so the attribution suffices and the *idafah* (genitival construction) becomes superfluous. The scholar al-Tibi quoted an explicit statement that it is not permissible, just as one does not say "I came to you on the day of your Busr." It was answered that every time that has a matter whose recurrence is considered significant, like the festival (*'id*), Nawruz, or the Hour for example, takes the place of a temporal entity (*zamaniyy*), and although in itself it is a time, by considering the difference of the two aspects the *idafah* and the attribution of action are valid. Just as it is valid to say "the day the Hour establishes" and "the day the festival comes" and "the festival is on such-and-such a day." The first is a time, and its pronoun, meaning the doer of the verb, is temporal. Accordingly, something like the poet's words is good:

*"So may He water the ghada (tamarisk) and its inhabitants,*
*even if they have kindled [the fire] between my ribs and my flanks."*

This is the better view. The two grammarians (al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr) and Nafi' read *ya'ti* with the *ya'* present when connected and omitted when pausing. Ibn Kathir read it with the *ya'* both connected and at pause. It is also present in the codex of Ubayy. The remaining seven readers read it without the *ya'*, both connected and at pause. It is absent from the codex of Uthman, may God be pleased with him. Keeping it both connected and at pause is the preferred form. The reason for omitting it at pause is to make it resemble the verse-endings (*fawasil*). Omitting it both connected and at pause is for lightness, as they say: *la adri wa la ubali* ("I do not know and I do not care"). Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that relying on the vowel *kasrah* in place of the *ya'* is common in the dialect of Hudhayl. From this is his statement:

*"Your palm is enough, so that the dirham you give is generous,*
*and another [palm] gives blood by the sword."*

The A'mash read *yawma ya'tuna* ("the day they come") with the *waw* of the plural, and likewise it is in the codex of Abdullah. That is, "the day the people come," or "the people of the place of standing" come. ﴿No soul will speak﴾: i.e., it will not speak with anything that benefits or saves it, whether an answer or an intercession. This verb, according to the more apparent view, is the governor of the earlier temporal adverb.

It was permitted that it be in the accusative by being governed by "the end" (*al-intiha'*), which is attributed to the term (*ajal*), and that it be an object (*maf'ul bihi*) of an omitted verb "remember" (*udhkur*). This sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun of "the day." Al-Hawfi and Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted it to be a descriptive clause (*na't*) of "a day." It was objected that this implies that its *idafah* does not confer definiteness, and that is disputed. Perhaps the one who claims this would say: clauses are like indefinite nouns, to the extent that they are called by that, so the *idafah* to them is like the *idafah* to them.

﴿except with His permission﴾: i.e., except with the permission of God, exalted be His majesty and glorious be His sovereignty, to speak. Like His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿They will not speak except for one whom the Most Merciful has permitted﴾. This is in one of the stations of that day. And His saying, blessed and exalted be He: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾ and ﴿nor will they be permitted, so they can make excuses﴾ is in another of its stations, just as His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿The day every soul comes pleading for itself﴾ is in another of its stations. This was related from al-Hasan.

Many have mentioned that what is permitted is the true answers, and what is forbidden is the false excuses. Yes, it may be permitted in them too, to show their falsehood, as in the words of the disbelievers: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ and its like. The claim that this is not of the category of excuses, but is rather an attribution of the sin to their leaders, and that they misled them, is nothing, as is not hidden. In *al-Durar wa al-Ghurar* by Sayyid al-Murtada, there is a supposed contradiction, apparently, between His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿On the day it comes, no soul will speak except with His permission﴾, and His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾ and ﴿nor will they be permitted, so they can make excuses﴾, and likewise His, majestic and exalted be He, saying: ﴿Some of them will turn to others, questioning one another﴾. Some of the exegetes answered this by saying that the Day of Resurrection is a long, extended day, so it is possible that they are prevented from speaking in part of it, and permitted in another part of it. This answer is weakened by the fact that the reference to the Day of Resurrection is in its entirety, so how can the verses about it be contradictory? According to what they mentioned, the meaning of ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾ would be: "This is a day in part of which they will not speak," which contradicts the apparent sense. The sound answer to this is to say: what is meant is only the negation of audible, accepted speech, by which they benefit, and through which they can establish an argument and find deliverance. It is not the negation of speech absolutely, in a way that includes what does not have this state. This is analogous to the sayings: "So-and-so was struck dumb regarding his argument," and "We attended so-and-so debating so-and-so, and we did not see him say anything," even though the one described as struck dumb and the one whose speech is denied have spoken much. But since there was no argument in it and it contained no benefit, it was permissible to apply to him what we have related. Similar to this is the poet's saying:

*"Blind when my neighbor goes out,*
*until the curtain hides my neighbor;*
*and deaf to what was between us,*
*my hearing, though nothing else is wrong with me."*

On this basis there is no contradiction, because questioning and blaming, for example, have no argument in them. As for His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿nor will they be permitted, so they can make excuses﴾, it has been said about it: they are not commanded to make excuses, so how would they make excuses? "Permission" is interpreted as "command," and they were not commanded to do so because in that state there is no obligation, and the servants, upon witnessing the terrors, are compelled to confess and acknowledge. Better than this is to interpret ﴿they are permitted﴾ as: He does not listen to them and does not accept their excuse. End of quotation.

You know that his weakening of what the people answered with, regarding the extension of the Day of Resurrection and the possibility that prohibition of speech occurs in part of it and permission in another part, is not approved by one of sound judgment. This is because it is evident that an extended time can validly be a container for two opposites, provided neither of them, or one of them, does not cover that entire time. The resolution of contradiction between the two statements in the manner they did is widespread, and it ultimately comes back to the view of the difference of time. Likewise, what was related from al-Hasan ultimately comes back to the view of the difference of place. The unity of time and place is among the conditions for the contradiction of two propositions. What they did is no more remote than what al-Murtada did, and moreover there is a remoteness in his statement that is not hidden.

Some of the learned said: there is no conflict between this verse and the verses that indicate speech on the Day of Resurrection, because what is meant by "the day it comes" is "the time it comes." The proposition containing this is temporal (*waqtiyyah*), in which the predicate is negated of all individuals of the subject at a specific time. This does not conflict with the predicate's affirmation of the subject at other than that time. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: one of two things is necessary. Either it is said that what came in the verses of mutual blame, questioning, disputing, and the like, which is explicit in speech, was by permission, or the speech here is interpreted as speech of intercession or establishing an argument. Both views, as you see, are not sound. The exception (*istithna'*) has been said to be from the more general of causes, meaning: no soul will speak for any reason except for a reason, which is His, exalted be He, permission, and this is continuous (*muttasil*). It is permissible for it to be discontinuous (*munqati'*), and what does not include the excepted item is presupposed, meaning: no soul will speak by power from itself except with His, exalted be He, permission. It is not hidden that this is an exception of the "emptied" type (*mufarragh*). You have heard what is most correct regarding it. It was read, as in the codices of Ibn al-Anbari: "the day they come, no creature will speak except with His permission."

﴿So among them﴾: i.e., the people of the place of standing, indicated by His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿no soul﴾, or the whole that the word "soul" includes, since it is a generic noun intended to mean the whole, according to what Abu Hayyan transmitted from Ibn 'Atiyyah, or "the people" mentioned in His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿That is a day for which the people will be gathered﴾. Ibn al-Anbari transmitted that the pronoun refers to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is extremely strange. It seems this speaker intended this as a preparation for justifying the following exception, but God is free of need for that.

The apparent sense is that "min" (of) is partitive, and the prepositional phrase is a fronted predicate. His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿wretched﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*). His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿and blessed﴾ is by the estimate "and among them is one who is blessed," and "among them" was omitted because the first indicates it. Happiness (*sa'adah*), according to what al-Raghib said, is the assistance of divine affairs to a human being in attaining good, and its opposite is wretchedness (*shaqawah*). Abu Hayyan, in *al-Bahr*, explained wretchedness as the hardship and evil of life, then said: happiness is its opposite. In *al-Qamus* there is something close to this. So the "wretched" and the "blessed" are the two characterized by what has been mentioned. Several have explained the first as one who deserves the Fire by the consequence of the threat, and the second as one who deserves Paradise by the requirement of the promise. This is what is customary among the jurists (*shar'iyyun*). The placing of the wretched before the blessed is because the context is one of warning and admonition.

﴿As for those who are wretched﴾, i.e., wretchedness has preceded for them. ﴿They will be in the Fire﴾, i.e., they will abide in it. ﴿For them therein is groaning and wailing﴾. The people of lexicography from the Kufan and Basran schools said: the *zafir* (groaning) is like the beginning of a donkey's voice, and the *shahiq* (wailing) is like the end of its bray. Ru'ba said:

*It rattled in the chest as a neigh, or gasped, until it is said it brays, though it has not brayed.*

Ibn Faris said: the *zafir* is the expelling of breath, and the *shahiq* is its drawing back. Al-Shammakh said, describing a wild ass:

*Far in its reach of melody, the first of its voice is a groaning, followed by a rattling wail.*

Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) said: the *zafir* is the repeated drawing of breath until the ribs swell from it, from the saying "Fulan zafara" when he carried a load with difficulty so that his breath was repeated within him. From this, female slaves who carry water are called *zawafir*. The *shahiq* is the prolonging of the *zafir*, and it is the drawing back of breath, while the *zafir* is its extension. Its root is from a *jabal shahiq*, that is, a mountain extremely tall.

It is narrated from al-Sa'ib that the *zafir* is for donkeys and the *shahiq* is for mules, and this is an unusual report. Both words are intended to indicate their distress and anguish, and to liken their state to that of one whose heart is overcome by heat and whose spirit is confined within it. Or the comparison is between their voices and the voices of donkeys, so the statement contains a *isti'ara tamthiliyya* (allegorical metaphor) or an *isti'ara musarriha* (explicit metaphor).

What is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, is that he said: it means regret, a high-pitched breath, and weeping that does not cease. Al-Hasan recited *shaqu* (شَقُوا) with a *damma* on the *shin*, and it is then used transitively, since it is said *shaqahu Allah* just as *ashqahu Allah* is said. The clause ﴿for them therein is groaning and wailing﴾, etc., is a resumptive clause (*jumla mustanafa*), as if a questioner asked: "What is their condition therein?" and it was said: "For them therein is such and such." It is also permitted that it be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring either to the Fire or to the pronoun in the prepositional phrase, as in the saying of the Mighty and Majestic:

[Page 142]

﴿Abiding therein﴾. Except that if what is meant is the occurrence of their being in the Fire, then the state is conditional (muqaddarah). ﴿As long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, that is, for the duration of their continuance. This is an expression of perpetuity and the negation of cessation, following the manner of the Arabs' saying: "I will not do such-and-such as long as a star shines, as long as dawn lights up, as long as night and day alternate, as long as a sea moistens a tuft of wool, as long as a dove coos," and other such expressions of perpetuity among them, which do not make their abiding dependent on the continuance of these heavens and this earth. The definitive texts indicate the perpetuity of their abiding therein and the cessation of the continuance of those two. This was narrated from Ibn Jarir. He also allowed that this be understood as a conditional clause (ta'liq). The intended "heavens and earth" are the heavens and earth of the Hereafter, which endure forever. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The evidence that the Hereafter has heavens and an earth is His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿On the day when the earth will be changed to a different earth, and the heavens as well﴾, and His saying: ﴿And He has caused us to inherit the earth, that we may dwell in the Garden wherever we will﴾. And because the people of the Hereafter must have something that carries them and shades them: either a heaven that Allah, exalted is He, creates, or the Throne shades them, and everything that shades you is a heaven." End of quote.

Al-Qadi (al-Baydawi) said: "In this there is room for scrutiny, for it is a comparison with something that most of creation does not know to exist or to endure, and whoever knows it knows it through what indicates the permanence of reward and punishment, so the comparison is of no benefit." The author of al-Kashf (al-Taftazani) answered him: "If what is meant is what shades them and what carries them, then this is clearly invalid, for this extent is known to exist for every rational person. As for permanence, it is not derived from the evidence for the permanence of reward and punishment, but rather from what indicates the permanence of Paradise and Hellfire, whether or not one knows that they are the abodes of reward and punishment and that their people are the blessed and the wretched among mankind, so that it is not a comparison of the known with the unknown, but the reverse." End of quote.

Al-Jalabi (Mustafa al-Jalabi) objected to him: "His saying 'for every rational person' is not correct, for none acknowledges this except the believers in the Hereafter. And his saying that permanence is derived from what indicates the permanence of Paradise and Hellfire does not refute what al-Qadi mentioned, for he means that the thing compared to (al-mushabbah bihi) is not better known than the thing compared (al-mushabbah), neither in the view of the religious person, since he knows both from the prophets, peace be upon them both, and there is nothing in it that requires that the permanence of the heavens and earth of the Hereafter is better known. He does not mean that their permanence is derived from the specific evidence that indicates reward and punishment itself, for that is not what is intended to refute, nor in the view of the non-religious person, for he neither acknowledges it nor them, nor knows it. And his saying: 'that it is not a comparison...' is based on the premise that it is a comparison of that abode with this abode, which is not so; rather what is meant is the implicit comparison of their permanence with the permanence of those two." End of quote. There is discussion in this.

The truth is that the correctness of this intended meaning is not a matter over which two rams should butt heads. And in the reports from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Suddi and others there is what supports it. Whoever reflects fairly, after granting that there is a comparison, will find that the thing compared to is better known and closer to the mind than the thing compared, and that the unity of the means of knowledge of the two does not harm this in any way. It is self-evident that the establishment of a place is better known and closer to the mind than the establishment of what is in that place, even if both come through hearing. And it is not hidden that the condition that the thing compared to be better known in every comparison is not accepted by the one who examines the meanings. Indeed, what is understood from "the heavens and the earth" is these bodies well known to us. So it is better to leave them on their apparent sense, and to make the speech come out in the manner the Arabs are accustomed to in their discourse when they intend to express remoteness and perpetuity, and this is more than can be counted. And perhaps this is also better than what is in Ibn Kathir's tafsir, of understanding the heavens and earth as the genus encompassing what is in this world and the Hereafter, that is, what shades and carries in every abode. In al-Durar it is said: It is possible that what is meant is that they abide for the length of the duration of the heavens and earth, whose cessation is known, and then He, glorified is He, adds to that and makes them eternal and makes their station everlasting. And perhaps he meant the length of their duration from the time Allah, exalted is He, created them until He changes them, not the length of their duration after their entry into the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, for they are changed before their entry. And the verse according to this is like His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Remaining therein for ages﴾, and ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾.

It was said: it is an exception from the pronoun concealed in (khalidin), and (ma) is applied to a type of those who have reason, as in His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Then marry what seems good to you of women﴾. Or (ma) is applied to those who have reason according to the view of one who holds that it applies to them absolutely.

By those whom He wills are meant the immoral among the monotheists, for they will come out of it, as the reports have stated. And that suffices for the correctness of the exception, for the removal of the ruling from the whole is satisfied by its removal from a part, and they are the intended referent of the second exception, for they are separated from Paradise during the days of their punishment. And permanence from a specific starting point is invalidated by considering the beginning, just as it is invalidated by considering the end. Do you not see that if you say: "I stayed in the garden on Thursday except for three hours," it is possible that the time in which there was non-staying is from its beginning and from its end. And these, though they were wretched through their disobedience, have been made happy through their faith. And one should not say: then according to this, His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Among them is a wretched one and a happy one﴾ is not a valid division, because a condition of it is that the attribute of each division be negated from the other two, for that condition, where the separation is real or prevents combination. Here what is meant is that the people of the standing place do not leave the two divisions, and that their condition is not free of happiness and wretchedness, and that does not prevent the combining of the two matters in one person under two considerations. End of quote. This is what al-Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) mentioned and preferred, and al-Qadi preferred it too. It was objected that there is no indication in the wording of a specific starting point, and even if it were granted, the exception requires a removal from the ruling of abiding, which is inevitably after entering. So how can it be invalidated by what preceded it? Especially since His saying, exalted is He: "in the Garden" has preceded. Then it was said: if you say, the time of their dispersal from the standing place is the beginning, and that is the last day that comes. I say: if he claims that the beginning is from the beginning of that time, it is possible that the indication of the wording to it be granted, but it does not help, because all of them in the two abodes are not abiding on this assumption. As for making the beginning of the period from its end, that is not so. And also because the opposition of the two rulings indicates the opposition of the two divisions in the sense of preventing the whole absolutely. It was answered (after closing one's eyes to what in that is a departure from the etiquette of debate) that the starting point of the time of the abiding of the people of Paradise is from the time of the entry of the people of the Fire into the Fire, and what indicates this is the unity of the measure of the two abidings, which is ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, for it indicates the time of their abiding, and there is no unity with difference in the starting point. And the exception from the ruling of abiding from a specific starting point is by removal from the ruling of entering that which the abiding therein necessarily includes.

The summary of the meaning according to this is that all the blessed abide in Paradise from the time the people of the Fire enter the Fire, except the disobedient among them, whom Allah, glorified is He, willed to enter the Fire for a specific period, the knowledge of which is with Him, majestic and exalted is He. And what has been mentioned about the opposition of the two rulings, if what is meant is their opposition in the sense of preventing combination, then there is no opposition between them in this sense, since they combine in the disobedient; and if what is meant is absolute opposition, then there is no indication of the opposition of the two divisions in that sense. End of quote.

It is not hidden from the fair-minded what in that statement is artificiality and departure from the apparent sense, and the defense of it by what has been mentioned does not benefit it at all.

It was said: it is an exception from the preceding pronoun, except that the ruling is abiding in the torment of the Fire. Likewise it is said of what follows: the ruling in it is abiding in the bliss of Paradise, and the people of the Fire are sometimes transferred from it to the zamharir (bitter cold) and other punishments. Likewise the people of Paradise enjoy what is higher than it, such as union with the presence of holiness and attainment of the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, which is greater, and what He bestows upon them beyond the reward of Paradise, of which none knows the reality except Him, glorified and exalted is He. To this al-Zamakhshari went, drawing the sword of rebellion and Mu'tazilism, and al-Tibi (al-Tibi) refuted it and extended his discussion on that.

The author of al-Kashf said: that is clearly so regarding the people of the Fire, for they are transferred from the heat of the Fire to the cold of the zamharir. The rejection that "the Fire" is an expression for the abode of punishment does not apply, for we do not deny that "the Fire" is used for it by way of predominance. As for the claim of such predominance so that the original meaning is abandoned, no. Do you not see His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿A fire blazing﴾, ﴿a fire whose fuel is people and stones﴾? And how many, how many. As for the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, toward the people of Paradise while they are in it, it refuses the exception. How? For His saying, glorified is He: ﴿abiding therein﴾ does not indicate by its apparent sense that they are blessed therein, let alone that they enjoy it exclusively, unless it is specified as the Paradise of reward and not mere grace. And specification without evidence suffices to refute it. It was objected that you could say: the original meaning was abandoned in the two verses you mentioned, which indicates it has become known from the description, and in this verse, its mention in contrast with Paradise supports that what is meant by it is the abode of punishment absolutely.

It was said: the exception is one of the most general times, and (ma) is in its original sense for what does not have reason, which is time, and the ruling is being in the Fire. The meaning: as for those who were wretched, they are in the Fire at every time after the coming of that day, except a time in which Allah, exalted is He, willed their non-being in it, and that is the time of the station of reckoning. It was objected that the disobedient believers who enter the Fire are either happy, so they must abide in Paradise in what is other than the excepted time, and that is not so; or wretched, so they must abide in the Fire, and that is contrary to the doctrine of the people of the Sunnah. Also, its being posterior to the state, while there is no place for it in the exception, is not eloquent; and the ambiguity in His, glorified is He, saying: "except what your Lord wills," and the majesty it gives, does not leave any splendor for it. It was answered: it may be said that the one who holds this restricts the wretched to the disbelievers and the happy to the pious, and the disobedient are left unmentioned here, so no objection is raised against him whether he is Sunni or Mu'tazili, for he has agreed with the custom of his nature. And what follows is answered by denial. It was said: the matter of the exception is what I know, except that the excepted is the duration of their stay in this world or in the barzakh (intermediate state). It disregards "the day when it comes." The meaning is that they are in the Fire during all periods of their existence, except a period in which Allah, exalted is He, willed their stay in this world or in the barzakh; and what is meant together with the period of the standing place, since they are not in the Fire during its time either, unless by the Fire is meant the torment, in which case no accompaniment is needed. But it is objected that they are punished in the barzakh too, unless it is said: that is not counted, for it is a punishment that is not complete, since their life in it is not complete. And it was objected to it with what was objected to the preceding view, and it was answered: that is only objectionable if the excepted in the second exception is that same time excepted in the first exception, and that is not granted. Let the excepted be the time of their stay in the Fire together with that time excepted in the first verse, for what is excepted does not contain anything indicating the specification of a time so that it is impossible to add to it. And this, as you see, is so.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 107 (part 2 of 2):

It has also been said that it is an exception from His words, glorified is He: ﴿For them therein is groaning and wailing﴾. It was objected that this counterpart (al-muqabil) does not apply here, and the difficulty remains. It was answered that the purpose is to mention what the verse may admit, and that consistency (al-itirad) is not required. This was criticized by saying that the purpose is only to show the weakness of this view, and that lack of consistency is sufficient weakness.

It has also been said that "illa" (except) means "siwa" (other than), as in your saying: "You owe me two thousand, other than (illa) the thousand that was..." meaning "other than it." This is transmitted from al-Zajjaj, al-Farra', and al-Sijawandi. The meaning is: other than what your Lord wills of the increase that has no end, beyond the duration of the heavens and the earth. The exception in this case is disjunctive (munqati', i.e., an exception not of the same kind as what precedes it).

It is also possible that they meant that "illa" in the sense of "ghayr" (other than) is an attribute of what precedes it, so the meaning is: they will abide therein for the length of the heavens and the earth, other than what God the Exalted wills of what has no end. The weakness of this view is that it requires taking "the heavens and the earth" to refer to these two known bodies, without regard to the meaning of eternity, and this is corrupt.

It has also been said that "illa" means "wa" (and), i.e., "and what your Lord wills, in addition to that." As evidence that it can mean "wa," the following line is cited:

"Every brother is parted from his brother, by the life of your father, except the two Farqadan."

It is objected that this view is rejected by the grammarians (al-nuhat).

The allamah al-Tibi said: "The truth from which there is no escape is that 'ma' should be understood as referring to a person (man), for the sake of describing the one who is shown mercy (al-marhumiyyah). And ﴿abiding﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) of anticipation (muqaddarah) from the pronoun of settling, i.e., in the Fire. The meaning is: As for those who are wretched, they are in the Fire, intending to abide therein, except the one shown mercy whom God the Exalted wills not to remain in it eternally. So this indicates that he will not remain therein at all, or that he will remain therein without eternity. The conditions of the disobedient are on this course, as is known from the texts. In this there is an indication that their removal is by sheer mercy of God the Exalted, and this fits His words, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Effecter of what He intends﴾." It is objected that this does not apply to the counterpart except through the interpretation of the Imam, and what is in that has already been discussed; or by making it part of the basic ruling, which requires that they not enter at all. And if it is interpreted as "those who are meant to abide," then if it is made an exception from "those who are meant to abide," it does not hold. And from His words, exalted is He: ﴿in the Fire﴾, it follows that they would have no entry at all. The indication of "ma" by its vagueness is either to exalt or to belittle, and this does not fit the context.

It has been said, and it has been said. The more apt view is that the exception in both places is based on supposition and hypothesis. So the meaning of "illa ma sha'a" (except what He wills) is: if He wills. That is, if it were supposed that God the Exalted willed to remove them from the Fire or from the Garden at some time, that would be an exception from the period of their abiding. But this does not happen, because of the decisive evidence that it does not occur.

[p. 145]

This, as al-Tibi said, is of the style of ﴿until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ and ﴿They will not taste death therein, except the first death﴾. He mentioned that he came across a text from before al-Zajjaj that agrees with this.

In al-Ma'alim, from al-Farra' also, there is something in agreement with this, where it is transmitted from him that he said: "This is an exception that God, glorified is He, made, and He will not do it, like your saying: 'By God, I will surely strike you, except if I see otherwise,' while your determination is to strike him." Following closely what was transmitted earlier from some of them: the meaning is, "If He willed, He would have removed them, but He does not will it, because He, glorified is He, has decreed for them abiding."

In al-Bahr, from Ibn Attiyya, citing some who hold a similar view, he said: "As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, it has been said about it that it is in the manner of the exception that the Law has encouraged the use of in every speech. It is like His words, majestic and exalted is He: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if God wills, in security﴾, an exception in an obligatory matter. This exception is in the sense of a condition, as if it were said: 'If your Lord wills.' It does not need to be described as contiguous or disjunctive."

Among those who went this way also is the excellent scholar Mirza Jan al-Shirazi in his glosses on the tafsir of al-Qadi. He stated that it is of the kind of conditioning on impossibilities (al-ta'liq bi'l-mahal), until one proves the impossibility of the conditioned, and it is like asserting a thing with a clear proof. This is one of the views mentioned by al-Sayyid al-Murtada in his Durar.

The explanation of the first exception as a condition was transmitted by Ibn Mardawayh from Jabir, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned in al-Durr al-Manthur.

Perhaps the point of this exception, as has been said, is to guide the servants to entrust their affairs to Him, majestic is His glory, and to inform them that these matters are bound to His will, exalted is He. He does what He wills and decrees what He intends; no one has a right over Him, and nothing is obligatory upon Him, as the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Effecter of what He intends﴾.

Some of the learned have mentioned that its benefit is to prevent the assumption that abiding is a matter obligatory upon Him, exalted is He, which He cannot abrogate, as the Mu'tazilah held. He, exalted is He, informed of it with emphasis. According to this view, the ones described as "wretched" are the disbelievers only, for they are the ones truly deserving of this name. And the ones described as "happy" are all the believers, obedient and disobedient. Thus the division in His words, glorified is He: ﴿Then among them is the wretched and the happy﴾ is a real separation. His words, exalted is He: ﴿then in the Garden﴾ do not contradict this, because it is true of entering in general.

In al-Kashf afterward, it was transmitted that the exception is of the kind of ﴿until the camel passes through﴾. If you say: the implication of al-Zamakhshari's point about the abiding of the sinners has been achieved, I say: No, because they are among the happy, and the verse requires the abiding of the happy, and that after their entry therein without doubt, and it does not deny their being in the Fire before their entry into the Garden. For the wording does not require that they, meaning the happy, all enter the Garden together, how could it, when the decisive proof indicates their entry one after another, according to their ranks. End of quote. So reflect, for the verse is among the difficult ones.

As for why the pronoun was not used in ﴿Indeed, your Lord...﴾, etc., as is the apparent expectation, it is to express awe and to increase the affirmation. As for the lam in ﴿li-ma﴾, it has been said to be for emphasis, i.e., "the Effecter of what He intends." Nothing resists Him in any way whatsoever.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 108:

﴿As for those who are made happy, they will be in the Garden, abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills﴾. The discussion of this is as you know, except that here it does not mention for them joy and delight as it mentioned for the people of the Fire: ﴿For them therein will be groaning and wailing﴾; because the context is one of warning and admonition. The reading of ﴿suʿidū﴾ (were made happy) in the passive voice is that of Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs, and it is attributed to Ibn Mas'ud, Talha ibn Musarrif, Ibn Wabbab and al-A'mash. The majority of the Seven read (saʿidū) in the active voice. ʿAli ibn Sulayman chose this, and he used to say: "How strange of al-Kisa'i, how did he read (suʿidū) despite his knowledge of Arabic! This is strange of him, for he read only what was authentically transmitted to him, and he did not read by opinion, nor did he stand alone in this." It is narrated from him that he argued for it by their saying: "Mas'ud," and this was countered by saying that there is no proof in it, since it is possible that he was (mas'ud) in it. He also mentioned that al-Farra' reported that the Hudhayl say: "saʿidahu Allah ta'ala" meaning "asʿadahu." Al-Jawhari said: "saʿida (with kasra) so he is saʿid, like their saying: salima so he is salim, and saʿida so he is mas'ud." Abu Nasr ʿAbd al-Rahim al-Qushayri said: "It has come: saʿidahu Allah ta'ala so he is mas'ud, and as'adahu Allah ta'ala so he is mus'ad." How subtle is the allusion in (shaqu wa-saʿidu): on the reading of the active voice in the first, and the passive voice in the second. Whoever perceives this, let him praise God Most High, and whoever does not perceive it, let him blame none but himself. ﴿A gift not cut off﴾: that is, not severed from them nor interrupted. Its verbal noun is al-jadhdh, and it has come as jadhadhtu and jadadtu with the dhal marked and the dal, as Ibn Qutayba said, and with the marked dhal is more common. (ʿAṭāʾan) is in the accusative as a verbal noun from the sense of the sentence, because His saying, glorified is He: ﴿so as for those in the Garden, abiding therein﴾ implies giving and bestowal, so it is as if it were said: He gives them a gift; and it is either an ism al-masdar which is the giving, or a verbal noun with the augmentations removed, like His saying Exalted is He: ﴿and made you grow from the earth a growth﴾. It has also been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative from the implied object of the will, or as a specification; for the attribution of the will of exit to God Most High may be on the basis of a gift that is cut off, and on the basis of a gift that is not cut off, so it removes the ambiguity regarding the attribution. Perhaps the accusative as a verbal noun is preferable, and it seems this was brought for emphasis and exaggeration regarding perpetuity, and to repel what might be imagined from the apparent exception being discontinuous. It has also been said that this is to show that the reward of the people of the Garden, which is either the very entry or what is like a clear necessary consequence of it, does not end; so it is known from this that the exception is not to indicate discontinuity as in the case of punishment, but to indicate the succession of blessings and good pleasure from God Most High; or to show the deficiency on the part of the origin. For this reason the composition differentiates between the perpetuity in that He completed the first with His saying glorified is He: ﴿Indeed your Lord is the doer of what He intends﴾ to indicate that He blesses some of those whom He punishes and keeps others as He wills and chooses; and the second with His saying Exalted is He (a gift) etc., as an explanation that His beneficence does not end. Some people have held to the beginning of the verse, that no one remains in the Fire, and they did not say this about the Garden; and they strengthened their claim by what Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Hasan who said: Umar said: "If the people of the Fire remained in the Fire as long as the sands of ʿAlij, there would still be a day for them in which they would come out." And by what Ishaq ibn Rahawayh reported from Abu Hurayra who said: "There will come upon Hell a day in which no one will remain therein," and he recited ﴿As for those who are wretched﴾ the verse. Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibrahim who said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more hopeful for the people of the Fire than this verse (﴿abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills﴾)." He said: Ibn Mas'ud said: "There will certainly come upon it a time in which its doors will clatter." Ibn Jarir reported from al-Sha'bi who said: "Hell is the swiftest of the two abodes in building and the swiftest of them in ruin," along with other reports.

Ibn al-Jawzi explicitly declared some of these to be fabricated, such as the report from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs: "There will come upon Hell a day in which no son of Adam will be in it, its doors clattering like the doors of the monotheists." Some interpreted these reports, and something of the discussion regarding this has passed. You know that the eternity of the disbelievers is among what the Muslims have agreed upon, and the dissenter is not considered; and the definitive texts are more than can be counted, and none of these many reports can withstand one of them; and there is no proof in the verse for what the dissenter says, in light of the aspects you have learned regarding it; and there is no need to claim abrogation in it, as was narrated from al-Suddi; rather, it is hardly sound to say abrogation in such a matter. It has been mentioned that the verse contains the form of the plural together with the division and classification. As for the plural, it is in His saying Exalted is He: ﴿On the day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission﴾, for the word "soul," as has been established, is general, being indefinite in the context of negation. As for the distinction, it is in His saying: (﴿So among them is the wretched and the happy﴾). As for the classification, it is in His saying glorified is He: (﴿As for those who are wretched﴾ etc.). A parallel to this is the saying of al-Sharif al-Qayrawani:

To those of varying needs a gathering at his gate: for this one there is an art, and for that one there is an art. So for the one of low station, the highest; for the destitute, wealth; for the sinner, reproach; and for the fearful, security.

From here the state of the two fa's becomes known: the fa' of (fa-minhum) and the fa' of (fa-amma) etc. It has been said: In the departure from "as for the wretched, he will be in the Fire, abiding therein" etc., and "as for the happy, or the one made happy, he will be in the Garden, abiding therein" etc., to what is in the sublime composition, there is an indication of the precedence of this wretchedness and happiness, and that this is a matter already concluded, as is shown by what Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i reported from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came out to us with two books in his hand. He said: 'Do you know what these two books are?' We said: 'No, O Messenger of Allah, will you not inform us?' He said to the one in his right hand: 'This is a book from the Lord of the worlds containing the names of the people of the Garden, their fathers and their tribes, then it is summed up to the last of them, so nothing is added to them nor is anything taken from them ever.' Then he said to the one in his left: 'This is a book from the Lord of the worlds containing the names of the people of the Fire, their fathers and their tribes, then it is summed up to the last of them, so nothing is added to them nor is anything taken from them ever.' His companions said: 'Then what is the deed for, O Messenger of Allah, if the matter has already been concluded?' He said: 'Be upright and draw near, for the companion of the Garden is sealed with the deed of the people of the Garden, however he acts; and the companion of the Fire is sealed with the deed of the people of the Fire, however he acts.' Then the Prophet ﷺ said with his hand, and he threw them away, and said: 'Your Lord has finished with the servants: a group in the Garden and a group in the blaze.'" And it has come in a hadith: "The wretched is he who is wretched in his mother's belly, and the happy is he who is happy in his mother's belly." Some interpreted that as the matter becoming manifest to the angel entrusted with the drop; otherwise the matter is before that. Others interpreted the mother as the scientific establishment (of knowledge) from which the known becomes manifest into this external existence, and this is a kind of interpretation, as is not hidden. Upon reflection, what does not contradict this allusion is what al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as good, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Mardawayh and others reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When (﴿So among them is the wretched and the happy﴾) was revealed, I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, then on what do we work, on something already concluded, or on something not yet concluded?' He said: 'Rather, on something already concluded and the pens have run with it, O ʿUmar; but each is made easy for what he was created for.'" It has been said: The apparent here was to express the verb in the present tense, but it expressed it in the past to indicate the certainty of occurrence; and it brought the relative pronoun in the plural to notify that what is meant by "wretched" and "happy" is a wretched group and a happy group; and it did not say "wretches" and "happy ones" because the singular is more suited to what precedes. It has also been said: The singular at first is to indicate that each group, in terms of its being characterized by wretchedness or happiness, is like one thing; and the plural second, because the entry of each group into the Garden and the Fire is not all at once but group after group and troop after troop; and there are witnesses to this from the Book and the Sunna.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 109:**

﴿So do not be in doubt﴾ means: in suspicion. The *fa'* (ﻓ) here expresses the consequence of the prohibition upon what has been narrated of the stories and of the worldly and otherworldly outcomes made clear within them. That is, "Do not be in doubt after what has been made clear to you has been made clear." ﴿about what these worship﴾ means: about the worship of these polytheists, that it is misguidance which leads to the same fate that befell those before them, whose evil end in worshipping I have related to you. *Min* (مِنْ) in *famin* is for the starting point (ابتدائية, *ibtida'iyyah*). It is also permitted that it means *fi* (in). The *ma* (ما) is a verbal-noun particle (مصدرية, *masdariyyah*). It is also permitted that it is a relative pronoun (موصولة, *mawsulah*), and in the speech there is an omitted *mudaf* (مضاف, possessive noun), meaning: "about the state of what they worship, that it neither harms nor benefits," since there is no sense in doubt regarding their own selves. ﴿They worship only as their forefathers worshipped before⟩ is a resumptive explanatory clause (استئناف بياني, *isti'naf bayani*) which in meaning serves as the reason for the prohibition against doubt. The exception (الاستثناء, *al-istithna'*) is either from an implied verbal noun or from an omitted object, meaning: they and their forefathers are equal in polytheism; they worship no worship except like the worship of their forefathers, or they worship nothing except the like of what those (forefathers) worshipped of idols. The sense of their forefathers' fate has reached you, and because of this the like of it will befall them, since similarity in causes necessitates similarity in effects. The meaning of ﴿as he worshipped﴾ (كَما يَعْبُدُ) is "as they had worshipped," so the verb was omitted, the word *qabl* (قَبْلُ, "before") indicating it. It seems that choosing this is to indicate that this was a continuous custom for them.

﴿And indeed We will give them﴾ meaning these disbelievers ﴿their portion⟩, their share of the punishment, as We gave their forefathers their shares, or of the provision. In that case it is an excuse for the delay of the punishment from them despite the existence of what necessitates it. In this there is an indication of God Most High's abundant grace and generosity, which is clear, in that He did not cut off their provision despite their worship of other than Him. Regarding the expression "portion," according to the first interpretation, there is mockery, because it is something sought and desired, whereas punishment is far removed from that. The explanation of it as mentioned has been related from Ibn Zayd, and "provision" from Abu al-'Aliyah. From Ibn 'Abbas it is related that what is meant is what has been decreed of good or evil. Ibn Muhaysin recited *lamuwaffuhum* (لَمُوَفُّوهُمْ) with a lightened form from *awfa*. ﴿Without diminution⟩ is an emphasizing circumstantial clause (حال مؤكدة, *hal mu'akkidah*) referring to "portion," like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then you turned back in retreat﴾. Its benefit is to repel the suspicion of figurative usage. This is the view of the scholar al-Tibi, who said: "It is the truth."

In the *al-Kashshaf* it is said that this circumstantial clause came regarding the portion that is given in full, because it is possible that it is given while deficient, and it is possible that it is given while complete. Do you not see that you say: "I gave him half his right" (وفَّيْتُهُ شَطْرَ حَقِّهِ), and "a third of his right," and "his right complete and deficient." End of quote. Abu Hayyan criticized it, saying: this is a fallacy, because when it is said "I gave him half his right," the giving occurred in the half, and likewise "a third of his right," and the meaning is "I gave him the half or the third complete, I did not diminish from it anything." As for your saying "I gave him his right complete," the circumstantial clause in it is emphasizing, because giving entails completion. As for your saying "I gave him his right deficient," it is incorrect due to contradiction. End of quote.

Ibn al-Munir said: this is an error, because giving entails the non-diminution of what is given, whether complete or partial. So your saying "I gave him half of his right" entails the non-diminution of the half that was given. Thus the question about the reason for the accusative of this circumstantial clause still stands. The more correct view is to say: "giving" (التوفية) has been used in the sense of "bestowing," just as "taking in full" (التوفي) has been used in the sense of "taking." Whoever says "I gave so-and-so his right" would be fitting to emphasize it with His saying: ﴿without diminution﴾. End of quote.

In *al-Kashf* I say: in attaching "giving" to "half," although the whole is his right, that which indicates its intended meaning, since there is no difference between your saying "half his right" and "his right halved." So it is permissible to say "I gave him his portion halved" and "his portion deficient," and the emphasis is fitting and shows who the one in error is, so reflect.

Page 148

And We certainly gave Moses the Book, that is, the Torah, ﴿but it was disputed over﴾, that is, concerning the Book and whether it was from Allah, the Exalted. Some people believed in it and others denied it. So do not be concerned about your people's disagreement regarding what We have given you of the Qur'an. And their saying: ﴿Why has a treasure not been sent down to him, or an angel not come with him?﴾ and their claim (You have invented it).

It is permissible for the pronoun (ḍamīr) to refer back to Moses, though this is contrary to the apparent meaning, if the dispute about him, peace be upon him, over whether he was a prophet or not, entailed a dispute over whether his Book was from Allah, the Exalted, or not. It was also said that, on this interpretation, the particle "fī" (in) carries the meaning of "ʿalā" (against), so that the meaning is: his people disputed against him and were obstinate, just as your people did with you. ﴿And had it not been for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord﴾, namely the word of decree to delay the punishment until a known term, in accordance with the wisdom that calls for that, ﴿the matter would have been decided between them﴾, that is, the judgment would have been carried out between the disputing parties among your people, by sending down the punishment that the falsifiers deserve, so that they would be distinguished from the righteous. In al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit), it is said that the apparent reading is that the pronoun refers to the people of Moses. It was said: "This is not the case."

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "Its reference to both groups is, in my view, better." It was objected that His saying, glorified is He, ﴿And indeed, all﴾ and so on, is apparent in generalising after specifying. There is room for debate on this. But in my view, the first interpretation is preferable. ﴿And indeed they﴾, that is, and indeed the disbelievers of your people, the pronoun being intended to refer to some of those to whom it returns, with the pronoun "bayna-hum" (between them) used because there is no risk of confusion, ﴿are certainly in grave doubt﴾ ﴿concerning it﴾, that is, concerning the Qur'an, even though it has not been mentioned explicitly. For the mention of the giving of the Book of Moses and the occurrence of disagreement over it, especially in the context of consolation, calls out to him in an unmistakable way.

Page 149

It was also said that the pronoun refers to the threat implied by the discourse. ﴿Disquieting﴾, that is, causing unease and doubt. It was also permitted that it be from "arāba", meaning he became one who has doubt.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 111 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Wa-inna kullan﴾ The tanwin is a substitute (iwad) for the genitive noun that has been omitted, as is well known regarding the tanwin of kull (each/all) according to some grammarians (nuhat). It has also been said that it is tanwin of tamkin (nunation of nominal status), but this does not prevent the omitted genitive noun from being understood as well, i.e., "and indeed all of the differing ones, the believers and the disbelievers."

Muqatil said: "By it is meant the disbelievers of this community." ﴿Lamma layuwaffiyannahum rabbuka a'malahum﴾, i.e., your Lord will recompense them for their deeds. The lam in ﴿layuwaffiyannahum﴾ falls in the answer to an oath, meaning: "By God, He will surely pay them in full." The (lamma) with tashdid (emphatic doubling), together with the tashdid of inna, is the reading of Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, Hafs, and Abu Ja'far. The derivation of the verse according to this reading is problematic, to the extent that al-Mubarrad said: "It is a grammatical error (lahn)," and this is a boldness, given the mutawatir (widely transmitted) status of the reading. Would that he had said what al-Kisa'i said: "I do not know what the aspect of this reading is." They differed in its derivation. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the original form of this (lamma) is lamma with tanwin, and it has been read so; then it was made indeclinable on the pattern fa'la, and it is derived from lamamtuhu (I gathered it) when you gathered it. It cannot be said that it is (lamman) with tanwin, pausal with an alif, and the connected reading treated as the pause, because, as Abu Hayyan said, that occurs only in poetry. This derivation is deemed unlikely for the reason that the pattern fa'la is not known from lamma, and because whoever pronounces fa'la with imalah (inclination) would have to incline it, and no one has inclined it by consensus, and because the analogy would have required it to be written with a ya, and it was not written with it. The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the verse on this view will be explained in what follows, God willing.

It has been said that (lamma) is the light (mukhaffafah) form which was doubled in pause, and then the connected reading was treated as the pause. In that case the i'rab is what you will also learn, God willing, and this is very remote. It has been said that it means illa (except), and illa may occur as a superfluous particle, as in the verse: "I swore an oath, not one of double meaning, an oath of a man, except by it, not sinning." So it is not far-fetched that (lamma) in the sense of it is superfluous, and this is a weak view built on a weak view regarding illa. From al-Mazini: that the doubled inna here is negating, and (lamma) in the sense of illa is not superfluous, and this is false, because doubling the negating inna is not known, and because kull is in the accusative, while the negating particle does not put into the accusative. Al-Hawfi said: inna is in its own sense, and (lamma) means illa, as in your saying: "I beseech you by God, except that you do it." Abu 'Ali weakened this by saying that this lamma does not leave the oath preceding it, and this is not as stated, for it does leave it. Abu Hayyan said what weakens it, rather nullifies it: the position is not one where illa is admissible. Do you not see that if you said "inna Zaydan illa darabta," it would not be an Arabic construction? It has also been said that this lamma is originally li-man ma, composed of the lam and the relative or qualifying (mawsulah or mawsufah) and the superfluous ma, so the nun was changed into mim for assimilation, three mims gathered, the middle one was deleted, and then the two identical mims were assimilated. This is the view of al-Mahdawi. Al-Farra' said, and a group followed him, among them Nasr al-Shirazi: its original is li-man ma with the preposition bi-man, and ma as relative or qualifying; in both possibilities it refers to one who has reason, so it is treated as similar to the earlier view. This original form occurs in the verse: "And I am for whoever strikes the ram a blow upon its head, so that the tongue comes out of the mouth." The lam, on these two views, is said to be a preparatory lam for the oath (muwatti'ah lil-qasam). It is transmitted from al-Farisi, and this is contrary to what is well known from the grammarians, that the preparatory lam is the one that enters upon a conditional preceding the answer of an oath, placed before it verbally or by implication, so as to signal that the answer belongs to it, as in: "By God, if you honour me, I will honour you." What the lam enters upon is not the answer of the oath, but what comes after it. His view, like that of al-Akhfash, is that its entry upon the conditional is not obligatory; rather it indicates that what follows is suitable to serve as the answer to an oath in general. It has also been said that it is the lam entering the predicate of inna, and man as a relative or qualifying, on the first of the two options, is the predicate, while the oath and its answer form a relative clause or qualifier. The meaning: "And indeed all of them, for those who [or for a creation], by God, your Lord will surely pay them in full." On the second option, the min and its genitive are in the position of predicate of inna, and the oath sentence with its answer is likewise a relative clause or qualifier, but with lamma. The meaning: "And indeed all of them are among those who [or among a creation], by God, your Lord will surely pay them in full." Al-Bahr said: these two views are very weak, and the deletion of the nun of man is not known, nor is the deletion of the nun of min the preposition, except in poetry when it meets the definite article or similar, not assimilated, as in their saying "milmal" meaning "min al-mal." In the commentary of al-Qadi and others: the original is li-man bi-min the preposition, the nun was changed into mim, three mims gathered, and the first was deleted. But in this too there is what there is. Al-Mughni says the deletion of this mim for lightness is not established. Al-Damamini said: how can the deletion be justified by heaviness, when eight mims are gathered in His saying, "upon nations from those with you" (Q 11:48)? Al-Farra' cited, in support of his view, the poet's words:

"And indeed when he issues the command, he directs it, when he is exhausted, his routes are guided by the path."

Some claimed that lamma means "when" (hina), and that there is an ellipsis in the speech, i.e., "when they have done what they did," or something similar. Ellipsis is frequent in speech, as in His saying:

"When you say: 'Go, indeed Layla, perhaps she...' a camel ran beyond Layla, its horn curved and broken."

He meant: "perhaps she will meet me or join me" or something like that. This is, as you see, far-fetched. Abu Hayyan, after mentioning that these explanations are among those which the sanctity of revelation is exalted above, said: "There had appeared to me an aspect accordant with the rules of Arabic and free from artificiality, namely that this lamma is the jussive (jazimah), whose verb is elided, the meaning indicating it, as they elided it in their saying: 'I approached Medina, and lamma' (i.e., lamma yadkhulha) meaning 'and not yet did I enter it.' The estimate here is: 'And indeed all of them, lamma (not yet) will be diminished from the recompense of their deeds,' and this is indicated by 'your Lord will pay them their deeds.'" I had believed I was not the first to this until I verified that Ibn al-Hajib had been granted success in this. I then saw in the book al-Tahrir a quotation from him that he said: "This lamma is the jussive, its verb elided because of indication, and the elision is established in their saying: 'I went out, and lamma,' and 'I travelled, and lamma,' and similar, and it is eloquent and sound. So the estimate is: 'lamma they will not leave off,' or 'lamma they will not neglect,' and the detailing of both groups and their recompense indicates it." Then he said: "I know of no aspect more similar to this, though souls find it unlikely since its like has not occurred in the Qur'an."

Your attention is drawn to the fact that it is preferable to estimate: lamma yuwaffu a'malahum, i.e., up to now they have not been paid in full, and they will be. Ibn Hisham went to this view, because the earlier estimates, according to the well-known meaning of lamma, entail that they will be diminished in the recompense of their deeds and that they will be left and neglected, and that is far from being intended, which is evident. This is the aspect of consideration which Ibn Hisham meant when he objected to Ibn al-Hajib, saying: "In this estimate there is consideration."

Al-Jalabi said: its aspect is that the indicator of the elided item precedes it by much, and that the elided item is not from the wording of what is said to indicate it, and this is not that. Then the preferred view among many exegetes is that of al-Farra'. Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read inna and lamma with lightness (takhfif). This reading is taken to mean that inna, though lightened, is still operative, considering the original in operation, which is its resemblance to the verb; the loss of verbal resemblance does no harm. This is the view of the Basrans. Abu Hayyan mentioned that their position is that it is permissible for it to operate when lightened, but rarely, except with a pronoun, so it is not permitted except if it occurs in poetry. It is transmitted from Sibawayh among them that he said: "The trustworthy one informed me that he heard some Arabs say: 'Inna 'Amran lamunṭaliq' (indeed 'Amr is departing)." Some of the grammarians claimed that the kasra-initial inna, when lightened, does not operate, and they interpreted the verse by making kull accusative by a supposed verb, i.e., "in an ra kullan mathalan" (if I see all, for example), and this is said by al-Bahr to be the view of the Kufans; and in al-Irtishaf: the Kufans do not permit lightening of the kasra-initial inna, neither unoperative nor operative; and some mentioned something similar, and that what the Basrans count as lightened the Kufans count as negating, excepting al-Kisa'i, who agreed with the Basrans, and their view in this is the truth. Here kull is its subject, and the lam is the one entering the predicate of inna, and ma is a relative, the predicate of inna, and the oath sentence with its answer is a relative clause. This is the view of al-Farra'. Al-Tabari preferred his view regarding the lam, and regarding ma that it is an indefinite qualifying noun, and the sentence is its qualifier, i.e., "and indeed all, a creation or a group whose deed is paid in full." Abu 'Ali preferred for the lam what they both preferred, and made the oath sentence the predicate, with ma superfluous between the two lams; its superfluity is known in various places.

Abu Bakr from 'Asim read inna lightened and lamma doubled, while al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr read the reverse. The explanation of the two readings is not hidden from one who knows well what was mentioned earlier regarding the explanation of the two readings.

Ubayy and al-Hasan (with a variant from him), Aban ibn Taghlib read: wa-an kullun lamma, with an lightened and kull nominative, lamma doubled. It is explained as: an is negating, kull is the subject, the oath sentence with its answer is its predicate, and lamma means illa, i.e., "no one but swore by God that He will surely pay them in full." Abu 'Ubaydah denied that lamma comes in the sense of illa in Arabic speech. Al-Farra' said: to make it here in the sense of illa is a view we do not know. The Arabs have indeed said with an oath by God: "Lamma qumta 'anna wa-illa qumta 'anna" (when you rose from us, or else you rose from us). But apart from that, we have not heard it coming in the sense of illa, neither in prose nor in poetry. It follows for the speaker that he must permit "qama al-nasu lamma Zaydan" (the people stood, except Zayd), and there is no regard for their denial of both. The mutawatir reading in "wa-in kullun lamma jami'un ladayna muhdarun" and "in kullu nafsin lamma 'alayha hafizun" establishes what they both denied.

Al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and al-Kisa'i explicitly stated the occurrence of that. Whoever memorized it is a proof against whoever did not memorize it, and that the Arabs restricted its occurrence in that manner to certain constructions does no harm, for many a thing is restricted to one construction and not to what resembles it.

Al-Zuhri and Sulayman ibn Arqam read: wa-inna kullan lamma, with the mim doubled and tanwin. Those transmitting from them did not mention the doubling or lightening of inna. In this reading lamma is a verbal noun from their saying "lamamtu al-shay'" when you gathered it, as already mentioned, and its accusative is as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun of the object in "layuwaffiyannahum," according to Abu al-Baqa', who weakened it.

Abu 'Ali said: it is an attribute of kull, and it is to be estimated as a genitive of an indefinite noun, so that the attribute by an indefinite may be sound, and the verbal noun in that case is in the sense of the passive participle. Al-Zamakhshari, regarding the meaning of the verse on this reading, said that "and indeed all gathered (malmumin), in the sense of 'gathered' (majmu'in)," as if it were said: "and indeed all together," like His saying, "So the angels prostrated, all of them together" (Q 15:30). Al-Tibi took this as an inclination toward the view of emphasis (ta'kid).

Ibn Jinni said: it is accusative with layuwaffiyannahum, on the pattern of their saying "qiyaman la-aqumanna" (standing, I will surely stand), and the estimate is "a comprehensive full payment of their deeds"; "layuwaffiyannahum." The predicate of inna in that is the oath sentence and its answer.

Abu Hatim transmitted that in the codex of Ubayy it reads: "wa-inna min kullin illa layuwaffiyannahum," and it is explained on the basis that an is negating and min is superfluous.

Al-A'mash recited something similar to this, except that he omitted مِن, and this is the reading (ḥarf) of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him. The meaning is clear.

It has been said: this sentence contains several emphatic particles: أنّ (inna, "indeed"), the lam of emphasis (اللّام), ما when it is used as a superfluous (zā'idah) particle, the oath (القَسَم), and the energetic nūn (نونُ التَّأكيد, the nūn of emphasis). This is for the sake of intensifying the promise to the obedient and the warning to the disobedient. ﴿Indeed, He is Acquainted with what they do.﴾ That is, He, glorified is He, knows perfectly every deed that each individual of the differing people does, whether good or evil, such that nothing of its great or minute aspects is hidden from Him.

It has been said that this sentence is an affirmation of the promise and the warning, for since He, glorified is He, knows all that is known, He knows the measures of obedience and disobedience and what each individual deserves of reward in accordance with wisdom. At that point, the giving to each one who is due his right becomes possible: if it is good, then good; if it is evil, then evil.

[Page 152]

Ibn Hurmuz recited (تَعْمَلُونَ, "you do") as an iltifāt (a shift from the third person to the second person, from the absent to the addressed).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 112:

﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded﴾. When Allah had explained the matter of those who differ regarding monotheism (tawhid) and prophethood, and had extensively elaborated the promise and the threat, He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to be steadfast in the same manner in which he had been commanded. This requires that he (ﷺ) was commanded by another revelation, even if it was not recited, as many have said. The apparent meaning is that this is a command to persist in steadfastness (istiqamah), which is adherence to the straight path (al-manhaj al-mustaqim), the middle course between excess (ifrat) and deficiency (tafrit). It is a comprehensive phrase that covers everything related to knowledge, action, and all other moral conduct. It therefore includes beliefs and deeds shared by him (ﷺ) and all the believers, and the matters specific to him, peace be upon him, such as conveying the rulings, carrying out the duties of prophethood, bearing the burdens of the message, and other things. They have said: the middle course between excess and deficiency, such that there is no inclination toward either side even by the breadth of a hair, is attained only by dependence upon Allah the Exalted and the complete negation of one's own power and strength. They illustrated the middle matter between these two extremes with a line that lies between the sun and the shade: it is neither sun nor shade, but a dividing matter between them. By my life, this is indeed subtle. For this reason they said: none can sustain steadfastness except one who has been strengthened by powerful witnessings (mushahadat) and radiant lights, and then has been protected by holding firmly to the truth. ﴿And had We not made you firm, you would nearly have inclined toward them a little﴾. Some of the gnostics (arifin) took the path, which is finer than a hair and sharper than a sword, as an allusion to this middle course.

Among what indicates the severity of this matter is what Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Hasan that he said: "When this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Exert yourselves, exert yourselves,' and he was not seen laughing after it."

And from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: "No verse was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that was more severe than this verse or more burdensome." Some exegetes used, to show the difficulty of steadfastness, what is widely circulated of his saying (ﷺ): "Hud has made me grey-haired." You know that the reports converge on attaching other surahs to it, even if they differ in specifying which surah is attached, as was mentioned at the beginning of the surah. In that case, the weakness of this argument is not hidden. For this reason the author of al-Kashf said: singling out Hud for this verse is not evident, since in its sister surahs there is no mention of steadfastness.

It is mentioned in Qut al-Qulub that since the beloved near one (ﷺ) was made grey-haired by the mention of distance and its people, then said: "Perhaps the more apparent view is that he, peace be upon him, was made grey-haired by the mention of the terrors of the Resurrection, and it is as if he—may my father and mother be his ransom—was witnessing a Day that makes the children grey-haired." End of quotation.

Some have singled out the vision of Abu Ali al-Shitri mentioned earlier. In response, even after accepting the soundness of the report: although the vision of the Prophet (ﷺ) is true, since Satan cannot take his form, peace be upon him, from where can one be certain of the dreamer's precision and accuracy in what he saw? Moreover, what weakens the matter of this vision and strengthens the assumption that it is not established is what Ibn Asakir narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hud and its sisters have made me grey-haired, and what was done to the nations before me." Al-Shihab mentioned what strengthens the objection of the author of al-Kashf: that in the transmitted routes on this subject, the restriction to Hud is not found, but rather its sisters are mentioned along with it, and the matter mentioned is not present in them, although it occurs in other surahs such as Al-Hamim (surahs beginning with Ha Mim). Then he mentioned that there appeared to him something that removes the difficulty. That is because the foundation of this noble surah is upon Allah the Exalted guiding His Prophet (ﷺ) to the manner of calling to Him from its beginning to its end, and to what befalls one who undertakes this lofty rank of hardships, and his bearing of what follows from it of benefits, not upon consolation, since that does not suit the context as was previously conveyed to you from the author of al-Kashf. And since this surah comprises his guidance from the beginning of his mission to its end, and this verse is a summation of it, when this surah was revealed it alarmed him by what it contained of hardships, and he feared failing to uphold its burdens. Until when he meets Allah the Exalted on the Day of Recompense, perhaps weariness touches him from being questioned about it. So the mention of the Resurrection in those surahs frightens him with its terror, due to the possibility of his falling short in what Allah the Exalted guided him to in this one. This does not contradict his infallibility, peace be upon him, or his nearness, since he is the most knowing of Allah the Exalted and the most fearful of Him. Thus fear of it reminds him of what this surah includes; so it is as if it is this surah that made him grey-haired from among them. For this reason it was mentioned first in all the narrations. And since that verse is a summation of it, it is in reality the one that made him grey-haired. So there is no contradiction between attributing the graying to those surahs, or to this surah alone as the one who did it, or to that verse, as occurred in that vision. End of quotation. Another aspect of attributing the graying to this surah will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, so let it be considered.

Some researchers went to the view that the kaf in (kama) has the meaning of "upon," as in their saying: "Be as you are," meaning "upon what you are." For this reason Ibn Atiyyah and a group said: the meaning is "be steadfast upon the Qur'an." Muqatil said: "proceed upon monotheism." Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "be steadfast in conveying the reports from Allah the Exalted with soundness of resolve." The more apparent view is to keep it general: that is, be steadfast in all that you have been commanded. The discussion about omitting such a pronoun is a common matter, and this was pointed out earlier. Some inclined to the view that the kaf is for comparison, as is apparent from it, but he said: it is in the sense of "like" (mithl), as in their saying: "Someone like you does not stint." So it is as if it was said: "be steadfast with the steadfastness you have been commanded," to avoid comparing a thing with itself. It is not hidden that this is not necessary. Among the strange things is what is reported from Abu Hayyan, that he said in his Tadhkirah: "If you say, how did this comparison of steadfastness to the command come about? I say: it is by omitting a noun, its estimated form being 'like the object of the command,' i.e., its meaning. If you say: the steadfastness commanded is the object of the command, so how can it be like it? I say: the object of the command is universal, and the commanded is particular, so the difference is established and the comparison is valid, as in your saying: 'Pray two rak'ahs as you have been commanded.'" Some went further and made the kaf mean "upon," and istaf'al for seeking, like istaghfir Allah, i.e., seek forgiveness from Him. He said: the meaning is: seek to be upright in the religion.

﴿And let those who have repented with you﴾: that is, those who repented from polytheism and believed along with you. The "with" (ma'iyyah) is in terms of what it entails, without regard to what preceded it or otherwise. It may be said that sharing in repentance suffices, and the "with" in it is with the disregard of what is repented from.
