He (ﷺ) "used to seek forgiveness from Allah the Exalted more than seventy times a day," and al-Jalabi deduced this. The "min" (in man) is as Abu Hayyan preferred. A group took it as conjoined to the hidden pronoun in ﴿wastaqim﴾ (be steadfast), and the separation by the prepositional phrase made it unnecessary to emphasize it with a detached pronoun, because the purpose is achieved by it. In the speech there is a prevalence (taghlib) of the address's ruling over the third person in the wording of the command. Many chose that it is the subject of a verb omitted, and let him be steadfast, from... etc., because a command does not take an explicit noun as subject. In that case the clause is conjoined to the first clause. Whoever went to the first view preferred it because it does not need an estimate, and he resolved the problem by saying that what is not tolerated in the head (matbu') may be tolerated in the follower (tabi').

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be in the accusative as an object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ahu), and the meaning is: be steadfast accompanied by those who repented. It has been said: this is more complete in meaning, though in wording there is some kind of separation from it.

It has also been said that it is a subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is omitted, i.e., "then let him be steadfast." He permitted that the predicate be (ma'aka) "with you," and "﴿and do not transgress﴾," i.e., do not deviate from what has been set for you by excess or deficiency, for both extremes of the course of affairs are blameworthy. That is called transgression (tughyan), which is exceeding the limit, using a stronger or more general expression so as to include the condition of all the believers along with his condition (ﷺ). It is reported from Ibn Abbas that the meaning is: do not transgress in the Qur'an by making lawful and making unlawful what you have not been commanded.

Ibn Zayd said: "do not disobey your Lord." Muqatil said: "do not mix monotheism with polytheism." Perhaps the first is better.

﴿Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do﴾: so He will recompense you for that. This is a reason (ta'lil) for the preceding command and prohibition, as if it were said: "be upright and do not transgress," because Allah the Exalted is watching your deeds, and so He will recompense you for them. It has been said that it is a completion of the command to steadfastness, but the first is better and more complete in benefit. Al-Hasan and al-A'mash read "ya'malun" (they do) with the third-person ya, and this was also reported from Isa al-Thaqafi. In the verse, as many have said, there is evidence for the obligation of following what is explicitly stated without deviation, merely by desire or by pure use of reason, for that is transgression and misguidance. As for acting according to ijtihad that follows the underlying causes (ilal) of the texts, that is from the category of steadfastness, just as one is commanded to act according to the texts that command ijtihad. The Imam (al-Razi) said: "In my view, it is not permissible to specify a text by analogy (qiyas), because when the general wording of a text indicates a ruling, it is obligatory to rule according to its requirement, due to His saying: ﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded﴾, and acting by analogy is a deviation from it. For this reason, when the Qur'an came with the command to perform ablution (wudu') and the body parts were mentioned in sequence in the wording, the sequence became obligatory in them. When the command regarding zakat came with paying camels from camels and cows from cows, it became obligatory to observe that. The same holds for everything that Allah the Exalted commanded, all of which is for the command to steadfastness as He commanded." End of quotation.

You know that imposing the order (tartib) in ablution for this reason is nothing, and it would entail imposing order on commands joined by "wa" (and), such as "establish prayer and give zakat," and likewise in such as ﴿and seek help through patience and prayer﴾ by the very same reasoning mentioned for ablution. And this, as you see, is not sound. It seems that he, may Allah pardon him, is certain that the Hanafis, who do not require order in the acts of ablution, are transgressors who have gone beyond what Allah the Exalted has set, and there is no possibility of saying that they are upright. That is a great injustice.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 113:

﴿Do not incline toward those who have done wrong, lest the Fire touch you.﴾ That is, do not lean even the slightest inclination. What is meant by them is the polytheists, as Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. He explained the inclination as the inclination of the heart toward them through love. It may also be explained more generally, just as ﴿those who have done wrong﴾ is explained as whoever has committed what is called wrong in an unrestricted sense. It has been said: for this meaning, He did not say "toward the wrongdoers." The prohibition then includes flattering them, abandoning the duty of changing what is wrong when able, imitating their dress, glorifying their mention, and sitting with them without a legitimate (shar'i) reason, as well as standing for them and the like. The basis of the prohibition is wrongdoing (zulm), and the plural is due to the plurality of those addressed. It has also been said that this plural form is for emphasis in the prohibition, in that being a group is a likely cause for leniency in flattering them, for example. This was objected to: it would only hold if the intended meaning were the prohibition of leaning toward them because they are a group, and it is not so.

﴿Lest it touch you﴾ means lest it afflict you because of that, as the fa' that follows the prohibition indicates. ﴿The Fire﴾ is the Fire of Hell. Most exegetes (mufassirun) adopted this second explanation, which is very difficult for people today in most of the storms (of corruption). They said: if the inclination in general toward one who has committed some wrong leads to the Fire touching people, then what do you think of one who inclines fully toward those thoroughly established in wrongdoing, who exhausts himself in their companionship and drinking-companionship, who wears out his heart and body in bringing joy to them, who spurs on horse and man to bring them benefits, who takes delight in dressing as they do and sharing in their error, who stretches his eyes toward what they have been given of the fleeting splendor of this world, who envies them for the near fruits they have been given, heedless of the reality of that, oblivious to the final outcome there? Such a person should be counted among those who have done wrong, not among those who incline toward them. This is based on what is reported: a man said to Sufyan, "I sew for the oppressors; am I counted among their helpers?" He said to him, "No, you are one of them; and the one who sells you the needle is among their helpers." How excellent is what one of the advisers wrote to al-Zuhri when he mixed with the rulers, and he is, may Allah keep us and you well: "Abu Bakr, from the trials, for you have come to a state in which whoever knows you should pray for you, that Allah have mercy on you. You have become an old man, and the blessings of Allah have weighed heavily upon you, in that He gave you understanding of His Book and taught you from the Sunnah of your Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. And it is not so [that you are excused]. Allah has taken the covenant from the scholars," He, glorified is He, said: ﴿You shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it﴾. Know that the least of what you have committed and the lightest of what you have borne is that you have comforted the loneliness of the wrongdoer and facilitated the path of error by drawing near to one who has not discharged a right and has not abandoned a falsehood. When they brought you near, they took you as a pivot around which the millstone of their falsehood turns, a bridge over which they cross to their calamities, and a ladder by which they climb to their misguidance. Through you they introduce doubt about the scholars, and through you they lead the hearts of the ignorant. How little they built for you compared to what they ruined for you, and how much they took from you in what they corrupted for you of your religion. What assures you that you will not be among those of whom Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected prayer and followed their desires, so they will meet error﴾? For you deal with one who is not ignorant, and who observes you, one who does not neglect. So treat your religion, for disease has entered it, and prepare your provision, for the far journey has arrived. Nothing is hidden from Allah on earth or in heaven. And peace."

From al-Awza'i: there is nothing more hateful to Allah, the Exalted, than a scholar who visits a worker (of the rulers). From Muhammad ibn Salama: a fly on dung is better than a reciter at the door of these people. In a report: whoever prays for a wrongdoer to remain (in life) has loved to disobey Allah on His earth. By my life, the verse is the most eloquent of things in warning against wrongdoers and wrongdoing. For this reason al-Hasan said: "The religion is gathered in two negatives," meaning: ﴿do not transgress, and do not incline﴾. It is related that the Mawaffaq Abu Ahmad Talha al-Abbasi prayed behind the imam and recited this verse, and he fainted. When he recovered, he was asked about it, and he said: "This is about one who inclined toward one who did wrong, so what about the wrongdoer himself?"

Furthermore, the address of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and those with him among the believers, with these two prohibitions follows the command to be upright, for steadfastness in it. It may also be taken as an emphasis of that if what is meant is continuance and firmness. From Abu 'Amr, he read (tirkanu) with a kasra on the ta' according to the dialect of Tamim.

Qatada, Talha and al-Ashhab read (tarkunu) with a damma on the kaf, the present tense of raka (with a fatha), and it is, according to al-Bahr, the dialect of Qays and Tamim. It was also narrated from Abu 'Amr (tarkunu).

Al-Kisa'i said: it is the dialect of the people of Najd. The reading (tarkanu) with a fatha, present tense of raka, is anomalous in this way. Ibn Abi 'Abla read (wa la turkanu) in the passive, from arkanahu, meaning he inclined it. The reading of the majority is ﴿tarkanu﴾ with a fatha on the kaf, and the past tense is raki (with a kasra), which is the dialect of Quraysh and is the eloquent form, according to al-Azhari. Ibn Thabit, 'Alqama, al-A'mash, Ibn Musarrif and Hamza, as reported from him, read (fa-timassukum) with a kasra on the ta', in the dialect of Tamim also.

﴿And you have no protectors other than Allah﴾: helpers who prevent the punishment from you. The intended meaning is the negation that any one of them has a helper, and the context is evidence for that. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the pronoun in (tamassukum).

﴿Then you will not be helped﴾ from His side, may He be exalted, since it has already preceded in His judgment that He will punish you for your inclining toward them and will not spare you. As for thumma, it has been said that it is for the improbability of His, glorified is He, helping them, when He has already threatened them with punishment for that and made it obligatory upon them. This was objected to: the effect of the particle belongs to what follows it, and what follows thumma is the absence of help, which is not improbable; what is improbable is Allah's help to them. So the apparent meaning is that it indicates a sequence in rank, because the absence of Allah's help is more severe and more dreadful than the absence of anyone else's help. It was answered with something that is not free of strain. In any case, the context calls for waw, but it deviated from it for the reason mentioned.

Al-Qadi allowed that it may be treated as if it were fa', in the sense of improbability. When He, glorified is He, made clear that He will punish them and that no one can help them, this produced the conclusion that they will not be helped at all. The reasoning is that the apparent expectation was to use the consequential fa' that introduces conclusions, since the meaning is that Allah has made His punishment obligatory upon you and there is no preventer from it for you, so therefore you will not be helped. He turned away from that to the conjunction thumma of improbability, to the sense he mentioned. The improbability of occurrence requires negation, and the absence that exists now fits the meaning of the causation of negation. With this he answered what was raised against it: that what enters upon conclusions is the causal fa', not the improbability particle. The strength of the objection is not hidden. He distinguished between the two aspects, the earlier improbability and the stated reinterpretation, by saying that the negated item in the first is Allah's help to them, while in the second it is help in general.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 114 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And establish the prayer﴾, i.e., the obligatory prayer (al-maktubah). Its establishment means performing it in its entirety.

It is also said: it means being constant in it. And it is said: it means performing it at the beginning of its time.

﴿at the two ends of the day﴾, i.e., its beginning and its end. The accusative of طَرَفَيِ النَّهارِ (ṭarafay al-nahār, "the two ends of the day") is in the adverbial sense (ẓarfiyyah) governed by "aqim" (establish). It is weak for it to be an adverb of time, and the way it takes the accusative in this sense is that it is in construct form with the noun it modifies (idafah to the time noun).

﴿and in some parts of the night﴾, i.e., hours of it close to the day, for it is derived from "azlafa", meaning "he brought near" (qarraba).

Al-Layth said: it is a portion from the beginning of the night. Thaʿlab likewise said so. Abu ʿUbaydah, al-Akhfash and Ibn Qutaybah said: it refers to the hours and periods of the night in general, and every hour is a zulfah. They cited al-ʿAjjaj:

*A swift [camel] that weariness had worn out, and that had been parched [by the journey], and the folding of the nights, stage after stage,*
*Until the crescent's bend had grown curved.*

It is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon ﴿the two ends of the day﴾, and ﴿from the night﴾ is in the position of a qualifier of it. The intended meaning of prayer at the two ends is said to be the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer. This is narrated from al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Dahhak. Abu Hayyan favoured this, based on the principle that the "ṭaraf" (end) of a thing must be part of that thing, and he held that the beginning of the day is from dawn. However, the term "ṭaraf" of a thing may be used figuratively for what is adjacent to its beginning and its end. So it is possible to consider the day to begin from sunrise, while still upholding what they mentioned about the prayer at the first end, by making the dual here like their saying: "The pen is one of the two tongues" (a figurative dual). But it has been said that such usage is anomalous.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Tabari favoured it, that the intended meaning is the dawn prayer and the sunset (maghrib) prayer. If the day is from the beginning of dawn until sunset, then sunset is figuratively an "end," and literally it is the end of the night. If the day is from sunrise until sunset, then the dawn prayer, like the sunset prayer, is figuratively an end.

Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi said: the first end is dawn, and the second end is the noon (zuhr) and afternoon (ʿasr) prayers. Ibn ʿAtiyyah favoured this. But you know that there is some obscurity in making noon part of the second end, since noon is the midpoint of the day, and the midpoint is not called an "end" except by a far-fetched figurative usage.

The intended meaning of the prayers "in some parts of the night" is, according to most, the sunset and night (ʿishaʾ) prayers.

Al-Hasan narrated in this regard a report traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) from Ibn ʿAbbas, that he interpreted the prayers in parts of the night as the prayer of al-ʿAtamah, which is the first third of the night after the disappearance of twilight (shafaq). It may also be used for the time of the late night (ʿishaʾ) prayer. And the strangest view is of the one who said: the prayer at the two ends is the noon and afternoon prayers, and the prayers in parts of the night are the sunset, night and dawn prayers.

It has been said: the meaning of "zulafan" is "closeness" (qurban). According to this view, as in the Kashshaf, its proper grammatical structure is that it is conjoined to "the prayer," meaning: "Establish the prayer at the two ends of the day, and establish in some parts of the night," i.e., prayers by which you draw near to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. End of quote. It has been said that according to this view the intended meaning is the night (ʿishaʾ) prayer and tahajjud, which was obligatory for him (ﷺ), or the night prayer, and the witr according to what Abu Hanifah (may Allah be pleased with him) held, or the combination of all of these, as the apparent sense of the plural suggests. It may also be interpreted as the sunset and night prayers, which some preferred. The use of the plural for two is attested, so there is no need to hold that this plurality is in consideration of the fact that each rak'ah is an act of closeness, so that closeness above three is realized in what has been mentioned.

Talhah, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu Jaʿfar read "zulufan" with a ḍammah on the lām. This is either because it is also the plural of zulfah, but its ʿayn was given a ḍammah to match its fāʾ, or because it is a singular noun like ʿunuq, or it is the plural of zalif in the sense of zulfah, like raghif and rughuf.

Mujahid and Ibn Muhayṣin read it with a sukūn on the lām, like busr (with ḍammah and sukūn), from busrah. According to al-Bahr, this would be a noun of genus (ism jins). In a report from them both, they read "zulfā" like ḥublā. This carries the meaning of zulfah, since the feminine tāʾ and the alif (of maqṣūrah) may alternate, as in qurbā and qurbah. It is also permitted that this alif be a substitute for the tanwin, treating the connected speech as if it were in pause.

﴿Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds﴾, i.e., they expiate them and remove the blame for them. Otherwise, evil deeds themselves are accidents that have existed and then ceased to exist. It has also been said: they wipe them out from the records of deeds. Some reports support this. It has also been said: good deeds prevent a person from committing them, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, prayer restrains from immorality and wrongdoing﴾. But this, despite its remoteness in itself, contradicts what has been transmitted from the Companions and the Successors (may Allah be pleased with them), so it should not be relied upon.

The apparent meaning is that "good deeds" includes the obligatory prayers and other obligatory and non-obligatory acts of worship. It has been said: the intended meaning is only the obligatory acts, based on the report: "The five prayers, and Friday to Friday, and Ramadan to Ramadan, are expiations for what lies between them." But it is objected that it has been authentically reported from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "When the imam says 'Amin,' then say 'Amin,' for the angels say 'Amin,' and whoever's 'Amin' coincides with the 'Amin' of the angels, his previous sins are forgiven." In a version narrated uniquely by Yahya ibn Nusayr, who is among the trustworthy narrators, there is an addition: "and what comes later." And it is authentically established that "fasting the day of ʿArafah expiates the previous year and the coming year." Abu Dawud also reported in his Sunan, with a good chain, from Sahl ibn Muʿadh ibn Anas, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever eats food and then says, 'Praise be to Allah who fed me this food and provided it for me without any strength or power from me, his previous sins will be forgiven. And whoever puts on a garment and says, 'Praise be to Allah who clothed me with this and provided it for me without any strength or power from me, his previous sins will be forgiven, and what comes later.'" And there are other reports about the expiation of many sins by acts that are not obligatory.

It has also been said: the intended meaning is the obligatory prayers, because of what occurs in some chains of the report of the occasion of revelation: that Abu al-Yusr, one of the Ansar, kissed a woman, then regretted it and came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him of what he had done. He (ﷺ) said: "I will await the command of my Lord." When he prayed a prayer, he (ﷺ) said: "Yes, go with it, for it is an expiation for what you did." This view is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud and Ibn al-Musayyab. The apparent sense is that these narrators limited the verse to an important portion of that general category, and the occasion of revelation does not preclude generality, as is clear.

In a report from Mujahid, it is the saying: "Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest, and there is no power or strength except by Allah, the Most High, the Mighty." In this there is what there is.

The intended meaning of "evil deeds" according to most is the minor sins, because major sins are not expiated, as they say, except by repentance. They argued for this by what Muslim narrated from the report of al-ʿAlaʾ: "The five prayers are an expiation for what is between them, as long as major sins are avoided." This was challenged: minor sins are expiated by avoiding major sins, by the explicit text: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will expiate from you your evil deeds﴾. So what do the five prayers expiate? Al-Balqini answered that this objection does not arise, because the intended meaning of the verse is avoiding them throughout one's whole life, and its meaning is continuing in this state from the time of faith or responsibility until death. What is in the hadith, "The prayers expiate what is between them," means on that day, if major sins are avoided on that day. So there is no contradiction. Al-Samhudi objected to this by saying: You may say that avoiding major sins throughout one's life is not realized except together with performing the five prayers each day. Therefore expiation is achieved by what the hadith includes, so what is the benefit of the avoidance mentioned in the verse? He then said: You may answer that this falls under the category of doing two things, each of which is an expiation. Some scholars have said: when expiating acts gather together, their ruling is that if they occur in succession, the first expiation applies. If they occur together, then whichever one Allah wills among them is the expiation. As for the rest, their reward remains for the person. The reward for each of them is such that it equals the expiation of minor sins if they existed. Likewise, if a person performs one of the expiating acts and has not committed any sin.

In the Sharh of Muslim by al-Nawawi there is something similar, except that he mentioned that if an expiating act coincides with a major sin or major sins and does not coincide with a minor sin, we hope that it will lighten the major sins. What he said is refuted: the claim that the intended meaning of ﴿if you avoid﴾ is throughout the whole life is a clear assertion. The apparent meaning is that the reward for avoiding major sins at every time expiates the minor sins committed during that time. The commentary of al-Qadi supports this, and so does what Imam Hujjat al-Islam mentioned in his discussion of repentance: that the ruling regarding a major sin is that the five prayers do not expiate it, and that avoiding major sins expiates minor sins, according to the words of His, Glorified is He: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden...﴾, etc. However, avoiding a major sin only expiates a minor sin if one avoids it while having the capacity and the desire. For example, one who has access to a woman and the ability to have intercourse with her, and restrains himself from falling into it, and is content with looking and touching: his striving against himself in refraining from intercourse has a greater effect in illuminating his heart than his engaging in looking at what darkens it. This is the meaning of its expiating. But if he is impotent and his abstention is only out of necessity due to incapacity, or if he is capable but refrains out of fear of someone else, this does not qualify for expiation at all. Thus, anyone who by nature has no appetite for wine, even if it were permitted to him, his abstention from it does not expiate for him the minor sins that are its preliminaries, such as listening to musical instruments and strings. This is clear, and what indicates it is that "good deeds remove evil deeds." Without doubt, avoiding major sins, when accompanied by intention, is a good deed. We added this qualification, although fulfilling the obligation of prohibition does not depend on it, because one is not rewarded for avoidance without it. So the better answer to the problem is to say: the phrase "as long as major sins are avoided" in the report is not a condition on the very fact of expiation, but rather it is for the comprehensiveness of the expiation of all the sins that lie between the five prayers. It is thus like an exception of major sins from sins, as if it were said: "The five prayers are an expiation for all the sins that lie between them," and their expiation of all of them is during the period in which major sins are avoided, or it is restricted to avoiding major sins. Otherwise, the prayers are not an expiation for all sins, but only for minor sins. Although this goes against the apparent meaning of the condition returning to the very fact of expiation, the context of the verse prompted turning away from that apparent meaning to this interpretation, to reconcile the evidences. In this matter we must take into account what they said about the combination of expiating acts for minor sins. Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar, after quoting the words of al-Balqini, said the following: "Even if the objection is granted, its resolution is easy. This is because avoiding major sins is not complete except by performing the five prayers. Whoever does not perform them is not considered one who avoids major sins, because abandoning them is a major sin. So expiation depends on performing them." End of quote. But it is not free from discussion. Among those who explicitly stated that "as long as they are avoided, etc." means an exception, citing some of them, is al-Muhibb al-Tabari. In his book on rulings he said: "The scholars differed regarding whether the expiation of minor sins by acts of worship is conditional on avoiding major sins, on two views. One of them is yes, and this is the apparent meaning of the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): 'as long as major sins are avoided.' Its apparent meaning is conditional, as is suggested by 'if they are avoided' that appears in some other reports. So if major sins are avoided, they are expiating, and otherwise not. This is the view of the majority, according to what Ibn ʿAtiyyah reported. Some said: it is not conditional, and the condition in the hadith means an exception. The meaning is: they are expiations for what is between them, except the major sins. And this is the more evident view."

Al-Zarkashi has mentioned that scholars disagree over whether repentance (tawbah) is a condition for expiation (takfir). One group holds that it is a condition, and another holds that it is not. In *al-Bahr*, it is stated that requiring repentance is the position of the most skilled scholars of legal theory (usul al-fiqh). Perhaps the disagreement rests on the disagreement over whether avoiding major sins (ijtinab al-kaba'ir) is a condition. Whoever makes avoiding major sins a condition for the expiation of minor sins does not require repentance, and treats this as a special feature of the one who avoids major sins. Only those who require avoidance of major sins also require repentance. This is supported by the report of Abu al-Yusr, since the narrations agree that he came in remorse, and remorse is repentance. The Prophet's (ﷺ) statement to him that the afternoon prayer (salat al-'asr) had expiated what he had done occurred after his remorse. However, the apparent general sense of the hadith indicates that the expiation was by the prayer itself, since repentance by itself erases what came before it. If we required repentance alongside the acts of worship, the acts of worship would not be expiating, yet it is established that they are expiations. Thus, the requirement of repentance together with them falls away. This ends the summary with some addition. It is not hidden that this requires holding that Abu al-Yusr's remorse was not a valid repentance; otherwise the expiation would have been by it, since it was earlier. Some have held that it was a valid repentance but was a repentance that was not accepted and did not expiate the sin. You know that the non-expiation of sin by repentance is open to discussion. What is transmitted from al-Subki is that he said: the acceptance of repentance from disbelief is certain by way of divine grace (tafaddul). Regarding the certainty of the acceptance of the repentance of a sinner, there are two views among the Ahl al-Sunnah. The preferred view of Imam al-Haramayn is that the expiation of sin by repentance is probable (maznun). Al-Nawawi claimed that this is the most sound view. In *Sharh al-Burhan*, it says: "The sound view according to us is certainty of expiation." Al-Halimi said: it is not obligatory upon God Most High to accept repentance, but since He has informed about Himself that He accepts repentance from His servants, and it is not permissible that He breaks His promise, we know that He, glorified and exalted, does not reject valid repentance, by His grace. Similar to this disagreement is the disagreement over whether expiation by avoiding major sins and the like is certain or probable. In the words of the scholar Najm al-Din al-Nasafi, Sadr al-Shari'ah and others, punishment for minor sins is possible whether or not the one who commits them avoids major sins, because they fall under His saying: ﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾, and His saying: ﴿It leaves out no small thing nor great, but records it﴾. The recording (ihsa') is for the purpose of questioning and recompense, and there are other verses and hadiths to this effect. The Mu'tazilah disagreed on this, and did not permit the punishment for minor sins if major sins are avoided. They used as evidence the verse ﴿If you avoid the major sins...﴾ etc. It is answered that the intended meaning of "major sins" is disbelief (kufr), in the singular, which includes its various types or the various people who are characterized by it. The meaning of the verse is: if you avoid disbelief, We will make you worthy of the expiation of your evil deeds. It is not hidden how weak their argument is, and by my life, their answer to the Mu'tazilah's argument is even weaker than it.

The author of *al-Dhakha'ir* held that some good deeds expiate both minor and major sins, since it is authentically reported in several hadiths: "Whoever does such and such, his past and future sins are forgiven," and in some of them: "He came out of his sins like the day his mother bore him." If the good deeds in the verse are taken in the sense of totality, then it is appropriate to take the evil deeds in that sense too, and specification is contrary to the apparent meaning, while God's grace is vast. Ibn al-Mundhir inclined to this view, and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr reported it from some of his contemporaries, meaning, it is said, Abu Muhammad the traditionist. But he was refuted, and one of them said: he says that major and minor sins are expiated by purification and prayer, based on the apparent sense of the hadiths. This is clear ignorance and agreement with the Murji'ah in their view. If it were as he claimed, there would be no meaning to the command to repent, and the Muslims have agreed that it is obligatory. It is also authentically reported from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "The prayers are expiations for what is between them, so long as major sins are avoided." This is the end.

In this there is the point that the claim that this is ignorance is not free from excess, since the difference between holding to the generality of expiation and the position of the Murji'ah is very clear. If it were established that this is an inclination toward their view, it would necessarily follow for him something similar regarding repentance, for he concedes that it expiates minor and major sins, and it is among the works of the servant. Just as God, glorified is He, may make this deed a cause for expiating all sins, He may make other deeds like that. His statement "if it were as he claimed" etc. is rejected, because it does not follow from the expiation of accumulated sins that there is no command to repent and that it is obligatory, since leaving it is among the new sins which the previous expiation, by performing ablution for example, does not cover. Do you not see that repentance from minor sins is obligatory according to what is transmitted from al-Ash'ari, and Imam al-Haramayn and his student al-Ansari reported consensus on it? Nevertheless, all minor sins are expiated by the explicit text of the Lawgiver, even if one does not repent, according to what you have heard of the disagreement. The realization of this is that repentance is obligatory in itself, immediately, and whoever delays it, his disobedience is repeated with the repetition of times, as the Shaykh 'Izz al-Din ibn 'Abd al-Salam explicitly stated. It does not follow from God Most High's expiation of His servant's sins that the obligation to repent, which he is charged with as a continuous obligation, falls away. Close to this is the lifting of sin from the sleeper, if he delays the prayer past its time, along with the command to make it up. What is narrated in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah came in a specific matter, so it does not go beyond it, since the original position is that what is other than it remains in its generality. This is a matter where analogy has no room, so that it could be specified by analogy to that. Therefore, attributing ignorance to that speaker is not proper. Hope in God, exalted is His glory, is strong, so it is said. In this context, after discussions which we have left out for fear of tedium, if you want them, then you should consult the books detailed in the science of hadith.

﴿That is a reminder for those who remember﴾: that is, an admonition for those who take heed. He singled them out for mention because they are the ones who benefit from it. The reference is to what preceded of the command to uprightness, the prohibition of transgression and inclining toward those who did wrong, and establishing the prayers at those times, interpreting the mentioned matter in that way. This is the view of al-Zamakhshari. Abu Hayyan preferred that the reference is to establishing the prayer, and the matter of reminding is easy. It was said: it is a reference to the information that good deeds remove evil deeds. Al-Tabari said: it is a reference to the commands and prohibitions in this surah. It was said: it refers to the Qur'an. Some who took the reference to be to the establishing of the prayer explained "reminder" as repentance.

﴿And be patient﴾: that is, persevere through the hardships of carrying out what you have been commanded. In al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's commentary), it is said: "This is a return by Him, exalted is He, to the reminder about patience, after He has mentioned what concludes the reminder, to show the special excellence and distinction of patience and to draw attention to its station and place. It is as if He said: 'And hold fast to what is more important than what you were reminded of and more deserving of being enjoined, which is patience in carrying out what you have been commanded and refraining from what you have been forbidden. Nothing of that is complete except through it.'" End of quote.

The reason it is a return to what was mentioned is that the command to uprightness (istiqamah) is a command to steadfastness in speech, action and belief, and this is patience in obedience to Allah, the Exalted. It necessarily includes patience in refraining from disobedience to Him. Moreover, everything He mentioned is not complete except through patience, so within the command to uprightness is a command to patience.

An objection was raised that treating refraining from what is forbidden as among the objects of patience is problematic, since there is no hardship in that. This was answered by saying that what is forbidden, such as transgression and inclining (to wrongdoers), may be understood as referring to what people cannot ordinarily avoid entirely: a slight natural inclination (by the nature of human temperament) away from the required uprightness, and a slight inclination, by the nature of being human, toward those who have committed wrongdoing. Avoiding such things involves hardship that is not hidden. But this was challenged: what follows from the natural constitution does not fall under the objects of a prohibition. For this reason, the scholars stated that a Muslim's love for his disbelieving child, for example, is not sinful. Rather, it is better to say that the existence of hardship in carrying out the whole of what one has been obligated to do is sufficient for the purpose.

It was also said that the patience commanded here means persistence in the prayer, as if it were said: "Establish the prayer," that is, perform it completely and persist in it, similar to His saying: ﴿And enjoin your family to prayer and be steadfast in it﴾ (20:132). And ﴿indeed, Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾, that is, He pays them the reward of their deeds without any diminution at all. He expressed this by negating waste, to make clear the perfection of His exaltedness above depriving them of any part of their reward. He turned away from the pronoun so that it would serve as a proof for the intended meaning, while also conveying a general benefit for everyone who possesses this quality. This is a reason given for the command to patience. In it is an indication that patience in what has been mentioned is of the category of ihsan (excellence in conduct, doing what is beautiful).

From Muqatil it is reported that he interpreted ihsan here as sincerity (ikhlas).

From Ibn 'Abbas it is reported that he said: "The good-doers are those who pray." It seems he looked to the context of the speech.

Furthermore, among the eloquence of the Qur'an is that the commands to good deeds were addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the singular, although they are general in meaning, whereas the prohibitions were addressed to the community in the plural. How great is the rank of the Messenger (ﷺ) with his Lord, may He be majestic and exalted.

**[Page 161]**

﴿Fa-lawlā kāna﴾ is an exhortation (taḥḍīḍ) that carries, figuratively, the sense of lament (tafajju'), meaning: "Why then did there not exist" (fa-halla)

**[Page 161 continues]** ﴿among the generations﴾, meaning among the peoples who were contemporaneous in one era, ﴿before you, people of remainder﴾, meaning people possessing a remaining trait of judgment and intellect, or people of excellence. In this reading, al-baqiyyah is a noun for excellence, and the ha' is for intensification (naql). This was used metaphorically from the "remainder" (baqiyyah) that a person selects for himself and sets aside from what benefits him. From this, one says: "So-and-so is of the remainder of the people," meaning, of their best. It is in this sense that the line of the Ḥamāsa is interpreted:

*"If you sin, then your remainder comes to me; there is no fault upon me in your sight for what is missed."*

From this is their saying: "In the corners are hidden things, and among men are remainders." It is also permitted that al-baqiyyah means al-baqwā, as al-taqiyyah means al-taqwā, meaning: "Why then did there not exist among them people of preservation for their own souls and guarding them from what brings upon them the wrath of God the Exalted and His punishment." The apparent meaning in this case is that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar). It has been said it is a noun of the verbal noun (ism maṣdar). What supports the verbal noun reading is that it was recited as baqiyyatin in the pattern of the single instance (marrah), and it is the verbal noun of baqāhu, yabqīhi, like rama-hu, yarmīhi, meaning he awaited him and watched over him. In the hadith from Mu'ādh ibn Jabal, who said: "We waited for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and he delayed the night prayer (ʿishā') until the one who thought would think he would not come out," the report continues. Mu'ādh meant: "we awaited him." As for the baqāʾ that is the opposite of fanāʾ (annihilation), its verb is baqiya, yabqā, like raḍiya, yarḍā. The meaning according to this recitation is: "Why then did there not exist among them people of watchfulness out of fear of God the Exalted and His vengeance." It was also recited as baqyatin, with the yā' lightened, as an active participle (ism fāʿil) from baqiya, like shajiyat, fa-hiya shajyah.

Abū Jaʿfar and Shaybah recited *buqyatin* with a ḍammah on the bā' and a sukūn on the qāf.

﴿who forbid corruption in the land﴾, which occurred among them as is mentioned in their stories. Corruption in the sea was interpreted as disbelief and what accompanies it of sins.

﴿Except a few of those We saved from among them﴾. This is a disconnected exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), meaning: "But a few of them, We saved them because they used to forbid." It has been said, meaning: "But a few of those We saved from among the generations forbade corruption, while the rest were abandoners of forbidding." The first *min* is explanatory (bayāniyyah), not partitive (tabʿīḍiyyah), because salvation is only for the forbidders alone, as evidenced by His words, glorified is He: ﴿We saved those who forbade evil and We seized those who wronged﴾. To this al-Zamakhsharī went. The connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil) on the apparent sense of the speech was prevented, because it entails corruption of the meaning, for it would be an exhortation of the people of remainder to forbid corruption, except for the few among the saved among them. Then he said: If you say: in their being exhorted to forbid corruption there is the sense of negating it from them, so it is as if it were said: "There were not among the generations people of remainder except a few," this would be a connected exception and a sound meaning. Its case (inṣāb) would be on the original basis of the exception, though the more eloquent would be to put it in the nominative as a substitute (badal). The upshot is that the speech has two considerations: exhortation and negation. If exhortation is considered, the exception cannot be connected, because the connected exception removes from the excepted what applies to the one excepted from, or affirms for him what is not his. The meaning of exhortation is "why did they not forbid," and it is not permissible to say "except a few, for they are not told: why did you not forbid," because the meaning would be corrupt, since the few are forbidders. If negation is considered, it is connected, because it indicates that the few saved are forbidders. Al-Quṭb raised an objection to this: the validity of negation or affirmation according to the wording is necessary in a declarative statement (khabar), but in a command (ṭalab) it is according to the meaning. For when you say, "Strike the people except Zayd," the meaning is not that you do not strike, but that the people are commanded to be struck except Zayd, for he is not commanded to be struck. Likewise here it is permissible to say: ﴿people of remainder﴾ are exhorted to forbid ﴿except a few﴾, for they are not exhorted to it because they forbade. So the exception is definitely connected, as some of the early scholars went. It may be answered to what he raised that the requirement of the exception is that they are not exhorted, and that is either because they forbade, or because they are not urged to it, since it is not expected from them. So either he made the possibility of corruption an act of corrupting, or he claimed that this is what is understood from the context. Then the scrutinizer, the author of al-Kashshāf (the commentary Kashshāf), said: the apparent sense of al-Zamakhsharī's presentation indicates that *yanhawna* is the predicate of *kāna*, and he made *min al-qurūn* another predicate or a preposed circumstantial (ḥāl), because the exhortation of the people of remainder to forbid, on that reckoning, is so; even if it were made a description and *min al-qurūn* the predicate, the meaning would be censure of the people of the generations for there being no people of remainder among them who forbade. And if it is made the predicate, the meaning of the exception is not "there were not among the generations people of remainder except a few," but rather "there were among them people of remainder who forbade, except a few, for they forbade," and this is corrupt. And the disconnection, as al-Zamakhsharī also preferred, corrupts, for it entails that the people of remainder were not forbidders, because in the exhortation and censure there is an indication of negating it from them. So the correct reading is to interpret it as meaning that the intended point of mentioning the noun is the predicate, and it is like a preface to it, as if it were said: "Why then did there not exist among the generations before you forbidders, except a few." In his speech there is an indication that the negation of the forbidder does not fail. The people of remainder were turned to the "station" only for emphasis, because the possessors of their excellence and remainders, when they are urged to forbid and censured for abandoning, they are more deserving of exhortation and censure. In this there is, in addition, an indication of their emptiness of the attribute, because their emptiness of the predicate, since the possessor of remainder is only a forbidder; so when the necessary consequence is negated, the necessitating thing is negated, and this is of the type: "You do not see the lizard entering its hole in it." And your saying: "Their brave men did not defend the realities in a context of blame," you mean there is no brave man and no defence, but you exaggerated in blame until you imagined that if they had a brave man he would be as nothing. This, then, is the noble view and the one that matches the eloquence of the Great Qur'an. The quotation ends. It is a precise and elegant verification.

Some claimed that the apparent sense is that *kāna* is complete (tāmmah), *people of remainder* is its subject, the clause *yanhawna* is its description, *min al-qurūn* is a preceding circumstantial relative to it, *min* is partitive, and *min qablikum* is a circumstantial relative to *al-qurūn*. It is also permitted that it is a description of it, meaning "those existing," based on the opinion of one who permits omitting the relative pronoun together with part of its relative clause. It was objected that this entails that the exhortation is upon the existence of those people among them, and likewise that the negated would be that; but this is not so. Rather the basis is the forbidding, as exhortation and negation, and holding that both matters are directed at it is because the description is a restriction in the speech. The common usage directs the restriction towards what was mentioned, as it is said: "an addition of a note to the ṭanbūr without joy." Something like this is counted among the connections: ﴿and those who wronged followed﴾, while they are abandoners of forbidding corruption.

﴿what they were made to enjoy in it﴾, meaning what they were blessed with in it, of wealth, pleasant living and worldly desires. The root of *taraf* is the expansion in blessing.

It is reported from al-Farrāʾ that the meaning of *utrifa* is returning to the *turfah*, which is blessing. It has been said: *utrifū* means they transgressed, from *atrafathu al-niʿam* when blessings made him insolent. Then *fī* is either causal or figuratively adverbial. It was objected that this meaning is contrary to what is well known, even if it is correct here. The meaning of *ittibāʿ* of that is preoccupation with it and leaving other things, i.e., they were preoccupied with that. ﴿And they were guilty﴾, meaning perpetrators of crimes other than that, or disbelievers characterized by what is greater than criminality. Each of these two interpretations was taken by some. Some took ﴿those who wronged﴾ to cover both those who abandon forbidding corruption and those who directly engage in it. Then he said: You know that it entails from the exhortation of the first group that the direct perpetrators of corruption are not included, by expression, in wrongdoing and criminality; perhaps the matter in this is light, so do not be heedless. The clause, according to Abū Ḥayyān, is a resumptive statement (istiʾnāf) informing about the condition of these ﴿who wronged﴾, and showing that they, along with being abandoners of forbidding corruption, were people of crimes other than that.

Some verifiers permitted that it be a coordination (ʿaṭf) upon an implied element indicated by the speech, meaning: "they did not forbid; and [they] followed," etc.

It was said: the estimate is "except a few of those We saved among them, who forbade corruption; and those who wronged followed," etc. It is also permitted that it is a resumption that follows from His words, glorified is He: ﴿except a few﴾, meaning: except a few of those We saved from them, who forbade corruption, ﴿and those who wronged followed﴾, from among the direct perpetrators of corruption and the abandoners of forbidding it. The manifest expression is made according to this the proper form, while according to the first, it is for including the direct perpetrators together with the abandoners in the ruling and the designation upon them of wrongdoing, and to indicate the cause of what befell them of punishment.

In al-Kashshāf there is something whose apparent sense indicates that the coordination is upon *nahaw* (they forbade), which is the predicate of *lākin*, so the coordinated element would also be a predicate, while lacking a connecting pronoun. It was answered once by saying it is in the sense of "the rest of them or those who opposed them," and another time by saying that *nahaw* is a resumptive clause resumed after considering the predicate, so it was coordinated upon it. In that there is what there is. His words, exalted is He: ﴿and they were guilty﴾ is coordinated upon ﴿followed those who﴾, etc., despite the difference between them. It is also permitted that the coordination is explanatory, on the meaning of ﴿and they were guilty﴾ by that following; in this there is distance. Also that it is upon *utrifū*, in the sense that they followed the blessing, and their being guilty because whoever follows desires is overwhelmed by sins; or that criminality is meant as their neglect of thankfulness. Ṣāḥib al-Taqrīb criticized this, saying: in it there is a matter to examine, because what is in ﴿what they were made to enjoy﴾ is a relative pronoun, not a verbal noun, since the pronoun returns from *fīhi* to it; so how can *kānū* be estimated as a verbal noun, unless it is said that the pronoun returns to the wrongdoing by the indication of *ẓalamū*, in which case *mā* would be a verbal noun. And it is also permitted that the clause is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ), based on the view that it can occur at the end of the speech according to the people of rhetoric (ahl al-maʿānī).

Abū Jaʿfar, al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Sayyābah, Abū ʿAmr, and in the transmission of al-Juʿfī recited *wa-ut'biʿa* with a ḍammah on the unpronounced hamzah, a sukūn on the tā', and a kasrah on the bā', in the passive form from *itbāʿ*. It was said: then one must estimate a genitive construction, meaning "they were made to receive the recompense of what they were made to enjoy." *Mā* is either a verbal noun or a relative pronoun, and the *wāw* is circumstantial. Some made it for coordination upon the estimated *lam yanhawū*. The meaning on the first view: ﴿except a few﴾ we saved, while the rest had perished. As for His words, glorified is He: ﴿and they were guilty﴾, they said that it is not good to make it a restriction of the saving, except insofar as it runs in the manner of a cause for the destruction of the rest, so it would be a parenthetical insertion, or a circumstantial clause of ﴿those who wronged﴾. The first circumstantial clause is of the estimated object of *anjaynā*. It is also permitted that the well-known recitation be interpreted by this. The precedence of salvation for the forbidders is appropriate to explain the destruction of those who did not forbid. The *wāw* is also circumstantial in the common view, as if it were said: "We saved the few, while those who wronged had followed their recompense, and so they perished." And when the well-known recitation is interpreted this way, it is said: the subject of *ittabaʿa* is "what they were made to enjoy," or the speech is in inversion; so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 117:

﴿Your Lord would never destroy the towns﴾ meaning: it is not proper, nor is it fitting; rather, it is impossible in wisdom that He should destroy the towns that He destroyed, whose accounts have reached you, or that He should destroy them together with others of the towns whose people are wrongdoers. The lam in such a construction is superfluous, used to emphasize the negation according to the Kufans (al-Kufiyyah, the grammarians of Kufa), while according to the Basrans (al-Basriyyah, the grammarians of Basra) it is connected to an omitted element toward which the negation is directed. As for His saying, glorified is He, ﴿with wrongdoing﴾, meaning accompanied by it. It has been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject, meaning "while wronging them." The indefiniteness of "wrongdoing" serves to magnify it and to indicate that destroying the reformers is a great wrong. The purpose is to declare God exalted above this in the most emphatic manner. Otherwise, there is no wrong from Him, exalted is He, in what He does to His servants, whatever it may be, in accordance with the established principle of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah). As for His saying, majestic and exalted is He, ﴿while its people are reformers﴾, it is a circumstantial clause from the object, and its governing element is the governing element of the object. However, it is not taken as restricting the negation to the earlier circumstantial clause, since it indicates the restriction of the negation of destruction as wrongdoing to the condition that its people are reformers. In this there is, as has been said, a corruption similar to that found in the view that it is absolute and unrestricted. This is the view chosen by Ibn 'Atiyyah. al-Tabari reported that the intended meaning of "wrongdoing" is polytheism (shirk), and the ba' is causal, meaning: He does not destroy towns because of the polytheism of their people, while they are reformers in their actions, dealing justly among themselves. Rather, for their destruction there must be added to their polytheism corruption and oppression. This is due to the abundance of His mercy and His leniency regarding His rights, glorified is He. For this reason, the jurists, when rights conflict, give precedence in general to the rights of servants, so long as no impediment prevents it.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is weak. It seems that its proponent went in the direction of what has been said: "Sovereignty may endure with disbelief, but it does not endure with injustice and oppression." Perhaps the reason for its weakness is what some of the investigators mentioned, that the context of forbidding evil deeds, the worst of which is associating partners with God, exalted is He, does not suit it, for polytheism is included in corruption on earth in a primary way. For this reason, each of the Messengers, peace be upon them, forbade his community from it first, and then from all other sins. Thus the correct view, as he said, is to take "wrongdoing" as general corruption encompassing all vices and sins, and to take "reform" as its reform and abandonment, by some being engaged in forbidding it, and others being inclined to admonition and not persisting in what they are upon of polytheism and other kinds of corruption. End of quotation. However, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Daylami narrated from Jarir, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ being asked about the interpretation of this verse, ﴿Your Lord would never destroy the towns with wrongdoing while their people are reformers﴾, and the Prayer and Peace of God be upon him said: 'And its people deal fairly with one another.'" Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Khara'iti in Masawi' al-Akhlaq also narrated it from Jarir as a statement of his own (mawquf), and it clearly conveys the meaning that al-Tabari reported. Perhaps it was not established from the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him; otherwise the matter is problematic. The engagement in forbidding evil by some and the admonition of others have been made into the fair dealing of some with others, as you see, so understand.

Page 164

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 118:

﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community﴾, united upon the true religion, such that no disbelief would arise from any of them. But He, glory be to Him, did not will that, so they were not united upon the true religion. A parallel to this is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And if We had willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. It was also narrated from al-Dahhak that the meaning is: if He had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance or upon misguidance. ﴿And they will continue to differ﴾, some of them upon the truth and some of them upon falsehood.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas. Probably the intended meaning is the difference between truth and falsehood in the beliefs (al-'aqa'id, the articles of faith) which are the foundations of the religion (usul al-din), by the indication of the context (qarinat al-maqam). It has also been said: the intended meaning includes difference in beliefs, in subsidiary rulings (al-furu', the derived legal rulings) and other matters of the religion, since there is nothing in the wording (al-nazm) that indicates specificity. Thus, the exception in His saying, glory be to Him:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 119:

﴿Except those upon whom your Lord has mercy﴾ is a connected (muttasil) exception according to the first view, which is the one chosen by Abu Hayyan and a group of scholars. According to the second view it is disconnected (munqati'), since those upon whom God has mercy have not gone out of the category of those who differ, such as the Imams of the People of the Truth, for they too differ regarding matters other than the fundamentals of religion, that is, the subsidiary rulings (furu'). This is the view taken by al-Hawfi and those who followed him.

﴿And for that He created them﴾, that is, created people. The demonstrative (al-ishara), as related from al-Hasan and 'Ata', refers to the verbal noun (masdar) implied by "differing" (mukhtalifin). A parallel is the expression idha nahy al-safih jara ilayhi (when the foolish one is forbidden, he is provoked by it). It is as if it were said: "And for differing He created people," meaning for the fruit of differing, which is that ﴿a party will be in the Garden and a party in the Blaze﴾ He created them. The lam is the lam of consequence and outcome (lam al-'aqiba wa al-sayrura), because the wisdom behind their creation is not this, in accordance with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾, and because if He had created them for this, He would not punish them for committing falsehood. Thus said more than one scholar. It has also been related from Imam Malik what suggests this. In my view, however, there is no harm in taking the wording in its apparent sense, and there is no contradiction between this verse and the verse they mentioned, as you will learn, God willing, from its explanation in Surat al-Dhariyat, and the reports transmitted concerning it, and that creation follows from the will, which follows from the knowledge, which follows from the object of knowledge as it is in itself. Punishment or reward is only for a matter that has been bestowed upon the one punished or rewarded according to his original predisposition (isti'dad asli). Perhaps this ultimately returns to the point that punishment and reward are consequences of that predisposition in which the one punished or rewarded stands by himself. From here they said: disobedience and obedience are signs of wretchedness and happiness, not their causes. By this the objection "for if He had created them for this, He would not punish them" is dispelled. There are many testimonies to what we have established from the Book and the Sunna, which are not hidden from those prepared to perceive realities. It has also been said: the pronoun in (khalaqahum) refers to "those" (man) according to its meaning, and the demonstrative refers to the mercy understood from (rahima), and the masculine form is due to interpreting it as "that" (an) with the verb, or because it has the sense of "good." This has been related from Mujahid and Qatada. It has also been related from Ibn 'Abbas that the pronoun refers to people and the demonstrative to mercy and differing, that is, the differing of all and the mercy of some: (khalaqahum). The demonstrative came for two, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿neither old nor young, but between that﴾. The lam according to this has been said to have a general figurative meaning (bi-ma'na majazi 'amm) covering both the apparent sense and the outcome, while according to what preceded it retains its own meaning. The most evident views regarding the demonstrative and the pronoun are what we have put forward; the other two views are lesser than it. As for the view that the demonstrative refers to what follows, and that there is an inversion in the speech, meaning: ﴿And the word of your Lord was fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together"﴾ and for that, i.e., for filling Hell, He created them, it is very far from the constructions of Arabic speech. Of this type is what has been said: that it refers to witnessing that Day, the day that is witnessed; and likewise what has been said: that it refers to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Among them is the wretched and the happy﴾, or to the wretchedness and happiness understood from that, or to the fact that there is a party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze, or to the prohibition understood from His saying, glorified is He: ﴿who forbid corruption in the land﴾, or to the Garden and the Fire, or to worship, along with other views at which one marvels.

Some verifiers (muhaqqiqun) have taken the meaning of the verse to be that by unity is meant unity in the true religion, and by differing is meant differing in it, in the sense of opposing it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who were given it did not differ concerning it except after clear proofs had come to them, out of rebellion among themselves﴾. By "those upon whom your Lord has mercy" is meant those whom God has guided and who did not oppose the truth. The demonstrative refers to differing in the sense of opposition, and the pronoun in (khalaqahum) refers to those who remained after the exception, namely those who differ and oppose. The lam is for consequence, as if it were said: "Had your Lord willed, He would have made people upon the truth and the religion of Islam, but He did not will, so He did not make them so. They will not cease opposing the truth, except for a people whom He, glorified is He, guided by His grace, so they did not oppose the truth." And for the differing that was mentioned, He created those who differ and oppose. The problem with this is not hidden, namely the commission of what contradicts the apparent sense, even though Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid something that suggests part of it.

Among the strange views is what is related from al-Hasan, that the intended differing is differing in sustenance and conditions and the subjection of some of them to others. Ibn Bahr said: the intended meaning is that some of them succeed others, so that the one who comes is a successor (khalaf) to the one who passed away; and from this is the phrase ma ikhtalafa al-jadidan, meaning that neither of the two replaced the other. Abu Muslim also took this view, except that he said: some of them replace others in disbelief through imitation (taqlid). There is much to be said about that. Whatever the case, the apparent sense of "people" is generality. Let one reflect on this verse together with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And mankind was not but one community﴾, and let the explanation of that be consulted.

Al-Fadil al-Jalabi said: there is nothing in this verse that indicates the generality of people, so as to contradict ﴿And mankind was not﴾ etc. There is consideration in this. The prepositional phrase (li-dhalika), that is, the phrase with the preposition, is connected to (khalaqa) after it. The apparent sense is that the restriction (hasr) derived from the fronting, if we say the fronting is for a particular restriction (idafi), and the thing it is added to varies according to the differing views on determining what is pointed to. On the first view it is agreement (al-ittifaq), and on the others it also appears with slight reflection. It has been used as evidence from the verse that the command is other than the will, that God did not will faith from everyone, and that what He wills must necessarily come to pass.

Some gnostics (al-'arifin) mentioned that the reason the Surah of Hud whitened the hair of the Prophet (ﷺ) is that it contains his command to be steadfast in the call, together with the information that God only created people for differing, and that He does not will their gathering upon the true religion; and this, as you see, is [problematic]. ﴿And the word of your Lord was fulfilled﴾, that is, His decree was carried out and His command was made binding. The word is sometimes interpreted metaphorically as the threat, and it may also mean the speech addressed to the angels, peace be upon them; the first is preferable. The sentence implies the meaning of an oath, and for this reason the lam is used in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿"I will surely fill Hell with the jinn and mankind all together"﴾. The word jinna and jinn have one meaning. In Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary it is stated that the ha' in (jinna) is for emphasis, even though jinn applies to a single one, so jinna is its collective noun, end of quote. This makes it one of the plurals distinguished from their singular by the ha', like kam' and ka'ma, as we mentioned in our notes on the Alfiyya. There is a well-known question regarding the verse: its apparent meaning requires that all of both groups enter Hell, while what is known from the verses and reports is otherwise. The judge (al-Qadi) answered this with a view whose gist is that by the jinn and mankind is meant either their disobedient ones, the reference being determined by the known context, and the indication being rational, since it is known from the Shari'a that punishment is specific to them and the threat applies only to them. To the same effect is what has been said: that by the jinn and mankind is meant the followers of Iblis, based on His saying in al-A'raf and Sad: ﴿"I will surely fill Hell with you and whoever follows you of them all together"﴾. So what is necessary is that all his followers enter Hell, and there is no objection to this. The Qur'an explains part of itself by part of itself. There is no need to posit a word "disobedient ones" governing the two groups, as has been said; (ajma'in) is for the comprehensiveness of the intended individuals, as far as you have understood. As for what is immediately understood from the two and what is intended by the emphasis, namely clarifying that filling Hell is from both categories and not from only one of them, this does not require the inclusion of the individuals of both groups, and those among them who enter are left unmentioned and entrusted to something else. The latter objection holds that this is based on (ajma'in) being an emphasis for a dual, which is contrary to what they have explicitly stated. In response: that applies when it is for a true dual, not when each member of it is a plural, for then it is in reality an emphasis for a plural, so the objection mentioned has no force.

Indeed, it may be objected to the first part that the emphasis requires the entry of all the disobedient into the Fire, while the known texts indicate otherwise. Unless it is said that the intended disobedient are those whom God has decreed to enter it. Some answered that this does not require the entry of all, but rather that He decreed what would fill Hell, just as when it is said: "I filled the bag with dirhams," this does not require the entry of all the dirhams into the bag. Al-Jalal al-Dawani rejected this, saying that it is like saying: "I filled the bag with all the dirhams," which by its apparent sense requires the entry of all the dirhams into it, and the objection stands as it is in the verse. He then said: the correct answer is that the intended meaning of the word (ajma'in) is the generality of the categories, and that does not require the inclusion of all the individuals, just as when you say: "I filled the sack with all kinds of food," this requires only that it contain something of every kind, not that it contain every individual food. Likewise, when you say: "The assembly was filled with all kinds of people," this does not require that every individual person be in the assembly, but only that there be one from every kind, which is clear. On this basis the benefit of the word (ajma'in) appears, for it is a rebuttal of the Jews and others who claimed that they would not enter the Fire. End of quote. Ibn al-Sadr criticized him, saying: there is a point to examine, for they explicitly stated that the benefit of the emphasis with (kull) and (ajma'in) is to remove the suspicion that the meaning does not include and encompass all the individuals. As for the two examples he mentioned, the comprehensiveness of categories arises in them from the addition of the word "all" to the categories. How so? If one said: "I filled the sack with all the food," omitting the word "kinds," the speech would be like what we are discussing. Moreover, what he said about this being a rebuttal of the Jews and so on is not correct, for the Jews said: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾, so how could they claim they would not enter it at all? Reflect on this. God, glorified is He, guides you.

Some answered with a Sufi approach, namely that by "the jinn and mankind" are meant those who remained at the level of jinnness and humanness, having immersed themselves in the darkness of nature and sunk into the abode of elemental crime, and were not raised to the higher world, were content with the present life, and were stripped away from the world of immaterial beings. These are the polytheists concerning whom it was said: ﴿The polytheists are only unclean, so let them not approach the Sacred Mosque﴾ etc., for they are not worthy of the abode of God and His nearness. Then he said: for this reason you see God, exalted is His majesty, blaming man and calling down curses upon him in more than one place.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verse 120:

﴿And all﴾, i.e., and every report. The tanwin here is for compensation (al-ta'wid) for the omitted genitive complement (al-mudaf ilayhi). The accusative of kull is because it is a direct object (maf'ul bihi) of the words of the Most High: ﴿We relate to you﴾, i.e., We inform you of it. And the words of the Exalted: [page 167]
﴿from the news of the messengers﴾ are an attribute (sifah) of that omitted noun, not of "kullan," because it (kull) is not described in eloquent usage, as in Idah al-Mufassal. And "min" is partitive (tab'idiyyah), though it has been said to be explanatory (bayaniyyah). And the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿with which We make firm your heart﴾ have been said to be an explicative apposition ('atf bayan) for "kullan," based on the view that agreement between the explanation and what is explained in definiteness and indefiniteness is not a condition. The meaning would be: it is that which We make firm, etc.

He also permitted that it be a substitute (badal) from it, a substitute of the whole (badal kull) or of part (badal ba'd). The benefit of this is to draw attention to the fact that the purpose of relating these accounts is to increase the certainty of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to give tranquility to his heart, and to strengthen his soul in conveying the message and bearing the harm of the disbelievers. He also permitted that the object of "We relate" be "kullan" in that case, and it is then accusative either as a verbal noun (masdariyyah), i.e., every type of relating ("We relate") to you that by which ("with which") ﴿We make firm your heart﴾ from the news of the messengers, or as a circumstantial accusative (hal) from "ma" or from the pronoun in the genitive "bihi," according to the view of those who permit the circumstance of a genitive governed by a particle to be placed in the accusative. In that case it is indefinite in meaning "jami'an," i.e., We relate to you from the news of the messengers the things with which We make firm your heart, all of them.

Abu Hayyan preferred that "kullan" be a direct object of "naqussa," and "min anba'i" be in the position of an attribute of it, and it is in the estimation annexed to an indefinite noun, and "ma" is superfluous (silah), as it is in the words of the Most High: ﴿little is it that you remember﴾. Its problem is not hidden.

﴿And there has come to you in this the truth﴾, i.e., the established matter that corresponds to reality. The reference of "this" is to this surah, as has been reported through several chains from Ibn Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Qatadah and Ibn Jubayr.

It has been said that the reference is to it along with its counterparts, but this is not right; likewise its being a reference to the abode of this world, though it occurs in a report from al-Hasan. It has been said that the reference is to the accounts that are related, and this is not objectionable. ﴿And an admonition and a reminder for the believers﴾ is conjoined to "the truth", i.e., there has come to you the comprehensive one, characterized by being true in itself and by being an admonition and a reminder for the believers. Perhaps the first attribute is given the definite article (al-) while the last two are not, because it has been said that the first is a state of the thing in itself, while the last two are attributes of it in relation to others.

Al-Shihab said: The apparent view is that it may be said: the first is defined because what is meant by it is what is specific to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, of his guidance to the call and his consolation with what is known and familiar to him. As for admonition and reminder, these are general matters that were not considered in terms of particularity, so a distinction was made between the two attributes for the distinction between the two described things. The specification by this surah supports this, because its basis is upon his guidance, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as I have heard from the author of al-Kashf. And the placement of the adverbial phrase before the subject is so that the delayed element may arrive in the fullest settledness, and because in the delayed element there is a kind of length that its advancement would disturb the harmony of the noble composition.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verses 121–122:

﴿And say to those who do not believe: "Act according to your standing (makanah)," that is, according to your direction (jihah) and your condition in which you are, ﴿Indeed, we are acting﴾ according to our direction and our condition in which we are, ﴿and wait﴾ for the turns of fate (al-dawa'ir) concerning us; ﴿indeed, we are waiting﴾, that there may befall you something similar to what befell those like you among the disbelievers.﴾ The form of command in both places is for threat and warning (tahdid wa wa'id), and the two verses are muhkamah (definitive, not abrogated).

It has been said: the intended meaning is conciliation (al-muwada'ah), so the two verses are mansukhah (abrogated, naskh).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 11, verses 121–122:

﴿And say to those who do not believe: "Act according to your standing (makanah)," that is, according to your direction (jihah) and your condition in which you are, ﴿Indeed, we are acting﴾ according to our direction and our condition in which we are, ﴿and wait﴾ for the turns of fate (al-dawa'ir) concerning us; ﴿indeed, we are waiting﴾, that there may befall you something similar to what befell those like you among the disbelievers.﴾ The form of command in both places is for threat and warning (tahdid wa wa'id), and the two verses are muhkamah (definitive, not abrogated).

It has been said: the intended meaning is conciliation (al-muwada'ah), so the two verses are mansukhah (abrogated, naskh).

[Page 168]

**(Commentary of al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 11, verse 123)**

﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is, He, glorified is He, knows everything that is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and no one other than Him knows it, exalted is He and high. (And to Him) and not to other than Him, exalted is His status, ﴿the matter is returned﴾, meaning all the affair, so your matter and their matter will undoubtedly return to Him. Most of the Seven Readers (*al-Sab'a*) read (*yurja'*) in the active form, from *raja'a*, *ruju'an*. ﴿So worship Him and put your trust in Him﴾, for He, glorified is He, is sufficient for you. The *fa'* (so) indicates the ordering of the command to worship and to trust, based on the fact that the return of all affairs is to Him. It has been said: "based on that," and on His being, may He be exalted, knowing every unseen thing as well. In delaying the command to trust until after the command to worship, there is an alert that trust does not benefit without worship, because mentioning it first indicates its precedence in rank or in occurrence.
